instruction: A cube is to be cut into 8 pieces of equal size and shape. Each cut should be straight and it should not stop till it reaches the other end of the cube. What is the minimum number of such cuts required? (GATE 2024 SET 2) (a) 3 (b) 4 (c) 7 (d) 8
response: 3 cuts. Cut 1 parallel to one face divides the cube into 2 equal halves. Cut 2 perpendicular to the first divides it into 4 equal quarters. Cut 3 perpendicular to both previous cuts divides each quarter into two, giving 8 pieces of equal size and shape. Answer: (a) 3.

instruction: A person sold two different items at the same price. He made 10% profit on one item and 10% loss on the other. In selling these two items, the person made a total of (GATE 2024 SET 2) (a) 1% profit (b) 2% profit (c) 1% loss (d) 2% loss
response: Let the selling price of each item be Rs. 99. Cost price of the first item = 99/1.10 = Rs. 90. Cost price of the second item = 99/0.90 = Rs. 110. Total cost price = Rs. 200, total selling price = Rs. 198. Loss = 2/200 = 1%. Answer: (c) 1% loss.

instruction: Sequence the following sentences in a coherent passage. (GATE 2024 SET 2) P: This fortuitous geological event generated a colossal amount of energy and heat that resulted in the rocks rising to an average height of 4 km across the contact zone. Q: Thus, the geophysicists tend to think of the Himalayas as an active geological event rather than as a static geological feature. R: The natural process of the cooling of this massive edifice absorbed large quantities of atmospheric carbon dioxide, altering the earth's atmosphere and making it better suited for life. S: Many millennia ago, a breakaway chunk of bedrock from the Antarctic Plate collided with the massive Eurasian Plate. (a) QPSR (b) QSPR (c) SPRQ (d) SRPQ
response: The passage opens with the event (S: the Antarctic chunk colliding with the Eurasian Plate), then its consequences (P: energy, heat, rocks rising), then the cooling effect (R: CO2 absorbed), and ends with the conclusion (Q: Himalayas as an active event). Answer: (c) SPRQ.

instruction: In the sequence 6, 9, 14, x, 30, 41, a possible value of x is (GATE 2024 SET 2) (a) 25 (b) 21 (c) 18 (d) 20
response: Differences increase by 2 each time: 6 + 3 = 9, 9 + 5 = 14, 14 + 7 = 21, 21 + 9 = 30, 30 + 11 = 41. So x = 21. Answer: (b) 21.

instruction: For positive non-zero real variables x and y, if ln((x + y)/2) = (1/2)[ln(x) + ln(y)], then the value of x/y + y/x is (GATE 2024 SET 2) (a) 1 (b) 1/2 (c) 2 (d) 4
response: ln((x+y)/2) = (1/2)(ln x + ln y) = ln(sqrt(xy)), so (x+y)/2 = sqrt(xy). Squaring: (x+y)^2 = 4xy, so x^2 + y^2 = 2xy. Dividing by xy: x/y + y/x = 2. Answer: (c) 2.

instruction: In an engineering college of 10,000 students, 1,500 like neither their core branches nor other branches. The number of students who like their core branches is 1/4th of the number of students who like other branches. The number of students who like both their core and other branches is 500. (GATE 2024 SET 2) The number of students who like their core branches is (a) 1,800 (b) 3,500 (c) 1,600 (d) 1,500
response: Let C = core-likers, O = other-branch likers. |C U O| = 10000 - 1500 = 8500. |C U O| = |C| + |O| - |C n O|, and |O| = 4|C|, |C n O| = 500. So 5|C| = 8500 + 500 = 9000, giving |C| = 1800. Answer: (a) 1,800.

instruction: Two wizards try to create a spell using all the four elements, water, air, fire, and earth. They decide to mix all these elements in all possible orders, working independently. After trying all possible combinations, they conclude that the spell does not work. (GATE 2024 SET 2) How many attempts does each wizard make before coming to this conclusion, independently? (a) 24 (b) 48 (c) 16 (d) 12
response: Mixing 4 distinct elements in all possible orders can be done in 4! = 24 ways. Answer: (a) 24.

instruction: If '->' denotes increasing order of intensity, then the meaning of the words [walk -> jog -> sprint] is analogous to [bothered -> ________ -> daunted]. Which option is appropriate to fill the blank? (GATE 2024 SET 2) (a) phased (b) phrased (c) fazed (d) fused
response: 'Bothered' is mild discomfort and 'daunted' is strongly intimidated. The middle word must be an intermediate intensity. 'Fazed' means perturbed or discomposed — stronger than bothered but weaker than daunted. Answer: (c) fazed.

instruction: A rectangular paper of 20 cm x 8 cm is folded 3 times. Each fold is made along the line of symmetry, which is perpendicular to its long edge. The perimeter of the final folded sheet (in cm) is (GATE 2024 SET 1) (a) 18 (b) 24 (c) 20 (d) 21
response: The long edge changes after each fold, so the fold direction changes too. Start 20 x 8 (long edge 20). Fold 1 halves the 20 -> 10 x 8. Fold 2 halves the 10 -> 5 x 8 (long edge now 8). Fold 3 halves the 8 -> 5 x 4. Final sheet is 5 cm x 4 cm, so perimeter = 2 x (5 + 4) = 18 cm. Answer: (a) 18.

instruction: A rectangular paper sheet of dimensions 54 cm x 4 cm is taken. The two longer edges of the sheet are joined together to create a cylindrical tube. A cube whose surface area is equal to the area of the sheet is also taken. (GATE 2024 SET 1) Then, the ratio of the volume of the cylindrical tube to the volume of the cube is (a) 1/pi (b) 2/pi (c) 3/pi (d) 4/pi
response: Cylinder: circumference 2*pi*r = 4, so r = 2/pi; height = 54. Volume = pi*r^2*h = pi*(4/pi^2)*54 = 216/pi. Cube: surface area 6a^2 = 54*4 = 216, so a = 6, volume = 216. Ratio = (216/pi)/216 = 1/pi. Answer: (a) 1/pi.

instruction: In the given text, the blanks are numbered (i)-(iv). Select the best match for all the blanks. (GATE 2024 SET 1) Steve was advised to keep his head ___(i)___ before heading ___(ii)___ to bat; for, while he had a head ___(iii)___ batting, he could only do so with a cool head ___(iv)___ his shoulders. (a) (i) down (ii) down (iii) on (iv) for (b) (i) on (ii) down (iii) for (iv) on (c) (i) down (ii) out (iii) for (iv) on (d) (i) on (ii) out (iii) on (iv) for
response: 'Keep his head down' (avoid attention), 'heading out to bat', 'a head for batting' (an ability for batting), 'a cool head on his shoulders'. Answer: (c) (i) down (ii) out (iii) for (iv) on.

instruction: For positive non-zero real variables p and q, if log(p^2 + q^2) = log p + log q + 2 log 3, then the value of (p^4 + q^4)/(p^2 q^2) is (GATE 2024 SET 1) (a) 79 (b) 81 (c) 9 (d) 93
response: log(p^2 + q^2) = log(pq) + log 9 = log(9pq), so p^2 + q^2 = 9pq. Squaring: p^4 + q^4 + 2p^2 q^2 = 81 p^2 q^2, so p^4 + q^4 = 79 p^2 q^2. Hence (p^4 + q^4)/(p^2 q^2) = 79. Answer: (a) 79.

instruction: The number of coins of Rs. 1, Rs. 5, and Rs. 10 denominations that a person has are in the ratio 5:3:13. Of the total amount, the percentage of money in Rs. 5 coins is (GATE 2024 SET 1) (a) 21% (b) 14 2/7% (c) 10% (d) 30%
response: Let the counts be 5x, 3x, 13x. Amounts: Rs. 5x + Rs. 15x + Rs. 130x = Rs. 150x total. Money in Rs. 5 coins = 15x, so percentage = (15x/150x)*100% = 10%. Answer: (c) 10%.

instruction: The triad of secondary colours in the additive colour system is _________. (GATE AR) (a) Cyan, Magenta, Yellow (b) Red, Green, Blue (c) Cyan, Magenta, Blue (d) Magenta, Blue, Yellow
response: In the additive colour system the primaries are red, green and blue; the secondary colours formed by mixing two primaries are cyan (green + blue), magenta (red + blue) and yellow (red + green). Answer: (a) Cyan, Magenta, Yellow.

instruction: The product of the digits of a three-digit number is 70. The sum of the digits of this three-digit number is (GATE AR 2026) (a) 12 (b) 14 (c) 16 (d) 18
response: 70 = 2 x 5 x 7, so the three digits must be 2, 5 and 7 (the only single-digit factors). Their sum is 2 + 5 + 7 = 14. Answer: (b) 14.

instruction: Verbosity : Brevity :: Insolence : ______ (GATE AR 2026) Choose the word that best fills the blank. (a) Innocence (b) Respect (c) Solace (d) Wealth
response: Verbosity and brevity are antonyms (wordiness vs conciseness). Insolence (rudeness) needs its antonym: respect. Answer: (b) Respect.

instruction: 'If his latest movie had been a commercial success, the actor would have made enough money to sponsor his next movie.' Based only on the above sentence, which one of the following statements is true? (GATE AR 2026) (a) His latest movie was a commercial success. (b) He has enough money to sponsor his next movie. (c) He will make his next movie. (d) His latest movie was not commercially successful.
response: The sentence is a counterfactual conditional: the success did not happen, so the consequence (having enough money) did not follow. The only statement the sentence supports is that the movie was not commercially successful. Answer: (d).

instruction: Consider the following sample of numbers: 9, 18, 11, 14, 15, 17, 10, 69, 11, 13. (GATE 2024 SET 1) The median of the sample is (a) 13.5 (b) 14 (c) 11 (d) 18.7
response: Sort the sample: 9, 10, 11, 11, 13, 14, 15, 17, 18, 69. With 10 values, the median is the average of the 5th and 6th values: (13 + 14)/2 = 13.5. Answer: (a) 13.5.

instruction: If two distinct non-zero real variables x and y are such that (x + y) is proportional to (x - y), then the value of x/y (GATE 2024 SET 1) (a) depends on x and y (b) depends only on x and not on y (c) depends only on y and not on x (d) is a constant
response: (x + y) = K(x - y) for some constant K. Rearranging: x + y = Kx - Ky, so y + Ky = Kx - x, giving x(K - 1) = y(K + 1). Hence x/y = (K + 1)/(K - 1), a constant. Answer: (d) is a constant.

instruction: If '->' denotes increasing order of intensity, then the meaning of the words [dry -> arid -> parched] is analogous to [diet -> fast -> _____]. (GATE 2024 SET 1) (a) starve (b) reject (c) feast (d) deny
response: Diet means restricting food intake, fast means going without food for a period, and starve means suffering from hunger — an increasing intensity of food deprivation, matching dry -> arid -> parched. Answer: (a) starve.

instruction: f(x) and g(y) are functions of x and y, respectively, and f(x) = g(y) for all real values of x and y. Which one of the following options is necessarily TRUE for all x and y? (GATE 2023) (a) f(x) = 0 and g(y) = 0 (b) f(x) = g(y) = constant (c) f(x) is not constant and g(y) is not constant (d) f(x) + g(y) = f(x) - g(y)
response: Fix y = 0: f(x) = g(0) for every real x, so f is constant. Fix x = 0: g(y) = f(0) for every real y, so g is the same constant. Answer: (b) f(x) = g(y) = constant.

instruction: Which one of the following sentence sequences creates a coherent narrative? (GATE 2023) (i) Once on the terrace, on her way to her small room in the corner, she notices the man right away. (ii) She begins to pant by the time she has climbed all the stairs. (iii) Mina has bought vegetables and rice at the market, so her bags are heavy. (iv) He was leaning against the parapet, watching the traffic below. (a) (i), (ii), (iv), (iii) (b) (ii), (iii), (i), (iv) (c) (iv), (ii), (i), (iii) (d) (iii), (ii), (i), (iv)
response: The narrative order is: (iii) Mina buys heavy bags at the market, (ii) she pants climbing the stairs, (i) on the terrace she notices the man, (iv) he was leaning against the parapet. Answer: (d) (iii), (ii), (i), (iv).

instruction: Consider two functions of time t, f(t) = 0.01 t^2 and g(t) = 4t, where 0 < t < infinity. Consider the statements: (i) For some t > 0, g(t) > f(t). (ii) There exists a T, such that f(t) > g(t) for all t > T. Which one of the following is TRUE? (GATE 2023) (a) only (i) is correct (b) only (ii) is correct (c) both (i) and (ii) are correct (d) neither (i) nor (ii) is correct
response: (i) g(t) > f(t) means 4t > 0.01 t^2, i.e. t < 400 — true for 0 < t < 400. (ii) f(t) > g(t) means 0.01 t^2 > 4t, i.e. t > 400 — true for all t > 400, so T = 400 works. Both statements are correct. Answer: (c).

instruction: The country of Zombieland is in distress since more than 75% of its working population is suffering from serious health issues. Studies concluded that a complete lack of physical exercise was one of the leading causes. As a measure, the Government decided to provide monetary incentives to those who ride bicycles to work. (GATE 2023) Based only on the information provided, which statement can be logically inferred with certainty? (a) All the working population will henceforth ride bicycles to work. (b) Riding bicycles will ensure all the working population is free of health issues. (c) The health experts suggested declaring bicycle riding mandatory. (d) The Government believes that riding bicycles is a form of physical exercise.
response: Only (d) follows with certainty: the government incentivises cycling to address a problem caused by lack of exercise, which implies it treats cycling as exercise. (a) and (b) overclaim — not everyone will cycle and cycling need not cure everything; (c) is not stated anywhere. Answer: (d).

instruction: Looking at the surface of a smooth 3-dimensional object from the outside, which one of the following options is TRUE? (GATE 2023) (a) The surface must be concave everywhere. (b) The surface must be convex everywhere. (c) The surface may be concave in some places and convex in other places. (d) The object can have edges, but no corners.
response: A smooth surface has a well-defined tangent plane at every point, but it may be concave in some places and convex in others (e.g. a torus). An edge is not smooth because the tangent plane changes abruptly there, so (d) is wrong. Answer: (c).

instruction: A survey found that 90% of pregnant women received medical care at least once before giving birth. Of these women, 60% received medical care from doctors, while 40% received care from other healthcare providers. (GATE 2023) Which statement can be inferred with certainty? (a) More than half of the pregnant women received medical care at least once from a doctor. (b) Less than half received care at least once from a doctor. (c) More than half received care at most once from a doctor. (d) Less than half received care at most once from a doctor.
response: Out of 100 women, 90 received care, and 60% of those 90 — i.e. 54 — received care from a doctor. 54 is more than half of 100. Answer: (a).

instruction: A series of natural numbers F1, F2, F3, ... obeys F(n+1) = F(n) + F(n-1) for all integers n >= 2. If F6 = 37 and F7 = 60, then what is F1? (GATE 2023) (a) 4 (b) 5 (c) 8 (d) 9
Kind : _______ : : Often : Frequently (GATE 2023) (By word meaning) (a) Mean (b) Type (c) Cruel (d) Kindly
response: Often and Frequently are synonyms (both adverbs of high frequency). The pair must show the same synonymy: Kind and Type are synonyms (both mean a category or sort). Answer: (b) Type.

instruction: We reached the station late, and _______ missed the train. (GATE 2023) (a) near (b) nearly (c) utterly (d) mostly
response: 'Nearly' means 'almost but not quite' — 'we reached the station late and nearly missed the train' (we almost missed it but caught it). 'Utterly' means completely and 'mostly' means almost all the time, neither fits. Answer: (b) nearly.

instruction: A box contains five balls of same size and shape: three green and two orange. Balls are drawn one at a time. If a green ball is drawn, it is not replaced. If an orange ball is drawn, it is replaced with another orange ball. First ball is drawn. What is the probability of getting an orange ball in the next draw? (GATE 2022) (a) 1/2 (b) 8/25 (c) 19/50 (d) 23/50
response: Use total probability. If the first ball is green (probability 3/5), 2 green + 2 orange remain, so P(orange next) = 2/4 = 1/2. If the first ball is orange (probability 2/5), it is replaced, so the box is unchanged and P(orange next) = 2/5. Total = (3/5)(1/2) + (2/5)(2/5) = 3/10 + 4/25 = 15/50 + 8/50 = 23/50. Answer: (d) 23/50.

instruction: In a recently conducted national entrance test, boys constituted 65% of those who appeared. Girls constituted the remaining candidates and they accounted for 60% of the qualified candidates. (GATE 2022) Which is the correct logical inference? (a) Equal number of boys and girls qualified (b) Equal number of boys and girls appeared (c) The number of boys who appeared is less than the number of girls who appeared (d) The number of boys who qualified is less than the number of girls who qualified
response: Take 100 who appeared: 65 boys, 35 girls. Of the qualified, girls are 60% and boys 40%, so more girls qualified than boys. (a) is false (60% vs 40%), (b) and (c) are false (65 vs 35 appeared). Answer: (d).

instruction: An automobile plant contracted to buy shock absorbers from two suppliers X and Y. X supplies 60% and Y supplies 40% of the shock absorbers. Of X's shock absorbers, 96% are reliable. Of Y's shock absorbers, 72% are reliable. The probability that a randomly chosen shock absorber, which is found to be reliable, is made by Y is (GATE) (a) 0.288 (b) 0.334 (c) 0.667 (d) 0.720
response: By Bayes' theorem: P(Y | reliable) = P(reliable | Y) P(Y) / [P(reliable | X) P(X) + P(reliable | Y) P(Y)] = (0.72 x 0.40) / (0.96 x 0.60 + 0.72 x 0.40) = 0.288 / (0.576 + 0.288) = 0.288 / 0.864 = 0.333. Answer: (b) 0.334.

instruction: What is Bernoulli's equation and lift? Explain it briefly. [GATE AE - Aerodynamics]
response:
Along a streamline in steady, incompressible, inviscid flow, the sum of static pressure, dynamic pressure and elevation pressure is constant. Faster flow therefore means lower static pressure, which is the basic explanation for the pressure difference that produces lift on a wing.

Formula: p + (1/2) rho V^2 + rho g h = constant; dynamic pressure q = (1/2) rho V^2

Worked example: Air (density 1.225 kg/m3) speeds up from 50 m/s below a wing to 70 m/s above it at the same height. Pressure drop = 0.5 x 1.225 x (70^2 - 50^2) = 0.5 x 1.225 x 2400 = 1470 Pa, so the upper surface pressure is 1470 Pa lower than the lower surface.

instruction: What is Lift coefficient and lift force? Explain it briefly. [GATE AE - Aerodynamics]
response:
Lift is proportional to dynamic pressure, wing area and the lift coefficient. The lift coefficient depends mainly on angle of attack, airfoil shape and Mach and Reynolds numbers, and it rises roughly linearly with angle of attack until stall.

Formula: L = (1/2) rho V^2 S CL

Worked example: For rho = 1.225 kg/m3, V = 60 m/s, wing area S = 20 m2 and CL = 0.5: L = 0.5 x 1.225 x 60^2 x 20 x 0.5 = 22,050 N.

instruction: What is Drag polar and induced drag? Explain it briefly. [GATE AE - Aerodynamics]
response:
Total drag coefficient is the sum of parasite (zero-lift) drag and lift-induced drag. Induced drag falls as aspect ratio rises, which is why gliders have long slender wings, while parasite drag dominates at high speed.

Formula: CD = CD0 + CL^2 / (pi e AR); D = (1/2) rho V^2 S CD

Worked example: With CD0 = 0.02, CL = 0.5, Oswald efficiency e = 0.8 and aspect ratio AR = 8: CD = 0.02 + 0.5^2 / (pi x 0.8 x 8) = 0.02 + 0.0124 = 0.0324.

instruction: What is Thin airfoil theory lift slope? Explain it briefly. [GATE AE - Aerodynamics]
response:
Thin airfoil theory predicts that a thin symmetric airfoil has a lift slope of 2 pi per radian (about 0.11 per degree) and zero lift at zero angle of attack. Camber shifts the zero-lift angle to a negative value but does not change the slope much.

Formula: Cl = 2 pi (alpha - alpha0); lift slope dCl/dalpha = 2 pi per radian

Worked example: At angle of attack 5 degrees = 0.0873 rad, Cl = 2 pi x 0.0873 = 0.55 for a thin symmetric airfoil at zero camber offset.

instruction: What is Thrust equation for a jet engine? Explain it briefly. [GATE AE - Propulsion]
response:
Thrust is the rate of change of momentum of the air and fuel passing through the engine, plus any pressure thrust at the nozzle exit. Increasing exhaust velocity or mass flow increases thrust, and thrust falls as flight speed approaches exhaust speed.

Formula: F = mdot_e Ve - mdot_0 V0 + (pe - p0) Ae

Worked example: A jet exhausts 100 kg/s at 600 m/s while flying at 200 m/s, with no pressure thrust: F = 100 x (600 - 200) = 40,000 N.

instruction: What is Mach number and speed of sound? Explain it briefly. [GATE AE - Aerodynamics]
response:
Mach number is flight speed divided by the local speed of sound, which depends on temperature. Flow is subsonic below M = 1, transonic near M = 1, supersonic above it, and hypersonic above about M = 5.

Formula: M = V / a; a = sqrt(gamma R T), with gamma = 1.4 for air

Worked example: At about 11,000 m altitude the speed of sound is about 295 m/s, so an aircraft flying at 250 m/s has M = 250 / 295 = 0.85, in the high-subsonic / transonic range.

instruction: What is Breguet range equation? Explain it briefly. [GATE AE - Flight Mechanics]
response:
The Breguet range equation gives the cruise range of a jet aircraft assuming constant speed, lift-to-drag ratio and specific fuel consumption. Range improves with higher L/D, lower fuel consumption, and a larger fraction of the takeoff weight carried as fuel.

Formula: R = (V / cT) (L / D) ln(Wi / Wf), where Wi is initial weight and Wf is final weight

Worked example: With V = 240 m/s, thrust specific fuel consumption cT = 0.6 per hour = 1.667 x 10^-4 per second, L/D = 15 and Wi/Wf = 1.25: R = (240 / 1.667 x 10^-4) x 15 x ln(1.25) = about 4.82 x 10^6 m, about 4,820 km.

instruction: What is Gradient, divergence and curl? Explain it briefly. [GATE AE - Engineering Mathematics]
response:
The gradient of a scalar field points in the direction of fastest increase, with magnitude equal to that rate of increase. Divergence measures the net outflow of a vector field from a point (a source or sink), and curl measures its local rotation. In aerodynamics they describe pressure fields, velocity fields and vorticity.

Formula: grad phi = (dphi/dx, dphi/dy, dphi/dz); div F = dFx/dx + dFy/dy + dFz/dz; curl F = grad x F. Vorticity omega = curl V.

Worked example: For solid-body rotation V = (-omega*y, omega*x, 0), curl V = (0, 0, 2*omega), so the vorticity is twice the angular velocity.

instruction: What is Stokes, Gauss and Green theorems? Explain it briefly. [GATE AE - Engineering Mathematics]
response:
These theorems convert integrals over a region into integrals over its boundary. Gauss's (divergence) theorem turns a volume integral of divergence into a surface flux integral; Stokes' theorem turns a surface integral of curl into a line integral around its boundary; Green's theorem is the 2-D form of Stokes' theorem. They underlie the integral forms of the conservation laws and the circulation definition of lift.

Formula: Gauss: integral_V div F dV = integral_S F . n dS. Stokes: integral_S (curl F) . n dS = integral_C F . dl. Circulation Gamma = integral_C V . dl.

Worked example: Circulation around an airfoil is found from the line integral of velocity around a closed loop enclosing it, and lift per unit span follows from the Kutta-Joukowski theorem L' = rho * V * Gamma.

instruction: What is Kepler's laws and escape velocity? Explain it briefly. [GATE AE - Flight Mechanics]
response:
Kepler's laws state that orbits are ellipses with the central body at one focus, a line joining body and centre sweeps equal areas in equal times, and the square of the orbital period is proportional to the cube of the semi-major axis. Escape velocity is the minimum speed at the surface needed to reach infinity with zero residual speed, found by equating kinetic energy to the gravitational potential energy that must be overcome.

Formula: T^2 = (4*pi^2 / (G*M)) * a^3; escape velocity v_e = sqrt(2*G*M / R) = sqrt(2*g*R). For Earth v_e is about 11.2 km/s.

Worked example: A satellite in a circular orbit of radius r has speed v = sqrt(G*M / r); doubling the radius reduces the speed by a factor of sqrt(2).

instruction: What is Longitudinal static stability (stick-fixed)? Explain it briefly. [GATE AE - Flight Mechanics]
response:
An aircraft is longitudinally statically stable if a disturbance in angle of attack produces a pitching moment that restores the original attitude, i.e. the pitching-moment slope dCm/dalpha is negative. The wing alone is usually destabilising about the centre of gravity, and the horizontal tail provides the restoring moment; the neutral point is the CG position where dCm/dalpha = 0. Static margin, the distance between neutral point and CG as a fraction of mean aerodynamic chord, measures the degree of stability.

Formula: Static margin = (x_np - x_cg) / c_bar (positive for stability). dCm/dalpha < 0 for static stability; Cm = Cm0 + (dCm/dalpha) * alpha.

Worked example: If the neutral point is at 45% MAC and the CG at 30% MAC, the static margin is 15% MAC, a typical stable value for a transport aircraft.

instruction: What is Load factor, turning flight and V-n diagram? Explain it briefly. [GATE AE - Flight Mechanics]
response:
Load factor n is lift divided by weight; in a steady level turn the lift must support the weight and provide the centripetal force, so n = 1/cos(phi) where phi is the bank angle. The turn radius then follows from the horizontal lift component. The V-n diagram plots the allowable load factor against airspeed, bounded by the stall line at low speed and the structural limit load factor at high speed.

Formula: n = L / W = 1 / cos(phi) in a level turn; turn radius R = V^2 / (g * tan(phi)); stall speed at load factor n is V_s(n) = V_s1 * sqrt(n).

Worked example: In a 60-degree banked level turn, n = 2, so the wings must produce twice the aircraft weight in lift, and the stall speed rises by sqrt(2), about 41%.

instruction: What is Potential flow: sources, sinks, doublets and vortices? Explain it briefly. [GATE AE - Aerodynamics]
response:
In incompressible, irrotational flow the velocity is the gradient of a velocity potential that satisfies Laplace's equation, so elementary solutions can be added together (superposed) to build flows around bodies. A source emits fluid radially, a sink absorbs it, a doublet is a source-sink pair, and a line vortex gives purely tangential flow. Superposing a uniform stream, a doublet and a vortex gives the flow around a lifting circular cylinder.

Formula: Uniform flow + doublet: stream function psi = V_inf * r * sin(theta) * (1 - a^2/r^2); vortex: V_theta = Gamma / (2*pi*r). Laplace equation: del^2 phi = 0.

Worked example: Flow past a non-lifting cylinder of radius a in a stream V_inf has surface speed 2*V_inf*sin(theta), maximum 2*V_inf at the top and bottom, and zero at the stagnation points.

instruction: What is Kutta-Joukowski theorem and the Kutta condition? Explain it briefly. [GATE AE - Aerodynamics]
response:
The Kutta-Joukowski theorem states that the lift per unit span on a two-dimensional body in steady flow equals air density times freestream speed times the circulation around the body. Circulation is generated because the flow must leave the sharp trailing edge smoothly (the Kutta condition), which fixes the circulation; the starting vortex shed at the start of motion carries the equal and opposite circulation. The theorem explains why lift is tied to circulation rather than to any single pressure value.

Formula: L' = rho * V_inf * Gamma (lift per unit span). Kutta condition: flow leaves the trailing edge smoothly, with finite velocity and equal pressure on both sides.

instruction: What is Normal and oblique shocks? Explain it briefly. [GATE AE - Aerodynamics]
response:

Worked example: For air (gamma = 1.4) entering a normal shock at M1 = 2, p2/p1 = 4.5 and M2 = 0.577; the flow leaves the shock subsonic with a large static pressure rise.

instruction: What is Isentropic flow, nozzles and diffusers? Explain it briefly. [GATE AE - Aerodynamics]
response:
In isentropic (adiabatic, reversible) compressible flow, stagnation pressure and stagnation temperature stay constant, and static properties follow from the Mach number through the isentropic relations. A converging-diverging (de Laval) nozzle chokes at the throat at Mach 1 when the pressure ratio is low enough, after which the exit Mach number is set by the area ratio. instruction: What is Viscous flow and boundary layers (Blasius)? Explain it briefly. [GATE AE - Aerodynamics]
response:
Viscosity makes fluid stick to a solid surface (no-slip), creating a thin boundary layer in which velocity rises from zero at the wall to the freestream value. For a laminar flat plate the Blasius solution gives the layer thickness growing as the square root of distance, and the local skin-friction coefficient falling as 1/sqrt(Rex). Transition to turbulence thickens the layer and raises skin friction, and an adverse pressure gradient can separate the layer from the surface.

Formula: delta/x = 5.0 / sqrt(Re_x); local skin friction Cf_x = 0.664 / sqrt(Re_x); total Cf = 1.328 / sqrt(Re_L) (laminar flat plate). Re_x = rho*V*x / mu.

Worked example: At Re_L = 1e6 on a flat plate, the laminar skin-friction coefficient is Cf = 1.328/sqrt(1e6) = 0.00133, and the boundary layer at the end is about 0.5% of the plate length.

instruction: What is Mohr's circle, principal stresses and failure theories? Explain it briefly. [GATE AE - Aerospace Structures]
response:
Mohr's circle is a graphical construction giving the normal and shear stresses on any plane through a point from the stress state on two perpendicular planes. Failure theories then compare a combined stress state with uniaxial test data: Tresca uses maximum shear stress, von Mises uses distortional strain energy, and maximum principal stress is used mainly for brittle materials.

Worked example: For sigma_x = 80 MPa, sigma_y = 20 MPa, tau_xy = 40 MPa: sigma_avg = 50 MPa, R = 50 MPa, so sigma_1 = 100 MPa, sigma_2 = 0, tau_max = 50 MPa.

instruction: What is Elastic flexural buckling of columns (Euler)? Explain it briefly. [GATE AE - Aerospace Structures]
response:
A slender column under axial compression can buckle sideways at a critical load well below its crushing strength; Euler theory gives this load from the flexural stiffness and the effective length set by the end conditions. The critical stress falls as the square of the slenderness ratio, so long thin columns fail by buckling while short stocky ones fail by yielding. instruction: What is Free and forced vibration of SDOF systems? Explain it briefly. [GATE AE - Aerospace Structures]
response:

response:

instruction: Give a worked example for Bernoulli's equation and lift [GATE AE - Aerodynamics]
response:

instruction: Give a worked example for Lift coefficient and lift force [GATE AE - Aerodynamics]

instruction: Give a worked example for Drag polar and induced drag [GATE AE - Aerodynamics]

Total drag coefficient is the sum of parasite (zero-lift) drag and lift-induced drag. Induced drag falls as aspect ratio rises, which is why gliders have long slender wings, while parasite drag dominates at high speed.

instruction: Give a worked example for Thin airfoil theory lift slope [GATE AE - Aerodynamics]
response:

instruction: Give a worked example for Thrust equation for a jet engine [GATE AE - Propulsion]
response:

Thrust is the rate of change of momentum of the air and fuel passing through the engine, plus any pressure thrust at the nozzle exit. Increasing exhaust velocity or mass flow increases thrust, and thrust falls as flight speed approaches exhaust speed.

instruction: Give a worked example for Mach number and speed of sound [GATE AE - Aerodynamics]
response:

instruction: Give a worked example for Gradient, divergence and curl [GATE AE - Engineering Mathematics]
response:

response:

Formula: L = (1/2) rho V^2 S CL

Lift is proportional to dynamic pressure, wing area and the lift coefficient. The lift coefficient depends mainly on angle of attack, airfoil shape and Mach and Reynolds numbers, and it rises roughly linearly with angle of attack until stall.

instruction: What is the formula for Drag polar and induced drag? When is it used? [GATE AE - Aerodynamics]
response:
Formula: CD = CD0 + CL^2 / (pi e AR); D = (1/2) rho V^2 S CD

Total drag coefficient is the sum of parasite (zero-lift) drag and lift-induced drag. Induced drag falls as aspect ratio rises, which is why gliders have long slender wings, while parasite drag dominates at high speed.

instruction: What is the formula for Thin airfoil theory lift slope? When is it used? [GATE AE - Aerodynamics]
response:
Formula: Cl = 2 pi (alpha - alpha0); lift slope dCl/dalpha = 2 pi per radian

Thin airfoil theory predicts that a thin symmetric airfoil has a lift slope of 2 pi per radian (about 0.11 per degree) and zero lift at zero angle of attack. Camber shifts the zero-lift angle to a negative value but does not change the slope much.

instruction: What is the formula for Thrust equation for a jet engine? When is it used? [GATE AE - Propulsion]
response:
Formula: F = mdot_e Ve - mdot_0 V0 + (pe - p0) Ae

Thrust is the rate of change of momentum of the air and fuel passing through the engine, plus any pressure thrust at the nozzle exit. Increasing exhaust velocity or mass flow increases thrust, and thrust falls as flight speed approaches exhaust speed.

instruction: What is the formula for Mach number and speed of sound? When is it used? [GATE AE - Aerodynamics]
response:
Formula: M = V / a; a = sqrt(gamma R T), with gamma = 1.4 for air

Mach number is flight speed divided by the local speed of sound, which depends on temperature. Flow is subsonic below M = 1, transonic near M = 1, supersonic above it, and hypersonic above about M = 5.

instruction: What is the formula for Breguet range equation? When is it used? [GATE AE - Flight Mechanics]
response:
Formula: R = (V / cT) (L / D) ln(Wi / Wf), where Wi is initial weight and Wf is final weight

The Breguet range equation gives the cruise range of a jet aircraft assuming constant speed, lift-to-drag ratio and specific fuel consumption. Range improves with higher L/D, lower fuel consumption, and a larger fraction of the takeoff weight carried as fuel.

instruction: What is the formula for Gradient, divergence and curl? When is it used? [GATE AE - Engineering Mathematics]
response:
Formula: grad phi = (dphi/dx, dphi/dy, dphi/dz); div F = dFx/dx + dFy/dy + dFz/dz; curl F = grad x F. Vorticity omega = curl V.

The gradient of a scalar field points in the direction of fastest increase, with magnitude equal to that rate of increase. Divergence measures the net outflow of a vector field from a point (a source or sink), and curl measures its local rotation. In aerodynamics they describe pressure fields, velocity fields and vorticity.

instruction: What is the formula for Stokes, Gauss and Green theorems? When is it used? [GATE AE - Engineering Mathematics]
response:
Formula: Gauss: integral_V div F dV = integral_S F . n dS. Stokes: integral_S (curl F) . n dS = integral_C F . dl. Circulation Gamma = integral_C V . dl.

These theorems convert integrals over a region into integrals over its boundary. Gauss's (divergence) theorem turns a volume integral of divergence into a surface flux integral; Stokes' theorem turns a surface integral of curl into a line integral around its boundary; Green's theorem is the 2-D form of Stokes' theorem. They underlie the integral forms of the conservation laws and the circulation definition of lift.

instruction: What is the formula for Kepler's laws and escape velocity? When is it used? [GATE AE - Flight Mechanics]
response:
Formula: T^2 = (4*pi^2 / (G*M)) * a^3; escape velocity v_e = sqrt(2*G*M / R) = sqrt(2*g*R). For Earth v_e is about 11.2 km/s.

Kepler's laws state that orbits are ellipses with the central body at one focus, a line joining body and centre sweeps equal areas in equal times, and the square of the orbital period is proportional to the cube of the semi-major axis. Escape velocity is the minimum speed at the surface needed to reach infinity with zero residual speed, found by equating kinetic energy to the gravitational potential energy that must be overcome.

instruction: What is the formula for Longitudinal static stability (stick-fixed)? When is it used? [GATE AE - Flight Mechanics]
response:
Formula: Static margin = (x_np - x_cg) / c_bar (positive for stability). dCm/dalpha < 0 for static stability; Cm = Cm0 + (dCm/dalpha) * alpha.

An aircraft is longitudinally statically stable if a disturbance in angle of attack produces a pitching moment that restores the original attitude, i.e. the pitching-moment slope dCm/dalpha is negative. The wing alone is usually destabilising about the centre of gravity, and the horizontal tail provides the restoring moment; the neutral point is the CG position where dCm/dalpha = 0. Static margin, the distance between neutral point and CG as a fraction of mean aerodynamic chord, measures the degree of stability.

instruction: What is the formula for Load factor, turning flight and V-n diagram? When is it used? [GATE AE - Flight Mechanics]
response:
Formula: n = L / W = 1 / cos(phi) in a level turn; turn radius R = V^2 / (g * tan(phi)); stall speed at load factor n is V_s(n) = V_s1 * sqrt(n).

Load factor n is lift divided by weight; in a steady level turn the lift must support the weight and provide the centripetal force, so n = 1/cos(phi) where phi is the bank angle. The turn radius then follows from the horizontal lift component. The V-n diagram plots the allowable load factor against airspeed, bounded by the stall line at low speed and the structural limit load factor at high speed.

instruction: What is the formula for Potential flow: sources, sinks, doublets and vortices? When is it used? [GATE AE - Aerodynamics]
response:
Formula: Uniform flow + doublet: stream function psi = V_inf * r * sin(theta) * (1 - a^2/r^2); vortex: V_theta = Gamma / (2*pi*r). Laplace equation: del^2 phi = 0.

In incompressible, irrotational flow the velocity is the gradient of a velocity potential that satisfies Laplace's equation, so elementary solutions can be added together (superposed) to build flows around bodies. A source emits fluid radially, a sink absorbs it, a doublet is a source-sink pair, and a line vortex gives purely tangential flow. Superposing a uniform stream, a doublet and a vortex gives the flow around a lifting circular cylinder.

instruction: What is the formula for Kutta-Joukowski theorem and the Kutta condition? When is it used? [GATE AE - Aerodynamics]
response:
Formula: L' = rho * V_inf * Gamma (lift per unit span). Kutta condition: flow leaves the trailing edge smoothly, with finite velocity and equal pressure on both sides.

The Kutta-Joukowski theorem states that the lift per unit span on a two-dimensional body in steady flow equals air density times freestream speed times the circulation around the body. Circulation is generated because the flow must leave the sharp trailing edge smoothly (the Kutta condition), which fixes the circulation; the starting vortex shed at the start of motion carries the equal and opposite circulation. The theorem explains why lift is tied to circulation rather than to any single pressure value.

instruction: What is the formula for Normal and oblique shocks? When is it used? [GATE AE - Aerodynamics]
response:
Formula: Normal shock: p2/p1 = 1 + (2*gamma/(gamma+1))*(M1^2 - 1); M2^2 = ((gamma-1)*M1^2 + 2) / (2*gamma*M1^2 - (gamma-1)). Oblique shock uses the normal component M1n = M1*sin(beta).

A shock wave is a thin region across which a supersonic flow decelerates abruptly to subsonic (normal shock) or to a lower supersonic Mach number (oblique shock), with jumps in pressure, density and temperature and a rise in entropy. Across a normal shock the Rankine-Hugoniot relations link the upstream and downstream Mach numbers. An oblique shock turns the flow by an angle theta; for a given upstream Mach number there are weak and strong solutions, and beyond the maximum deflection angle the shock detaches as a bow shock.

instruction: What is the formula for Isentropic flow, nozzles and diffusers? When is it used? [GATE AE - Aerodynamics]
response:
Formula: T0/T = 1 + ((gamma-1)/2)*M^2; p0/p = (T0/T)^(gamma/(gamma-1)); A/A* = (1/M)*((2/(gamma+1))*(1 + ((gamma-1)/2)*M^2))^((gamma+1)/(2*(gamma-1))). Choked mass flow m_dot_max = (A* * p0 / sqrt(T0)) * sqrt(gamma/R) * (1 + (gamma-1)/2)^(-(gamma+1)/(2*(gamma-1))).

In isentropic (adiabatic, reversible) compressible flow, stagnation pressure and stagnation temperature stay constant, and static properties follow from the Mach number through the isentropic relations. A converging-diverging (de Laval) nozzle chokes at the throat at Mach 1 when the pressure ratio is low enough, after which the exit Mach number is set by the area ratio. A diffuser does the reverse, slowing the flow and recovering static pressure.

instruction: What is the formula for Viscous flow and boundary layers (Blasius)? When is it used? [GATE AE - Aerodynamics]
response:
Formula: delta/x = 5.0 / sqrt(Re_x); local skin friction Cf_x = 0.664 / sqrt(Re_x); total Cf = 1.328 / sqrt(Re_L) (laminar flat plate). Re_x = rho*V*x / mu.

Viscosity makes fluid stick to a solid surface (no-slip), creating a thin boundary layer in which velocity rises from zero at the wall to the freestream value. For a laminar flat plate the Blasius solution gives the layer thickness growing as the square root of distance, and the local skin-friction coefficient falling as 1/sqrt(Rex). Transition to turbulence thickens the layer and raises skin friction, and an adverse pressure gradient can separate the layer from the surface.

instruction: What is the formula for Mohr's circle, principal stresses and failure theories? When is it used? [GATE AE - Aerospace Structures]
response:
Formula: sigma_avg = (sigma_x + sigma_y)/2; R = sqrt(((sigma_x - sigma_y)/2)^2 + tau_xy^2); sigma_1,2 = sigma_avg +/- R; tau_max = R. Von Mises: sigma_vm = sqrt(sigma_x^2 - sigma_x*sigma_y + sigma_y^2 + 3*tau_xy^2).

Mohr's circle is a graphical construction giving the normal and shear stresses on any plane through a point from the stress state on two perpendicular planes. Its centre and radius yield the principal stresses (planes of zero shear) and the maximum shear stress. Failure theories then compare a combined stress state with uniaxial test data: Tresca uses maximum shear stress, von Mises uses distortional strain energy, and maximum principal stress is used mainly for brittle materials.

instruction: What is the formula for Elastic flexural buckling of columns (Euler)? When is it used? [GATE AE - Aerospace Structures]
response:
Formula: P_cr = (pi^2 * E * I) / (K*L)^2; critical stress sigma_cr = (pi^2 * E) / (L_e/r)^2, where L_e = K*L and r = sqrt(I/A) is the radius of gyration.

A slender column under axial compression can buckle sideways at a critical load well below its crushing strength; Euler theory gives this load from the flexural stiffness and the effective length set by the end conditions. The critical stress falls as the square of the slenderness ratio, so long thin columns fail by buckling while short stocky ones fail by yielding. The effective-length factor K is 0.5 for both ends fixed, about 0.7 for one fixed and one pinned, 1.0 for both pinned, and 2.0 for one free end.

instruction: What is the formula for Free and forced vibration of SDOF systems? When is it used? [GATE AE - Aerospace Structures]
response:
Formula: Natural frequency omega_n = sqrt(k/m); damped frequency omega_d = omega_n * sqrt(1 - zeta^2); zeta = c / (2*sqrt(k*m)); resonance magnification (zeta small) about 1/(2*zeta).

A single-degree-of-freedom system (mass, spring, damper) oscillates at its natural frequency when displaced and released; damping removes energy and is measured by the damping ratio zeta. Under harmonic forcing the response is largest near resonance, where the forcing frequency equals the natural frequency, and the magnification depends on damping. Undamped free vibration is simple harmonic motion; a 2-DOF undamped system has two natural frequencies and two mode shapes.

instruction: What is the formula for Brayton cycle and gas-turbine efficiency? When is it used? [GATE AE - Propulsion]
response:
Formula: Thermal efficiency eta_th = 1 - 1 / (r_p^((gamma-1)/gamma)), where r_p is the compressor pressure ratio. Net specific work w_net = w_turbine - w_compressor.

The Brayton cycle is the ideal cycle of a gas turbine: isentropic compression, constant-pressure heat addition in the combustor, isentropic expansion through the turbine, and constant-pressure heat rejection. Its thermal efficiency depends only on the pressure ratio (for a perfect gas), rising as the pressure ratio rises. Real engines lose efficiency to compressor and turbine irreversibilities, pressure drops and combustion losses.

instruction: What is the formula for Rocket thrust equation and specific impulse? When is it used? [GATE AE - Propulsion]
response:
Formula: F = m_dot * v_e + (p_e - p_a) * A_e; specific impulse I_sp = F / (m_dot * g0) = v_e,eff / g0; Tsiolkovsky delta-v = v_e * ln(m0 / mf).

A rocket produces thrust from the momentum of its exhaust plus the pressure thrust at the nozzle exit: mass flow times exhaust velocity, plus exit area times the difference between exit and ambient pressure. Specific impulse is thrust per unit weight flow rate of propellant, equal to the effective exhaust velocity divided by g0, and measures propellant efficiency. Multi-staging discards empty tank mass so the remaining stages accelerate a lighter vehicle, raising the achievable velocity increment for a given propellant mass.

instruction: What is the formula for Axial compressor stage: work, reaction and efficiency? When is it used? [GATE AE - Propulsion]
response:
Formula: Specific work w = U * (V_w2 - V_w1) (Euler turbomachine equation); degree of reaction R = (static enthalpy rise in rotor) / (static enthalpy rise in stage); stage pressure ratio from isentropic efficiency eta_c = (T02s - T01)/(T02 - T01).

In an axial compressor stage the rotor adds swirl (angular momentum) to the flow, raising its stagnation enthalpy, and the stator removes the swirl and converts kinetic energy into static pressure. The degree of reaction is the fraction of the stage static enthalpy rise that occurs in the rotor; 50% reaction gives symmetric velocity triangles and is common in design. Stage efficiency compares the ideal (isentropic) work with the actual work, and multi-staging is needed because one stage gives only a modest pressure ratio.

instruction: Why does Bernoulli's equation and lift matter in Aerodynamics? Where is it used? [GATE AE]
response:
Along a streamline in steady, incompressible, inviscid flow, the sum of static pressure, dynamic pressure and elevation pressure is constant. Faster flow therefore means lower static pressure, which is the basic explanation for the pressure difference that produces lift on a wing.

Formula: p + (1/2) rho V^2 + rho g h = constant; dynamic pressure q = (1/2) rho V^2

response:

Discharge is proportional to the hydraulic conductivity, the cross-sectional area, and the hydraulic gradient. It is the foundation of groundwater flow, drainage design, and seepage calculations in agricultural engineering.

Formula: Q = K * A * (dh/dl);  v = K * i, where Q is discharge, K is hydraulic conductivity, A is cross-sectional area, dh/dl is the hydraulic gradient, v is Darcy velocity, and i is the gradient.

Worked example: A soil column has K = 1 x 10^-5 m/s, area A = 2 m2 and hydraulic gradient 0.05. Q = 1 x 10^-5 x 2 x 0.05 = 1 x 10^-6 m3/s, which is 0.086 m3/day.

instruction: What is Irrigation efficiency? Explain it briefly. [GATE AG - Soil & Water]
response:
Irrigation efficiency measures how much of the water applied to a field is actually stored in the root zone and used by the crop. Application efficiency is the ratio of water stored in the root zone to water applied. Low efficiency means losses to runoff, deep percolation, and evaporation.

Formula: Application efficiency Ea = (water stored in root zone / water applied) x 100%. Overall project efficiency = conveyance efficiency x application efficiency.

Worked example: 100 mm of water is applied and 65 mm is stored in the root zone. Ea = (65/100) x 100 = 65%.

instruction: What is Available soil water? Explain it briefly. [GATE AG - Soil & Water]
response:
Available water is the water held in soil between field capacity and permanent wilting point that plants can extract. Field capacity is the water remaining after free drainage, and wilting point is the moisture at which plants can no longer extract water and wilt permanently. It depends on soil texture: clay holds more than sand.

Formula: Available water depth = (field capacity - wilting point) x root-zone depth, with moisture contents as fractions by volume.

Worked example: Field capacity is 30%, wilting point is 15%, and root depth is 0.6 m (600 mm). Available water = (0.30 - 0.15) x 600 = 90 mm.

instruction: What is Manning equation for open channels? Explain it briefly. [GATE AG - Soil & Water]
response:
Manning's equation is the standard empirical formula for velocity in open channels such as irrigation canals, under steady uniform flow. Velocity increases with hydraulic radius and channel slope and decreases with roughness. The roughness coefficient n is taken from standard tables for the channel material.

Formula: V = (1/n) x R^(2/3) x S^(1/2);  Q = A x V;  R = A/P, where V is mean velocity, n is Manning's roughness, R is hydraulic radius, S is slope, A is flow area and P is wetted perimeter (SI units).

Worked example: For n = 0.025, R = 1.0 m and S = 0.001, V = (1/0.025) x 1^(2/3) x sqrt(0.001) = 40 x 0.0316 = 1.27 m/s.

instruction: What is Soil bulk density and porosity? Explain it briefly. [GATE AG - Soil & Water]
response:
Bulk density is the mass of dry soil per unit total volume, including pore space, while particle density is the mass per unit volume of the solid particles only (about 2.65 g/cm3 for most mineral soils). Porosity is the fraction of soil volume occupied by pores, which hold air and water. Compaction raises bulk density and lowers porosity.

Formula: Porosity n = 1 - (bulk density / particle density). Bulk density = mass of dry soil / total volume.

Worked example: Bulk density is 1.32 g/cm3 and particle density is 2.65 g/cm3. Porosity = 1 - (1.32/2.65) = 1 - 0.498 = 0.50, or about 50%.

instruction: What is Crop water requirement and evapotranspiration? Explain it briefly. [GATE AG - Soil & Water]
response:
Crop water requirement is the depth of water needed to meet the evapotranspiration of a crop, and it is estimated from reference evapotranspiration and a crop coefficient that varies with growth stage. Reference evapotranspiration ETo is the demand of a well-watered reference grass surface. Irrigation requirement is crop water requirement minus effective rainfall.

Formula: ETc = Kc x ETo, where ETc is crop evapotranspiration, Kc is the crop coefficient and ETo is reference evapotranspiration. Irrigation requirement = ETc - effective rainfall.

Worked example: If Kc = 1.1 and ETo = 5 mm/day, ETc = 1.1 x 5 = 5.5 mm/day. Over 10 days the crop needs 55 mm of water.

instruction: What is Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors? Explain it briefly. [GATE AG - Engineering Mathematics]
response:
A non-zero vector v is an eigenvector of a square matrix A if Av = λv, where λ is the eigenvalue. Eigenvalues are the roots of the characteristic equation det(A − λI) = 0. The Cayley-Hamilton theorem states that every square matrix satisfies its own characteristic equation, which lets powers of A be reduced to lower-degree polynomials.

Worked example: For A = [[2, 0], [0, 3]], det(A − λI) = (2 − λ)(3 − λ) = 0, so the eigenvalues are λ = 2 and 3, with eigenvectors along the x and y axes.

instruction: What is Laplace Transforms for ODEs? Explain it briefly. [GATE AG - Engineering Mathematics]
response:

Formula: L{f'(t)} = sF(s) − f(0); L{e^(at)} = 1/(s − a)

instruction: What is Simpson's Rule for Numerical Integration? Explain it briefly. [GATE AG - Engineering Mathematics]
response:

It needs an even number of intervals n with step h = (b − a)/n. It is generally more accurate than the trapezoidal rule for the same number of intervals.

instruction: What is Field Capacity and Efficiency of Farm Implements? Explain it briefly. [GATE AG - Farm Machinery]
response:
Theoretical field capacity (TFC) is the area covered per hour if the machine worked continuously at full width and speed. Field efficiency is the ratio EFC/TFC, typically 65-85% for tillage and sowing operations.

instruction: What is Tractor Traction, Slip and Drawbar Pull? Explain it briefly. [GATE AG - Farm Machinery]
response:
Wheel slip is the loss of forward motion because the driving wheels spin faster than the tractor advances, and it rises with drawbar load and soft soil. Gross traction is the thrust developed at the soil-wheel interface; subtracting rolling resistance gives the net drawbar pull available for the implement. The traction coefficient is drawbar pull divided by the dynamic weight on the drive wheels.

Formula: Slip (%) = (V0 − Va)/V0 × 100; drawbar pull = gross traction − rolling resistance; traction coefficient = pull / dynamic weight

Worked example: A tractor whose wheels would theoretically advance at 6 km/h but actually moves at 5.4 km/h has slip = (6 − 5.4)/6 = 10%, which is near the 10-15% range considered acceptable for good traction.

instruction: What is IC Engine Cycles: Otto and Diesel Efficiency? Explain it briefly. [GATE AG - Farm Machinery]
response:
The Otto cycle (constant-volume heat addition) models spark-ignition petrol engines, and its air-standard efficiency depends only on the compression ratio r and the specific-heat ratio γ. The Diesel cycle (constant-pressure heat addition) models compression-ignition engines and also depends on the cut-off ratio ρ. Higher compression ratio raises efficiency in both, which is why diesel engines run at much higher compression ratios.

instruction: What is Darcy-Weisbach Head Loss in Pipes? Explain it briefly. [GATE AG - Soil & Water]
response:

instruction: What is Unit Hydrograph Theory? Explain it briefly. [GATE AG - Soil & Water]
response:

Because a catchment is treated as a linear system, the hydrograph for any storm is obtained by scaling the UH ordinates by the effective rainfall depth and adding (convolving) the responses of successive rainfall blocks. The base period of the UH stays constant regardless of rainfall depth.

instruction: What is Universal Soil Loss Equation (USLE)? Explain it briefly. [GATE AG - Soil & Water]
response:

instruction: What is Psychrometry: Properties of Air-Water Vapour Mixtures? Explain it briefly. [GATE AG - Food Processing]
response:

instruction: What is Kinetics of Microbial Death: D-value, z-value and F0? Explain it briefly. [GATE AG - Food Processing]
response:

instruction: What is Thiem Equation for Steady Flow to a Well? Explain it briefly. [GATE AG - Soil & Water]

instruction: What is the formula for Manning equation for open channels? When is it used? [GATE AG - Soil & Water]
response:
Formula: V = (1/n) x R^(2/3) x S^(1/2);  Q = A x V;  R = A/P, where V is mean velocity, n is Manning's roughness, R is hydraulic radius, S is slope, A is flow area and P is wetted perimeter (SI units).

Manning's equation is the standard empirical formula for velocity in open channels such as irrigation canals, under steady uniform flow. Velocity increases with hydraulic radius and channel slope and decreases with roughness. The roughness coefficient n is taken from standard tables for the channel material.

instruction: What is the formula for Soil bulk density and porosity? When is it used? [GATE AG - Soil & Water]
response:
Formula: Porosity n = 1 - (bulk density / particle density). Bulk density = mass of dry soil / total volume.

Bulk density is the mass of dry soil per unit total volume, including pore space, while particle density is the mass per unit volume of the solid particles only (about 2.65 g/cm3 for most mineral soils). Porosity is the fraction of soil volume occupied by pores, which hold air and water. Compaction raises bulk density and lowers porosity.

instruction: What is the formula for Crop water requirement and evapotranspiration? When is it used? [GATE AG - Soil & Water]
response:
Formula: ETc = Kc x ETo, where ETc is crop evapotranspiration, Kc is the crop coefficient and ETo is reference evapotranspiration. Irrigation requirement = ETc - effective rainfall.

Crop water requirement is the depth of water needed to meet the evapotranspiration of a crop, and it is estimated from reference evapotranspiration and a crop coefficient that varies with growth stage. Reference evapotranspiration ETo is the demand of a well-watered reference grass surface. Irrigation requirement is crop water requirement minus effective rainfall.

instruction: What is the formula for Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors? When is it used? [GATE AG - Engineering Mathematics]
response:
Formula: det(A − λI) = 0; for a 2x2 matrix, A^2 − tr(A)A + det(A)I = 0 (Cayley-Hamilton)

A non-zero vector v is an eigenvector of a square matrix A if Av = λv, where λ is the eigenvalue. Eigenvalues are the roots of the characteristic equation det(A − λI) = 0. The Cayley-Hamilton theorem states that every square matrix satisfies its own characteristic equation, which lets powers of A be reduced to lower-degree polynomials.

instruction: What is the formula for Laplace Transforms for ODEs? When is it used? [GATE AG - Engineering Mathematics]
response:
Formula: L{f'(t)} = sF(s) − f(0); L{e^(at)} = 1/(s − a)

The Laplace transform converts a differential equation into an algebraic equation in s, which is easier to solve. Key transforms are L{1} = 1/s, L{e^(at)} = 1/(s − a), L{sin at} = a/(s^2 + a^2), and L{f'(t)} = sF(s) − f(0). The inverse transform then recovers the time-domain solution.

instruction: What is the formula for Simpson's Rule for Numerical Integration? When is it used? [GATE AG - Engineering Mathematics]
response:
Formula: ∫f(x)dx ≈ (h/3)[f0 + 4f1 + 2f2 + 4f3 + ... + fn], n even, h = (b − a)/n

Simpson's 1/3 rule approximates a definite integral by fitting parabolas through groups of three points, and is exact for polynomials up to degree 3. It needs an even number of intervals n with step h = (b − a)/n. It is generally more accurate than the trapezoidal rule for the same number of intervals.

instruction: What is the formula for Field Capacity and Efficiency of Farm Implements? When is it used? [GATE AG - Farm Machinery]
response:
Formula: TFC (ha/h) = speed (km/h) × width (m) / 10; EFC = TFC × field efficiency; time per ha = 1/EFC

Theoretical field capacity (TFC) is the area covered per hour if the machine worked continuously at full width and speed. Effective field capacity (EFC) is what is actually achieved, reduced by turning, loading and overlap losses. Field efficiency is the ratio EFC/TFC, typically 65-85% for tillage and sowing operations.

instruction: What is the formula for Tractor Traction, Slip and Drawbar Pull? When is it used? [GATE AG - Farm Machinery]
response:
Formula: Slip (%) = (V0 − Va)/V0 × 100; drawbar pull = gross traction − rolling resistance; traction coefficient = pull / dynamic weight

Wheel slip is the loss of forward motion because the driving wheels spin faster than the tractor advances, and it rises with drawbar load and soft soil. Gross traction is the thrust developed at the soil-wheel interface; subtracting rolling resistance gives the net drawbar pull available for the implement. The traction coefficient is drawbar pull divided by the dynamic weight on the drive wheels.

instruction: What is the formula for IC Engine Cycles: Otto and Diesel Efficiency? When is it used? [GATE AG - Farm Machinery]
response:
Formula: Otto: η = 1 − 1/r^(γ−1); Diesel: η = 1 − [1/r^(γ−1)] × [(ρ^γ − 1)/(γ(ρ − 1))]

The Otto cycle (constant-volume heat addition) models spark-ignition petrol engines, and its air-standard efficiency depends only on the compression ratio r and the specific-heat ratio γ. The Diesel cycle (constant-pressure heat addition) models compression-ignition engines and also depends on the cut-off ratio ρ. Higher compression ratio raises efficiency in both, which is why diesel engines run at much higher compression ratios.

instruction: What is the formula for Darcy-Weisbach Head Loss in Pipes? When is it used? [GATE AG - Soil & Water]
response:
Formula: h_f = f × (L/D) × (v^2/(2g)); laminar: f = 64/Re; Re = ρvD/μ

The Darcy-Weisbach equation gives the friction head loss in a pipe as a function of the friction factor f, pipe length and diameter, and flow velocity. For laminar flow f = 64/Re, while for turbulent flow f is read from Moody's diagram using the Reynolds number and the relative roughness of the pipe.

instruction: What is the formula for Unit Hydrograph Theory? When is it used? [GATE AG - Soil & Water]
response:
Formula: Q(t) = UH ordinate × effective rainfall depth (cm); for multiple blocks, Q = sum over blocks of (UH shifted by block time × block rainfall)

A unit hydrograph (UH) is the direct-runoff hydrograph resulting from 1 cm of effective rainfall uniformly distributed over a catchment in a specified duration D. Because a catchment is treated as a linear system, the hydrograph for any storm is obtained by scaling the UH ordinates by the effective rainfall depth and adding (convolving) the responses of successive rainfall blocks. The base period of the UH stays constant regardless of rainfall depth.

instruction: What is the formula for Universal Soil Loss Equation (USLE)? When is it used? [GATE AG - Soil & Water]
response:
Formula: A = R × K × LS × C × P, where A is soil loss in t/ha/yr

The USLE is an empirical model that predicts the long-term average annual soil loss from sheet and rill erosion on a hillslope. It multiplies five factors: rainfall erosivity R, soil erodibility K, topographic factor LS, cover-management factor C, and support-practice factor P. It does not predict gully erosion or single-storm losses.

instruction: What is the formula for Psychrometry: Properties of Air-Water Vapour Mixtures? When is it used? [GATE AG - Food Processing]
response:
Formula: W = 0.622 × pv/(p − pv); relative humidity = pv/pvs × 100%

Psychrometry describes moist air using the humidity ratio W (kg of water per kg of dry air), relative humidity, dew-point temperature and wet-bulb temperature. The humidity ratio follows from the partial pressure of water vapour in the air. These properties govern drying, storage and air-conditioning of agricultural produce.

instruction: What is the formula for Kinetics of Microbial Death: D-value, z-value and F0? When is it used? [GATE AG - Food Processing]
response:
Formula: D = time for 1-log reduction at temperature T; log(D1/D2) = (T2 − T1)/z; F0 = D × log(N0/N)

Microbial death by heat follows first-order kinetics: each D-value is the time at a given temperature needed to reduce a population by 90% (one log cycle). The z-value is the temperature rise needed to reduce the D-value tenfold. The F0 value is the equivalent time at 121.1 °C, and a 12D process (F0 = 12 min for C. botulinum) is the standard for low-acid canned foods.

instruction: What is the formula for Thiem Equation for Steady Flow to a Well? When is it used? [GATE AG - Soil & Water]
response:
Formula: T = Q × ln(r2/r1) / (2π × (s1 − s2)), where T = K × b (transmissivity)

The Thiem equation describes steady-state radial flow to a fully penetrating well in a confined aquifer. It relates the pumping rate to the drawdowns measured in two observation wells, and is used to estimate aquifer transmissivity T from a pumping test. It assumes a homogeneous, isotropic, infinite aquifer and constant pumping rate.

instruction: Why does Darcy flow in soils matter in Soil & Water? Where is it used? [GATE AG]
response:
Darcy's law describes laminar flow of water through a saturated porous medium such as soil. Discharge is proportional to the hydraulic conductivity, the cross-sectional area, and the hydraulic gradient. It is the foundation of groundwater flow, drainage design, and seepage calculations in agricultural engineering.

Formula: Q = K * A * (dh/dl);  v = K * i, where Q is discharge, K is hydraulic conductivity, A is cross-sectional area, dh/dl is the hydraulic gradient, v is Darcy velocity, and i is the gradient.

instruction: Why does Irrigation efficiency matter in Soil & Water? Where is it used? [GATE AG]
response:

Formula: Application efficiency Ea = (water stored in root zone / water applied) x 100%. Overall project efficiency = conveyance efficiency x application efficiency.

instruction: What is Floor Area Ratio (FAR / FSI)? Explain it briefly. [GATE AR - Planning]
response:
Floor Area Ratio (called Floor Space Index, FSI, in India) is the ratio of a building's total floor area to the area of its plot. It is the main planning control on how much can be built on a site: a higher FAR allows a taller or bulkier building. It is set by development control regulations and varies by zone, road width, and land use.

Formula: FAR (FSI) = total built-up floor area / plot area. Permissible built-up area = FAR x plot area.

Worked example: A plot of 1000 sq m with FAR = 2.0 may have up to 2.0 x 1000 = 2000 sq m of total floor area, for example four floors of 500 sq m each.

instruction: What is Water-cement ratio and Abrams' law? Explain it briefly. [GATE AR - Building Materials]
response:
The water-cement ratio is the mass of free water divided by the mass of cement in a concrete mix. Abrams' law states that, for given materials and curing, the compressive strength of fully compacted concrete depends mainly on this ratio: a lower ratio gives denser paste and higher strength, while excess water leaves pores that weaken the concrete. Codes such as IS 456 set maximum ratios by exposure condition.

Formula: w/c = W / C;  Abrams' law: strength S = A / B^(w/c), where W is mass of water, C is mass of cement, and A and B are empirical constants for the materials and curing.

Worked example: A mix uses 180 kg of water and 400 kg of cement. w/c = 180/400 = 0.45, which is the IS 456 maximum for reinforced concrete in severe exposure.

instruction: What is U-value and heat transfer through building fabric? Explain it briefly. [GATE AR - Architecture]
response:
The U-value (thermal transmittance) measures how much heat passes through one square metre of a wall, roof, or window per degree of temperature difference. It is the reciprocal of the total thermal resistance of the layers. A lower U-value means better insulation and lower heating or cooling load, which is central to climate-responsive design.

Formula: U = 1 / R_total;  Q = U x A x delta T, where U is in W/(m2 K), R_total is total thermal resistance, Q is heat flow, A is area and delta T is temperature difference.

Worked example: A wall with R_total = 2.5 m2 K/W has U = 1/2.5 = 0.4 W/(m2 K). For A = 10 m2 and delta T = 10 K, heat flow Q = 0.4 x 10 x 10 = 40 W.

instruction: What is Daylight factor? Explain it briefly. [GATE AR - Architecture]
response:
The daylight factor is the ratio of indoor illuminance at a point to the simultaneous outdoor illuminance under an overcast sky, expressed as a percentage. It is the standard measure of how well a room is daylit, independent of the time of day. Larger windows, lighter surfaces, and shallower rooms raise it; a living room typically needs an average daylight factor of about 2% or more.

Formula: Daylight factor DF = (Ei / Eo) x 100%, where Ei is indoor illuminance and Eo is outdoor illuminance under an overcast sky.

Worked example: If indoor illuminance is 300 lux and outdoor illuminance is 10,000 lux, DF = (300/10,000) x 100 = 3%.

instruction: What is Golden ratio in proportion? Explain it briefly. [GATE AR - History of Architecture]
response:
The golden ratio, phi, is the proportion in which a line is divided so that the ratio of the whole to the longer part equals the ratio of the longer part to the shorter part. It has been used since antiquity as a proportioning system in architecture, from the Parthenon to Le Corbusier's Modulor, because rectangles in this ratio are widely judged harmonious. It is closely linked to the Fibonacci sequence.

Formula: phi = (1 + sqrt(5)) / 2 = 1.618... A golden rectangle has sides in the ratio 1 : 1.618.

Worked example: A golden rectangle 1.618 m long is 1.0 m wide. Removing a 1 m x 1 m square leaves a smaller rectangle, 0.618 m by 1 m, which is again in the golden ratio.

instruction: What is Neighbourhood unit (Clarence Perry)? Explain it briefly. [GATE AR - Planning]
response:
Clarence Perry's neighbourhood unit (1929) is a foundational planning concept: a residential area of about 5,000-10,000 people organised around an elementary school at its centre, bounded by arterial roads, with shops at the edges and parks and open space inside. Every home is within about a quarter-mile (400 m), a five-minute walk, of the school. It shaped garden-city and new-town planning and remains the basis of walkable neighbourhood design.

Formula: Population about 5,000-10,000 per unit; radius about 400 m (1/4 mile) to the central school; area about 160 acres in Perry's original scheme.

Worked example: A neighbourhood of 6,000 people with one elementary school at the centre and homes within 400 m of it follows Perry's unit: children walk to school without crossing an arterial road.

instruction: What is PERT and CPM in Project Management? Explain it briefly. [GATE AR - Architecture]
response:
The Critical Path Method (CPM) schedules a project as a network of activities: for each activity the earliest start/finish and latest start/finish are computed, and the path with zero total float is the critical path that fixes the project duration. Any delay on it delays the whole project. PERT handles uncertain durations by taking optimistic (a), most likely (m) and pessimistic (b) estimates and computing an expected time. CPM is used for construction projects with well-defined activities.

Formula: PERT expected time te = (a + 4m + b)/6; total float = LS − ES = LF − EF; critical path float = 0

Worked example: An activity with a = 2, m = 4 and b = 12 days has expected time te = (2 + 16 + 12)/6 = 5 days; if it lies on the critical path, slipping by 2 days delays the project by 2 days.

instruction: What is Modular Coordination in Building Construction? Explain it briefly. [GATE AR - Building Materials]
response:
Modular coordination sizes building components on a standard module, conventionally M = 100 mm, so that parts from different manufacturers fit together on a common grid. Planning, structural and service dimensions are multiples of the module, which reduces cutting and waste, speeds prefabrication and allows standardised windows, doors and panels. It is a core principle of industrialised and prefabricated construction.

Formula: Rule: basic module M = 100 mm; dimensions are multiples of M (e.g. 3M = 300 mm planning grid)

Worked example: A room planned on a 3M grid is 3.0 m, 3.3 m or 3.6 m wide, so standard 900 mm (9M) doors and 1,200 mm (12M) windows fit without on-site cutting.

instruction: What is Natural and Mechanical Ventilation: Air Changes per Hour? Explain it briefly. [GATE AR - Architecture]
response:
Ventilation replaces stale indoor air with fresh air, removing heat, moisture, odours and pollutants. Its rate is often expressed as air changes per hour (ACH): the volume of fresh air supplied per hour divided by the room volume. Natural ventilation relies on wind and stack effect through openings, while mechanical ventilation uses fans and ducts. Bedrooms and living rooms typically need 0.5-1 ACH, while kitchens and toilets need much higher rates.

Formula: ACH = airflow (m3/h) / room volume (m3)

Worked example: A 60 m3 bedroom supplied with 120 m3/h of fresh air has 2 air changes per hour, meaning its air is fully replaced every 30 minutes.

instruction: What is Room Acoustics: Reverberation Time (Sabine's Formula)? Explain it briefly. [GATE AR - Architecture]
response:
Reverberation time RT60 is the time for sound to decay by 60 dB after the source stops, and it decides whether a room sounds echoey or dead. Sabine's formula relates it to the room volume V and the total absorption A, which is the sum of each surface's area times its absorption coefficient. Large, hard rooms reverberate longest; adding soft, absorptive material shortens it. Speech needs a short RT60 (about 0.5-1 s), while concert halls need longer (about 1.5-2 s).

Formula: RT60 = 0.161 × V/A; A = Σ(S × α), where S = surface area and α = absorption coefficient

Worked example: A hall of volume 500 m3 with total absorption 100 sabins has RT60 = 0.161 × 500/100 ≈ 0.81 s, suitable for speech; doubling the absorption would halve it to about 0.4 s.

instruction: What is Kevin Lynch's Five Elements of Urban Design? Explain it briefly. [GATE AR - Urban Design]
response:
Kevin Lynch's The Image of the City (1960) identified five elements by which people read and remember a city: paths (streets and routes of movement), edges (boundaries such as rivers or walls), districts (areas with a recognisable character), nodes (focal points such as squares or junctions) and landmarks (reference points such as a tower or monument). A legible city with clear elements is easier to navigate and gives a stronger sense of place.

Formula: Rule: legibility = clear paths + edges + districts + nodes + landmarks

Worked example: In a historic city the main street is a path, the river is an edge, the old quarter is a district, the central square is a node, and the cathedral tower is a landmark that orients visitors.

instruction: What is Garden City Movement (Ebenezer Howard)? Explain it briefly. [GATE AR - Planning]
response:
Ebenezer Howard's Garden City (1898) proposed self-contained towns combining the advantages of town and country — jobs and services with fresh air and gardens — surrounded by a permanent agricultural green belt. Each town was planned for about 32,000 people, with radial streets, a central park and civic buildings, and limited growth by building new towns instead of sprawling. Letchworth and Welwyn in England were the first examples, and the idea influenced new-town planning worldwide.

Formula: Rule: town of ~32,000 people + permanent green belt + town-country balance; growth by new towns, not sprawl

Worked example: Letchworth Garden City, founded in 1903, follows Howard's plan with a central square, radial avenues and a green belt that still limits its expansion today.

instruction: What is Residential Density: Net and Gross? Explain it briefly. [GATE AR - Planning]
response:
Residential density measures how intensively land is used for housing, expressed as dwelling units per hectare or persons per hectare. Net density counts only the residential plots, while gross density includes roads, open spaces and community facilities in the area, so gross is always lower. Density shapes infrastructure demand, transport viability and liveability: very low density makes public transport uneconomic, while very high density strains services and open space.

Formula: Density = dwelling units (or persons) / area in hectares; gross density counts the whole area, net density only residential plots

Worked example: 100 dwelling units on 2 hectares of residential plots is a net density of 50 DU/ha; if the same 100 units sit in a 4-hectare neighbourhood including roads and a park, the gross density is 25 DU/ha.

instruction: What is Gothic Architecture? Explain it briefly. [GATE AR - History of Architecture]
response:
Gothic architecture, dominant in Europe from the 12th to the 16th century, is defined by the pointed arch, ribbed vault and flying buttress, which together channelled the weight of the roof outward and downward so walls could be thin and filled with stained glass. The result is soaring verticality and light-filled interiors expressing spiritual aspiration. Early masterpieces include Chartres and Notre-Dame de Paris, and the style revived in the 19th-century Gothic Revival.

response:

instruction: What is Fire Safety and Means of Escape in Buildings? Explain it briefly. [GATE AR - Architecture]
response:

instruction: What is Transit Oriented Development (TOD)? Explain it briefly. [GATE AR - Planning]
response:

instruction: Give a worked example for Floor Area Ratio (FAR / FSI) [GATE AR - Planning]
response:

instruction: Give a worked example for Water-cement ratio and Abrams' law [GATE AR - Building Materials]
response:

instruction: Give a worked example for U-value and heat transfer through building fabric [GATE AR - Architecture]
response:

instruction: Give a worked example for Daylight factor [GATE AR - Architecture]

instruction: Give a worked example for Golden ratio in proportion [GATE AR - History of Architecture]

instruction: Give a worked example for Neighbourhood unit (Clarence Perry) [GATE AR - Planning]

It is the reciprocal of the total thermal resistance of the layers. A lower U-value means better insulation and lower heating or cooling load, which is central to climate-responsive design.

Formula: U = 1 / R_total;  Q = U x A x delta T, where U is in W/(m2 K), R_total is total thermal resistance, Q is heat flow, A is area and delta T is temperature difference.

instruction: Why does Daylight factor matter in Architecture? Where is it used? [GATE AR]
response:
The daylight factor is the ratio of indoor illuminance at a point to the simultaneous outdoor illuminance under an overcast sky, expressed as a percentage. It is the standard measure of how well a room is daylit, independent of the time of day. Larger windows, lighter surfaces, and shallower rooms raise it; a living room typically needs an average daylight factor of about 2% or more.

Formula: Daylight factor DF = (Ei / Eo) x 100%, where Ei is indoor illuminance and Eo is outdoor illuminance under an overcast sky.

instruction: Why does Golden ratio in proportion matter in History of Architecture? Where is it used? [GATE AR]
response:
The golden ratio, phi, is the proportion in which a line is divided so that the ratio of the whole to the longer part equals the ratio of the longer part to the shorter part. It has been used since antiquity as a proportioning system in architecture, from the Parthenon to Le Corbusier's Modulor, because rectangles in this ratio are widely judged harmonious. It is closely linked to the Fibonacci sequence.

Formula: phi = (1 + sqrt(5)) / 2 = 1.618... A golden rectangle has sides in the ratio 1 : 1.618.

instruction: Why does Neighbourhood unit (Clarence Perry) matter in Planning? Where is it used? [GATE AR]
response:
Clarence Perry's neighbourhood unit (1929) is a foundational planning concept: a residential area of about 5,000-10,000 people organised around an elementary school at its centre, bounded by arterial roads, with shops at the edges and parks and open space inside. Every home is within about a quarter-mile (400 m), a five-minute walk, of the school. It shaped garden-city and new-town planning and remains the basis of walkable neighbourhood design.

Formula: Population about 5,000-10,000 per unit; radius about 400 m (1/4 mile) to the central school; area about 160 acres in Perry's original scheme.

instruction: Why does PERT and CPM in Project Management matter in Architecture? Where is it used? [GATE AR]
response:
The Critical Path Method (CPM) schedules a project as a network of activities: for each activity the earliest start/finish and latest start/finish are computed, and the path with zero total float is the critical path that fixes the project duration. Any delay on it delays the whole project. PERT handles uncertain durations by taking optimistic (a), most likely (m) and pessimistic (b) estimates and computing an expected time. CPM is used for construction projects with well-defined activities.

Formula: PERT expected time te = (a + 4m + b)/6; total float = LS − ES = LF − EF; critical path float = 0
