A planar cyclic conjugated system with 4n pi electrons is antiaromatic and especially unstable. Non-planar or non-conjugated rings are simply non-aromatic. The rule also applies to charged species such as the cyclopentadienyl anion (6 pi electrons, aromatic).

Formula: Aromatic: cyclic, planar, conjugated, (4n + 2) π electrons; antiaromatic: 4n π electrons

instruction: Why does First-Order Reaction Kinetics and Half-Life matter in Physical Chemistry? Where is it used? [GATE CY]
response:
In a first-order reaction the rate is proportional to the concentration of one reactant, so a plot of ln[A] against time is a straight line with slope −k. The half-life is independent of the initial concentration, which is the signature of first-order kinetics. Many processes, including radioactive decay and some drug eliminations, follow first-order kinetics.

Formula: ln[A] = ln[A]0 − kt; t1/2 = ln 2/k = 0.693/k

instruction: Why does Rotational Spectroscopy of Diatomic Molecules matter in Spectroscopy? Where is it used? [GATE CY]
response:
A diatomic molecule treated as a rigid rotor has quantised rotational energies E_J = BJ(J + 1), where B = h/(8π²I) is the rotational constant and I = μr² is the moment of inertia. Microwave absorption follows the selection rule ΔJ = ±1, so spectral lines appear spaced by 2B. Measuring the spacing gives B, hence the bond length.

Formula: E_J = B·J(J + 1); B = h/(8π^2·I); line spacing = 2B; selection rule ΔJ = ±1

instruction: What is Continuous RVs, PDF? Explain it briefly. [GATE DA - Probability & Stats]
response:
A continuous RV takes uncountably many values. P(X = c) = 0 for every single point c — probabilities only live on intervals. PDF axioms: f(x) >= 0 and the integral over all x equals 1. A PDF is a density, not a probability, so f(x) CAN exceed 1.

Formula: P(a <= X <= b) = integral_a^b f(x) dx = F(b) - F(a). If a PDF does not integrate to 1, normalise first.

Worked example: f(x) = k*x^2 for 0 <= x <= 2. Normalise: integral_0^2 k*x^2 dx = 8k/3 = 1, so k = 3/8. Then P(0.5 < X < 1.5) = 13/32 ~ 0.406.

instruction: What is CDF of a continuous RV? Explain it briefly. [GATE DA - Probability & Stats]
response:
CDF F(x) = P(X <= x) = integral_{-inf}^x f(t) dt. Reverse it: f(x) = F'(x). For continuous X, F is continuous and non-decreasing, F(-inf) = 0, F(inf) = 1. A jump in a CDF means a discrete mass point — it is not purely continuous.

Formula: Median: solve F(m) = 1/2. Mode: where f is tallest. E[g(X)] = integral g(x) f(x) dx (LOTUS). Var(X) = E[X^2] - mu^2.

Worked example: F(x) = x^2/9 for 0 <= x <= 3. PDF f(x) = F'(x) = 2x/9 on (0,3). P(1 < X < 2) = F(2) - F(1) = 4/9 - 1/9 = 1/3. Median of F(x) = 1 - e^{-3x} is ln 2 / 3 ~ 0.231.

instruction: What is Continuous Uniform distribution? Explain it briefly. [GATE DA - Probability & Stats]
response:
Continuous Uniform[a, b]: every point in [a, b] equally likely. CDF has three pieces: 0 for x < a, (x-a)/(b-a) for a <= x <= b, 1 for x > b. Single points have probability zero, so P(X <= 3) = P(X < 3).

Formula: f(x) = 1/(b-a) on [a,b]. E[X] = (a+b)/2. Var(X) = (b-a)^2/12. P(x1 < X < x2) = (x2-x1)/(b-a).

Worked example: X ~ Uniform(2, 8). P(X > 5) = (8-5)/6 = 1/2. E[X] = 5. Var(X) = (8-2)^2/12 = 3. A wait X ~ Uniform(0, 30) has Var = 30^2/12 = 75.

instruction: What is Exponential distribution, memoryless? Explain it briefly. [GATE DA - Probability & Stats]
response:
Exponential(lambda) is the continuous version of Geometric. It is the ONLY continuous distribution with the memoryless property: past waiting buys you nothing. GATE uses rate lambda (mean 1/lambda); some textbooks use mean theta instead — read the question's definition first.

Formula: f(x) = lambda*e^{-lambda*x}, x >= 0. F(x) = 1 - e^{-lambda*x}. E[X] = 1/lambda. Var(X) = 1/lambda^2. P(X > s+t | X > s) = P(X > t). Median = ln 2 / lambda ~ 0.693/lambda, below the mean (right-skewed).

Worked example: X ~ Exponential(lambda = 0.5). By memoryless, P(X > 6 | X > 2) = P(X > 4) = e^{-0.5*4} = e^{-2} ~ 0.135.

instruction: What is Normal distribution, standardisation? Explain it briefly. [GATE DA - Probability & Stats]
response:
Normal X ~ N(mu, sigma^2) is a symmetric bell curve with mean = median = mode = mu. Always standardise first: Z = (X - mu)/sigma ~ N(0,1), then read the table. GATE writes N(10, 4) — the 4 is the VARIANCE, sigma = 2, not 4. 68-95-99.7 rule: within 1/2/3 sigma of mu.

Formula: f(x) = 1/(sigma*sqrt(2*pi)) * e^{-(x-mu)^2/(2*sigma^2)}. P(a < X < b) = Phi((b-mu)/sigma) - Phi((a-mu)/sigma). Phi(1) ~ 0.8413, Phi(2) ~ 0.9772, Phi(1.96) ~ 0.975. Phi(-z) = 1 - Phi(z). P(|Z| < z) = 2*Phi(z) - 1.

Worked example: X ~ N(10, 4): sigma = sqrt(4) = 2. P(X > 12): Z = (12-10)/2 = 1, so P = 1 - Phi(1) = 1 - 0.8413 = 0.1587.

instruction: What is Combining independent normals? Explain it briefly. [GATE DA - Probability & Stats]
response:
A linear combination of independent normals is normal. Means add or subtract; variances ALWAYS add, never subtract. Sum of n iid N(mu, sigma^2) is N(n*mu, n*sigma^2) — mean scales by n, variance by n, SD by sqrt(n).

Formula: aX + bY ~ N(a*mu_x + b*mu_y, a^2*sigma_x^2 + b^2*sigma_y^2) for independent X, Y. E[X - Y] = mu_x - mu_y, Var(X - Y) = sigma_x^2 + sigma_y^2.

Worked example: X, Y iid N(2, 9). X - Y ~ N(0, 18), sigma = sqrt(18) ~ 4.24. P(X - Y > 6): Z = 6/4.24 ~ 1.414, P ~ 1 - Phi(1.414) ~ 0.079.

instruction: What is Chi-squared distribution? Explain it briefly. [GATE DA - Probability & Stats]
response:
Chi-squared with n degrees of freedom is the sum of n squared iid standard normals: Z1^2 + ... + Zn^2. Always >= 0, right-skewed, NOT symmetric — do not import bell-curve instincts. Chi-squared(1) = Z^2; chi-squared(2) is Exponential(1/2). Sampling link: (n-1)S^2/sigma^2 ~ chi-squared(n-1).

Formula: E[chi^2] = n. Var(chi^2) = 2n. Mode = n - 2 (for n >= 2). E[X^2] = Var + (E[X])^2 = 2n + n^2. Independent chi-squares add: df adds.

Worked example: X ~ chi^2(6). E[X^2] = 2*6 + 6^2 = 12 + 36 = 48. Z1^2+Z2^2+Z3^2+Z4^2 with Zi iid N(0,1) is chi^2(4): mean 4, variance 8.

instruction: What is Conditional PDF? Explain it briefly. [GATE DA - Probability & Stats]
response:
Conditional PDF = joint divided by the marginal of the GIVEN variable. It must integrate to 1 over x for the fixed y — if it does not, you divided by the wrong marginal. The support can shrink after conditioning. If X, Y are independent, conditioning does nothing: f_{X|Y}(x|y) = f_X(x).

Formula: f_{X|Y}(x|y) = f_{X,Y}(x,y) / f_Y(y). P(X in A | Y = y) = integral_A f_{X|Y}(x|y) dx. Law of total expectation: E[X] = E[E[X|Y]].

Worked example: Joint PDF f(x,y) = 2 on the triangle 0 < y < x < 1. f_X(x) = integral_0^x 2 dy = 2x. So f_{Y|X}(y|x) = 2/(2x) = 1/x on 0 < y < x — y's ceiling is x, not 1.

instruction: What is Joint and marginal probability? Explain it briefly. [GATE DA - Probability & Stats]
response:
Joint = both happen at once. Marginal = sum (discrete) or integrate (continuous) out the other variable — you 'forget' that column. Marginal limits follow the region, not the rectangle: on 0 <= x < y <= 1, f_X(x) integrates y from x to 1, not 0 to 1. Draw the region first.

Formula: Discrete: P_X(x) = sum_y P(x, y). Continuous: f_X(x) = integral f_{X,Y}(x, y) dy. Independent continuous variables: joint = product of marginals.

Worked example: Joint pmf: P(0,0)=0.1, P(0,1)=0.2, P(1,0)=0.3, P(1,1)=0.4. Marginal P(X=1) = 0.3+0.4 = 0.7; P(Y=1) = 0.2+0.4 = 0.6. On the triangle 0 <= x < y <= 1 with f=2, f_X(x) = 2(1-x) for 0 <= x <= 1.

instruction: What is Conditional probability and Bayes' theorem? Explain it briefly. [GATE DA - Probability & Stats]
response:
Conditional = zoom in on the given slice, then renormalise so it sums to 1. P(A|B) is NOT P(B|A) — Bayes' theorem exists precisely because they differ. Law of total probability needs a partition that is mutually exclusive AND exhaustive; a missing case corrupts the whole answer. Parse the English first: 'given that' = condition, 'both/and' = joint, 'overall/regardless' = marginal or total probability.

Formula: P(X=x | Y=y) = P(X=x, Y=y) / P(Y=y), needs P(Y=y) > 0. Bayes: P(B_i|A) = P(A|B_i)*P(B_i) / sum_j P(A|B_j)*P(B_j). Law of total probability: P(A) = sum_i P(A|B_i)*P(B_i).

Worked example: A test is 95% accurate both ways, but only 1% have the disease. P(disease | +) = (0.95*0.01)/(0.95*0.01 + 0.05*0.99) = 0.0095/0.059 ~ 0.161. The base rate dominates — a positive test is still usually a false positive.

instruction: What is Independence and covariance? Explain it briefly. [GATE DA - Probability & Stats]
response:
Independent means P(x,y) = P_X(x)*P_Y(y) for EVERY x, y — equivalently, conditioning changes nothing. Independent implies Cov = 0, but the converse is FALSE in general: zero covariance does not imply independence (the one exception is jointly Gaussian variables).

Formula: Cov(X,Y) = E[XY] - E[X]*E[Y]. Independent: E[XY] = E[X]*E[Y] and Var(X+Y) = Var(X) + Var(Y). Var(X - Y) = Var(X) + Var(Y) for independent X, Y — the minus does NOT carry inside. General: Var(aX + bY) = a^2*Var(X) + b^2*Var(Y) + 2ab*Cov(X,Y).

Worked example: Joint pmf P(1,1)=0.2, P(1,2)=0.3, P(2,1)=0.1, P(2,2)=0.4. E[X]=1.5, E[Y]=1.7, E[XY]=2.6, so Cov = 2.6 - 1.5*1.7 = 0.05. Check independence: P_X(1)*P_Y(1) = 0.42 vs P(1,1) = 0.4 — not independent.

instruction: What is Mean, median, mode? Explain it briefly. [GATE DA - Probability & Stats]
response:
Mean = share everything out flat. Median = the middle value AFTER SORTING (odd n: middle value; even n: average of the two middle values). Mode = most frequent value — it may not exist (all distinct) or there may be several (bimodal). Mean is dragged by outliers, median is not. Empirical relation (moderately skewed, unimodal only — an approximation, not a theorem): mode = 3*median - 2*mean.

Formula: Mean x-bar = (sum x_i)/n. Weighted mean = sum w_i*x_i / sum w_i. Empirical: mean - mode = 3*(mean - median).

Worked example: Data 7, 3, 9, 3, 12, 5. Sorted: 3, 3, 5, 7, 9, 12. Mean = 39/6 = 6.5. Median = (5+7)/2 = 6. Mode = 3. For median 24 and mean 27 (moderately skewed), mode ~ 3*24 - 2*27 = 18.

instruction: What is Variance and standard deviation? Explain it briefly. [GATE DA - Probability & Stats]
response:
Variance = E[(X-mu)^2] = E[X^2] - mu^2 — the formula never changes. SD = sqrt(variance), always >= 0. Sample variance divides by (n-1); population variance divides by n — if GATE says 'sample', the denominator is n-1. A shift (+b) never changes spread; scaling multiplies SD by |a| and variance by a^2.

Formula: Var(X) = E[X^2] - mu^2. E[aX+b] = a*E[X] + b. Var(aX+b) = a^2*Var(X). SD(aX+b) = |a|*SD(X). Var(X+Y) = Var(X) + Var(Y) + 2*Cov(X,Y).

Worked example: Observations 4, 8, 6, 10, 12. Mean = 8, sum of squared deviations = 40. Sample variance = 40/4 = 10. Population variance = 40/5 = 8. If SD = 4 and x -> 3 - 2x, new SD = |-2|*4 = 8 — the +3 shift does nothing.

instruction: What is Covariance, correlation, Chebyshev? Explain it briefly. [GATE DA - Probability & Stats]
response:
Correlation is covariance squashed into [-1, 1] — a score for 'how close is this to a perfect straight line?'. Correlation is unitless; covariance has units (units of X times units of Y), so covariance's magnitude alone is meaningless. Independent implies rho = 0, but rho = 0 only kills LINEAR dependence. If X is constant (sigma = 0), rho is undefined, not zero.

Formula: Cov(X,Y) = E[XY] - E[X]*E[Y]. rho = Cov(X,Y)/(sigma_x*sigma_y), -1 <= rho <= 1. rho = +1 or -1 iff Y = aX + b exactly. Cov(aX+b, cY+d) = a*c*Cov(X,Y). Chebyshev: P(|X-mu| >= k*sigma) <= 1/k^2.

Worked example: X takes -1, 0, 1 with equal probability; Y = X^2. Cov = 0, so rho = 0 — yet Y is a perfect function of X. Correlation only sees straight lines. Exam scores mean 70, SD 8: by Chebyshev (k=2), at least 1 - 1/4 = 75% score between 54 and 86.

instruction: What is Discrete RVs and PMF? Explain it briefly. [GATE DA - Probability & Stats]
response:
A discrete RV takes values in a countable set. PMF axioms: p(x) >= 0 and sum p(x_i) = 1 over the whole support — always add first, three of four options in a GATE question are usually fakes. The CDF jumps by p(x_i) at each mass point and is flat between them. For discrete RVs, P(X <= 3) and P(X < 3) differ exactly by p(3) — read the inequality carefully. Never integrate a PMF; never treat a staircase CDF as continuous.

Formula: E[X] = sum x_i*p(x_i). E[g(X)] = sum g(x_i)*p(x_i) (LOTUS — no need to find g(X)'s distribution). Var(X) = E[X^2] - mu^2. Linearity: E[aX + bY + c] = a*E[X] + b*E[Y] + c, no independence needed. Var(aX+b) = a^2*Var(X).

Worked example: X in {0,1,2,3} with p = {0.1, 0.3, 0.4, 0.2}. E[X] = 1.7. E[X^2] = 3.7. Var = 3.7 - 1.7^2 = 0.81.

instruction: What is Bernoulli, Binomial, Geometric, Poisson, Discrete Uniform? Explain it briefly. [GATE DA - Probability & Stats]
response:
Binomial = sum of n iid Bernoulli(p) — spot 'n identical yes/no trials' and it is binomial instantly. Poisson = binomial limit (n large, p small, np = lambda); mean = variance = lambda is the giveaway. Sums of independent Poissons stay Poisson (lambdas add); sums of binomials need the SAME p. Geometric has two conventions: trials-to-first-success {1,2,...} (GATE usually means this, E = 1/p) vs failures-before-first {0,1,2,...} — check the support first.

Formula: Bernoulli(p): E = p, Var = p(1-p). Binomial(n,p): P(X=k) = C(n,k)*p^k*(1-p)^{n-k}, E = np, Var = np(1-p). Geometric(p): P(X=k) = (1-p)^{k-1}*p, E = 1/p, Var = (1-p)/p^2. Poisson(lambda): P(X=k) = e^{-lambda}*lambda^k/k!, E = lambda, Var = lambda. Discrete Uniform{1..n}: E = (n+1)/2, Var = (n^2-1)/12.

Worked example: A fair die rolled 4 times; X = number of sixes ~ Binomial(4, 1/6). P(X=2) = C(4,2)*(1/6)^2*(5/6)^2 = 25/216 ~ 0.116. E[X] = 4/6 = 2/3. Calls Poisson(2)/hour: P(exactly 2) = e^{-2}*2^2/2! = 2*e^{-2} ~ 0.271.

instruction: What is Geometric distribution, memoryless (discrete)? Explain it briefly. [GATE DA - Probability & Stats]
response:
Geometric is the ONLY discrete distribution with the memoryless property: past failures buy you nothing. Continuous twin: Exponential. Mode of a discrete RV = the value with the largest p(x).

Formula: P(X > m+n | X > m) = P(X > n). For the trials convention, P(X > k) = (1-p)^k. E[X] = 1/p.

Worked example: X ~ Geometric(p = 0.3), trials to first success. P(X > 4 | X > 2) = P(X > 2) = (1-0.3)^2 = 0.49. A fair coin tossed until the first head: E[X] = 1/0.5 = 2 tosses; P(first head on 3rd toss) = (1/2)^3 = 1/8.

instruction: What is Binomial distribution in depth? Explain it briefly. [GATE DA - Probability & Stats]
response:
'At least one' shortcut: P(X >= 1) = 1 - P(X=0) = 1 - (1-p)^n. Never sum the whole PMF for this. Mode (most likely k) = floor((n+1)p); if (n+1)p is an integer, k and k-1 are both modes. Normal approximation (large n, p not near 0/1): Binomial ~ N(np, npq) with continuity correction +/-0.5. If success probability changes trial to trial, X is a sum of non-identical Bernoullis — E[X] still sums by linearity, but no binomial PMF applies.

Formula: P(X=k) = C(n,k)*p^k*(1-p)^{n-k}. E[X] = np. Var(X) = np(1-p). E[X^2] = npq + n^2*p^2.

Worked example: X ~ Binomial(12, 1/3). E = 4. Var = 12*(1/3)*(2/3) = 8/3 ~ 2.667. Mode = floor(13/3) = 4. X ~ Binomial(4, 0.1): P(X >= 1) = 1 - 0.9^4 = 1 - 0.6561 = 0.3439.

instruction: What is Uniform vs Bernoulli — the two variance traps? Explain it briefly. [GATE DA - Probability & Stats]
response:
Two different 'uniform variance' formulas — swapping them is the most common 1-mark loss here. Continuous Uniform[a,b]: (b-a)^2/12. Discrete Uniform{1..n}: (n^2-1)/12. Bernoulli variance p(1-p) is maximised at p = 1/2, max 0.25. Discrete inequalities bite (P(X<=3) != P(X<3) for Binomial); continuous ones do not (single points are zero).

Formula: Continuous Uniform: E = (a+b)/2, Var = (b-a)^2/12. Discrete Uniform{1..n}: E = (n+1)/2, Var = (n^2-1)/12. Bernoulli(p): E = p, Var = p(1-p) <= 1/4.

Worked example: X ~ Uniform[-2, 2]: P(|X| < 1) = 2/4 = 0.5, Var = (2-(-2))^2/12 = 4/3. X ~ discrete Uniform{1..10}: E = 5.5, Var = (100-1)/12 = 8.25.

instruction: What is Standard limits and L'Hopital? Explain it briefly. [GATE DA - Calculus & Optimization]
response:
L'Hopital applies ONLY to 0/0 or infinity/infinity forms — check the form first, then differentiate top and bottom separately (NOT the quotient rule). One-sided limits must both agree for the two-sided limit to exist. Squeeze theorem kills things like x*sin(1/x) as x -> 0.

Formula: lim(x->0) sin x / x = 1. lim(x->0) (1-cos x)/x^2 = 1/2. lim(x->0) (e^x-1)/x = 1. lim(x->0) ln(1+x)/x = 1. lim(x->inf) (1+1/x)^x = e. Conversions: 0*inf -> inf/inf or 0/0; 1^inf / 0^0 / inf^0 -> take ln.

Worked example: lim(x->0) (sin 3x - 3x)/x^3 = -9/2 (series: sin 3x = 3x - (3x)^3/6 + ...). lim(x->inf) x*[ln(x+1) - ln x] = 1. lim(x->0+) x^x = 1 (x ln x -> 0).

instruction: What is Continuity, IVT, EVT? Explain it briefly. [GATE DA - Calculus & Optimization]
response:
f is continuous at a iff lim(x->a-) f = lim(x->a+) f = f(a) — all three must exist AND match. Discontinuity types: removable (hole), jump (one-sided limits differ), essential/infinite (blows up), oscillatory (sin(1/x) at 0). IVT: continuous on [a,b] with f(a)*f(b) < 0 guarantees at least one root in (a,b). Continuous on a closed interval is bounded and attains its max/min (Extreme Value Theorem).

Formula: Continuity at a: LHL = RHL = f(a). IVT: f(a)*f(b) < 0 => exists c in (a,b) with f(c) = 0.

Worked example: f(x) = (x^3-8)/(x-2) for x != 2, f(2) = 6. Limit at 2 is 12, but f(2) = 6, so it is discontinuous at 2 — removable. f continuous on [0,1] with f(0) = -2, f(1) = 3 guarantees at least one root in (0,1) by IVT.

instruction: What is Differentiability, Rolle, MVT, Taylor? Explain it briefly. [GATE DA - Calculus & Optimization]
response:
Differentiable at a implies continuous at a. The converse is FALSE — |x| at 0 is the classic counterexample. Check left and right derivatives separately for piecewise/absolute-value functions. Differentiable does NOT mean continuously differentiable: x^2*sin(1/x) is differentiable at 0 with derivative 0, but f' is discontinuous there.

Formula: f'(a) = lim(h->0) [f(a+h) - f(a)]/h. Rolle: f continuous on [a,b], differentiable on (a,b), f(a) = f(b) => some c in (a,b) with f'(c) = 0. MVT: f'(c) = [f(b)-f(a)]/(b-a). Taylor: e^x = 1+x+x^2/2!+...; sin x = x-x^3/3!+...; cos x = 1-x^2/2!+...; ln(1+x) = x-x^2/2+x^3/3-... (|x|<1).

Worked example: f(x) = x^2*sin(1/x), f(0)=0: continuous at 0 (squeeze) and differentiable at 0 with f'(0)=0. |x-1| + |x-2| is differentiable everywhere except x=1 and x=2 (kinks). MVT on sqrt(x) over [1,4]: f'(c) = 1/3, c = 9/4.

instruction: What is First and second derivative tests? Explain it briefly. [GATE DA - Calculus & Optimization]
response:
Fermat: if f has a local max/min at interior point c and f'(c) exists, then f'(c) = 0 — necessary, NOT sufficient. Critical points = f'(c) = 0 OR f'(c) undefined (cusps, kinks) — plus endpoints on a closed interval. First derivative test: f' changes + to - => local max; - to + => local min; no sign change => neither (x^3 at 0). Second derivative test: f''(c) > 0 => local min, < 0 => local max, = 0 => INCONCLUSIVE (x^4 min, -x^4 max, x^3 neither all have f'(0)=f''(0)=0).

Formula: First derivative test: sign change of f' across c decides. Second derivative test: f'(c)=0 and f''(c)>0 => min; f''(c)<0 => max; f''(c)=0 => inconclusive, go back to the first derivative test.

Worked example: f(x) = x^3 - 3x^2 + 1. f'(x) = 3x(x-2); f''(x) = 6x-6. Local max at x=0, f(0)=1; local min at x=2, f(2)=-3. g(x) = (x-1)^4: second derivative test is inconclusive at x=1 (g''(1)=0); first derivative test confirms global minimum 0 at x=1.

instruction: What is Global maxima/minima and applied optimisation? Explain it briefly. [GATE DA - Calculus & Optimization]
response:
Global max/min on [a,b]: evaluate f at every critical point inside (a,b) AND at a and b. The largest/smallest value wins — never skip the endpoints; on a closed interval the global extremum is very often at an endpoint. Local max can sit below a local min elsewhere — 'local' means in a neighbourhood only. Domain first: x + 1/x has a clean minimum 2 on x > 0, but on R minus {0} there is no global min at all. Applied setup: use the constraint to eliminate the second variable, then differentiate.

Formula: Global on [a,b]: compare f(critical points) and f(a), f(b). AM-GM shortcut: x + 1/x >= 2*sqrt(x*1/x) = 2 for x > 0.

Worked example: f(x) = |x^2 - 4| on [-3, 3]. Candidates: kinks at x = +/-2 (f=0), f(0)=4, endpoints f(+/-3)=5. Global max 5 at x=-3 and x=3 — endpoints win. h(x) = x + 1/x, x > 0: h'(x) = 1 - 1/x^2 = 0 => x=1, minimum value 2. Two positive numbers summing to 10 minimise sum of squares at (5, 5): minimum 50.

instruction: What is Uninformed search (BFS/DFS)? Explain it briefly. [GATE DA - Artificial Intelligence]
response:
Uninformed search explores a state space using only the problem definition, with no heuristic estimate of distance to the goal. Breadth-first search (BFS) expands nodes level by level using a queue and is complete and optimal when all step costs are equal. Depth-first search (DFS) expands the deepest node first using a stack, uses little memory, but is neither complete in infinite spaces nor optimal.

Formula: BFS time and space: O(b^d), where b is the branching factor and d is the depth of the shallowest goal. DFS space: O(b*m), where m is the maximum depth explored.

Worked example: In a graph A connected to B and C, and B and C both connected to goal D: BFS visits A, B, C, D and finds D at depth 2. DFS visits A, B, D and also reaches D, but it may first explore a long deep branch before finding the shallowest goal.

instruction: What is Informed search and A*? Explain it briefly. [GATE DA - Artificial Intelligence]
response:
Informed search uses a heuristic function to guide exploration toward the goal. A* search expands the node with the lowest f(n) = g(n) + h(n), where g(n) is the cost from the start to n and h(n) is the estimated cost from n to the goal. A* is complete and optimal if the heuristic is admissible, meaning it never overestimates the true cost to the goal.

Formula: f(n) = g(n) + h(n). Admissible heuristic: 0 <= h(n) <= h*(n), where h*(n) is the true cheapest cost from n to the goal.

Worked example: From start S, S to A costs 1 and S to B costs 4; A to G costs 5 and B to G costs 1, with h(A) = 5 and h(B) = 1. Then f(A) = 1 + 5 = 6 and f(B) = 4 + 1 = 5, so A* expands B first and finds the optimal path S-B-G with total cost 5, rather than S-A-G with cost 6.

instruction: What is Heuristic functions? Explain it briefly. [GATE DA - Artificial Intelligence]
response:
A heuristic function h(n) estimates the cost of the cheapest path from node n to a goal. An admissible heuristic never overestimates the true cost, which is required for A* optimality. A consistent (monotone) heuristic also satisfies h(n) <= c(n, a, n') + h(n') for every action a from n to n', which guarantees that f values never decrease along a path.

Formula: Admissible: h(n) <= h*(n). Consistent: h(n) <= c(n, a, n') + h(n'). Manhattan distance: h = |x1 - x2| + |y1 - y2|.

Worked example: On a grid with moves up, down, left and right, the goal is at (3, 4) and the agent is at (0, 0). The Manhattan distance heuristic is |3 - 0| + |4 - 0| = 7, which equals the true cost of 7 steps, so it is admissible and exact here.

instruction: What is Minimax and alpha-beta pruning? Explain it briefly. [GATE DA - Artificial Intelligence]
response:
Minimax chooses the move that maximises the player's minimum guaranteed outcome in a two-player zero-sum game, assuming the opponent also plays optimally. MAX nodes take the maximum of their children and MIN nodes take the minimum. Alpha-beta pruning skips branches that cannot affect the final decision: a MAX node prunes when a child value is at most beta, and a MIN node prunes when a child value is at least alpha.

Formula: Minimax: V(s) = max_a min_b V(result(s, a, b)) for a MAX node, and the minimum over opponent moves at a MIN node. Prune a MIN branch when value <= alpha; prune a MAX branch when value >= beta.

Worked example: Root MAX has MIN children A and B. A has leaves 3 and 5, so A = min(3, 5) = 3 and alpha becomes 3. B's first leaf is 2, which is already <= alpha = 3, so B's second leaf (9) is pruned and B = 2. The root value is max(3, 2) = 3.

instruction: What is Knowledge representation and propositional logic? Explain it briefly. [GATE DA - Artificial Intelligence]
response:
Knowledge representation stores facts about the world in a formal language so an agent can reason with them. In propositional logic, statements are built from atomic propositions with connectives such as NOT, AND, OR, implication and biconditional. A sentence is entailed by a knowledge base if it is true in every model in which the knowledge base is true, and modus ponens lets us infer Q from P and P implies Q.

Formula: Modus ponens: from P and (P -> Q), infer Q. Implication truth table: P -> Q is false only when P is true and Q is false.

Worked example: Knowledge base: Rain -> WetRoad, and Rain is true. By modus ponens, WetRoad is true. If instead Rain were false, Rain -> WetRoad would still be true as an implication, but WetRoad could not be inferred from it alone.

instruction: What is First-order logic basics? Explain it briefly. [GATE DA - Artificial Intelligence]
response:
First-order logic extends propositional logic with objects, predicates, functions and quantifiers, so it can express general rules about many individuals at once. The universal quantifier (for all x) states that a property holds for every object, and the existential quantifier (there exists x) states that it holds for at least one object. Variables can be instantiated to specific constants to derive concrete facts.

Formula: Universal instantiation: from forall x P(x), infer P(a) for any constant a. Example rule: forall x (Human(x) -> Mortal(x)).

Worked example: Given forall x (Human(x) -> Mortal(x)) and Human(Socrates), universal instantiation gives Human(Socrates) -> Mortal(Socrates), and modus ponens then gives Mortal(Socrates).

instruction: What is Bayesian networks? Explain it briefly. [GATE DA - Artificial Intelligence]
response:
A Bayesian network is a directed acyclic graph in which nodes are random variables and edges represent direct dependencies, with each node carrying a conditional probability table given its parents. The joint distribution factorises as the product of each variable's probability given its parents, which encodes conditional independence: a variable is independent of its non-descendants given its parents.

Formula: P(X1, ..., Xn) = product over i of P(Xi | Parents(Xi)). Bayes' rule: P(A | B) = P(B | A) * P(A) / P(B).

Worked example: Let A -> B with P(A) = 0.5, P(B | A) = 0.8 and P(B | not A) = 0.2. Then P(A and B) = 0.5 * 0.8 = 0.4, and by total probability P(B) = 0.5 * 0.8 + 0.5 * 0.2 = 0.5.

instruction: What is Markov decision processes? Explain it briefly. [GATE DA - Artificial Intelligence]
response:
A Markov decision process (MDP) models sequential decision making with states, actions, transition probabilities and rewards, under the Markov property that the future depends only on the current state and action. The goal is a policy maximising expected discounted return. The optimal value function satisfies the Bellman optimality equation, which relates the value of a state to the best immediate reward plus the discounted value of the next state.

Formula: V*(s) = max_a sum over s' of P(s' | s, a) * [R(s, a, s') + gamma * V*(s')]. Q*(s, a) = sum over s' of P(s' | s, a) * [R(s, a, s') + gamma * max_a' Q*(s', a')]. Discount factor: 0 <= gamma < 1.

Worked example: In state s, action a gives reward 5 for sure and moves to state s' with V*(s') = 10, with discount gamma = 0.9. Then Q*(s, a) = 5 + 0.9 * 10 = 14.

instruction: What is Reinforcement learning and Q-learning? Explain it briefly. [GATE DA - Artificial Intelligence]
response:
In reinforcement learning an agent learns a policy by trial and error, receiving rewards from the environment and aiming to maximise cumulative discounted reward. Q-learning is a model-free, off-policy method that learns the action-value function Q(s, a) directly from experience. It updates Q toward the target reward plus the discounted best Q of the next state, balancing exploration of new actions with exploitation of known good ones.

Formula: Q(s, a) <- Q(s, a) + alpha * [r + gamma * max_a' Q(s', a') - Q(s, a)], where alpha is the learning rate and gamma is the discount factor.

Worked example: With Q(s, a) = 1, learning rate alpha = 0.5, reward r = 10, gamma = 0.9 and max_a' Q(s', a') = 2, the target is 10 + 0.9 * 2 = 11.8, so the new Q(s, a) = 1 + 0.5 * (11.8 - 1) = 6.4.

instruction: What is NLP basics (tokenization, n-grams)? Explain it briefly. [GATE DA - Artificial Intelligence]
response:
Natural language processing starts by turning raw text into units a model can use. Tokenization splits text into tokens such as words or subwords, and normalisation steps like lowercasing may follow. An n-gram model predicts a word from the previous n - 1 words, estimating the probability by counting how often that word sequence occurs in a corpus.

Formula: Bigram probability: P(w_n | w_{n-1}) = Count(w_{n-1}, w_n) / Count(w_{n-1}). General n-gram: P(w_n | w_{n-n+1}, ..., w_{n-1}) = Count(w_{n-n+1}, ..., w_n) / Count(w_{n-n+1}, ..., w_{n-1}).

Worked example: The sentence 'the cat sat' tokenizes into ['the', 'cat', 'sat'] and has two bigrams: ('the', 'cat') and ('cat', 'sat'). If 'cat' occurs 3 times in a corpus and 'cat sat' occurs 2 times, then P(sat | cat) = 2 / 3, about 0.67.

instruction: What is Law of large numbers? Explain it briefly. [GATE DA - Probability & Stats]
response:
The law of large numbers says that the sample mean of independent, identically distributed random variables converges to the true population mean as the sample size grows. The weak law states convergence in probability, while the strong law states convergence with probability 1. It is the theoretical basis for estimating probabilities and means from large samples.

Formula: Sample mean: Xbar_n = (1/n) * sum_{i=1 to n} X_i. Weak law: for any epsilon > 0, P(|Xbar_n - mu| > epsilon) -> 0 as n -> infinity, where mu = E[X_i].

Worked example: For a fair die, the true mean is (1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 6) / 6 = 3.5. Averaging 6000 rolls, the sample mean will typically be very close to 3.5, for example 3.48, whereas the average of only 6 rolls could easily be far from 3.5.

instruction: What is Central limit theorem? Explain it briefly. [GATE DA - Probability & Stats]
response:
The central limit theorem says that the sum or average of many independent, identically distributed random variables is approximately normally distributed, regardless of the shape of the original distribution, provided the mean and variance are finite. The approximation improves as the sample size grows, which is why normal-based confidence intervals and tests are so widely used.

Formula: Z_n = (Xbar_n - mu) / (sigma / sqrt(n)) converges in distribution to N(0, 1). Approximately: Xbar_n ~ N(mu, sigma^2 / n), and S_n ~ N(n*mu, n*sigma^2).

Worked example: If a population has mean mu = 50 and standard deviation sigma = 10, the mean of n = 100 observations is approximately N(50, 1), since sigma / sqrt(n) = 10 / 10 = 1. So about 95% of such sample means lie roughly between 48 and 52.

instruction: What is Moment-generating functions? Explain it briefly. [GATE DA - Probability & Stats]
response:
The moment-generating function (MGF) of a random variable X is the expected value of e^(tX), when it exists in a neighbourhood of zero. Differentiating the MGF k times and evaluating at t = 0 gives the k-th moment E[X^k]. The MGF uniquely determines the distribution, and the MGF of a sum of independent variables is the product of their MGFs.

Formula: M_X(t) = E[e^{tX}]. Moments: M_X^{(k)}(0) = E[X^k]. Sum of independent variables: M_{X+Y}(t) = M_X(t) * M_Y(t).

Worked example: For X Bernoulli(p), M_X(t) = (1 - p) + p * e^t. Differentiating gives M_X'(t) = p * e^t, so M_X'(0) = p, which is E[X] = p. For p = 0.3, the mean is 0.3.

instruction: What is Conditional expectation? Explain it briefly. [GATE DA - Probability & Stats]
response:
The conditional expectation E[X | Y] is the expected value of X given the information in Y; for discrete Y it is the average of X weighted by the conditional distribution P(X | Y = y). It is itself a random variable that depends on Y. The law of total expectation says that averaging the conditional expectation over Y recovers the unconditional expectation E[X].

Formula: E[X | Y = y] = sum_x x * P(X = x | Y = y). Law of total expectation: E[X] = E[E[X | Y]].

Worked example: Roll a fair die and let Y be whether the result is even. Given Y = even, the possible values are 2, 4 and 6, each equally likely, so E[X | even] = (2 + 4 + 6) / 3 = 4, which is higher than the unconditional mean 3.5.

instruction: What is Covariance matrix and multivariate normal? Explain it briefly. [GATE DA - Probability & Stats]
response:
The covariance matrix of a random vector collects the variances of each component on its diagonal and the covariances between pairs off the diagonal; it is symmetric and positive semidefinite. A multivariate normal distribution is fully determined by its mean vector mu and covariance matrix Sigma, and every linear combination of its components is normally distributed.

Formula: Cov(X, Y) = E[(X - E[X])(Y - E[Y])] = E[XY] - E[X]E[Y]. Correlation: rho = Cov(X, Y) / (sigma_X * sigma_Y). Multivariate normal density: f(x) = (1 / sqrt((2*pi)^k * det(Sigma))) * exp(-(1/2) * (x - mu)^T * Sigma^{-1} * (x - mu)).

Worked example: If Var(X) = 4, Var(Y) = 9 and Cov(X, Y) = 2, the covariance matrix is [[4, 2], [2, 9]] and the correlation is 2 / (2 * 3) = 1/3, about 0.33, so X and Y are positively but only weakly linearly related.

instruction: What is Integration by parts? Explain it briefly. [GATE DA - Calculus & Optimization]
response:
Integration by parts comes from the product rule for differentiation and is used when an integrand is a product of two functions, one easy to differentiate and the other easy to integrate. Choose u to differentiate and dv to integrate, then apply the formula. The LIATE guideline (logarithmic, inverse trigonometric, algebraic, trigonometric, exponential) often helps in choosing u.

Formula: Integral of u dv = u*v - Integral of v du. Definite form: Integral from a to b of u dv = [u*v] from a to b - Integral from a to b of v du.

Worked example: For Integral of x * e^x dx, take u = x and dv = e^x dx, so du = dx and v = e^x. Then the integral is x*e^x - Integral of e^x dx = x*e^x - e^x + C = (x - 1)*e^x + C. From 0 to 1 this equals 0 - (-1) = 1.

instruction: What is Definite integral properties? Explain it briefly. [GATE DA - Calculus & Optimization]
response:
A definite integral gives the signed area under a curve between two limits. Reversing the limits changes the sign, the integral over a zero-width interval is zero, and integrals add over adjacent intervals. Integrals are linear: the integral of a sum is the sum of the integrals, and constants factor out. The fundamental theorem of calculus evaluates a definite integral from an antiderivative.

Formula: Integral from a to b of f(x) dx = - Integral from b to a of f(x) dx. Integral from a to b of f(x) dx = Integral from a to c of f(x) dx + Integral from c to b of f(x) dx. Fundamental theorem: Integral from a to b of f(x) dx = F(b) - F(a), where F' = f.

Worked example: Integral from 0 to 2 of (x + 1) dx = [x^2/2 + x] from 0 to 2 = (2 + 2) - 0 = 4. Splitting at 1 gives Integral from 0 to 1 plus Integral from 1 to 2, which is 1.5 + 2.5 = 4, as expected.

instruction: What is Partial derivatives and chain rule? Explain it briefly. [GATE DA - Calculus & Optimization]
response:
A partial derivative measures how a multivariable function changes when one variable changes while the others are held fixed. The gradient collects all the partial derivatives into a vector. The multivariable chain rule adds the contributions through each intermediate variable: if z = f(x, y) and x and y depend on t, then dz/dt is the sum of the partial derivative with respect to each variable times that variable's rate of change.

Formula: Partial derivative: df/dx = limit as h -> 0 of [f(x + h, y) - f(x, y)] / h. Chain rule: dz/dt = (df/dx)(dx/dt) + (df/dy)(dy/dt). Gradient: grad f = (df/dx, df/dy).

Worked example: For f(x, y) = x^2 * y, the partial derivatives are df/dx = 2xy and df/dy = x^2, so at (2, 3) they are 12 and 4. With x = t and y = t^2, f = t^4, and the chain rule gives df/dt = 2xy * 1 + x^2 * 2t = 2t^3 + 2t^3 = 4t^3, matching the direct derivative of t^4.

instruction: What is Lagrange multipliers? Explain it briefly. [GATE DA - Calculus & Optimization]
response:
Lagrange multipliers find the maximum or minimum of a function subject to an equality constraint. At a constrained extremum, the gradient of the objective function is parallel to the gradient of the constraint function, so their difference is zero for some multiplier lambda. Solving the resulting system together with the constraint gives the candidate points, which are then compared by evaluating the objective.

Formula: Lagrangian: L(x, y, lambda) = f(x, y) - lambda * (g(x, y) - c). Conditions: grad f = lambda * grad g, and g(x, y) = c.

Worked example: Maximise f(x, y) = xy subject to x + y = 10. The Lagrangian is L = xy - lambda * (x + y - 10). Setting partial derivatives to zero gives y = lambda and x = lambda, so x = y, and with x + y = 10, x = y = 5 and the maximum is 25.

instruction: What is Gradient descent? Explain it briefly. [GATE DA - Calculus & Optimization]
response:
Gradient descent is an iterative optimisation method that moves a point in the direction of steepest decrease of a function, which is the negative gradient. The step size, or learning rate, controls how far each step goes: too large a step can overshoot or diverge, while too small a step converges slowly. It stops when the gradient is near zero or the change in the function value becomes negligible.

Formula: Update rule: x_{t+1} = x_t - eta * grad f(x_t), where eta > 0 is the learning rate. For a single variable: x_{t+1} = x_t - eta * f'(x_t).

Worked example: For f(x) = x^2, f'(x) = 2x. Starting at x_0 = 4 with learning rate eta = 0.1, the first update is x_1 = 4 - 0.1 * 8 = 3.2, and the function value falls from 16 to 10.24, moving toward the minimum at x = 0.

instruction: What is Entity-Relationship (ER) model? Explain it briefly. [GATE DA - Database Management & Warehousing]
response:
The ER model describes data as entities (real-world objects), attributes (their properties) and relationships between entities. Each entity set has a key attribute that uniquely identifies its entities, and relationships have a cardinality such as one-to-one, one-to-many or many-to-many. An ER diagram is converted into relational tables by creating one table per entity set and using foreign keys for relationships.

Formula: Entity set -> table; key attribute -> primary key; many-to-many relationship -> separate table with the keys of both entity sets as a composite primary key; one-to-many relationship -> foreign key on the 'many' side.

Worked example: In a university database, Student(roll_no, name) and Course(course_id, title) are entity sets, and 'Enrolls' is a many-to-many relationship between them. It becomes a table Enrolls(roll_no, course_id, grade) whose primary key is (roll_no, course_id), with roll_no and course_id as foreign keys.

instruction: What is Relational model and keys? Explain it briefly. [GATE DA - Database Management & Warehousing]
response:
In the relational model, data is stored in tables (relations) of rows (tuples) and columns (attributes), and each cell holds a single atomic value. A superkey is a set of attributes that uniquely identifies each row; a candidate key is a minimal superkey, and one candidate key is chosen as the primary key. A foreign key is an attribute in one table that refers to the primary key of another table, enforcing referential integrity.

Formula: Primary key: unique and NOT NULL for every row. Foreign key: every value must either match a primary key value in the referenced table or be NULL. Candidate key: minimal superkey (no attribute can be removed without losing uniqueness).

Worked example: Student(roll_no, name, email, dept_id) has primary key roll_no, unique key email, and dept_id is a foreign key referring to Department(dept_id). A row with dept_id = 99 is rejected if no department with dept_id 99 exists.

instruction: What is Relational algebra? Explain it briefly. [GATE DA - Database Management & Warehousing]
response:
Relational algebra is a procedural query language whose operators take relations as input and produce a relation as output. The basic operators are selection (sigma, filters rows), projection (pi, keeps chosen columns), union, set difference, Cartesian product and rename. The join combines two relations on a matching condition and is the most used operator in practice.

Formula: Selection: sigma_condition(R) keeps rows satisfying the condition. Projection: pi_attributes(R) keeps only listed columns, removing duplicates. Natural join: R natural-join S matches rows on common attributes. Theta join: R join_condition S.

Worked example: For Student(roll_no, name, age), the query 'names of students older than 20' is pi_name(sigma_age > 20(Student)). On rows (1, Ana, 21), (2, Ben, 19), (3, Cara, 22), selection keeps Ana and Cara, and projection gives {Ana, Cara}.

instruction: What is SQL basics and joins? Explain it briefly. [GATE DA - Database Management & Warehousing]
What is Functional dependencies? Explain it briefly. [GATE DA - Database Management & Warehousing]
response:
A functional dependency X -> Y means that any two rows agreeing on the attributes X must also agree on Y, so X determines Y. Armstrong's axioms (reflexivity, augmentation, transitivity) let us derive all implied dependencies, and the closure X+ is the set of all attributes functionally determined by X. A dependency is trivial if Y is a subset of X. Closures are used to find candidate keys and to test normal forms.

Formula: Armstrong's axioms: Reflexivity: if Y is a subset of X then X -> Y. Augmentation: if X -> Y then XZ -> YZ. Transitivity: if X -> Y and Y -> Z then X -> Z. Closure: X+ is computed by repeatedly adding Y for every X -> Y until no change.

Worked example: For R(A, B, C) with FDs A -> B and B -> C: A+ starts as {A}, A -> B adds B, then B -> C adds C, so A+ = {A, B, C}. Hence A is a candidate key, and by transitivity A -> C also holds.

instruction: What is First and second normal forms (1NF, 2NF)? Explain it briefly. [GATE DA - Database Management & Warehousing]
response:
A relation is in first normal form (1NF) if every attribute holds only atomic (indivisible) values, with no repeating groups or multi-valued attributes. A relation is in second normal form (2NF) if it is in 1NF and every non-prime attribute is fully functionally dependent on each candidate key, meaning no partial dependency on only part of a composite key exists. Normalization removes redundancy and the update, insertion and deletion anomalies it causes.

Formula: 1NF: all attribute values are atomic. 2NF: in 1NF and no partial dependency, i.e. no non-prime attribute A such that part of a candidate key K' -> A where K' is a proper subset of a candidate key K.

Worked example: Order(order_id, item, qty, customer_name) with composite key (order_id, item) violates 2NF because customer_name depends only on order_id, a part of the key. Split it into Order(order_id, customer_name) and OrderItem(order_id, item, qty), and both tables are in 2NF.

instruction: What is Third normal form (3NF) and Boyce-Codd normal form (BCNF)? Explain it briefly. [GATE DA - Database Management & Warehousing]
response:
A relation is in third normal form (3NF) if it is in 2NF and no non-prime attribute is transitively dependent on any candidate key. BCNF is stricter: for every non-trivial functional dependency X -> Y, X must be a superkey, with no exception for prime attributes. Every BCNF relation is in 3NF, but a 3NF relation can fail BCNF when a non-superkey determines a prime attribute. Decomposing into BCNF can lose a functional dependency, unlike 3NF decomposition.

Formula: 3NF rule: for every non-trivial FD X -> Y, X is a superkey OR every attribute of Y not in X is prime. BCNF rule: for every non-trivial FD X -> Y, X is a superkey (no prime-attribute exception). Classical 3NF wording: in 2NF and no transitive dependency of a non-prime attribute on any candidate key.

Worked example: Student(roll_no, dept, dept_head) with roll_no -> dept and dept -> dept_head has the transitive dependency roll_no -> dept -> dept_head, so it violates 3NF; split into Student(roll_no, dept) and Dept(dept, dept_head). Separately, Enroll(student, course, instructor) with FDs {student, course} -> instructor and instructor -> course has candidate keys {student, course} and {student, instructor}: instructor -> course violates BCNF because instructor is not a superkey, but it passes 3NF because course is prime, so this relation is in 3NF but not in BCNF.

instruction: What is Transactions, ACID and concurrency control? Explain it briefly. [GATE DA - Database Management & Warehousing]
response:
A transaction is a unit of work that must satisfy ACID: Atomicity (all operations or none), Consistency (the database moves from one valid state to another), Isolation (concurrent transactions behave as if run one after another) and Durability (committed changes survive crashes). Concurrency control, usually two-phase locking, prevents lost updates, dirty reads and other anomalies, and a schedule is serializable if its result equals some serial execution of the same transactions.

Formula: ACID: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability. Two-phase locking: a transaction acquires all locks before releasing any (growing phase, then shrinking phase). Serializable schedule: equivalent to some serial schedule; conflict-serializable if its precedence graph is acyclic.

Worked example: Account balance is 1000. T1 withdraws 100 (reads 1000, writes 900) and T2 deposits 200 (reads 1000, writes 1200) concurrently without locking. Whichever writes last wins, so the final balance is 900 or 1200 instead of the correct 1100: one update is lost. Two-phase locking prevents this by serializing the two transactions.

instruction: What is Indexing and B+ trees? Explain it briefly. [GATE DA - Database Management & Warehousing]
response:
An index is an auxiliary structure that lets the database find rows by a key without scanning the whole table. A B+ tree is the standard index structure: a balanced multi-way tree in which internal nodes hold only separator keys for routing, all data pointers live in the leaf nodes, and leaves are linked in sorted order. Its high fanout keeps the tree shallow (typically 3-4 levels), so search, insert and delete cost O(log n) disk accesses, and range scans walk the linked leaves in order.

Formula: Search/insert/delete cost: O(log_F N), where F is the fanout (children per node) and N is the number of records. Height is about log_F(N); range query with k results costs O(log_F N + k).

Worked example: With fanout F = 100 and 1,000,000 records, the B+ tree height is log_100(1,000,000) = 3, so a lookup touches only about 3 disk pages instead of scanning 1,000,000 rows. A range query such as marks BETWEEN 80 AND 90 finds the first leaf and then follows leaf links to collect all matching rows in order.

instruction: What is Data warehousing, star schema and OLAP? Explain it briefly. [GATE DA - Database Management & Warehousing]
response:
A data warehouse is a subject-oriented, integrated, time-variant and non-volatile store built for analysis rather than day-to-day transactions. A star schema models it with one central fact table holding numeric measures and foreign keys, surrounded by dimension tables (such as time, product and store) that describe the context. OLAP operations analyse this cube: roll-up aggregates to coarser levels, drill-down goes to finer detail, slice and dice select subsets, and pivot rotates the view.

Formula: Star schema: fact table (foreign keys to dimensions + numeric measures) at the centre, dimension tables around it. OLAP: roll-up (aggregate up a hierarchy, e.g. month -> quarter), drill-down (quarter -> month), slice (fix one dimension value), dice (select a sub-cube).

Worked example: A Sales fact table has measures amount and quantity, with dimensions Time, Product and Store. Monthly sales of 100 in January, 150 in February and 200 in March roll up to Q1 sales of 100 + 150 + 200 = 450. Drilling down from Q1 back to months recovers the three monthly figures.

instruction: What is Linear regression? Explain it briefly. [GATE DA - Machine Learning]
response:
Linear regression fits a straight line (or hyperplane) to numeric data by modelling the target as a weighted sum of the features plus an intercept. It is trained by minimising the mean squared error between predictions and true values, which has a closed-form least-squares solution. The fitted coefficients show how much the prediction changes when one feature increases by one unit, holding the others fixed.

Formula: Model: y_hat = w0 + w1*x1 + ... + wn*xn. Cost (MSE): J(w) = (1/n) * sum_i (y_i - y_hat_i)^2. Closed-form solution: w = (X^T X)^-1 X^T y.

Worked example: Points (1, 2), (2, 4), (3, 6) lie exactly on y = 2x, so the fitted line has slope w1 = 2 and intercept w0 = 0, with MSE = 0. Predicting at x = 4 gives y_hat = 2 * 4 = 8.

instruction: What is Logistic regression? Explain it briefly. [GATE DA - Machine Learning]
response:
Logistic regression is a classification algorithm, not a regressor: it passes a linear score through the sigmoid function to output the probability that an example belongs to the positive class. It is trained by minimising log loss (binary cross-entropy), which heavily penalises confident wrong predictions. The model is linear in the log-odds, and the usual decision rule is to predict class 1 when the probability exceeds 0.5.

Formula: Sigmoid: sigma(z) = 1 / (1 + e^-z), where z = w.x + b. Model: P(y = 1 | x) = sigma(w.x + b). Log-odds: ln(p / (1 - p)) = w.x + b. Log loss: L = -(1/n) * sum_i [y_i ln p_i + (1 - y_i) ln(1 - p_i)].

Worked example: With w.x + b = 2, sigma(2) = 1 / (1 + e^-2) = 1 / 1.1353 = 0.881, so the model predicts class 1 with probability 0.881. With z = 0, sigma(0) = 0.5, exactly on the decision boundary.

instruction: What is Bias-variance tradeoff, overfitting and regularization? Explain it briefly. [GATE DA - Machine Learning]
response:
Overfitting is when a model memorises training noise and performs much worse on unseen data, while underfitting is when a model is too simple to capture the pattern at all. The bias-variance tradeoff explains this: expected test error splits into squared bias (error from wrong assumptions), variance (error from sensitivity to the training sample) and irreducible noise. Simpler models have high bias and low variance; complex models have low bias and high variance. Regularization controls overfitting by penalising large weights: L2 (ridge) shrinks all weights, while L1 (lasso) can drive some to exactly zero.

Formula: Expected test error: E[(y - y_hat)^2] = Bias^2 + Variance + sigma^2 (irreducible noise), where Bias = E[y_hat] - f(x) and Variance = E[(y_hat - E[y_hat])^2]. Ridge (L2): cost + lambda * sum_j w_j^2. Lasso (L1): cost + lambda * sum_j |w_j|.

Worked example: A model with Bias^2 = 0.04, Variance = 0.09 and irreducible noise sigma^2 = 0.01 has expected test error 0.04 + 0.09 + 0.01 = 0.14. Fitting a degree-15 polynomial to 20 noisy points drives training error near zero but inflates variance, so test error rises; adding an L2 penalty lambda * sum w_j^2 shrinks the wild coefficients and lowers test error.

instruction: What is Cross-validation? Explain it briefly. [GATE DA - Machine Learning]
response:
Cross-validation estimates how well a model generalises by repeatedly training on one part of the data and testing on a held-out part. In k-fold cross-validation the data is split into k equal folds; each fold serves once as the test set while the other k-1 folds train the model, and the k test scores are averaged. Leave-one-out cross-validation is the extreme case with k equal to the number of samples. It gives a more reliable estimate than a single train-test split and is the standard way to choose hyperparameters.

Formula: k-fold CV error: CV = (1/k) * sum_j Error_j, where Error_j is the test error on fold j. Each fold is the test set exactly once; training uses the other k - 1 folds. Leave-one-out: k = n.

Worked example: With 100 samples and 5-fold cross-validation, each round trains on 80 samples and tests on 20. If the five test accuracies are 0.82, 0.85, 0.80, 0.84 and 0.83, the cross-validated accuracy is (0.82 + 0.85 + 0.80 + 0.84 + 0.83) / 5 = 4.14 / 5 = 0.828.

instruction: What is Decision trees? Explain it briefly. [GATE DA - Machine Learning]
response:
A decision tree predicts by asking a sequence of yes/no questions about the features, splitting the data at each node until the leaves are nearly pure in one class (or one value, for regression). At each node it picks the split that most reduces impurity, measured by Gini impurity or entropy, and the gain from a split is the impurity drop. Trees are easy to interpret and need no feature scaling, but a deep tree overfits, so pruning or a depth limit is used.

Formula: Gini impurity: Gini = 1 - sum_k p_k^2. Entropy: H = -sum_k p_k log2(p_k), where p_k is the fraction of class k in the node. Information gain: IG = I(parent) - sum_v (|S_v| / |S|) * I(S_v).

Worked example: On the classic Play Tennis data, 14 examples have 9 Yes and 5 No, so entropy H = -(9/14) log2(9/14) - (5/14) log2(5/14) = 0.940 bits. Splitting on Outlook separates the data into purer groups and lowers the weighted entropy, giving a positive information gain, so Outlook is chosen as the root split.

instruction: What is k-nearest neighbours (k-NN)? Explain it briefly. [GATE DA - Machine Learning]
response:
k-NN is a lazy, non-parametric classifier: it stores the whole training set and only works at prediction time. For a new point it finds the k training points closest to it (usually by Euclidean distance) and predicts the majority class among them, or the average target for regression. It makes no assumption about the shape of the decision boundary, but it needs feature scaling, slows down on large datasets, and suffers in very high dimensions.

Formula: Euclidean distance: d(x, q) = sqrt(sum_j (x_j - q_j)^2). Prediction: majority vote of the k nearest neighbours' labels (classification) or their mean (regression).

Worked example: Training points: A(1, 1) class 0, B(2, 2) class 0, C(5, 5) class 1. Query point (2, 3): distances are d(A) = sqrt(5) = 2.24, d(B) = 1, d(C) = sqrt(13) = 3.61. With k = 3 the neighbours vote 0, 0, 1, so the prediction is class 0.

instruction: What is Support vector machine (SVM)? Explain it briefly. [GATE DA - Machine Learning]
response:
An SVM is a classifier that finds the hyperplane separating two classes with the largest possible margin, the gap between the hyperplane and the nearest training points, called support vectors. Maximising the margin improves generalisation. For data that is not linearly separable, the kernel trick maps points into a higher-dimensional space (for example with an RBF kernel) where a linear separator exists, and a soft margin with slack variables allows a few misclassifications in exchange for a wider margin.

Formula: Hyperplane: w.x + b = 0. Margin width: 2 / ||w||. Hard-margin SVM: minimise (1/2)||w||^2 subject to y_i (w.x_i + b) >= 1 for all i. RBF kernel: K(x, z) = exp(-gamma ||x - z||^2).

Worked example: If a trained SVM has weight vector w = (3, 4), then ||w|| = 5 and the margin width is 2 / 5 = 0.4. The support vectors are the training points lying exactly on w.x + b = 1 or w.x + b = -1; only these points determine the boundary, and removing any other point leaves it unchanged.

instruction: What is k-means clustering? Explain it briefly. [GATE DA - Machine Learning]
response:
k-means is an unsupervised algorithm that partitions data into k clusters by minimising the within-cluster sum of squared distances to the cluster centroids. It alternates two steps: assign each point to its nearest centroid, then recompute each centroid as the mean of its assigned points, repeating until the assignments stop changing. The result depends on the initial centroids and on the choice of k, often picked with the elbow method, and features should be scaled first.

Formula: Objective (WCSS): J = sum_{j=1..k} sum_{x in C_j} ||x - mu_j||^2, where mu_j is the centroid of cluster C_j. Centroid update: mu_j = (1 / |C_j|) * sum_{x in C_j} x.

Worked example: Points (1, 1), (2, 1), (8, 8), (9, 8) with k = 2 and initial centroids (1, 1) and (8, 8): cluster 1 = {(1, 1), (2, 1)} with new centroid (1.5, 1), cluster 2 = {(8, 8), (9, 8)} with new centroid (8.5, 8). WCSS = 0.25 + 0.25 + 0.25 + 0.25 = 1.0, and the next assignment step changes nothing, so it has converged.

instruction: What is Gradient descent? Explain it briefly. [GATE DA - Machine Learning]
response:
Gradient descent is the workhorse optimiser of machine learning: it minimises a cost function by repeatedly stepping in the direction of steepest decrease, which is the negative gradient. The learning rate controls the step size: too small and training crawls, too large and it overshoots or diverges. Batch gradient descent uses the whole dataset per step, stochastic gradient descent uses one example, and mini-batch gradient descent uses a small batch, which is the usual compromise.

Formula: Update rule: w := w - alpha * (dJ/dw), where alpha is the learning rate and dJ/dw is the gradient of the cost J at w. For linear regression, dJ/dw_j = (1/n) * sum_i (y_hat_i - y_i) * x_ij (up to a constant factor of 2, depending on the MSE convention).

Worked example: Minimise f(w) = (w - 3)^2, whose gradient is 2(w - 3). Starting at w0 = 0 with learning rate alpha = 0.1: w1 = 0 - 0.1 * 2 * (0 - 3) = 0.6, then w2 = 0.6 - 0.1 * 2 * (0.6 - 3) = 1.08. The iterates move toward the minimum at w = 3.

instruction: What is Ensemble methods: bagging and boosting? Explain it briefly. [GATE DA - Machine Learning]
response:
Ensemble methods combine many weak learners into one stronger model. Bagging (bootstrap aggregating) trains each learner on a bootstrap sample of the data and averages or majority-votes their predictions, which reduces variance; a random forest is bagging plus random feature subsets at each split. Boosting trains learners sequentially, each new one focusing on the examples the previous ones got wrong, which reduces bias; AdaBoost reweights misclassified examples and gradient boosting fits each new tree to the residual errors of the ensemble so far.

Formula: Bagging prediction: average (regression) or majority vote (classification) over B bootstrap-trained models. AdaBoost: final prediction H(x) = sign(sum_t alpha_t * h_t(x)), with learner weight alpha_t = (1/2) ln((1 - err_t) / err_t). Gradient boosting: F_m(x) = F_{m-1}(x) + nu * h_m(x), where h_m fits the negative gradient (residuals) and nu is the learning rate.

Worked example: A random forest of 100 trees classifies a loan application: 62 trees vote 'approve' and 38 vote 'reject', so the ensemble predicts 'approve' by majority vote. In AdaBoost, a weak learner with error err = 0.2 gets weight alpha = (1/2) ln(0.8 / 0.2) = (1/2) ln(4) = 0.693, so it counts more than a learner with error 0.4.

instruction: What is Vectors and vector operations? Explain it briefly. [GATE DA - Linear Algebra]
response:
A vector is an ordered list of numbers that represents a point or a direction in space. Vectors can be added component-wise and scaled by a scalar, and the dot product measures how much two vectors point in the same direction. The length (norm) of a vector generalises Pythagoras' theorem to n dimensions, and two non-zero vectors are orthogonal when their dot product is zero.

Formula: u . v = u1*v1 + u2*v2 + ... + un*vn; ||u|| = sqrt(u . u); cos(theta) = (u . v) / (||u|| * ||v||)

Worked example: For u = (3, 4) and v = (1, 2): u . v = 3*1 + 4*2 = 3 + 8 = 11. ||u|| = sqrt(9 + 16) = 5, ||v|| = sqrt(1 + 4) = sqrt(5) = 2.236. So cos(theta) = 11 / (5 * 2.236) = 11 / 11.18 = 0.984, so the angle between them is about 10.3 degrees.

instruction: What is Matrix operations? Explain it briefly. [GATE DA - Linear Algebra]
response:
A matrix is a rectangular array of numbers, and matrix multiplication composes linear transformations: the (i, j) entry of AB is the dot product of row i of A with column j of B. Multiplication is associative and distributive but generally not commutative. The transpose flips rows and columns, and a square matrix A is invertible when there is a matrix A^-1 with A * A^-1 = I, which happens exactly when det(A) is non-zero.

Formula: (AB)[i][j] = sum over k of A[i][k] * B[k][j]; (AB)^T = B^T * A^T; A * A^-1 = A^-1 * A = I; for 2x2 [[a, b], [c, d]], inverse = (1 / (ad - bc)) * [[d, -b], [-c, a]]

Worked example: A = [[1, 2], [3, 4]] and B = [[5, 6], [7, 8]]. AB = [[1*5 + 2*7, 1*6 + 2*8], [3*5 + 4*7, 3*6 + 4*8]] = [[19, 22], [43, 50]]. det(A) = 1*4 - 2*3 = -2, so A^-1 = (1 / -2) * [[4, -2], [-3, 1]] = [[-2, 1], [1.5, -0.5]].

instruction: What is Linear independence and span? Explain it briefly. [GATE DA - Linear Algebra]
What is Rank, null space and column space? Explain it briefly. [GATE DA - Linear Algebra]
response:
The rank of a matrix is the number of linearly independent rows or columns, equivalently the dimension of its column space. The null space is the set of all vectors x with Ax = 0, and its dimension is the nullity. The rank-nullity theorem links them: for an m x n matrix, rank + nullity = n. The column space is the span of the columns, and Ax = b has a solution exactly when b lies in the column space.

Formula: rank(A) + nullity(A) = n (number of columns); null space = {x : Ax = 0}; column space = span of the columns of A

Worked example: A = [[1, 2], [2, 4]]. Row 2 is 2 times row 1, so rank(A) = 1. By rank-nullity, nullity = 2 - 1 = 1. Ax = 0 gives x + 2y = 0, so x = -2y and the null space is all multiples of (-2, 1). The column space is the span of (1, 2).

instruction: What is Determinant? Explain it briefly. [GATE DA - Linear Algebra]
response:
The determinant is a single number assigned to a square matrix that measures how the matrix scales volumes: it is zero exactly when the matrix is singular (not invertible), and non-zero exactly when it is invertible. Swapping two rows flips the sign of the determinant, multiplying a row by a scalar multiplies the determinant by that scalar, and the determinant of a product is the product of the determinants. For a triangular matrix the determinant is the product of the diagonal entries.

Formula: det([[a, b], [c, d]]) = ad - bc; det(AB) = det(A) * det(B); det(A^T) = det(A); det of a triangular matrix = product of diagonal entries

Worked example: For A = [[2, 3], [1, 4]], det(A) = 2*4 - 3*1 = 8 - 3 = 5. Since 5 is non-zero, A is invertible, with A^-1 = (1/5) * [[4, -3], [-1, 2]] = [[0.8, -0.6], [-0.2, 0.4]].

instruction: What is Eigenvalues and eigenvectors? Explain it briefly. [GATE DA - Linear Algebra]
response:
An eigenvector of a square matrix A is a non-zero vector v whose direction is unchanged by A; A only stretches it by a scalar factor lambda, the eigenvalue. Eigenvalues are found by solving the characteristic equation det(A - lambda*I) = 0. The trace of A equals the sum of its eigenvalues and the determinant equals their product, and eigenvectors for distinct eigenvalues are linearly independent.

Formula: Av = lambda*v; det(A - lambda*I) = 0 (characteristic equation); trace(A) = sum of eigenvalues; det(A) = product of eigenvalues

Worked example: A = [[2, 1], [1, 2]]. det(A - lambda*I) = (2 - lambda)^2 - 1 = lambda^2 - 4*lambda + 3 = (lambda - 1)(lambda - 3), so eigenvalues are 1 and 3. For lambda = 3, (A - 3I)v = 0 gives -x + y = 0, so v = (1, 1) is an eigenvector. Check: A*(1, 1) = (3, 3) = 3*(1, 1). Trace 4 = 1 + 3 and det 3 = 1 * 3, as expected.

instruction: What is Diagonalization? Explain it briefly. [GATE DA - Linear Algebra]
response:
A square n x n matrix A is diagonalizable when it can be written as A = P D P^-1, where D is diagonal and P is invertible. This is possible exactly when A has n linearly independent eigenvectors; the columns of P are those eigenvectors and the diagonal entries of D are the matching eigenvalues. Diagonalization makes matrix powers easy, since A^k = P D^k P^-1, and D^k just raises each diagonal entry to the power k. A matrix with n distinct eigenvalues is always diagonalizable, as are all real symmetric matrices.

Formula: A = P D P^-1, where columns of P are eigenvectors and D = diag(lambda1, ..., lambdan); A^k = P D^k P^-1

Worked example: A = [[2, 1], [1, 2]] has eigenvalues 3 and 1 with eigenvectors (1, 1) and (1, -1). So P = [[1, 1], [1, -1]] and D = [[3, 0], [0, 1]]. Then A^2 = P D^2 P^-1 with D^2 = [[9, 0], [0, 1]], giving A^2 = [[5, 4], [4, 5]], which matches direct multiplication: [[2*2 + 1*1, 2*1 + 1*2], [1*2 + 2*1, 1*1 + 2*2]] = [[5, 4], [4, 5]].

instruction: What is Singular Value Decomposition (SVD)? Explain it briefly. [GATE DA - Linear Algebra]
response:
Every real matrix A, square or rectangular, can be factored as A = U Sigma V^T, where U and V are orthogonal matrices and Sigma is a diagonal matrix of non-negative singular values in decreasing order. The singular values are the square roots of the eigenvalues of A^T A, the columns of V are eigenvectors of A^T A, and the columns of U are eigenvectors of A A^T. The number of non-zero singular values equals the rank of A, and keeping only the largest k singular values gives the best rank-k approximation of A, which is the basis of PCA and data compression.

Formula: A = U Sigma V^T; sigma_i = sqrt(lambda_i(A^T A)), where lambda_i are eigenvalues of A^T A; rank(A) = number of non-zero singular values

Worked example: A = [[3, 2], [2, 3]]. A^T A = [[13, 12], [12, 13]]. Its characteristic equation is lambda^2 - 26*lambda + 25 = (lambda - 25)(lambda - 1) = 0, so eigenvalues are 25 and 1. The singular values are sqrt(25) = 5 and sqrt(1) = 1. Both are non-zero, so rank(A) = 2, and the Frobenius norm is sqrt(25 + 1) = sqrt(26).

instruction: What is Orthogonality and Gram-Schmidt process? Explain it briefly. [GATE DA - Linear Algebra]
response:
Two vectors are orthogonal when their dot product is zero, and an orthonormal set is an orthogonal set in which every vector has unit length. The Gram-Schmidt process turns any linearly independent set into an orthogonal (or, after normalising, orthonormal) basis for the same span, by keeping the first vector and subtracting from each later vector its projections onto all previously built orthogonal vectors. Orthonormal bases make projections and least-squares problems simple, because coordinates are just dot products.

Formula: proj_u(v) = ((v . u) / (u . u)) * u; u1 = v1; u_i = v_i - sum over j < i of proj_{u_j}(v_i); e_i = u_i / ||u_i||

Worked example: Orthogonalise v1 = (1, 1) and v2 = (1, 0). u1 = v1 = (1, 1). proj_{u1}(v2) = ((1*1 + 0*1) / (1 + 1)) * (1, 1) = (1/2) * (1, 1) = (0.5, 0.5). So u2 = (1, 0) - (0.5, 0.5) = (0.5, -0.5). Check: u1 . u2 = 1*0.5 + 1*(-0.5) = 0, so they are orthogonal. Normalising gives e1 = (1/sqrt(2), 1/sqrt(2)) and e2 = (1/sqrt(2), -1/sqrt(2)).

instruction: What is Quadratic forms? Explain it briefly. [GATE DA - Linear Algebra]
response:
A quadratic form is a homogeneous degree-two polynomial that can always be written as Q(x) = x^T A x, where A is a symmetric matrix; the off-diagonal entries of A are half the coefficients of the cross terms. A symmetric matrix (and its form) is positive definite when Q(x) > 0 for every non-zero x, which happens exactly when all its eigenvalues are positive, and equivalently when all leading principal minors are positive. Positive definite forms have a unique minimum at the origin, which is why they appear in optimisation and in covariance matrices.

Formula: Q(x) = x^T A x; for 2 variables, Q(x, y) = a*x^2 + 2*b*x*y + c*y^2 with A = [[a, b], [b, c]]; positive definite iff all eigenvalues > 0 iff all leading principal minors > 0

Worked example: Q(x, y) = 3x^2 + 4xy + 5y^2 has A = [[3, 2], [2, 5]], since 2*b = 4 gives b = 2. At (1, 1), Q = 3 + 4 + 5 = 12. Leading minors: 3 > 0 and det(A) = 3*5 - 2*2 = 11 > 0, so A is positive definite. Its eigenvalues are 4 + sqrt(5) = 6.236 and 4 - sqrt(5) = 1.764, both positive, confirming it.

instruction: What is Time and space complexity and Big-O notation? Explain it briefly. [GATE DA - Programming/DSA]
response:
Big-O notation describes how an algorithm's running time or memory use grows as the input size n grows, ignoring constant factors and lower-order terms. Common growth rates, from fastest to slowest, are O(1) constant, O(log n) logarithmic, O(n) linear, O(n log n), O(n^2) quadratic, and O(2^n) exponential. Time complexity counts the dominant operations and space complexity counts the extra memory used; the worst case is the usual measure quoted, and Big-O gives an upper bound on that growth.

Formula: T(n) = O(f(n)) means T(n) <= c * f(n) for all large n and some constant c; binary search: O(log n); linear search: O(n); sorting by comparison: Omega(n log n) lower bound

Worked example: Searching a sorted array of n = 1,000,000 elements by binary search takes about log2(1,000,000) = 19.93, about 20 comparisons, while linear search takes up to 1,000,000 comparisons in the worst case. Summing 1 to n with a single loop does n additions, so it is O(n) time and O(1) extra space.

instruction: What is Arrays? Explain it briefly. [GATE DA - Programming/DSA]
response:
An array stores a fixed-size sequence of elements of the same type in contiguous memory, so the element at index i is found by direct address arithmetic in O(1) time. Searching an unsorted array takes O(n) time, while binary search on a sorted array takes O(log n). Inserting or deleting in the middle costs O(n) because the elements after the position must be shifted, which is the main weakness of arrays compared with linked lists.

Formula: address of a[i] = base address + i * element size; binary search: mid = (low + high) / 2, compare a[mid] with target, halve the interval each step; time O(log n)

Worked example: Binary search for 23 in [2, 5, 8, 12, 16, 23, 38, 56, 72, 91]: mid index (0 + 9) / 2 = 4 gives 16 < 23, so search right; mid (5 + 9) / 2 = 7 gives 56 > 23, so search left; mid (5 + 6) / 2 = 5 gives 23, found in 3 comparisons. Accessing index 2 of [10, 20, 30, 40] returns 30 in O(1).

instruction: What is Linked lists? Explain it briefly. [GATE DA - Programming/DSA]
What is Stacks and queues? Explain it briefly. [GATE DA - Programming/DSA]
response:
A stack is a last-in, first-out (LIFO) structure with push to add to the top and pop to remove from the top, both O(1); it is used for function calls, undo, expression evaluation and checking balanced parentheses. A queue is a first-in, first-out (FIFO) structure with enqueue at the rear and dequeue from the front, both O(1) in a linked or circular-array implementation; it is used for breadth-first search, scheduling and buffering. A deque allows insertion and deletion at both ends.

Formula: Stack: push(x), pop() returns the most recently pushed item, peek() returns the top; Queue: enqueue(x) at rear, dequeue() returns the oldest item; all four operations O(1)

Worked example: Push 1, 2, 3 onto a stack, then pop three times: the pops return 3, then 2, then 1 (LIFO). Enqueue 1, 2, 3 into a queue, then dequeue three times: the dequeues return 1, then 2, then 3 (FIFO). Checking '(()())' with a stack: each '(' is pushed and each ')' pops one, ending with an empty stack, so the parentheses are balanced.

instruction: What is Trees and binary search trees? Explain it briefly. [GATE DA - Programming/DSA]
response:
A tree is a hierarchical structure of nodes connected by edges, with one root and no cycles; a binary tree gives each node at most two children. In a binary search tree (BST), every node's left subtree holds smaller keys and its right subtree holds larger keys, so search, insert and delete take O(log n) on average in a balanced tree but degrade to O(n) if the tree becomes skewed like a linked list. An inorder traversal of a BST visits keys in sorted order, and the height of a balanced tree with n nodes is about log2(n).

Formula: BST property: keys in left subtree < node key < keys in right subtree; search/insert/delete: O(log n) average, O(n) worst case; inorder traversal visits keys in ascending order; height of balanced tree = O(log n)

Worked example: Insert 50, 30, 70, 20, 40, 60, 80 into an empty BST. The inorder traversal is 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70, 80, in sorted order. Searching for 60: compare with 50 (go right), then 70 (go left), then find 60, taking 3 comparisons.

instruction: What is Heaps and priority queues? Explain it briefly. [GATE DA - Programming/DSA]
response:
A heap is a complete binary tree stored in an array that satisfies the heap property: in a min-heap every parent is smaller than or equal to its children, so the minimum is always at the root, while a max-heap keeps the maximum at the root. Insert and extract-min (or extract-max) both take O(log n) by bubbling an element up or sifting it down, and building a heap from n elements takes O(n). A heap implements a priority queue, and heapsort sorts in O(n log n) time with O(1) extra space.

Formula: 0-indexed array: parent(i) = (i - 1) / 2, left child(i) = 2i + 1, right child(i) = 2i + 2; insert: O(log n); extract-min/max: O(log n); build heap: O(n); heapsort: O(n log n)

Worked example: Min-heap array [10, 15, 20, 30, 40] is valid: 10 is the parent of 15 and 20, and 15 is the parent of 30 and 40. Insert 5: append it to get [10, 15, 20, 30, 40, 5], swap 5 with its parent 20, then swap 5 with 10, giving [5, 15, 10, 30, 40, 20] with 5 at the root.

instruction: What is Hashing and hash tables? Explain it briefly. [GATE DA - Programming/DSA]
response:
A hash table stores key-value pairs by passing each key through a hash function that maps it to a bucket index, giving average O(1) time for insert, search and delete. Different keys can collide in the same bucket; collisions are handled by chaining (a list per bucket) or open addressing (probing for another slot). Performance depends on the load factor, the number of items divided by the number of buckets: a high load factor means more collisions, so tables resize and rehash when it grows too large. In the worst case, with all keys colliding, operations degrade to O(n).

Formula: index = hash(key) mod m, where m is the table size; load factor alpha = n / m; average insert/search/delete: O(1); worst case: O(n)

Worked example: With table size m = 7 and h(k) = k mod 7, keys 10, 17 and 24 all hash to 3, since 10 mod 7 = 3, 17 mod 7 = 3 and 24 mod 7 = 3, so they collide and share bucket 3 as a chain [10, 17, 24]. With n = 3 items in m = 7 buckets, the load factor is 3 / 7 = 0.43.

instruction: What is Sorting algorithms? Explain it briefly. [GATE DA - Programming/DSA]
response:
Sorting arranges elements in order, and the classic comparison sorts differ in cost and stability. Bubble, selection and insertion sort all take O(n^2) time in the worst case, though insertion sort is O(n) on nearly sorted input. Mergesort always takes O(n log n) time but needs O(n) extra space, while quicksort averages O(n log n) with O(log n) stack space but degrades to O(n^2) on already sorted input with a bad pivot. A stable sort preserves the relative order of equal elements; mergesort is stable and standard quicksort is not.

Formula: Bubble/selection/insertion sort: O(n^2) worst case; mergesort: T(n) = 2*T(n/2) + O(n), O(n log n) time, O(n) space; quicksort: O(n log n) average, O(n^2) worst case

Worked example: Mergesort on [38, 27, 43, 3, 9, 82, 10] splits it down to single elements and merges sorted halves back up. One merge step combines the sorted halves [27, 38] and [3, 43] by comparing heads: 3 < 27, then 27 < 43, then 38 < 43, giving [3, 27, 38, 43]. The final sorted array is [3, 9, 10, 27, 38, 43, 82].

instruction: What is Graphs, BFS and DFS? Explain it briefly. [GATE DA - Programming/DSA]
response:
A graph is a set of vertices connected by edges, stored as an adjacency list or an adjacency matrix. Breadth-first search (BFS) explores level by level using a queue, visiting vertices in order of increasing distance from the start, so it finds shortest paths in an unweighted graph. Depth-first search (DFS) goes as deep as possible first, using a stack or recursion, and is used for cycle detection, topological sorting and connected components. Both visit every vertex and edge once, taking O(V + E) time with an adjacency list.

Formula: BFS and DFS: O(V + E) time with an adjacency list, O(V^2) with an adjacency matrix; BFS distance from start = number of edges on the shortest path (unweighted graph)

Worked example: Graph with edges 1-2, 1-3, 2-4, 3-4. BFS from 1: visit 1, then its neighbours 2 and 3, then 4, giving order 1, 2, 3, 4; vertex 4 is at distance 2. DFS from 1 (neighbours in order 2 then 3): go 1 -> 2 -> 4, backtrack, then 3, giving order 1, 2, 4, 3.

instruction: What is Dynamic programming? Explain it briefly. [GATE DA - Programming/DSA]
response:
Dynamic programming solves a problem by breaking it into overlapping subproblems, solving each subproblem once, and storing its result for reuse, either top-down with memoisation or bottom-up with a table. It applies when the problem has optimal substructure, meaning an optimal solution is built from optimal solutions of smaller subproblems, and overlapping subproblems, meaning the same subproblems recur. Classic examples are Fibonacci numbers, 0/1 knapsack, longest common subsequence and shortest paths in DAGs. Memoisation turns the naive exponential Fibonacci recursion into linear time.

Formula: Fibonacci: fib(0) = 0, fib(1) = 1, fib(n) = fib(n-1) + fib(n-2); with memoisation/tabulation: O(n) time, O(n) space (O(1) space with two variables); naive recursion: O(2^n) time

Worked example: Fibonacci with a table: fib(0) = 0, fib(1) = 1, fib(2) = 1 + 0 = 1, fib(3) = 1 + 1 = 2, fib(4) = 2 + 1 = 3, fib(5) = 3 + 2 = 5. Each value is computed once from the previous two, so fib(5) = 5 in 5 steps, instead of the naive recursion which recomputes fib(3) twice, fib(2) three times, and so on.

instruction: What is Counting: permutations and combinations? Explain it briefly. [GATE DA - Probability & Stats]
response:
Counting arguments give the size of a sample space, which is the denominator of most elementary probability calculations. A permutation counts ordered arrangements: choosing an ordered r-tuple from n distinct objects can be done in n!/(n-r)! ways. A combination counts unordered selections: choosing r objects from n, ignoring order, can be done in n!/(r!(n-r)!) ways. Every combination corresponds to r! permutations of the same r objects, which is why the combination count divides by r!.

Formula: P(n, r) = n! / (n - r)! (permutations, order matters). C(n, r) = n! / (r! (n - r)!) (combinations, order does not matter). C(n, r) = C(n, n - r).
