Formula: fs >= 2 * fm, where fs is sampling frequency and fm is the highest frequency in the signal. Nyquist rate = 2 * fm. Nyquist frequency = fs / 2. Sampling period Ts = 1 / fs.

The Nyquist-Shannon sampling theorem states that a band-limited signal can be perfectly reconstructed from its samples if the sampling rate is at least twice its highest frequency. Sampling slower than this causes aliasing, where high frequencies falsely appear as low frequencies. The minimum rate is called the Nyquist rate.

instruction: Give a worked example for Amplitude modulation: modulation index and bandwidth [GATE EC - Communication]
response:
Worked example: With Am = 2 V, Ac = 10 V and fm = 5 kHz, mu = 2 / 10 = 0.2 (20 percent modulation) and bandwidth BW = 2 * 5 = 10 kHz.

Formula: Modulation index mu = Am / Ac = (Amax - Amin) / (Amax + Amin), where Am is message amplitude, Ac is carrier amplitude, and Amax and Amin are the maximum and minimum envelope amplitudes. Bandwidth BW = 2 * fm, where fm is the highest message frequency. AM wave: s(t) = Ac * (1 + mu * cos(2 * pi * fm * t)) * cos(2 * pi * fc * t).

In amplitude modulation the message signal varies the amplitude of a high-frequency carrier. The modulation index measures how deeply the carrier is modulated, and it must not exceed 1 or the envelope distorts on demodulation. An AM signal occupies twice the message bandwidth, one sideband on each side of the carrier.

instruction: Give a worked example for Steady-state error of a unity-feedback system [GATE EC - Control Systems]
response:
Worked example: For G(s) = 10 / (s * (s + 2)), the system is type 1 because of the 1 / s term. Kp is infinite, so the steady-state error to a unit step input is 0.

Formula: For unity feedback, step-input steady-state error e_ss = 1 / (1 + Kp), where Kp = limit as s -> 0 of G(s). For a type 1 or higher system, Kp is infinite, so e_ss = 0 for a step input.

Steady-state error is the difference between the desired output and the actual output after transients have died out. A system with at least one integrator (type 1 or higher) tracks a step input with zero steady-state error in unity feedback. A type 0 system has a finite step error determined by its position error constant Kp.

instruction: Give a worked example for Linear algebra: rank, basis and solution of linear equations [GATE EC - Engineering Mathematics]
response:
Worked example: A = [[1, 2], [2, 4]] has its second row twice the first, so rank = 1 and det = 0. The system A x = [3, 6] is consistent (infinitely many solutions), but A x = [3, 5] is inconsistent.

Formula: rank(A) = number of independent rows = number of independent columns; A x = b consistent iff rank(A) = rank([A | b]); unique solution iff rank = n (unknowns); det(A - lambda I) = 0 gives eigenvalues.

The rank of a matrix is the number of linearly independent rows or columns. A system A x = b has a solution if and only if rank(A) = rank([A|b]); it is unique if that rank also equals the number of unknowns, and has infinitely many solutions if the rank is smaller. Vectors are linearly independent if only the trivial combination gives zero, and a basis is an independent set that spans the space. Eigenvalues and eigenvectors come from det(A - lambda I) = 0, as in the EE entry on eigenvalues.

instruction: Give a worked example for Vector analysis: gradient, divergence, curl and integral theorems [GATE EC - Engineering Mathematics]
response:
Worked example: For F = (x, 0, 0), div F = 1 and curl F = 0. The flux of F out of the unit cube is integral of div F over the volume = 1 x 1 = 1, matching the surface integral.

Formula: grad f = (df/dx, df/dy, df/dz); div F = dFx/dx + dFy/dy + dFz/dz; curl F = grad x F; Gauss: integral_V div F dV = integral_S F . dS; Stokes: integral_S curl F . dS = integral_C F . dr.

The gradient of a scalar points in the direction of fastest increase; the divergence of a vector field measures net outflow per unit volume; the curl measures local rotation. A field with zero curl is conservative and can be written as a gradient, and a field with zero divergence is solenoidal. Gauss, Stokes and Green theorems convert volume integrals of divergence and surface integrals of curl into surface and line integrals, and are used throughout electromagnetics.

instruction: Give a worked example for Complex analysis: analytic functions, Taylor and Laurent series, residue theorem [GATE EC - Engineering Mathematics]
response:
Worked example: f(z) = 1/(z^2 + 4) has a simple pole at z = 2i with residue 1/(4i). On a small circle around 2i only, the integral is 2 pi i x 1/(4i) = pi/2.

Formula: Cauchy-Riemann: du/dx = dv/dy, du/dy = -dv/dx; integral_C f(z) dz = 2 pi i x sum of residues; simple pole residue = lim_{z->z0} (z - z0) f(z); ratio test: series converges if lim |a_{n+1}/a_n| < 1.

A function is analytic where it is differentiable in the complex sense (Cauchy-Riemann equations hold); analytic functions have power-series (Taylor) expansions, and functions with isolated singularities have Laurent expansions with negative powers. The residue theorem says the integral around a closed contour is 2 pi i times the sum of residues inside, which evaluates many real integrals. Convergence tests (ratio, root, comparison) decide whether a series converges.

instruction: Give a worked example for Thevenin, Norton and reciprocity theorems [GATE EC - Networks]
response:
Worked example: A network with Vth = 6 V and Rth = 2 ohm feeding a 4 ohm load delivers V = 6 x 4/6 = 4 V. Its Norton form is a 3 A source in parallel with 2 ohm.

Formula: Vth = open-circuit voltage; Rth = Vth / I_sc; IN = Vth / Rth; reciprocity: response at port 2 to a source at port 1 equals response at port 1 to the same source at port 2.

Any linear network seen from two terminals is equivalent to a voltage source Vth in series with Rth, or a current source IN = Vth/Rth in parallel with Rth. Vth is the open-circuit voltage and Rth the resistance looking back with independent sources turned off. The reciprocity theorem says that in a linear network with only one source, swapping the source and the measurement point leaves the measured response unchanged. Superposition lets each independent source be considered alone, with the others turned off.

instruction: Give a worked example for Phasor analysis, complex power and maximum power transfer [GATE EC - Networks]
response:
Worked example: V_rms = 230 V, I_rms = 10 A at power factor 0.8 lagging: P = 230 x 10 x 0.8 = 1840 W, Q = 230 x 10 x 0.6 = 1380 VAR, and apparent power is 2300 VA.

Formula: Z_L = j omega L; Z_C = 1/(j omega C); S = V_rms I_rms* = P + j Q; |S| = V_rms I_rms; power factor = cos(phi) = P/|S|; maximum power when Z_L = Zth*.

In sinusoidal steady state, voltages and currents are phasors and impedances are complex: Z = R + jX, with X = omega L for an inductor and -1/(omega C) for a capacitor. Complex power S = V_rms I_rms* = P + jQ, where P is average power in watts, Q is reactive power in VAR, and |S| is apparent power in VA. Maximum average power is delivered when the load impedance is the complex conjugate of the source impedance.

instruction: Give a worked example for Transient analysis of RL, RC and RLC circuits with Laplace transform [GATE EC - Networks]
response:
Worked example: Series RLC with R = 20 ohm, L = 10 mH, C = 100 nF: omega_0 = 1/sqrt(1e-9) = 31623 rad/s, zeta = 10 x sqrt(100e-9/10e-3) = 10 x 0.00316 = 0.0316, so the transient is a lightly damped oscillation near 5033 Hz.

Formula: s-domain: R -> R; L -> sL; C -> 1/(sC); series RLC: s^2 + (R/L) s + 1/(LC) = 0; omega_0 = 1/sqrt(LC); zeta = (R/2) sqrt(C/L); zeta < 1 underdamped, = 1 critically damped, > 1 overdamped.

Network equations in the time domain become algebraic in the s-domain: a resistor stays R, an inductor becomes sL (plus an initial-flux voltage source), and a capacitor becomes 1/(sC) (plus an initial-charge source). Solving for the s-domain current or voltage and inverting gives the transient, whose character is set by the poles: real distinct poles give overdamped decay, a repeated pole gives critically damped decay, and complex poles give damped oscillation. The damping ratio and natural frequency of a series RLC circuit are zeta = (R/2) sqrt(C/L) and omega_0 = 1/sqrt(LC).

instruction: Give a worked example for Fourier series, Fourier transform, DTFT and DFT [GATE EC - Signals & Systems]
response:
Worked example: x = [1, 1, 0, 0], N = 4: X[0] = 2, X[1] = 1 + e^{-j pi/2} = 1 - j, X[2] = 1 + e^{-j pi} = 0, X[3] = 1 + j.

Formula: Fourier series: periodic -> discrete spectrum; FT: X(omega) = integral x(t) e^{-j omega t} dt; DTFT: X(e^{j w}) = sum_n x[n] e^{-j w n}; DFT: X[k] = sum_{n=0}^{N-1} x[n] e^{-j 2 pi k n / N}.

Fourier series handles periodic signals, the Fourier transform handles aperiodic ones, the DTFT handles discrete-time signals (periodic in frequency with period 2 pi), and the DFT is the sampled, finite-length version used in computation. The DFT of length N is X[k] = sum_{n=0}^{N-1} x[n] e^{-j 2 pi k n / N}, and the FFT computes it in O(N log N) instead of O(N^2). Sampling in one domain causes periodicity in the other, which is why aliasing appears when sampling is too slow.

instruction: Give a worked example for Z-transform, LTI systems, convolution, poles and zeros [GATE EC - Signals & Systems]
response:
Worked example: x = [1, 2] convolved with h = [1, 1] gives y = [1, 3, 2]. A system with H(z) = 1/(1 - 0.5 z^{-1}) has one pole at 0.5, inside the unit circle, so it is stable and causal.

Formula: y[n] = sum_k x[k] h[n-k]; H(z) = Y(z)/X(z); stable iff all poles satisfy |p| < 1; frequency response H(e^{j w}) = H(z) at z = e^{j w}; group delay tau_g = -d(angle H)/d w.

An LTI system is fully described by its impulse response h[n]: the output is the convolution sum of the input with h. In the z-domain the transfer function H(z) = Y(z)/X(z) is a ratio of polynomials; its poles decide stability (all inside the unit circle) and causality, and its zeros shape the frequency response. The frequency response is H(e^{j w}), obtained by evaluating H(z) on the unit circle. Group delay is minus the derivative of phase with respect to frequency, and phase delay is minus phase divided by frequency.

instruction: Give a worked example for Semiconductors: energy bands, drift, diffusion and continuity [GATE EC - Electronic Devices]
response:
Worked example: Silicon with n = 1e16 cm^-3 and electron mobility 1350 cm^2/Vs has resistivity rho = 1 / (1.6e-19 x 1e16 x 1350) = about 0.46 ohm-cm. At 300 K, D_n = mu_n x 0.02585 = about 34.9 cm^2/s.

Formula: Drift: J_n(drift) = q n mu_n E; diffusion: J_n(diff) = q D_n dn/dx; Einstein: D/mu = kT/q = about 25.85 mV at 300 K; n p = n_i^2; resistivity rho = 1 / [q (n mu_n + p mu_p)]; Poisson: d^2 V/dx^2 = -rho_charge / epsilon.

In a semiconductor, electrons in the conduction band and holes in the valence band carry current. Intrinsic carrier concentration n_i grows with temperature; doping adds donors (n-type, electrons majority) or acceptors (p-type, holes majority), with n p = n_i^2 in equilibrium. Drift current follows the electric field with mobility mu; diffusion current follows the concentration gradient with diffusivity D, linked by the Einstein relation D/mu = kT/q (about 25.85 mV at 300 K). Poisson equation links charge to potential, and the continuity equation is conservation of carriers including generation and recombination.

instruction: Give a worked example for P-N junction, Zener diode, LED, photodiode and solar cell [GATE EC - Electronic Devices]
response:
Worked example: With N_A = 1e17 cm^-3, N_D = 1e15 cm^-3 and n_i = 1e10 cm^-3, Vbi = 0.02585 x ln(1e32/1e20) = 0.02585 x 27.63 = about 0.71 V. A 5.1 V Zener in reverse breakdown holds about 5.1 V across a load despite supply changes.

Formula: Diode: I = I_s (e^{V/(eta Vt)} - 1), Vt = kT/q = about 26 mV at 300 K; Vbi = Vt ln(N_A N_D / n_i^2); depletion width W proportional to sqrt(Vbi - V); Zener: reverse breakdown at a fixed Vz.

A p-n junction has a built-in potential Vbi = Vt ln(N_A N_D / n_i^2) across its depletion region; forward bias shrinks the barrier and current grows exponentially, reverse bias widens it and only a small saturation current flows until breakdown. A Zener diode is designed to break down at a controlled reverse voltage and so holds a nearly constant voltage, used as a regulator. An LED emits light when carriers recombine, a photodiode generates current from absorbed light (reverse biased), and a solar cell is a large photodiode operated to deliver power to a load.

instruction: Give a worked example for BJT, MOSFET and MOS capacitor; small-signal amplifiers [GATE EC - Electronic Devices]
response:
Worked example: A BJT biased at Ic = 1 mA has gm = 1e-3 / 0.026 = about 38.5 mS, so with Rc = 2 k ohm the small-signal voltage gain is about -77. A MOSFET with mu C_ox (W/L) = 1 mA/V^2 and overdrive 1 V carries Id = 0.5 mA.

Formula: BJT: Ic = beta Ib; gm = Ic/Vt; MOSFET saturation: Id = (1/2) mu C_ox (W/L)(Vgs - Vth)^2; gm = 2 Id / (Vgs - Vth); common-emitter gain about -gm Rc (with load); common-source gain about -gm Rd.

A BJT is a current-controlled device: collector current Ic = beta Ib in active mode, with transconductance gm = Ic/Vt. A MOSFET is voltage-controlled: in saturation Id = (1/2) mu C_ox (W/L) (Vgs - Vth)^2, with gm = sqrt(2 mu C_ox (W/L) Id). A MOS capacitor goes from accumulation through depletion to inversion as gate voltage rises, and inversion is what forms the MOSFET channel. Small-signal analysis replaces each device by its gm and output resistance to find voltage gain, input and output resistance; gain falls at high frequency because of device capacitances (Miller effect) and at low frequency because of coupling capacitors.

instruction: Give a worked example for Diode circuits: clipping, clamping and rectifiers [GATE EC - Analog Circuits]
response:
Worked example: A full-wave rectifier with Vm = 10 V gives Vdc = 20/pi = 6.37 V before filtering. With a 100 uF capacitor, 50 Hz mains and 10 mA load, ripple is about 0.01 / (2 x 50 x 100e-6) = 1 V peak-to-peak.

Formula: Half-wave average: Vdc = Vm / pi; full-wave average: Vdc = 2 Vm / pi; ripple (capacitor filter, full-wave): Vr(pp) about I_load / (2 f C); bridge PIV = Vm; centre-tapped PIV = 2 Vm.

A clipper uses a diode (and a reference voltage) to cut off the part of a waveform above or below a level; a clamper uses a diode plus a capacitor to shift the whole waveform up or down by a DC level without changing its shape. A half-wave rectifier passes only one half-cycle (average output Vm/pi), a full-wave rectifier uses both (average 2 Vm/pi), and a capacitor filter smooths the ripple, with ripple falling as capacitance and load resistance rise. Peak inverse voltage ratings decide diode choice: a bridge rectifier needs PIV of Vm, a centre-tapped full-wave needs 2 Vm.

instruction: Give a worked example for Op-amp circuits: amplifiers, integrators, filters, Schmitt trigger and oscillators [GATE EC - Analog Circuits]
response:
Worked example: An integrator with R = 10 k ohm and C = 100 nF fed a constant 1 V gives a ramp of slope -1/(RC) = -1000 V/s, reaching -1 V in 1 ms. A Schmitt trigger with Vsat = 12 V, R1 = 1 k ohm and R2 = 9 k ohm has thresholds at +/- 1.2 V.

Formula: Inverting gain = -Rf/R1; non-inverting gain = 1 + Rf/R1; integrator: Vo = -(1/RC) integral Vi dt; differentiator: Vo = -RC dVi/dt; Schmitt thresholds = +/- [R1/(R1+R2)] Vsat; Sallen-Key fc = 1/(2 pi sqrt(R1 R2 C1 C2)); Barkhausen: loop gain = 1 at 0 deg (or 360 deg) phase.

An ideal op-amp has infinite gain, infinite input resistance and zero output resistance, so with negative feedback the two inputs sit at the same voltage (virtual short) and draw no current. That gives the inverting gain -Rf/R1, the non-inverting gain 1 + Rf/R1, summers, differentiators and integrators (output -1/(RC) times the integral of the input). A Schmitt trigger uses positive feedback to give two thresholds and hysteresis, cleaning up noisy signals; an oscillator needs loop gain of at least 1 with zero total phase shift (Barkhausen criterion). Active filters use op-amps with RC networks: a Sallen-Key second-order low-pass has fc = 1/(2 pi sqrt(R1 R2 C1 C2)) and Q = 0.707 gives a Butterworth (maximally flat) response.

instruction: Give a worked example for Number systems, combinational logic and Karnaugh maps [GATE EC - Digital Circuits]
response:
Worked example: F(A,B,C) = sum m(1,3,5,7) is 1 exactly when C = 1, so the minimised form is F = C, one wire and no gates. The 4-bit binary number 1101 is 13 in decimal.

Formula: Binary 1011 = 1x8 + 0x4 + 1x2 + 1 = 11 decimal; De Morgan: NOT(A B) = (NOT A) + (NOT B), NOT(A + B) = (NOT A)(NOT B); 2^n-to-1 multiplexer needs n select lines; K-map group size must be a power of 2.

Digital numbers are binary; integers convert by repeated division by 2 and fractions by repeated multiplication by 2, and floating-point numbers store a sign, exponent and mantissa (IEEE 754). Combinational outputs depend only on present inputs: Boolean algebra and Karnaugh maps minimise the sum-of-products form, grouping 1s in powers of two (pairs, quads, octets), including wrap-around and don't-care cells. Standard blocks are adders, comparators, code converters, multiplexers (a 2^n-to-1 mux needs n select lines) and decoders. A static CMOS gate uses a PMOS pull-up network dual to the NMOS pull-down network.

instruction: Give a worked example for Sequential circuits: latches, flip-flops, counters, FSMs and timing [GATE EC - Digital Circuits]
response:
Worked example: A 3-bit ripple counter with 10 ns clock-to-Q per flip-flop accumulates 30 ns of delay, so its reliable maximum clock is about 1/30 ns = 33 MHz. A mod-10 counter needs 4 flip-flops (2^3 = 8 is too few).

Formula: Mod-n counter needs ceil(log2 n) flip-flops; max clock frequency f_max = 1 / (t_clk-to-Q + t_comb(max) + t_setup); setup slack = T_clk - (t_clk-to-Q + t_comb + t_setup) must be >= 0.

Sequential outputs depend on present inputs and past history, stored in latches (level-sensitive) and flip-flops (edge-triggered: D, JK, T). Counters and shift registers are built from flip-flops; an n-bit ripple counter divides by 2^n, and a finite state machine is described by a state diagram with states, inputs, outputs and transitions (Mealy outputs depend on input and state, Moore on state only). Timing must satisfy setup time (data stable before the clock edge) and hold time (data stable after it); the critical path is the longest combinational delay between flip-flops and sets the maximum clock frequency.

instruction: Give a worked example for ADCs, DACs, semiconductor memories and computer organisation [GATE EC - Digital Circuits]
response:
Worked example: An 8-bit ADC with Vref = 5 V has LSB = 5/256 = 19.5 mV, so an input of 1.00 V reads about code 51. A 4-bit flash ADC needs 15 comparators.

Formula: ADC resolution (LSB) = Vref / 2^n; quantisation error is at most +/- LSB/2; flash ADC needs 2^n - 1 comparators; R-2R DAC output steps by Vref / 2^n per LSB; pipeline throughput approaches one instruction per clock once filled.

An ADC converts an analog voltage to a digital code; an n-bit ADC with reference Vref has LSB step Vref / 2^n, and successive-approximation, flash (fastest, 2^n - 1 comparators) and integrating types trade speed against accuracy. A DAC does the reverse, for example with an R-2R ladder. ROM is non-volatile, SRAM is fast and uses 6 transistors per cell, DRAM is dense but needs refresh. In computer organisation, the ALU does arithmetic and logic, the control unit fetches and decodes instructions, addressing modes (immediate, direct, indirect, register) say where operands live, and pipelining overlaps instruction stages to raise throughput.

instruction: Give a worked example for Stability: Routh-Hurwitz and Nyquist criteria [GATE EC - Control Systems]
response:
Worked example: For a system with P = 0 open-loop unstable poles, the Nyquist plot must not encircle -1 at all. If the plot crosses the negative real axis at -0.5, the gain margin is 1/0.5 = 2, or 6 dB.

Formula: Routh: stable iff first column has no sign changes; Nyquist: Z = N + P, where N = clockwise encirclements of -1, P = open-loop right-half-plane poles; stable iff Z = 0; gain margin from the -180 deg crossing, phase margin from the |GH| = 1 crossing.

Routh-Hurwitz tests stability from the characteristic polynomial: no sign changes in the first column of the Routh array means no right-half-plane poles. The Nyquist criterion tests stability from the open-loop frequency response: plot G(j omega) H(j omega) as omega goes from -inf to +inf and count encirclements N of the -1 point; with P open-loop right-half-plane poles, the closed loop has Z = N + P unstable poles, so Z = 0 means stable. Nyquist also gives gain and phase margins directly from the plot.

instruction: Give a worked example for Root locus, Bode plots and lead-lag compensation [GATE EC - Control Systems]
response:
Worked example: For G(s) = K / [s (s+1) (s+2)], the three branches go to infinity along asymptotes at 60, 180 and 300 deg from centroid -1. If the phase at gain crossover is -150 deg, the phase margin is 30 deg.

Formula: Root-locus angle condition: sum of angles from zeros - sum from poles = (2k+1) x 180 deg; asymptotes at (2k+1) x 180 deg / (n - m); phase margin PM = 180 deg + angle G(j omega_gc); lead adds positive phase, lag adds negative phase at high frequency but gain at low frequency.

The root locus shows closed-loop pole movement as gain K rises from 0 to infinity, starting at open-loop poles and ending at zeros or at infinity along asymptotes. Bode plots show magnitude (dB) and phase versus log frequency; phase margin is 180 deg plus the phase at the 0 dB crossover, and gain margin is measured at the -180 deg phase crossover. A lead compensator adds phase near crossover, improving phase margin and transient response; a lag compensator raises low-frequency gain and improves steady-state accuracy; lag-lead combines both.

instruction: Give a worked example for Random processes: autocorrelation, power spectral density and white noise [GATE EC - Communication]
response:
Worked example: White noise with two-sided PSD N0/2 = 1e-9 W/Hz through a low-pass filter of bandwidth 1 MHz passes total power 1e-9 x 2 x 1e6 = 2 mW (counting both sidebands) in the idealised flat-band calculation; in practice the one-sided PSD N0 is used with positive frequencies only.

Formula: Wiener-Khinchin: S_xx(f) = integral R_xx(tau) e^{-j 2 pi f tau} d tau; white noise: S = N0/2 (two-sided), R(tau) = (N0/2) delta(tau); output PSD: S_yy(f) = |H(f)|^2 S_xx(f); total power = R_xx(0) = integral S_xx(f) df.

A random process is described by its autocorrelation R_xx(tau), the average of x(t) x(t + tau), and its power spectral density (PSD) S_xx(f), which are a Fourier pair (Wiener-Khinchin theorem): the PSD shows how power is spread over frequency. White noise has a flat PSD (N0/2, two-sided) and an autocorrelation that is a delta function, so its samples are uncorrelated. Passing a random signal through an LTI system multiplies its PSD by |H(f)|^2, and the output autocorrelation is the inverse transform of that.

instruction: Give a worked example for Angle modulation, FM spectra and superheterodyne receivers [GATE EC - Communication]
response:
Worked example: Broadcast FM with peak deviation 75 kHz and audio up to 15 kHz has Carson bandwidth 2 x (75 + 15) = 180 kHz. A receiver tuned to 100 MHz with a 10.7 MHz IF has its image at 100 + 2 x 10.7 = 121.4 MHz (for low-side LO injection).

Formula: FM: instantaneous frequency f_i(t) = fc + k_f m(t); modulation index beta = delta_f / f_m; Carson bandwidth BW about 2 (delta_f + f_m); superheterodyne: f_IF = |f_RF - f_LO|; image frequency = f_RF +/- 2 f_IF.

In amplitude modulation the carrier amplitude follows the message; in angle modulation (FM and PM) the frequency or phase follows it, giving FM a constant envelope and better noise immunity at the cost of more bandwidth. Carson rule estimates FM bandwidth as 2 (delta_f + f_m), where delta_f is the peak frequency deviation. A superheterodyne receiver mixes the incoming signal down to a fixed intermediate frequency (IF), so most gain and selectivity sit in fixed IF filters; the image frequency, spaced 2 f_IF away, is the main spurious response and must be rejected by the RF front end.

instruction: Give a worked example for Digital modulation, matched filter, ISI, MAP and ML detection [GATE EC - Communication]
response:
Worked example: BPSK at Eb/N0 = 10 dB (a ratio of 10) has BER = Q(sqrt(20)) = Q(4.47), about 3.9 x 10^-6, roughly 4 errors per million bits. 16-QAM carries 4 bits per symbol but needs considerably higher Eb/N0 for the same BER.

Formula: BPSK BER = Q(sqrt(2 Eb/N0)); QPSK carries 2 bits per symbol at the same BER as BPSK per bit; matched filter output SNR = 2 E / N0; Nyquist ISI-free criterion: pulse sampled at symbol spacing is zero at all non-zero multiples of T.

Digital modulation maps bits to symbols: ASK varies amplitude, FSK varies frequency, PSK varies phase and QAM varies both amplitude and phase, packing more bits per symbol at the cost of needing higher SNR. The matched filter maximises SNR at the sampling instant and is the optimal linear receiver in white Gaussian noise; MAP and ML detection then pick the most likely symbol, ML when all symbols are equally likely. Inter-symbol interference (ISI) is avoided when pulses satisfy the Nyquist criterion (zero crossings at other sampling instants, e.g. raised-cosine pulses). Bit error rate for BPSK in AWGN is Q(sqrt(2 Eb/N0)), falling steeply as Eb/N0 rises.

instruction: Give a worked example for Information theory: entropy, channel capacity, Hamming codes and CRC [GATE EC - Communication]
response:
Worked example: A binary symmetric source has entropy 1 bit per symbol. A 1 MHz channel with SNR = 15 has capacity 1e6 x log2(16) = 4 Mbps. Hamming (7,4) with data 1011 and parity bits placed at positions 1, 2, 4 can correct any single flipped bit in the 7-bit codeword.

Formula: Entropy H = -sum_i p_i log2 p_i; capacity C = B log2(1 + SNR) bits/s; Hamming (n, k) with r parity bits needs 2^r >= n + 1 and corrects 1 error; CRC: append remainder of data polynomial divided by generator polynomial.

Entropy H is the average information per symbol: H = -sum p_i log2 p_i bits, maximum log2 M for M equally likely symbols. Mutual information is the reduction in uncertainty about one variable from knowing another. Shannon channel capacity C = B log2(1 + SNR) is the maximum error-free rate over a bandlimited AWGN channel. Errors are corrected with redundancy: a Hamming (7,4) code adds 3 parity bits to 4 data bits and corrects any single-bit error, and a CRC appends a remainder computed by polynomial division that detects burst errors.

instruction: Give a worked example for Maxwell equations and Poynting vector [GATE EC - Communication]
response:
Worked example: In free space, a plane wave with E = 10 V/m peak has H = E / 377 = 26.5 mA/m, and its time-average power density is (1/2) x 10 x 0.0265 = 0.133 W/m^2.

Formula: Differential: div D = rho; div B = 0; curl E = -dB/dt; curl H = J + dD/dt; wave speed c = 1/sqrt(mu epsilon) = 3 x 10^8 m/s in free space; Poynting vector S = E x H (W/m^2); average power = (1/2) Re(E x H*).

Maxwell equations unify electricity and magnetism: Gauss law (electric flux from charge), Gauss law for magnetism (no magnetic monopoles, so magnetic flux through a closed surface is zero), Faraday law (changing magnetic flux induces an electric field) and Ampere-Maxwell law (currents and changing electric flux produce magnetic fields). In differential form they give the wave equation, so light is an electromagnetic wave with speed c = 1/sqrt(mu epsilon). The Poynting vector S = E cross H gives power flow per unit area, and boundary conditions say the tangential E and normal B are continuous across an interface (without surface current or charge).

instruction: Give a worked example for Plane waves: reflection, refraction, polarisation and skin depth [GATE EC - Communication]
response:
Worked example: Copper (sigma = 5.8e7 S/m) at 1 MHz has skin depth about 65 micrometres (65.2/sqrt(f in Hz) mm = 65.2/1000 mm), so a 1 MHz current flows only in a thin surface layer and AC resistance is far above DC resistance.

Formula: Intrinsic impedance eta = sqrt(mu/epsilon); phase velocity v = 1/sqrt(mu epsilon); Snell: sin(theta_t)/sin(theta_i) = n1/n2; skin depth delta = sqrt(2/(omega mu sigma)) = 1/sqrt(pi f mu sigma); field decays as e^{-x/delta}.

A uniform plane wave in a lossless medium has E and H perpendicular to each other and to the direction of travel, with ratio equal to the intrinsic impedance eta = sqrt(mu/epsilon) (377 ohm in free space). At an interface part of the wave reflects and part refracts (Snell law); polarisation describes the direction of the E-field, and at the Brewster angle the reflected wave is fully polarised. In a good conductor the wave decays exponentially with skin depth delta = sqrt(2/(omega mu sigma)) = 1/sqrt(pi f mu sigma), the depth at which the field falls to 1/e of its surface value.

instruction: Give a worked example for Transmission lines: characteristic impedance, matching and Smith chart [GATE EC - Communication]
response:
Worked example: A 100 ohm load on a 50 ohm line gives Gamma = (100-50)/(100+50) = 1/3 and VSWR = (1+1/3)/(1-1/3) = 2. A quarter-wave transformer of impedance sqrt(50 x 100) = 70.7 ohm matches it.

Formula: Z0 = sqrt(L/C); v = 1/sqrt(LC); reflection coefficient Gamma = (ZL - Z0)/(ZL + Z0); VSWR = (1 + |Gamma|)/(1 - |Gamma|); input impedance of a line of length l: Zin = Z0 (ZL + j Z0 tan(beta l)) / (Z0 + j ZL tan(beta l)); quarter-wave: Zin = Z0^2 / ZL.

A transmission line has distributed inductance and capacitance per unit length, giving characteristic impedance Z0 = sqrt(L/C) and propagation velocity v = 1/sqrt(LC). A load ZL reflects with coefficient Gamma = (ZL - Z0)/(ZL + Z0); the standing-wave ratio is VSWR = (1 + |Gamma|)/(1 - |Gamma|), and power is fully delivered only when ZL = Z0. Impedance matching (quarter-wave transformer, stub, or L-network) removes reflections. The Smith chart plots normalised impedance on the reflection-coefficient plane, so matching and line transformations are read off graphically; S-parameters describe multi-port networks in the same reflection/transmission language.

instruction: Give a worked example for Waveguides, optical fibres, dipole and monopole antennas and arrays [GATE EC - Communication]
response:
Worked example: A rectangular waveguide with broad side a = 2 cm has TE10 cutoff fc = 3e8/(2 x 0.02) = 7.5 GHz; a 10 GHz signal propagates, a 5 GHz signal does not. A half-wave dipole at 100 MHz is 1.5 m long.

Formula: Rectangular waveguide TE10 cutoff: fc = c/(2a); circular waveguide TE11 cutoff about 1.841 c/(2 pi r); dipole length = lambda/2; monopole length = lambda/4 over a ground plane; array factor for N elements spaced d: AF = sum exp(j n (beta d cos theta + alpha)).

A rectangular waveguide guides waves only above its cutoff frequency: for the dominant TE10 mode, fc = c/(2a), where a is the broad dimension, and below cutoff the wave is evanescent. Light propagates in an optical fibre by total internal reflection, with single-mode fibre carrying one mode and multimode fibre many. A half-wave dipole is the reference antenna (about 73 ohm input resistance, gain 2.15 dBi); a monopole over a ground plane is half a dipole. A linear array of elements with controlled phase shifts steers its beam without moving the antenna.

instruction: Give a worked example for Correlation and regression analysis [GATE EC - Engineering Mathematics]
response:
Worked example: r = 0.9 means a strong positive linear relation; r = 0 does not mean the variables are independent, only that there is no linear relation.

Formula: r = Cov(X, Y) / (sigma_x x sigma_y); slope b = Cov(X, Y) / Var(X); R^2 = 1 - SS_res / SS_tot

The correlation coefficient r (between -1 and +1) measures the strength of a linear association; regression fits the best line y = a + b x by least squares. R-squared is the fraction of variance the line explains. A zero correlation means no linear relation, not independence: a perfect curve can still have r = 0.

instruction: Give a worked example for FIR and IIR filter design [GATE EC - Signals & Systems]
response:
Worked example: A 51-tap FIR low-pass at 1 kHz (sampling 8 kHz) has linear phase; an equivalent IIR needs about 6th order but adds phase distortion.

Formula: FIR: y[n] = sum of b_k x x[n-k]; IIR: y[n] = sum of b_k x x[n-k] - sum of a_k x y[n-k]; bilinear transform: s = (2/T) x (1 - z^-1)/(1 + z^-1)

FIR filters have a finite impulse response: always stable, and linear phase when the taps are symmetric. They are designed by the window method (truncate an ideal response) or by Parks-McClellan. IIR filters use feedback, so they reach a sharp cutoff with far fewer coefficients, but they can be unstable and distort phase; they are designed by the bilinear transform from analog prototypes such as Butterworth and Chebyshev.

instruction: Give a worked example for MOSFET scaling and short-channel effects [GATE EC - Electronic Devices]
response:
Worked example: S = 60 mV per decade means 60 mV of gate voltage changes the leakage current tenfold: that is the floor for turning a MOSFET off.

Formula: Subthreshold swing S is about 60 mV per decade at room temperature (the ideal limit); subthreshold drain current is proportional to 10^((Vgs - Vth)/S)

Dennard scaling shrank MOSFET dimensions while keeping electric fields constant, so each generation got faster and cheaper. Below about 90 nm the scaling breaks: short-channel effects appear (drain-induced barrier lowering, threshold roll-off) and leakage grows through subthreshold conduction and gate tunnelling. FinFET and gate-all-around devices restore gate control by wrapping the gate around the channel.

instruction: Give a worked example for Miller compensation and phase margin [GATE EC - Analog Circuits]
response:
Worked example: An op-amp with 60 degrees of phase margin settles with little ringing; at 10 degrees it rings for many cycles before settling.

Formula: C_Miller = C_f x (1 + |A_v|); phase margin PM = 180 degrees + phase of A at the unity-gain frequency

The Miller effect multiplies a feedback capacitance by (1 + gain), so a small capacitor between an amplifier's input and output looks huge at the input and creates a dominant pole that stabilises the op-amp. Phase margin is 180 degrees plus the loop phase at the unity-gain frequency: at least 45 degrees (ideally 60) is wanted, or the step response rings badly.

instruction: Give a worked example for PID controller [GATE EC - Control Systems]
response:
Worked example: A temperature loop with proportional-only control sits 2 C below its setpoint under load; adding integral action closes the gap.

Formula: u(t) = Kp x e + Ki x integral of e dt + Kd x de/dt; Ziegler-Nichols: Kp = 0.6 Ku, Ti = Tu/2, Td = Tu/8 (Ku, Tu from ultimate oscillation)

A PID controller acts on the error e: proportional corrects the present error, integral accumulates past error and removes steady-state offset, derivative anticipates the error trend and adds damping. Too much integral action causes overshoot; derivative action amplifies measurement noise. Ziegler-Nichols tuning finds the ultimate gain Ku and period Tu at the edge of oscillation and sets the gains from them.

instruction: Give a worked example for Source coding [GATE EC - Communication]
response:
Worked example: Symbols with probabilities {0.5, 0.25, 0.25}: H = 1.5 bits and Huffman gives L = 1.5 bits, which is optimal.

Formula: Entropy H(X) = -sum of p(x) x log2 p(x) bits per symbol; Huffman average length L satisfies H <= L < H + 1

Source coding removes redundancy before transmission. Shannon's source coding theorem says the average code length cannot go below the source entropy H. Huffman coding assigns short codewords to frequent symbols and approaches H when probabilities are known; fixed-length codes waste bits on skewed sources.

instruction: What is the formula for Ohm's law in resistive networks? When is it used? [GATE EC - Networks]
response:
Formula: V = I * R. Resistors in series: R_eq = R1 + R2 + ... Resistors in parallel: 1 / R_eq = 1 / R1 + 1 / R2 + ... Power: P = V * I = I^2 * R.

Ohm's law relates voltage, current and resistance in a linear resistor, and it is the starting point for network analysis. In a network it is applied branch by branch, together with KCL and KVL, to find unknown voltages and currents. Series resistors add directly, while parallel resistors combine by reciprocal addition.

instruction: What is the formula for Shockley diode equation? When is it used? [GATE EC - Electronic Devices]
response:
Formula: I = Is * (exp(V / (n * VT)) - 1), where I is diode current, Is is reverse saturation current, V is diode voltage, n is ideality factor (about 1) and VT = k * T / q is thermal voltage, about 26 mV at room temperature (300 K).

The Shockley diode equation models the exponential current-voltage characteristic of a p-n junction diode. A small increase in forward voltage causes a large increase in current because voltage appears in the exponent. In reverse bias the current saturates at about minus the reverse saturation current.

instruction: What is the formula for Non-inverting op-amp gain? When is it used? [GATE EC - Analog Circuits]
response:
Formula: Gain Av = Vout / Vin = 1 + Rf / R1, where Rf is the feedback resistor and R1 is the resistor to ground. For an inverting amplifier, Av = -Rf / R1.

An ideal op-amp with negative feedback has virtually no input current and virtually no voltage difference between its two inputs. In the non-inverting configuration the input goes to the positive terminal, so the output is in phase with the input. The gain is set only by the two feedback resistors, not by the op-amp itself.

instruction: What is the formula for Boolean algebra and De Morgan's laws? When is it used? [GATE EC - Digital Circuits]
response:
Formula: De Morgan's laws: (A + B)' = A' * B' and (A * B)' = A' + B', where + is OR, * is AND and ' is NOT. Basic identities: A + 0 = A, A * 1 = A, A + A' = 1, A * A' = 0.

Boolean algebra is the mathematics of digital logic, with variables taking only 0 or 1. De Morgan's laws show how to convert between AND and OR forms using complements, which is essential for simplifying logic and implementing circuits with only NAND or only NOR gates. They are used in almost every digital design and GATE question on logic minimisation.

instruction: What is the formula for Nyquist sampling theorem? When is it used? [GATE EC - Signals & Systems]
response:
Formula: fs >= 2 * fm, where fs is sampling frequency and fm is the highest frequency in the signal. Nyquist rate = 2 * fm. Nyquist frequency = fs / 2. Sampling period Ts = 1 / fs.

The Nyquist-Shannon sampling theorem states that a band-limited signal can be perfectly reconstructed from its samples if the sampling rate is at least twice its highest frequency. Sampling slower than this causes aliasing, where high frequencies falsely appear as low frequencies. The minimum rate is called the Nyquist rate.

instruction: What is the formula for Amplitude modulation: modulation index and bandwidth? When is it used? [GATE EC - Communication]
response:
Formula: Modulation index mu = Am / Ac = (Amax - Amin) / (Amax + Amin), where Am is message amplitude, Ac is carrier amplitude, and Amax and Amin are the maximum and minimum envelope amplitudes. Bandwidth BW = 2 * fm, where fm is the highest message frequency. AM wave: s(t) = Ac * (1 + mu * cos(2 * pi * fm * t)) * cos(2 * pi * fc * t).

In amplitude modulation the message signal varies the amplitude of a high-frequency carrier. The modulation index measures how deeply the carrier is modulated, and it must not exceed 1 or the envelope distorts on demodulation. An AM signal occupies twice the message bandwidth, one sideband on each side of the carrier.

instruction: What is the formula for Steady-state error of a unity-feedback system? When is it used? [GATE EC - Control Systems]
response:
Formula: For unity feedback, step-input steady-state error e_ss = 1 / (1 + Kp), where Kp = limit as s -> 0 of G(s). For a type 1 or higher system, Kp is infinite, so e_ss = 0 for a step input.

Steady-state error is the difference between the desired output and the actual output after transients have died out. A system with at least one integrator (type 1 or higher) tracks a step input with zero steady-state error in unity feedback. A type 0 system has a finite step error determined by its position error constant Kp.

instruction: What is the formula for Linear algebra: rank, basis and solution of linear equations? When is it used? [GATE EC - Engineering Mathematics]
response:
Formula: rank(A) = number of independent rows = number of independent columns; A x = b consistent iff rank(A) = rank([A | b]); unique solution iff rank = n (unknowns); det(A - lambda I) = 0 gives eigenvalues.

The rank of a matrix is the number of linearly independent rows or columns. A system A x = b has a solution if and only if rank(A) = rank([A|b]); it is unique if that rank also equals the number of unknowns, and has infinitely many solutions if the rank is smaller. Vectors are linearly independent if only the trivial combination gives zero, and a basis is an independent set that spans the space. Eigenvalues and eigenvectors come from det(A - lambda I) = 0, as in the EE entry on eigenvalues.

instruction: What is the formula for Vector analysis: gradient, divergence, curl and integral theorems? When is it used? [GATE EC - Engineering Mathematics]
response:
Formula: grad f = (df/dx, df/dy, df/dz); div F = dFx/dx + dFy/dy + dFz/dz; curl F = grad x F; Gauss: integral_V div F dV = integral_S F . dS; Stokes: integral_S curl F . dS = integral_C F . dr.

The gradient of a scalar points in the direction of fastest increase; the divergence of a vector field measures net outflow per unit volume; the curl measures local rotation. A field with zero curl is conservative and can be written as a gradient, and a field with zero divergence is solenoidal. Gauss, Stokes and Green theorems convert volume integrals of divergence and surface integrals of curl into surface and line integrals, and are used throughout electromagnetics.

instruction: What is the formula for Complex analysis: analytic functions, Taylor and Laurent series, residue theorem? When is it used? [GATE EC - Engineering Mathematics]
response:
Formula: Cauchy-Riemann: du/dx = dv/dy, du/dy = -dv/dx; integral_C f(z) dz = 2 pi i x sum of residues; simple pole residue = lim_{z->z0} (z - z0) f(z); ratio test: series converges if lim |a_{n+1}/a_n| < 1.

A function is analytic where it is differentiable in the complex sense (Cauchy-Riemann equations hold); analytic functions have power-series (Taylor) expansions, and functions with isolated singularities have Laurent expansions with negative powers. The residue theorem says the integral around a closed contour is 2 pi i times the sum of residues inside, which evaluates many real integrals. Convergence tests (ratio, root, comparison) decide whether a series converges.

instruction: What is the formula for Thevenin, Norton and reciprocity theorems? When is it used? [GATE EC - Networks]
response:
Formula: Vth = open-circuit voltage; Rth = Vth / I_sc; IN = Vth / Rth; reciprocity: response at port 2 to a source at port 1 equals response at port 1 to the same source at port 2.

Any linear network seen from two terminals is equivalent to a voltage source Vth in series with Rth, or a current source IN = Vth/Rth in parallel with Rth. Vth is the open-circuit voltage and Rth the resistance looking back with independent sources turned off. The reciprocity theorem says that in a linear network with only one source, swapping the source and the measurement point leaves the measured response unchanged. Superposition lets each independent source be considered alone, with the others turned off.

instruction: What is the formula for Phasor analysis, complex power and maximum power transfer? When is it used? [GATE EC - Networks]
response:
Formula: Z_L = j omega L; Z_C = 1/(j omega C); S = V_rms I_rms* = P + j Q; |S| = V_rms I_rms; power factor = cos(phi) = P/|S|; maximum power when Z_L = Zth*.

In sinusoidal steady state, voltages and currents are phasors and impedances are complex: Z = R + jX, with X = omega L for an inductor and -1/(omega C) for a capacitor. Complex power S = V_rms I_rms* = P + jQ, where P is average power in watts, Q is reactive power in VAR, and |S| is apparent power in VA. Maximum average power is delivered when the load impedance is the complex conjugate of the source impedance.

instruction: What is the formula for Transient analysis of RL, RC and RLC circuits with Laplace transform? When is it used? [GATE EC - Networks]
response:
Formula: s-domain: R -> R; L -> sL; C -> 1/(sC); series RLC: s^2 + (R/L) s + 1/(LC) = 0; omega_0 = 1/sqrt(LC); zeta = (R/2) sqrt(C/L); zeta < 1 underdamped, = 1 critically damped, > 1 overdamped.

Network equations in the time domain become algebraic in the s-domain: a resistor stays R, an inductor becomes sL (plus an initial-flux voltage source), and a capacitor becomes 1/(sC) (plus an initial-charge source). Solving for the s-domain current or voltage and inverting gives the transient, whose character is set by the poles: real distinct poles give overdamped decay, a repeated pole gives critically damped decay, and complex poles give damped oscillation. The damping ratio and natural frequency of a series RLC circuit are zeta = (R/2) sqrt(C/L) and omega_0 = 1/sqrt(LC).

instruction: What is the formula for Fourier series, Fourier transform, DTFT and DFT? When is it used? [GATE EC - Signals & Systems]
response:
Formula: Fourier series: periodic -> discrete spectrum; FT: X(omega) = integral x(t) e^{-j omega t} dt; DTFT: X(e^{j w}) = sum_n x[n] e^{-j w n}; DFT: X[k] = sum_{n=0}^{N-1} x[n] e^{-j 2 pi k n / N}.

Fourier series handles periodic signals, the Fourier transform handles aperiodic ones, the DTFT handles discrete-time signals (periodic in frequency with period 2 pi), and the DFT is the sampled, finite-length version used in computation. The DFT of length N is X[k] = sum_{n=0}^{N-1} x[n] e^{-j 2 pi k n / N}, and the FFT computes it in O(N log N) instead of O(N^2). Sampling in one domain causes periodicity in the other, which is why aliasing appears when sampling is too slow.

instruction: What is the formula for Z-transform, LTI systems, convolution, poles and zeros? When is it used? [GATE EC - Signals & Systems]
response:
Formula: y[n] = sum_k x[k] h[n-k]; H(z) = Y(z)/X(z); stable iff all poles satisfy |p| < 1; frequency response H(e^{j w}) = H(z) at z = e^{j w}; group delay tau_g = -d(angle H)/d w.

An LTI system is fully described by its impulse response h[n]: the output is the convolution sum of the input with h. In the z-domain the transfer function H(z) = Y(z)/X(z) is a ratio of polynomials; its poles decide stability (all inside the unit circle) and causality, and its zeros shape the frequency response. The frequency response is H(e^{j w}), obtained by evaluating H(z) on the unit circle. Group delay is minus the derivative of phase with respect to frequency, and phase delay is minus phase divided by frequency.

instruction: What is the formula for Semiconductors: energy bands, drift, diffusion and continuity? When is it used? [GATE EC - Electronic Devices]
response:
Formula: Drift: J_n(drift) = q n mu_n E; diffusion: J_n(diff) = q D_n dn/dx; Einstein: D/mu = kT/q = about 25.85 mV at 300 K; n p = n_i^2; resistivity rho = 1 / [q (n mu_n + p mu_p)]; Poisson: d^2 V/dx^2 = -rho_charge / epsilon.

In a semiconductor, electrons in the conduction band and holes in the valence band carry current. Intrinsic carrier concentration n_i grows with temperature; doping adds donors (n-type, electrons majority) or acceptors (p-type, holes majority), with n p = n_i^2 in equilibrium. Drift current follows the electric field with mobility mu; diffusion current follows the concentration gradient with diffusivity D, linked by the Einstein relation D/mu = kT/q (about 25.85 mV at 300 K). Poisson equation links charge to potential, and the continuity equation is conservation of carriers including generation and recombination.

instruction: What is the formula for P-N junction, Zener diode, LED, photodiode and solar cell? When is it used? [GATE EC - Electronic Devices]
response:
Formula: Diode: I = I_s (e^{V/(eta Vt)} - 1), Vt = kT/q = about 26 mV at 300 K; Vbi = Vt ln(N_A N_D / n_i^2); depletion width W proportional to sqrt(Vbi - V); Zener: reverse breakdown at a fixed Vz.

A p-n junction has a built-in potential Vbi = Vt ln(N_A N_D / n_i^2) across its depletion region; forward bias shrinks the barrier and current grows exponentially, reverse bias widens it and only a small saturation current flows until breakdown. A Zener diode is designed to break down at a controlled reverse voltage and so holds a nearly constant voltage, used as a regulator. An LED emits light when carriers recombine, a photodiode generates current from absorbed light (reverse biased), and a solar cell is a large photodiode operated to deliver power to a load.

instruction: What is the formula for BJT, MOSFET and MOS capacitor; small-signal amplifiers? When is it used? [GATE EC - Electronic Devices]
response:
Formula: BJT: Ic = beta Ib; gm = Ic/Vt; MOSFET saturation: Id = (1/2) mu C_ox (W/L)(Vgs - Vth)^2; gm = 2 Id / (Vgs - Vth); common-emitter gain about -gm Rc (with load); common-source gain about -gm Rd.

A BJT is a current-controlled device: collector current Ic = beta Ib in active mode, with transconductance gm = Ic/Vt. A MOSFET is voltage-controlled: in saturation Id = (1/2) mu C_ox (W/L) (Vgs - Vth)^2, with gm = sqrt(2 mu C_ox (W/L) Id). A MOS capacitor goes from accumulation through depletion to inversion as gate voltage rises, and inversion is what forms the MOSFET channel. Small-signal analysis replaces each device by its gm and output resistance to find voltage gain, input and output resistance; gain falls at high frequency because of device capacitances (Miller effect) and at low frequency because of coupling capacitors.

instruction: What is the formula for Diode circuits: clipping, clamping and rectifiers? When is it used? [GATE EC - Analog Circuits]
response:
Formula: Half-wave average: Vdc = Vm / pi; full-wave average: Vdc = 2 Vm / pi; ripple (capacitor filter, full-wave): Vr(pp) about I_load / (2 f C); bridge PIV = Vm; centre-tapped PIV = 2 Vm.

A clipper uses a diode (and a reference voltage) to cut off the part of a waveform above or below a level; a clamper uses a diode plus a capacitor to shift the whole waveform up or down by a DC level without changing its shape. A half-wave rectifier passes only one half-cycle (average output Vm/pi), a full-wave rectifier uses both (average 2 Vm/pi), and a capacitor filter smooths the ripple, with ripple falling as capacitance and load resistance rise. Peak inverse voltage ratings decide diode choice: a bridge rectifier needs PIV of Vm, a centre-tapped full-wave needs 2 Vm.

instruction: What is the formula for Op-amp circuits: amplifiers, integrators, filters, Schmitt trigger and oscillators? When is it used? [GATE EC - Analog Circuits]
response:
Formula: Inverting gain = -Rf/R1; non-inverting gain = 1 + Rf/R1; integrator: Vo = -(1/RC) integral Vi dt; differentiator: Vo = -RC dVi/dt; Schmitt thresholds = +/- [R1/(R1+R2)] Vsat; Sallen-Key fc = 1/(2 pi sqrt(R1 R2 C1 C2)); Barkhausen: loop gain = 1 at 0 deg (or 360 deg) phase.

An ideal op-amp has infinite gain, infinite input resistance and zero output resistance, so with negative feedback the two inputs sit at the same voltage (virtual short) and draw no current. That gives the inverting gain -Rf/R1, the non-inverting gain 1 + Rf/R1, summers, differentiators and integrators (output -1/(RC) times the integral of the input). A Schmitt trigger uses positive feedback to give two thresholds and hysteresis, cleaning up noisy signals; an oscillator needs loop gain of at least 1 with zero total phase shift (Barkhausen criterion). Active filters use op-amps with RC networks: a Sallen-Key second-order low-pass has fc = 1/(2 pi sqrt(R1 R2 C1 C2)) and Q = 0.707 gives a Butterworth (maximally flat) response.

instruction: What is the formula for Number systems, combinational logic and Karnaugh maps? When is it used? [GATE EC - Digital Circuits]
response:
Formula: Binary 1011 = 1x8 + 0x4 + 1x2 + 1 = 11 decimal; De Morgan: NOT(A B) = (NOT A) + (NOT B), NOT(A + B) = (NOT A)(NOT B); 2^n-to-1 multiplexer needs n select lines; K-map group size must be a power of 2.

Digital numbers are binary; integers convert by repeated division by 2 and fractions by repeated multiplication by 2, and floating-point numbers store a sign, exponent and mantissa (IEEE 754). Combinational outputs depend only on present inputs: Boolean algebra and Karnaugh maps minimise the sum-of-products form, grouping 1s in powers of two (pairs, quads, octets), including wrap-around and don't-care cells. Standard blocks are adders, comparators, code converters, multiplexers (a 2^n-to-1 mux needs n select lines) and decoders. A static CMOS gate uses a PMOS pull-up network dual to the NMOS pull-down network.

instruction: What is the formula for Sequential circuits: latches, flip-flops, counters, FSMs and timing? When is it used? [GATE EC - Digital Circuits]
response:
Formula: Mod-n counter needs ceil(log2 n) flip-flops; max clock frequency f_max = 1 / (t_clk-to-Q + t_comb(max) + t_setup); setup slack = T_clk - (t_clk-to-Q + t_comb + t_setup) must be >= 0.

Sequential outputs depend on present inputs and past history, stored in latches (level-sensitive) and flip-flops (edge-triggered: D, JK, T). Counters and shift registers are built from flip-flops; an n-bit ripple counter divides by 2^n, and a finite state machine is described by a state diagram with states, inputs, outputs and transitions (Mealy outputs depend on input and state, Moore on state only). Timing must satisfy setup time (data stable before the clock edge) and hold time (data stable after it); the critical path is the longest combinational delay between flip-flops and sets the maximum clock frequency.

instruction: What is Ohm's law? Explain it briefly. [GATE EE - Electric Circuits]
response:
Ohm's law states that the voltage across a resistor is directly proportional to the current through it, provided the temperature and other physical conditions remain constant. The constant of proportionality is the resistance. It applies to linear, ohmic resistors in DC and, in phasor form, to AC circuits.

Formula: V = I * R, I = V / R, R = V / I, where V is voltage in volts, I is current in amperes and R is resistance in ohms. Power dissipated: P = V * I = I^2 * R = V^2 / R.

Worked example: A 12 V battery is connected across a 4 ohm resistor. Current I = V / R = 12 / 4 = 3 A, and power dissipated P = V * I = 12 * 3 = 36 W.

instruction: What is Kirchhoff's current law (KCL) and voltage law (KVL)? Explain it briefly. [GATE EE - Electric Circuits]
response:
Kirchhoff's current law states that the algebraic sum of currents entering a node is zero, which is conservation of charge. Kirchhoff's voltage law states that the algebraic sum of voltages around any closed loop is zero, which is conservation of energy. Together they are the basis for nodal and mesh analysis of any circuit.

Formula: KCL: sum of currents entering a node = sum of currents leaving the node, or Sigma I = 0 at a node. KVL: Sigma V = 0 around a closed loop, or sum of voltage rises = sum of voltage drops.

Worked example: A 12 V source drives 2 ohm and 4 ohm resistors in series. By KVL, loop current I = 12 / (2 + 4) = 2 A. Voltage across the 2 ohm resistor is 4 V and across the 4 ohm resistor is 8 V, and 4 + 8 = 12 V, satisfying KVL.

instruction: What is Transformer EMF equation? Explain it briefly. [GATE EE - Electrical Machines]
response:
When a sinusoidal flux links a transformer winding, Faraday's law gives an induced EMF whose RMS value depends on frequency, turns and maximum flux. The factor 4.44 comes from the sinusoidal form factor 1.11 multiplied by 4. It applies to both primary and secondary windings, which share the same core flux.

Formula: E = 4.44 * f * N * Phi_m, where E is RMS induced EMF in volts, f is supply frequency in Hz, N is number of turns and Phi_m is maximum core flux in webers. E1 = 4.44 * f * N1 * Phi_m and E2 = 4.44 * f * N2 * Phi_m, so E2 / E1 = N2 / N1.

Worked example: For f = 50 Hz, N = 100 turns and Phi_m = 0.02 Wb, E = 4.44 * 50 * 100 * 0.02 = 444 V RMS.

instruction: What is Power factor and three-phase power? Explain it briefly. [GATE EE - Power Systems]
response:
Power factor is the cosine of the angle between voltage and current in an AC circuit, and it equals real power divided by apparent power. A low power factor means more current is needed for the same useful power. For a balanced three-phase load, power is expressed with line voltage and line current and the factor sqrt(3).

Formula: Power factor = cos(phi) = P / S, where P is real power in watts and S is apparent power in volt-amperes. Single-phase: P = V * I * cos(phi), S = V * I, Q = V * I * sin(phi). Balanced three-phase: P = sqrt(3) * VL * IL * cos(phi), S = sqrt(3) * VL * IL, Q = sqrt(3) * VL * IL * sin(phi), S^2 = P^2 + Q^2.

Worked example: A balanced load has VL = 400 V, IL = 10 A and cos(phi) = 0.8. Real power P = 1.732 * 400 * 10 * 0.8 = 5542 W (about 5.54 kW) and apparent power S = 1.732 * 400 * 10 = 6928 VA.

instruction: What is Transfer function of a linear system? Explain it briefly. [GATE EE - Control Systems]
response:
The transfer function is the Laplace transform of the output divided by the Laplace transform of the input, with all initial conditions zero. It completely describes a linear time-invariant system in the s-domain. Its poles determine stability and its value at s = 0 gives the DC gain.

Formula: G(s) = Y(s) / X(s), where Y(s) is the Laplace transform of the output and X(s) is the Laplace transform of the input. DC gain = G(0). For a first-order system G(s) = K / (tau * s + 1), the pole is at s = -1 / tau.

Worked example: For G(s) = 1 / (s + 2), the DC gain is G(0) = 1 / 2 = 0.5. A unit step input therefore settles to a steady-state output of 0.5.

instruction: What is Faraday's law of electromagnetic induction? Explain it briefly. [GATE EE - Electromagnetic Fields]
response:
Faraday's law states that a changing magnetic flux linking a coil induces an EMF in the coil. The minus sign in the law is Lenz's law: the induced EMF opposes the change in flux that produced it. This is the operating principle of transformers, generators and inductors.

Formula: e = -N * dPhi/dt, where e is induced EMF in volts, N is number of turns and Phi is magnetic flux in webers. For sinusoidal flux Phi = Phi_m * sin(2 * pi * f * t), peak EMF Em = 2 * pi * f * N * Phi_m and RMS EMF E = Em / sqrt(2) = 4.44 * f * N * Phi_m.

Worked example: A coil has N = 200 turns, Phi_m = 0.01 Wb and f = 50 Hz. Peak EMF Em = 2 * pi * 50 * 200 * 0.01 = 628.3 V, so RMS EMF E = 628.3 / 1.414 = 444.3 V.

instruction: What is RMS value of a sinusoidal signal? Explain it briefly. [GATE EE - Signals & Systems]
response:
The RMS (root mean square) value of an AC signal is the equivalent DC value that would deliver the same average power to a resistor. For a sinusoid it is the peak value divided by sqrt(2). Household mains are quoted in RMS, so 230 V RMS in India corresponds to a peak of about 325 V.

Formula: Vrms = Vm / sqrt(2) = 0.707 * Vm, where Vm is the peak voltage. Similarly Irms = Im / sqrt(2). Average power in a resistor: P = Vrms * Irms = Vrms^2 / R.

Worked example: A sine wave has peak voltage Vm = 10 V. Its RMS value is Vrms = 10 / 1.414 = 7.07 V. Across a 10 ohm resistor it delivers P = 7.07^2 / 10 = 5 W.

instruction: What is Eigenvalues and eigenvectors? Explain it briefly. [GATE EE - Engineering Mathematics]
response:
A non-zero vector v is an eigenvector of a square matrix A if A v is a scalar multiple of v; that scalar is the eigenvalue lambda. Eigenvalues are the roots of the characteristic equation det(A - lambda I) = 0. They give the determinant (product of eigenvalues), the trace (sum of eigenvalues), and whether A is singular (zero is an eigenvalue). Symmetric matrices have real eigenvalues and orthogonal eigenvectors.

Formula: A v = lambda v; det(A - lambda I) = 0; det(A) = product of eigenvalues; trace(A) = sum of eigenvalues.

Worked example: A = [[2, 0], [0, 3]] has det(A - lambda I) = (2 - lambda)(3 - lambda) = 0, so eigenvalues are 2 and 3, with eigenvectors [1, 0] and [0, 1]. det(A) = 6 = 2 x 3.

instruction: What is Fourier series of a periodic function? Explain it briefly. [GATE EE - Engineering Mathematics]
response:
A periodic function of period 2L can be written as a sum of sines and cosines. An even function has only cosine terms (all b_n = 0); an odd function has only sine terms (a_0 = a_n = 0). The coefficients are found by integrating the function against each basis term over one period. Discontinuities cause the Gibbs overshoot of about 9 percent near the jump, which does not vanish as more terms are added.

Formula: f(x) = a0/2 + sum_{n>=1} [a_n cos(n pi x / L) + b_n sin(n pi x / L)]; a_n = (1/L) integral_{-L}^{L} f(x) cos(n pi x / L) dx; b_n = (1/L) integral_{-L}^{L} f(x) sin(n pi x / L) dx.

Worked example: A square wave of amplitude 1 and period 2 pi is odd, so only sine terms appear: f(x) = (4/pi)[sin x + sin 3x / 3 + sin 5x / 5 + ...]. The first term alone already gives the fundamental sine.

instruction: What is Vector integral theorems: Gauss, Stokes and Green? Explain it briefly. [GATE EE - Engineering Mathematics]
response:
Gauss divergence theorem turns a volume integral of the divergence into a flux integral over the closed surface bounding it. Stokes theorem turns a surface integral of the curl into a line integral of the field around the boundary curve. Green theorem is the 2D form of Stokes in the plane. Together they convert between line, surface and volume integrals and are the basis of Gauss law and Faraday law in integral form.

Formula: Gauss: integral_V div F dV = integral_S F . dS. Stokes: integral_S curl F . dS = integral_C F . dr. Green: integral_C (P dx + Q dy) = integral_D (dQ/dx - dP/dy) dA.

Worked example: For F = (x, y, z) through the unit sphere, div F = 3, so the flux is 3 x volume = 3 x (4 pi / 3) = 4 pi, matching the direct surface integral.

instruction: What is Residue theorem and contour integration? Explain it briefly. [GATE EE - Engineering Mathematics]
response:
A function analytic inside and on a closed contour except for isolated singularities has its contour integral equal to 2 pi i times the sum of the residues at the singularities inside. The residue at a simple pole z0 of f is the limit of (z - z0) f(z) as z tends to z0. This turns difficult real integrals, such as integrals of rational functions over the real line, into residue sums.

Formula: integral_C f(z) dz = 2 pi i x sum of residues inside C. Simple pole: Res(f, z0) = lim_{z->z0} (z - z0) f(z). Cauchy integral formula: f(a) = (1 / 2 pi i) integral_C f(z)/(z - a) dz.

Worked example: f(z) = 1/(z^2 + 1) has a simple pole at z = i with residue 1/(2i). On a small circle around i only, the integral is 2 pi i x 1/(2i) = pi.

instruction: What is Thevenin and Norton equivalent circuits? Explain it briefly. [GATE EE - Electric Circuits]
response:
Any linear network seen from two terminals behaves exactly like a voltage source Vth in series with a resistance Rth (Thevenin), or equivalently a current source IN in parallel with the same Rth (Norton). Vth is the open-circuit voltage at the terminals and Rth is the resistance seen looking back with all independent sources turned off (voltage sources shorted, current sources opened). IN = Vth / Rth, and the two forms give identical terminal voltage and current for any load.

Formula: Vth = open-circuit voltage; Rth = Vth / I_sc; IN = Vth / Rth; load voltage V_L = Vth x R_L / (Rth + R_L).

Worked example: A network with Vth = 12 V and Rth = 4 ohm feeding a 8 ohm load gives V_L = 12 x 8 / 12 = 8 V and current 1 A. Its Norton form is a 3 A source in parallel with 4 ohm.

instruction: What is Maximum power transfer theorem? Explain it briefly. [GATE EE - Electric Circuits]
response:
A load receives maximum power when its resistance equals the Thevenin resistance of the source network, R_L = Rth (for AC, the load impedance must be the complex conjugate of the source impedance). At that point the efficiency is only 50 percent, because as much power is lost in Rth as is delivered, so the theorem is used for signal and communication circuits, not for power systems where efficiency matters. Maximum power is Vth^2 / (4 Rth).

Formula: R_L = Rth for maximum power; P_max = Vth^2 / (4 Rth); AC: Z_L = Zth* (complex conjugate).

Worked example: With Vth = 10 V and Rth = 5 ohm, choose R_L = 5 ohm: P_max = 100 / 20 = 5 W, and 5 W is also lost in Rth, so efficiency is 50 percent.

instruction: What is Series and parallel resonance in RLC circuits? Explain it briefly. [GATE EE - Electric Circuits]
response:
Resonance is the frequency at which the inductive and capacitive reactances cancel, so a series RLC circuit has minimum impedance (purely resistive) and maximum current, while a parallel RLC circuit has maximum impedance and minimum line current. The resonant frequency is the same for both: 1 / (2 pi sqrt(LC)). The quality factor Q measures sharpness: high Q means a narrow bandwidth, BW = f0 / Q.

Formula: f0 = 1 / (2 pi sqrt(L C)); series Q = (1/R) sqrt(L/C); parallel Q = R sqrt(C/L); bandwidth BW = f0 / Q = R / (2 pi L) for series RLC.

Worked example: L = 10 mH, C = 100 nF, R = 10 ohm: f0 = 1 / (2 pi sqrt(10e-3 x 100e-9)) = about 5033 Hz. sqrt(L/C) = 316 ohm, so Q = 316 / 10 = 31.6 and BW = 5033 / 31.6 = about 159 Hz.

instruction: What is Transient response of RL and RC circuits? Explain it briefly. [GATE EE - Electric Circuits]
response:
When a DC source is switched onto an RL or RC circuit, voltages and currents move exponentially from their initial value toward the final steady value, with time constant tau. For RC, tau = R C; for RL, tau = L / R. After one time constant the transient has covered about 63 percent of the change; after five time constants it is essentially over. Inductor current and capacitor voltage cannot change instantly, which fixes the initial conditions.

Formula: tau_RC = R C; tau_RL = L / R; x(t) = x(inf) + [x(0) - x(inf)] e^{-t/tau}; after t = tau, 63.2 percent of the change is complete.

Worked example: R = 1 k ohm and C = 1 uF give tau = 1 ms. A capacitor charging from 0 V toward 10 V reaches 6.32 V after 1 ms and about 9.93 V after 5 ms.

instruction: What is Gauss law and electric field of charge distributions? Explain it briefly. [GATE EE - Electromagnetic Fields]
response:
Gauss law says the total electric flux through any closed surface equals the charge enclosed divided by epsilon_0. By symmetry it gives the field directly: a point charge gives E falling as 1/r^2, an infinite line charge gives E falling as 1/r, and an infinite plane sheet gives a constant field. Electric field is the negative gradient of potential, and potential is found by integrating the field. A dielectric reduces the field by its relative permittivity.

Formula: Integral form: integral_S D . dS = Q_enclosed; E = Q / (4 pi epsilon r^2) for a point charge; E = lambda / (2 pi epsilon r) for a line charge; E = sigma / (2 epsilon) for a plane sheet; E = -grad V.

Worked example: A 1 uC point charge at 1 m in air: E = 9 x 10^9 x 1e-6 / 1^2 = 9000 V/m radially outward. At 2 m the field is 2250 V/m, one quarter as large.

instruction: What is Biot-Savart law and Ampere law? Explain it briefly. [GATE EE - Electromagnetic Fields]
response:
Biot-Savart law gives the magnetic field of a current element: dB is proportional to I dl cross r-hat over r^2. Ampere law in integral form says the line integral of B around a closed path equals mu_0 times the current enclosed. For a long straight wire this gives B = mu_0 I / (2 pi r), circling the wire by the right-hand rule. The curl form, curl B = mu_0 J, is one of Maxwell equations.

Formula: dB = (mu_0 / 4 pi) I dl x r-hat / r^2; integral_C B . dl = mu_0 I_enclosed; long wire: B = mu_0 I / (2 pi r); curl B = mu_0 J.

Worked example: A wire carrying 10 A produces B = (4 pi x 10^-7 x 10) / (2 pi x 0.1) = 2 x 10^-5 T = 20 uT at 0.1 m, directed tangentially around the wire.

instruction: What is Magnetic circuits, reluctance, self and mutual inductance? Explain it briefly. [GATE EE - Electromagnetic Fields]
response:
A magnetic circuit obeys the same form as an electric circuit: magnetomotive force (MMF = N I) drives flux Phi through a reluctance R = l / (mu A), just as voltage drives current through resistance. Self-inductance is L = N Phi / I, the flux linkage per ampere; a changing current induces v = L di/dt. Two coupled coils have mutual inductance M = k sqrt(L1 L2), with coupling coefficient k between 0 and 1, and the induced voltage in one coil is M times the rate of change of current in the other.

Formula: MMF = N I; reluctance R = l / (mu A); Phi = MMF / R; L = N Phi / I; v = L di/dt; M = k sqrt(L1 L2); v2 = M di1/dt.

Worked example: A coil with N = 100 turns carrying 2 A has MMF = 200 ampere-turns. If the core reluctance is 1 x 10^6 A-turns/Wb, flux Phi = 200 / 1e6 = 0.2 mWb. Two coils of 4 mH and 9 mH with k = 0.5 have M = 0.5 x sqrt(36) = 3 mH.

instruction: What is Fourier transform of continuous-time signals? Explain it briefly. [GATE EE - Signals & Systems]
response:
The Fourier transform decomposes a non-periodic signal into its frequency components; the inverse transform rebuilds the time signal from them. It turns convolution into multiplication and differentiation into multiplication by j omega, which is why it solves linear systems and differential equations so cleanly. The transform of a rectangular pulse is a sinc, and of an exponential e^{-a t} u(t) is 1/(a + j omega). Parseval theorem says total energy is the same in time and frequency.

Formula: X(omega) = integral_{-inf}^{inf} x(t) e^{-j omega t} dt; x(t) = (1/2 pi) integral X(omega) e^{j omega t} d omega; convolution: x * h <-> X(omega) H(omega); energy: integral |x(t)|^2 dt = (1/2 pi) integral |X(omega)|^2 d omega.

Worked example: x(t) = e^{-2t} u(t) has X(omega) = 1/(2 + j omega). Its magnitude is 1/sqrt(4 + omega^2), falling to half its DC value when omega = 2 sqrt(3) rad/s.

instruction: What is Laplace transform and solving differential equations? Explain it briefly. [GATE EE - Signals & Systems]
response:
The Laplace transform turns a linear differential equation with initial conditions into an algebraic equation in s, which is why it is the standard tool for transient analysis and control. Differentiation becomes multiplication by s (minus the initial value), integration becomes division by s, and a time delay becomes multiplication by e^{-sT}. The transfer function of a system is the Laplace transform of its impulse response, and poles of the transfer function decide stability: all poles in the left half-plane means stable.

Formula: X(s) = integral_0^{inf} x(t) e^{-s t} dt; L{dx/dt} = s X(s) - x(0); L{1} = 1/s; L{e^{-a t}} = 1/(s + a); L{sin omega t} = omega / (s^2 + omega^2); transfer function H(s) = Y(s)/X(s).

Worked example: Solve y' + 2y = 0, y(0) = 3: s Y(s) - 3 + 2 Y(s) = 0, so Y(s) = 3/(s + 2), and y(t) = 3 e^{-2t}. The single pole at s = -2 is in the left half-plane, so the response decays.

instruction: What is Z-transform of discrete-time signals? Explain it briefly. [GATE EE - Signals & Systems]
response:
The Z-transform is the discrete-time twin of the Laplace transform: it turns difference equations into algebra and convolution into multiplication. The region of convergence (ROC) decides causality and stability: a causal sequence has an ROC outside the outermost pole, and a system is stable if the unit circle lies inside the ROC. Poles inside the unit circle give decaying responses; poles outside give growing ones.

Formula: X(z) = sum_{n=-inf}^{inf} x[n] z^{-n}; x[n] = a^n u[n] <-> X(z) = 1 / (1 - a z^{-1}), ROC |z| > |a|; delay: x[n-1] <-> z^{-1} X(z); convolution: x * h <-> X(z) H(z).

Worked example: x[n] = (0.5)^n u[n] has X(z) = 1 / (1 - 0.5 z^{-1}) = z / (z - 0.5), ROC |z| > 0.5. The pole at 0.5 is inside the unit circle, so the sequence decays and the system is stable.

instruction: What is DC machines: motoring, generating and speed control? Explain it briefly. [GATE EE - Electrical Machines]
response:
A DC machine converts between electrical and mechanical energy through the interaction of armature current and flux. As a generator the induced EMF is E = P Phi N Z / (60 A); as a motor the same EMF acts as back-EMF opposing the supply, and speed is roughly (V - Ia Ra) / (k Phi). A shunt motor holds speed nearly constant, a series motor gives very high starting torque but must never run unloaded, and speed is controlled by varying armature voltage or field flux (field weakening raises speed above base speed).

Formula: Generated EMF Eg = P Phi N Z / (60 A); motor: V = Eb + Ia Ra; Eb = k Phi omega; torque T = k Phi Ia; speed N proportional to (V - Ia Ra) / Phi.

Worked example: A 220 V shunt motor draws Ia = 10 A with Ra = 1 ohm: back-EMF Eb = 220 - 10 x 1 = 210 V. Halving the flux (field weakening) roughly doubles the speed, at the cost of lower torque.

instruction: What is Three-phase induction motor: slip and torque-speed characteristics? Explain it briefly. [GATE EE - Electrical Machines]
response:
The stator rotating field at synchronous speed Ns = 120 f / P induces currents in the rotor, and the rotor chases the field but never catches it: slip s = (Ns - Nr) / Ns. Rotor frequency is s f, torque is proportional to s R2 / (R2^2 + (s X2)^2), and maximum torque occurs at slip s_max = R2 / X2. Adding rotor resistance (slip-ring motor) raises starting torque and lowers starting current. No-load and blocked-rotor tests give the equivalent-circuit parameters.

Formula: Ns = 120 f / P; slip s = (Ns - Nr) / Ns; rotor frequency = s f; T proportional to s R2 / (R2^2 + (s X2)^2); maximum torque at s_max = R2 / X2.

Worked example: A 4-pole, 50 Hz motor has Ns = 1500 rpm. Running at Nr = 1440 rpm, slip s = (1500 - 1440) / 1500 = 0.04, and rotor frequency is 0.04 x 50 = 2 Hz.

instruction: What is Synchronous machines: regulation and parallel operation? Explain it briefly. [GATE EE - Electrical Machines]
response:
A synchronous generator runs exactly at synchronous speed, with frequency fixed by speed and pole count, f = P N / 120. Its terminal voltage falls with load because of armature reaction and synchronous reactance Xs; voltage regulation is (E - V) / V at constant excitation, often found by the synchronous-impedance method. Generators in parallel must match voltage, frequency, phase sequence and phase angle before synchronising, after which real power is shared by the prime mover input and reactive power by excitation.

Formula: f = P N / 120; regulation = (E - V) / V x 100 percent; power output P = (E V / Xs) sin(delta), where delta is the load (power) angle; E = V + j Ia Xs (cylindrical rotor, ignoring resistance).

Worked example: A generator with no-load voltage E = 253 V and full-load terminal voltage V = 230 V has regulation (253 - 230) / 230 = 10 percent. Raising excitation raises E and supplies more reactive power to the grid.

instruction: What is Transformer tests, regulation and efficiency? Explain it briefly. [GATE EE - Electrical Machines]
response:
The open-circuit test (rated voltage on one side, other side open) measures core (iron) loss and the magnetising branch, because copper loss is negligible at no-load current. The short-circuit test (rated current, low voltage) measures copper loss and the series impedance, because core loss is negligible at low voltage. Voltage regulation is the rise in secondary voltage from full load to no load at constant primary voltage; efficiency is output over output plus iron plus copper loss, and is maximum when iron loss equals copper loss.

Formula: OC test: iron loss Pi at rated V; SC test: copper loss Pcu at rated I; regulation = (V_no-load - V_full-load) / V_full-load x 100 percent; efficiency eta = output / (output + Pi + Pcu); maximum efficiency when Pi = Pcu.

Worked example: A transformer delivers 8 kW with iron loss 200 W and copper loss 300 W: eta = 8000 / (8000 + 200 + 300) = 8000 / 8500 = 94.1 percent. If the load halves, copper loss falls to one quarter, 75 W.

instruction: What is Per-unit quantities and bus admittance matrix? Explain it briefly. [GATE EE - Power Systems]
response:
Per-unit values express voltages, currents, impedances and powers as fractions of chosen base values, so transformers disappear from the numbers and equipment of very different ratings can be compared directly. Base impedance is V_base^2 / S_base, and a per-unit impedance changes with the square of the voltage-base ratio when the base changes. In load-flow work the network is described by the bus admittance matrix Ybus, where the diagonal element is the sum of admittances connected to that bus and an off-diagonal element is minus the admittance between the two buses.

Formula: pu value = actual value / base value; Z_base = V_base^2 / S_base; Z_pu(new) = Z_pu(old) x (S_base(new)/S_base(old)) x (V_base(old)/V_base(new))^2; Ybus_ii = sum of admittances at bus i; Ybus_ij = -y_ij.

Worked example: On a 10 MVA, 11 kV base, Z_base = 11^2 / 10 = 12.1 ohm. An impedance of 1.21 ohm is 1.21 / 12.1 = 0.1 pu.

instruction: What is Symmetrical components and fault analysis? Explain it briefly. [GATE EE - Power Systems]
response:
Any unbalanced three-phase set can be resolved into positive-, negative- and zero-sequence components using the operator a = e^{j120 deg}. A balanced system has only positive sequence; zero sequence needs a return path (neutral or earth) and is absent in a three-wire system. Fault currents are found by connecting the sequence networks: a single line-to-ground fault connects all three in series, a line-to-line fault connects positive and negative in parallel, and a three-phase fault uses positive sequence only.

Formula: a = e^{j120 deg} = -0.5 + j 0.866; V0 = (Va + Vb + Vc)/3; V1 = (Va + a Vb + a^2 Vc)/3; V2 = (Va + a^2 Vb + a Vc)/3; a^2 + a + 1 = 0.

Worked example: Va = 230 at 0 deg, Vb = 230 at -120 deg, Vc = 230 at 120 deg is balanced, so V1 = 230 V and V0 = V2 = 0. If Vc becomes 0 (a fault), zero and negative sequence components appear and the sequence networks must be solved together.

instruction: What is Equal area criterion for transient stability? Explain it briefly. [GATE EE - Power Systems]
response:
The swing equation describes the rotor angle of a synchronous machine: accelerating power Pm - Pe drives the angle, with inertia constant H. During a fault Pe collapses and the rotor gains kinetic energy, shown as the accelerating area A1 on the power-angle curve. After clearing, Pe exceeds Pm and the rotor gives the energy back, shown as the decelerating area A2. The machine stays in synchronism on the first swing if a decelerating area equal to A1 is available before the angle reaches the unstable equilibrium point.
