A current element produces magnetic field by the Biot-Savart law, and Ampere law gives B = mu_0 I/(2 pi r) around a long straight wire. A magnetic circuit follows MMF = N I driving flux through reluctance R = l/(mu A), and self-inductance is L = N Phi/I with mutual inductance M = k sqrt(L1 L2) between coupled coils.

Formula: integral_S D . dS = Q_enclosed; E = Q/(4 pi epsilon r^2) point charge; B = mu_0 I/(2 pi r) long wire; MMF = N I; reluctance R = l/(mu A); Phi = MMF/R; L = N Phi/I; M = k sqrt(L1 L2).

Worked example: A 1 uC point charge gives E = 9000 V/m at 1 m. A coil of 100 turns carrying 2 A (MMF 200 A-turns) on a core of reluctance 1e6 A-turns/Wb carries flux 0.2 mWb.

instruction: What is Kirchhoff laws, Thevenin, Norton, superposition and reciprocity? Explain it briefly. [GATE IN - Electrical Circuits]
response:
KCL says the currents entering a node sum to zero (charge conservation) and KVL says the voltages around a loop sum to zero (energy conservation); nodal and mesh analysis are systematic ways of writing these equations. Any linear network seen from two terminals is a Thevenin source Vth in series with Rth, or equivalently a Norton source IN = Vth/Rth in parallel with Rth. Superposition considers each independent source alone, and reciprocity says swapping a single source and the measurement point leaves the response unchanged. Maximum power is delivered when the load equals Rth (or the conjugate impedance for AC).

Formula: KCL: sum of currents at a node = 0; KVL: sum of voltages around a loop = 0; Vth = open-circuit voltage; Rth = Vth/I_sc; IN = Vth/Rth; maximum power when R_L = Rth, P_max = Vth^2/(4 Rth).

Worked example: A network with Vth = 12 V and Rth = 4 ohm delivers maximum power 12^2/(4 x 4) = 9 W to a 4 ohm load, at 50 percent efficiency.

instruction: What is Phasor analysis, resonance, locus diagrams and RLC filters? Explain it briefly. [GATE IN - Electrical Circuits]
response:
In sinusoidal steady state, impedances are complex (j omega L, 1/(j omega C)) and voltages and currents are phasors. Apparent power S = P + jQ, with P the average power and Q the reactive power; series and parallel resonance both occur at f0 = 1/(2 pi sqrt(LC)), where the impedance is purely resistive. A locus diagram traces the tip of the current or voltage phasor as a parameter (such as frequency or resistance) varies. Simple RC and RL networks are first-order low-pass or high-pass filters with cutoff fc = 1/(2 pi RC) (or R/(2 pi L)), passing frequencies below (or above) the cutoff with -3 dB at fc.

Formula: Z_L = j omega L; Z_C = 1/(j omega C); S = V_rms I_rms* = P + jQ; f0 = 1/(2 pi sqrt(LC)); RC low-pass cutoff fc = 1/(2 pi RC); at fc the output is 1/sqrt(2) (about -3 dB) of the input.

Worked example: An RC low-pass with R = 1 k ohm and C = 0.16 uF has fc = 1/(2 pi x 1000 x 0.16e-6) = about 995 Hz. At 995 Hz a 10 V input gives about 7.07 V out; at 10 kHz it gives about 1 V.

instruction: What is Single-phase transformer and three-phase induction motor? Explain it briefly. [GATE IN - Electrical Circuits]
response:
A transformer transfers power by mutual induction: V2/V1 = N2/N1 = I1/I2 for an ideal transformer. The open-circuit test (rated voltage, secondary open) gives iron loss and the magnetising branch; the short-circuit test (rated current, low voltage) gives copper loss and series impedance. Voltage regulation is (V_no-load - V_full-load)/V_full-load, and efficiency is maximum when iron loss equals copper loss. A three-phase induction motor runs at slip s = (Ns - Nr)/Ns with Ns = 120 f/P; torque is proportional to s R2/(R2^2 + (s X2)^2), maximum at s = R2/X2, and the no-load and blocked-rotor tests give the equivalent circuit.

Formula: V2/V1 = N2/N1; regulation = (V_nl - V_fl)/V_fl x 100 percent; eta = output/(output + Pi + Pcu), maximum when Pi = Pcu; Ns = 120 f/P; s = (Ns - Nr)/Ns; rotor frequency = s f.

Worked example: A 4-pole, 50 Hz motor has Ns = 1500 rpm; at Nr = 1440 rpm, slip is 0.04 and rotor frequency is 2 Hz. A transformer delivering 8 kW with 200 W iron and 300 W copper loss is 8000/8500 = 94.1 percent efficient.

instruction: What is Laplace, Fourier and Z-transforms? Explain it briefly. [GATE IN - Signals & Systems]
response:
The Laplace transform turns differential equations into algebra (differentiation becomes multiplication by s, minus initial values), the Fourier transform decomposes a signal into frequencies (convolution becomes multiplication), and the Z-transform does the same for discrete-time signals and difference equations. The transfer function H(s) = Y(s)/X(s) is the Laplace transform of the impulse response, and poles in the left half-plane mean stability for continuous systems, inside the unit circle for discrete ones. The region of convergence decides causality and stability of a Z-transform.

Formula: Laplace: X(s) = integral_0^inf x(t) e^{-s t} dt; L{dx/dt} = s X(s) - x(0); Fourier: X(omega) = integral x(t) e^{-j omega t} dt; Z: X(z) = sum x[n] z^{-n}; a^n u[n] <-> 1/(1 - a z^{-1}), ROC |z| > |a|.

Worked example: y' + 2y = 0 with y(0) = 3 gives Y(s) = 3/(s + 2), so y(t) = 3 e^{-2t}. The discrete sequence (0.5)^n u[n] has Z-transform z/(z - 0.5) with pole at 0.5, inside the unit circle, so it is stable.

instruction: What is Impulse response, convolution and correlation? Explain it briefly. [GATE IN - Signals & Systems]
response:
The impulse response h(t) of an LTI system is its output for a unit impulse, and the output for any input is the convolution of the input with h. In the frequency domain convolution becomes multiplication by the transfer function H, whose magnitude and phase give the frequency response; first-order systems roll off at 20 dB/decade past their corner, second-order at 40 dB/decade. Correlation measures similarity between two signals as a function of lag: autocorrelation peaks at zero lag with the signal power, and cross-correlation peaks at the lag where the signals best align, which is how time delay is measured.

Formula: y(t) = integral x(tau) h(t - tau) d tau; y[n] = sum_k x[k] h[n-k]; H(s) = Y(s)/X(s); autocorrelation R_xx(tau) = integral x(t) x(t + tau) dt, R_xx(0) = signal power.

Worked example: x = [1, 2] convolved with h = [1, 1] gives y = [1, 3, 2]. The autocorrelation of a signal at zero lag equals its energy; a delayed copy of a signal cross-correlates maximally at a lag equal to the delay.

instruction: What is DFT, FFT, IIR and FIR digital filters? Explain it briefly. [GATE IN - Signals & Systems]
response:
The DFT samples the DTFT at N equally spaced frequencies, X[k] = sum_{n=0}^{N-1} x[n] e^{-j 2 pi k n / N}, and the FFT computes it in O(N log N). FIR filters use only feedforward taps, so they are always stable and can have exactly linear phase, but need many taps for sharp cutoffs. IIR filters use feedback, so they achieve sharp cutoffs with few coefficients but can be unstable and have non-linear phase. Filter design starts from the required passband, stopband and transition width, then picks the order and the window (FIR) or prototype (IIR, e.g. Butterworth or Chebyshev).

Formula: DFT: X[k] = sum_{n=0}^{N-1} x[n] e^{-j 2 pi k n / N}; FIR: y[n] = sum_{k=0}^{M} b_k x[n-k]; IIR: y[n] = sum b_k x[n-k] - sum a_k y[n-k]; FIR always stable, linear phase possible; IIR stable iff poles inside the unit circle.

Worked example: x = [1, 0, 1, 0], N = 4: X[0] = 2, X[1] = 0, X[2] = 2, X[3] = 0. A 3-tap moving-average FIR y[n] = (x[n] + x[n-1] + x[n-2])/3 is a simple low-pass filter.

instruction: What is Signal flow graphs and Mason gain formula? Explain it briefly. [GATE IN - Control Systems]
response:
A signal flow graph represents a system as nodes (signals) joined by directed branches (gains). Mason gain formula gives the overall transfer function from the forward paths and loops: sum over forward paths of (path gain x its cofactor) divided by the determinant Delta. Delta is 1 minus the sum of individual loop gains, plus the sum of products of pairs of non-touching loops, minus the sum of products of triples of non-touching loops, and so on; a path cofactor is Delta with all loops touching that path removed.

Formula: T = (sum_k M_k Delta_k) / Delta; Delta = 1 - sum L1 + sum L2 - sum L3 + ...; M_k = gain of k-th forward path; Delta_k = Delta with loops touching path k removed.

Worked example: A system with one forward path of gain 10 and one feedback loop of gain -2 has Delta = 1 - (-2) = 3 and T = 10/3 = 3.33. Adding a second loop that does not touch the first contributes its product to Delta.

instruction: What is Stability criteria, compensators, state space and time-delay systems? Explain it briefly. [GATE IN - Control Systems]
response:
Routh-Hurwitz tests stability from the characteristic polynomial (no sign changes in the first column means stable); Nyquist counts encirclements of -1 by the open-loop frequency response; root locus traces closed-loop poles as gain varies. Bode plots give gain and phase margins, the usual robustness measures. Lead compensation adds phase near crossover and speeds up the response, lag raises low-frequency gain and cuts steady-state error, and lag-lead does both. In state space, x-dot = A x + B u and y = C x + D u, and stability is decided by the eigenvalues of A. A pure time delay e^{-sT} adds phase lag proportional to frequency and hurts stability margins.

Formula: Routh: stable iff first column has no sign changes; Nyquist: Z = N + P, stable iff Z = 0; phase margin = 180 deg + angle G(j omega_gc); state space: x-dot = A x + B u, y = C x + D u; delay: e^{-sT} adds phase -omega T.

Worked example: s^3 + 4 s^2 + 5 s + 2 has Routh rows 1, 5; 4, 2; 4.5; 2, all positive in the first column, so it is stable. A 0.1 s delay at 10 rad/s adds phase lag of 1 rad, about 57 deg, which can erase a phase margin.

instruction: What is Diode, Zener diode, BJT and MOSFET: characteristics and small-signal analysis? Explain it briefly. [GATE IN - Instrumentation]
response:
A diode conducts exponentially in forward bias, I = Is (e^{V/(eta Vt)} - 1) with Vt about 26 mV at 300 K, and blocks in reverse until breakdown; a Zener diode breaks down at a controlled reverse voltage and regulates it. A BJT in active mode has Ic = beta Ib and transconductance gm = Ic/Vt, so it is a current-controlled current source. A MOSFET in saturation has Id = (1/2) mu Cox (W/L) (Vgs - Vth)^2 and is voltage-controlled. Small-signal analysis replaces each device by its gm and output resistance to find gain and input/output resistance; feedback trades gain for bandwidth, linearity and stable resistance.

Formula: Diode: I = Is (e^{V/(eta Vt)} - 1); BJT: Ic = beta Ib, gm = Ic/Vt; MOSFET saturation: Id = (1/2) mu Cox (W/L)(Vgs - Vth)^2, gm = 2 Id/(Vgs - Vth); common-emitter gain about -gm Rc.

Worked example: A BJT at Ic = 2 mA has gm = 2e-3/0.026 = about 77 mS, so with Rc = 1 k ohm the voltage gain is about -77. A 5.1 V Zener holds about 5.1 V across its load in reverse breakdown.

instruction: What is Op-amp applications, instrumentation amplifier, PLL and noise? Explain it briefly. [GATE IN - Instrumentation]
response:
An ideal op-amp with negative feedback keeps its inputs at equal voltage and draws no input current, giving adder, subtractor, integrator (Vo = -1/(RC) integral Vi dt), differentiator, difference amplifier and precision rectifier (a diode inside the loop removes the 0.7 V diode drop). An instrumentation amplifier uses two non-inverting stages plus a difference stage to give high input impedance, high CMRR and gain set by one resistor Rg. A phase-locked loop locks a VCO to a reference: with a divide-by-N counter in the loop, f_out = N f_ref. Noise in circuits comes from thermal noise (4 k T R per hertz), shot noise and 1/f noise, and shielding and grounding keep interference out of low-level measurements.

Formula: Inverting gain = -Rf/R1; non-inverting = 1 + Rf/R1; integrator Vo = -(1/RC) integral Vi dt; instrumentation amplifier gain = (1 + 2R/Rg) x (Rf/R1); PLL: f_out = N f_ref; thermal noise voltage density = sqrt(4 k T R) V/sqrt(Hz).

Worked example: An instrumentation amplifier with R = 10 k ohm and Rg = 1 k ohm and a unity second stage has gain 1 + 20 = 21, so a 10 mV bridge output becomes 210 mV. A PLL with f_ref = 1 MHz and N = 50 outputs 50 MHz.

instruction: What is Active filters, oscillators and signal generators? Explain it briefly. [GATE IN - Instrumentation]
response:
Active filters use op-amps with RC networks instead of inductors: a first-order stage rolls off at 20 dB/decade, a second-order Sallen-Key stage at 40 dB/decade, with fc = 1/(2 pi sqrt(R1 R2 C1 C2)) and Q = 0.707 for a Butterworth (maximally flat) response. An oscillator needs loop gain of at least 1 with zero total phase shift (Barkhausen criterion); RC phase-shift and Wien-bridge oscillators set frequency with RC networks, and LC oscillators with a tank circuit. A voltage-controlled oscillator tunes its frequency with a control voltage, and a function generator combines oscillators, integrators and comparators to produce sine, square and triangle waves.

Formula: Sallen-Key low-pass: fc = 1/(2 pi sqrt(R1 R2 C1 C2)); Butterworth Q = 0.707; Barkhausen: loop gain >= 1 at 0 deg (360 deg) total phase; Wien bridge: f0 = 1/(2 pi RC); first-order roll-off 20 dB/decade, second-order 40 dB/decade.

Worked example: A Sallen-Key low-pass with R1 = R2 = 15.9 k ohm and C1 = C2 = 10 nF has fc = 1/(2 pi x 15900 x 10e-9) = about 1000 Hz. A Wien-bridge oscillator with R = 16 k ohm and C = 10 nF oscillates near 995 Hz.

instruction: What is Boolean minimisation and IC families: TTL and CMOS? Explain it briefly. [GATE IN - Instrumentation]
response:
Boolean functions are minimised with algebra or Karnaugh maps, grouping 1s in powers of two (pairs, quads, octets) with wrap-around and don't-care cells, to get the smallest sum-of-products form. TTL logic uses bipolar transistors, runs on 5 V, and has fast switching but higher static power; CMOS uses complementary PMOS/NMOS pairs, draws almost no static power, has high noise margins and wide supply range, and dominates modern digital ICs. Key datasheet figures are propagation delay, fan-out (how many inputs one output can drive), noise margin and power dissipation.

Formula: De Morgan: NOT(A B) = (NOT A) + (NOT B); K-map groups must be powers of 2; CMOS static power about 0, dynamic power = C V^2 f; TTL supply 5 V, typical noise margin about 0.4 V.

Worked example: F = sum m(1,3,5,7) over three variables is 1 exactly when C = 1, so the minimised form is F = C. A CMOS gate switching 10 pF at 5 V and 10 MHz dissipates about 10e-12 x 25 x 10e6 = 2.5 mW of dynamic power.

instruction: What is Sequential circuits, multivibrators, timers and counters? Explain it briefly. [GATE IN - Instrumentation]
response:
Flip-flops (D, JK, T) store one bit on a clock edge; latches are level-sensitive. Shift registers move bits along on each clock, counters divide the clock (a mod-n counter needs ceil(log2 n) flip-flops), and comparators and Schmitt triggers clean up and compare levels. An astable multivibrator free-runs as a clock; the 555 timer in astable mode gives frequency f = 1.44/((R1 + 2 R2) C) with duty cycle set by R1 and R2. Setup and hold times must be met, and the critical path sets the maximum clock frequency.

Formula: Mod-n counter needs ceil(log2 n) flip-flops; 555 astable: f = 1.44 / ((R1 + 2 R2) C); T = 0.693 (R1 + 2 R2) C; f_max = 1 / (t_clk-to-Q + t_comb(max) + t_setup).

Worked example: A 555 astable with R1 = 1 k ohm, R2 = 10 k ohm and C = 10 uF gives T = 0.693 x (1000 + 20000) x 10e-6 = 0.146 s, so f = about 6.9 Hz. A mod-10 counter needs 4 flip-flops.

instruction: What is ADCs, DACs, embedded systems, DCS and PLC? Explain it briefly. [GATE IN - Instrumentation]
response:
An ADC quantises an analog voltage into an n-bit code with step LSB = Vref/2^n: successive-approximation ADCs are the common middle ground, flash ADCs are fastest (2^n - 1 comparators), integrating (dual-slope) ADCs are slow but reject mains noise, and sigma-delta ADCs oversample for high resolution. DACs use weighted resistors or an R-2R ladder. Key ADC/DAC figures are resolution, quantisation error (+/- LSB/2), conversion/settling time and effective number of bits. A microprocessor/microcontroller runs the data-acquisition system: sensor, signal conditioning, ADC, processor, memory and I/O; a DCS distributes control across many controllers in a plant, and a PLC runs rugged ladder-logic control of machines and processes.

Formula: ADC LSB = Vref / 2^n; quantisation error <= LSB/2; flash comparators = 2^n - 1; DAC R-2R output steps by Vref/2^n per LSB; sample-and-hold freezes the input during conversion.

Worked example: A 10-bit ADC with Vref = 5 V has LSB = 5/1024 = 4.88 mV, so a 1.00 V input reads about code 205. A 4-bit flash ADC needs 15 comparators.

instruction: What is AC bridges: Maxwell, Anderson, Schering, Wien and Q-meter? Explain it briefly. [GATE IN - Measurements]
response:
AC bridges measure inductance, capacitance and frequency by balancing arms at null, like the Wheatstone bridge does for resistance. The Maxwell bridge measures inductance against a known capacitance (Lx = R2 R3 C1); the Anderson bridge is a modified Maxwell that suits low-Q coils; the Schering bridge measures capacitance and dissipation factor (tan delta); the Wien bridge measures frequency, f = 1/(2 pi RC), and is also the basis of the Wien-bridge oscillator. A Q-meter measures the quality factor of a coil directly by resonance: Q = Vc/V, the ratio of the capacitor voltage to the applied voltage at resonance.

Formula: Maxwell bridge: Lx = R2 R3 C1; Schering bridge: Cx = C1 (R3/R4), tan(delta) = omega C1 R1; Wien bridge: f = 1/(2 pi R C); Q-meter: Q = Vc / V at resonance; Q = omega L / R for a coil.

Worked example: A Maxwell bridge with R2 = 100 ohm, R3 = 200 ohm and C1 = 1 uF measures Lx = 100 x 200 x 1e-6 = 20 mH. A Wien bridge with R = 16 k ohm and C = 10 nF balances at f = 1/(2 pi x 16000 x 10e-9) = about 995 Hz.

instruction: What is Instrument transformers, true-RMS meters, timer/counter and oscilloscope? Explain it briefly. [GATE IN - Measurements]
response:
Instrument transformers scale high voltages and currents down for meters: a potential transformer (PT) scales voltage by its turns ratio, a current transformer (CT) scales current, and its secondary must never be open-circuited while the primary carries current. A true-RMS meter reads the RMS value of any waveform, while an average-responding meter is calibrated for sine waves only and reads wrong on distorted waveforms. A timer/counter measures frequency, period and time interval by counting cycles against a reference clock. An oscilloscope shows voltage against time (or X-Y), with time base, volts/division, triggering and bandwidth setting what can be seen; shielding and grounding keep interference out of the measurement.

Formula: PT: V_secondary = V_primary x (N2/N1); CT: I_secondary = I_primary x (N1/N2); true RMS = sqrt(mean of v^2); frequency = counts / gate time; oscilloscope bandwidth should exceed the highest signal frequency of interest.

Worked example: A 100/5 A CT with 4 A in its secondary carries 4 x (100/5) = 80 A in the primary. A timer counting 50000 cycles in a 1 s gate reads 50 kHz.

instruction: What is Sensors: resistive, capacitive, inductive, piezoelectric and Hall effect? Explain it briefly. [GATE IN - Instrumentation]
response:
Resistive sensors change resistance with the measured quantity (strain gauge, RTD, thermistor, LDR); capacitive sensors change C = epsilon A/d with gap or overlap or dielectric; inductive sensors change inductance with a moving core (LVDT gives a linear AC output versus core position); piezoelectric sensors generate charge under force or vibration (high impedance, needs a charge amplifier); Hall sensors give a voltage proportional to magnetic field times current. Signal conditioning matches the sensor to the ADC: bridge completion, amplification (often an instrumentation amplifier), filtering, isolation and linearisation.

Formula: Capacitance C = epsilon A / d; Hall voltage V_H = I B / (n q t); piezoelectric charge Q = d x F (d = piezoelectric coefficient); LVDT output is linear in core displacement with a null at centre; strain gauge: delta R/R = G_f x strain.

Worked example: A parallel-plate sensor with A = 1 cm^2, d = 1 mm in air has C = 8.85e-12 x 1e-4 / 1e-3 = 0.885 pF; halving the gap doubles the capacitance to 1.77 pF. A Hall sensor with a 10 mA current in a 0.1 T field gives a voltage proportional to B, used to measure current without breaking the circuit.

instruction: What is Temperature measurement: thermocouple, RTD, thermistor, pyrometer and bolometer? Explain it briefly. [GATE IN - Instrumentation]
response:
A thermocouple joins two dissimilar metals; the Seebeck effect gives a voltage roughly proportional to the temperature difference between the hot junction and the cold (reference) junction, so the reference temperature must be known or compensated. An RTD (usually Pt100, 100 ohm at 0 C) has resistance rising almost linearly with temperature, R = R0 (1 + alpha T) with alpha = 0.00385 per deg C for platinum, and 3- or 4-wire connection cancels lead resistance. A thermistor is a semiconductor whose resistance falls steeply (NTC) with temperature, very sensitive over a narrow range. A pyrometer measures temperature from thermal radiation without contact, and a bolometer detects radiation by the heating it causes.

Formula: Thermocouple: V about S x (T_hot - T_ref), S = Seebeck coefficient; RTD: R = R0 (1 + alpha T), Pt100 alpha = 0.00385 /deg C; thermistor (NTC): R falls exponentially with T; radiation: emitted power proportional to T^4 (Stefan-Boltzmann).

Worked example: A Pt100 at 100 C reads R = 100 x (1 + 0.00385 x 100) = 138.5 ohm. A type-K thermocouple gives about 41 uV per deg C, so a 250 deg C difference gives about 10.3 mV.

instruction: What is Flow, pressure, level, pH, conductivity and viscosity measurement? Explain it briefly. [GATE IN - Instrumentation]
response:
Variable-head meters (orifice, venturi) infer flow from the pressure drop, Q proportional to sqrt(delta p); variable-area (rotameter) meters read flow from a float position; electromagnetic meters use the voltage induced in a conductive fluid moving in a magnetic field, E = B d v; turbine meters count rotor speed; ultrasonic meters use transit time or Doppler shift; open-channel meters use a weir or flume. Pressure is measured by Bourdon tubes, diaphragms and strain-gauge transducers, and very low pressure by a McLeod gauge. Liquid level uses floats, capacitance, ultrasonic or differential pressure. pH is measured with a glass electrode (about 59 mV per pH at 25 C), conductivity with a conductance cell, and viscosity with rotational or capillary viscometers.

Formula: Orifice/venturi: Q proportional to sqrt(delta p); electromagnetic: E = B d v; turbine: flow proportional to rotor frequency; pH electrode: about 59.16 mV per pH unit at 25 C (Nernst); differential-pressure level: delta p = rho g h.

Worked example: A venturi whose differential pressure quadruples has its flow doubled, since Q is proportional to sqrt(delta p). A tank of water 2 m deep gives a differential pressure of 1000 x 9.81 x 2 = 19.6 kPa at the bottom.

instruction: What is Modulation, PCM, multiplexing and digital modulation? Explain it briefly. [GATE IN - Instrumentation]
response:
Amplitude modulation varies the carrier amplitude with the message, frequency modulation varies its frequency; both shift the message to a carrier frequency for transmission, and Shannon sampling theorem says a bandlimited signal is recovered from samples taken faster than twice its highest frequency. Pulse code modulation samples, quantises and encodes the signal into bits, with bit rate = sampling frequency x bits per sample. Frequency-division multiplexing stacks channels in frequency, time-division multiplexing interleaves them in time. Digital modulation (ASK, PSK, FSK, QAM) maps bits to carrier amplitude, phase, frequency or combinations, with QAM packing the most bits per symbol.

Formula: Sampling theorem: fs > 2 f_max; PCM bit rate = fs x n bits; AM bandwidth = 2 f_m; FM Carson bandwidth about 2 (delta_f + f_m); FDM stacks in frequency, TDM interleaves in time.

Worked example: Telephone PCM samples at 8 kHz with 8 bits per sample, giving a bit rate of 64 kbps. An AM signal carrying 5 kHz audio occupies 10 kHz of bandwidth.

instruction: What is Optical instrumentation: sources, detectors, interferometry, fibre sensing and spectrometry? Explain it briefly. [GATE IN - Instrumentation]
response:
Optical sources are LEDs (incoherent, broad spectrum) and lasers (coherent, narrow spectrum); detectors are photodiodes (current proportional to light), light-dependent resistors (resistance falls with light) and square-law detectors (output proportional to optical power). An interferometer splits light into two paths and recombines it; the fringe shift measures displacement or refractive-index change to a fraction of a wavelength, which is the basis of precision metrology and fibre-optic sensing (where the measurand changes the fibre phase, intensity or wavelength). A UV-VIS spectrophotometer measures absorbance (Beer-Lambert law, A = epsilon c l), and a mass spectrometer separates ions by mass-to-charge ratio m/z, giving composition from the mass spectrum.

Formula: Beer-Lambert: A = epsilon c l; interferometer fringe shift: one fringe per half-wavelength of path change (delta = lambda/2 per fringe); mass spectrometer: ions separated by m/z; photodiode current proportional to incident optical power.

Worked example: A solution with molar absorptivity 1000 L/mol/cm in a 1 cm cuvette at 0.001 mol/L has absorbance A = 1000 x 0.001 x 1 = 1, so it transmits 10 percent of the light. An interferometer with 600 nm light moves one fringe per 300 nm of mirror displacement.

instruction: Give a worked example for Wheatstone bridge balance condition [GATE IN - Measurements]
response:
Worked example: With R1 = 100 ohm, R2 = 200 ohm and R3 = 150 ohm at balance, the unknown resistance R4 = R2 * R3 / R1 = 200 * 150 / 100 = 300 ohm.

Formula: Balance condition: R1 / R2 = R3 / R4, where R1, R2, R3 and R4 are the four arm resistances. Unknown resistance Rx = R2 * R3 / R1 (with the labelling R1 / R2 = R3 / Rx). At balance the galvanometer current is zero.

A Wheatstone bridge has four resistors in a diamond, with a supply across one diagonal and a galvanometer across the other. It is balanced when no current flows through the galvanometer, which happens when the two voltage dividers give equal midpoint voltages. At balance an unknown resistance can be found accurately from the three known resistances.

instruction: Give a worked example for ADC resolution and LSB step size [GATE IN - Instrumentation]
response:
Worked example: A 10-bit ADC with Vref = 5 V has 2^10 = 1024 levels and LSB = 5 / 1024 = 0.00488 V, about 4.88 mV per count.

Formula: Number of levels = 2^N. LSB step = Vref / 2^N (for a unipolar range 0 to Vref), where N is the number of bits and Vref is the reference voltage. Maximum quantisation error is about plus or minus LSB / 2.

An N-bit ADC divides its full-scale input range into 2^N discrete levels. The resolution, or one LSB step, is the smallest change in input voltage that changes the output code by one count. More bits give a smaller step and smaller quantisation error, at the cost of slower or more expensive conversion.

instruction: Give a worked example for Strain gauge and gauge factor [GATE IN - Instrumentation]
response:
Worked example: A 120 ohm gauge with GF = 2 is strained by epsilon = 0.001 (1000 microstrain). Delta R = 2 * 120 * 0.001 = 0.24 ohm, so the resistance becomes 120.24 ohm.

Formula: Gauge factor GF = (Delta R / R) / (Delta L / L) = (Delta R / R) / epsilon, where epsilon = Delta L / L is strain (dimensionless). Change in resistance: Delta R = GF * R * epsilon. Typical GF is about 2 for metallic gauges.

A strain gauge is a resistive transducer whose resistance changes when it is stretched or compressed. The gauge factor relates the fractional change in resistance to the mechanical strain, and for common metallic foil gauges it is about 2. Because the resistance change is tiny, strain gauges are usually read with a Wheatstone bridge.

instruction: Give a worked example for Measurement error: absolute, relative and percentage error [GATE IN - Measurements]
response:
Worked example: A voltmeter reads 10.2 V for a true voltage of 10.0 V. Absolute error = 0.2 V and percentage error = (0.2 / 10.0) * 100 = 2 percent.

Formula: Absolute error = measured value - true value. Relative error = absolute error / true value. Percentage error = (absolute error / true value) * 100 percent.

Absolute error is the difference between the measured value and the true value, while relative error expresses that difference as a fraction of the true value. Percentage error is the relative error multiplied by 100 and is the usual way to report accuracy. Systematic errors repeat in the same direction, while random errors vary unpredictably.

instruction: Give a worked example for PID controller [GATE IN - Control Systems]
response:
Worked example: With Kp = 2 and an instantaneous error e = 0.5, the proportional term alone contributes Kp * e = 2 * 0.5 = 1 unit to the control output at that instant.

Formula: u(t) = Kp * e(t) + Ki * integral of e(t) dt + Kd * de(t)/dt, where u(t) is the control output, e(t) is the error, and Kp, Ki and Kd are the proportional, integral and derivative gains. In the s-domain: U(s)/E(s) = Kp + Ki/s + Kd * s.

A PID controller combines proportional, integral and derivative action on the error between setpoint and measured output. The proportional term reacts to the present error, the integral term removes steady-state error by acting on past error, and the derivative term damps overshoot by acting on the rate of change of error. It is the most widely used controller in industry.

instruction: Give a worked example for Nyquist sampling theorem for data acquisition [GATE IN - Signals & Systems]
response:
Worked example: A vibration signal has fm = 3 kHz, so the minimum sampling rate is 2 * 3 = 6 kHz. Sampling at 10 kHz satisfies the theorem with margin.

Formula: fs >= 2 * fm, where fs is sampling frequency and fm is the highest frequency in the signal. Nyquist rate = 2 * fm. Nyquist frequency = fs / 2.

To digitise an analogue signal without losing information, it must be sampled at least twice as fast as its highest frequency component. Sampling slower causes aliasing, in which higher frequencies appear as lower ones in the sampled data. Practical data-acquisition systems therefore use an anti-aliasing filter before the ADC and sample above the Nyquist rate.

instruction: Give a worked example for Ohm's law for measurement circuits [GATE IN - Electrical Circuits]
response:
Worked example: A current of 2 A flows through a 0.1 ohm shunt resistor. The voltage across the shunt is V = 2 * 0.1 = 0.2 V, which a voltmeter can measure to infer the current.

Formula: V = I * R, I = V / R, R = V / I. Voltage divider: Vout = Vin * R2 / (R1 + R2). Power: P = V * I = I^2 * R.

Ohm's law is the basic relation used to size shunts, series resistors and loads in measurement circuits. A current is often measured as the voltage drop across a known shunt resistor, and a voltage is scaled down with a resistive divider. The law holds for linear resistors at constant temperature.

instruction: Give a worked example for Linear algebra: matrix algebra, rank, eigenvalues [GATE IN - Engineering Mathematics]
response:
Worked example: A = [[1, 2], [2, 4]] has rank 1 (second row is twice the first) and determinant 0, so it is singular and has eigenvalue 0. Its other eigenvalue is the trace, 5.

Formula: Consistent iff rank(A) = rank([A | b]); unique iff rank = n; det(A - lambda I) = 0; det(A) = product of eigenvalues; trace(A) = sum of eigenvalues.

The rank of a matrix is the number of independent rows or columns. A system A x = b is consistent if and only if rank(A) = rank([A|b]), with a unique solution when the rank equals the number of unknowns. Eigenvalues come from det(A - lambda I) = 0; their product is the determinant and their sum is the trace. Eigenvectors give the directions a matrix only scales, which is how vibration modes and system poles are understood.

instruction: Give a worked example for Fourier series and vector integral theorems [GATE IN - Engineering Mathematics]
response:
Worked example: A square wave of amplitude 1 is odd, so its Fourier series is (4/pi)[sin x + sin 3x/3 + sin 5x/5 + ...]. For F = (x, y, z), div F = 3, so flux out of the unit sphere is 3 x (4 pi/3) = 4 pi.

Formula: f(x) = a0/2 + sum [a_n cos(n pi x / L) + b_n sin(n pi x / L)]; Gauss: integral_V div F dV = integral_S F . dS; Stokes: integral_S curl F . dS = integral_C F . dr; Green: integral_C (P dx + Q dy) = integral_D (dQ/dx - dP/dy) dA.

A periodic function expands into sines and cosines; even functions need only cosines, odd functions only sines, and the coefficients come from integrating over one period. The vector theorems convert between integrals: Gauss turns a volume integral of divergence into surface flux, Stokes turns a surface integral of curl into a line integral around the boundary, and Green is the planar form of Stokes. These are the integral forms behind Gauss law and Faraday law.

instruction: Give a worked example for Complex variables: analytic functions and residue theorem [GATE IN - Engineering Mathematics]
response:
Worked example: f(z) = 1/(z^2 + 1) has a simple pole at z = i with residue 1/(2i). On a small circle around i only, the integral is 2 pi i x 1/(2i) = pi.

Formula: Cauchy-Riemann: du/dx = dv/dy, du/dy = -dv/dx; integral_C f(z) dz = 2 pi i x sum of residues; Res at simple pole z0 = lim_{z->z0} (z - z0) f(z); Cauchy integral formula: f(a) = (1/2 pi i) integral_C f(z)/(z - a) dz.

A function is analytic where it satisfies the Cauchy-Riemann equations; such functions have Taylor expansions, and functions with isolated singularities have Laurent expansions including negative powers. The residue theorem says the integral around a closed contour equals 2 pi i times the sum of residues at singularities inside it, and the residue at a simple pole z0 is the limit of (z - z0) f(z). This evaluates real integrals of rational and trigonometric functions that are hard to do directly.

instruction: Give a worked example for Numerical methods: matrix inversion, nonlinear equations, integration and regression [GATE IN - Engineering Mathematics]
response:
Worked example: Solving x^2 - 2 = 0 from x0 = 1.5: x1 = 1.5 - 0.25/3 = 1.4167, already close to sqrt(2) = 1.4142. Trapezoidal rule on x^2 from 0 to 1 with h = 0.5 gives (0.25)[0 + 2 x 0.25 + 1] = 0.375, against the exact 1/3.

Formula: Newton-Raphson: x_{n+1} = x_n - f(x_n)/f'(x_n); trapezoidal: integral about (h/2)[f0 + 2 f1 + ... + 2 f_{n-1} + fn]; Simpson: integral about (h/3)[f0 + 4 f1 + 2 f2 + 4 f3 + ... + fn]; least squares slope b = sum (x - xbar)(y - ybar) / sum (x - xbar)^2.

Newton-Raphson solves f(x) = 0 by iterating x_{n+1} = x_n - f(x_n)/f'(x_n), converging fast near a simple root but needing a good start and a non-zero derivative. Matrix inversion (Gauss-Jordan) solves linear systems directly. Numerical integration uses the trapezoidal rule (error order h^2) or Simpson rule (error order h^4, needs an even number of intervals). Linear regression fits y = a + b x by least squares, minimising the sum of squared residuals, and correlation r in [-1, 1] measures linear association.

instruction: Give a worked example for Electricity and magnetism: Gauss law, Biot-Savart law and magnetic circuits [GATE IN - Electrical Circuits]
response:
Worked example: A 1 uC point charge gives E = 9000 V/m at 1 m. A coil of 100 turns carrying 2 A (MMF 200 A-turns) on a core of reluctance 1e6 A-turns/Wb carries flux 0.2 mWb.

Formula: integral_S D . dS = Q_enclosed; E = Q/(4 pi epsilon r^2) point charge; B = mu_0 I/(2 pi r) long wire; MMF = N I; reluctance R = l/(mu A); Phi = MMF/R; L = N Phi/I; M = k sqrt(L1 L2).

Gauss law says the electric flux through a closed surface equals the enclosed charge over epsilon; by symmetry a point charge gives E = Q/(4 pi epsilon r^2), a line charge gives E falling as 1/r, and a plane sheet gives a constant field. A current element produces magnetic field by the Biot-Savart law, and Ampere law gives B = mu_0 I/(2 pi r) around a long straight wire. A magnetic circuit follows MMF = N I driving flux through reluctance R = l/(mu A), and self-inductance is L = N Phi/I with mutual inductance M = k sqrt(L1 L2) between coupled coils.

instruction: Give a worked example for Kirchhoff laws, Thevenin, Norton, superposition and reciprocity [GATE IN - Electrical Circuits]
response:
Worked example: A network with Vth = 12 V and Rth = 4 ohm delivers maximum power 12^2/(4 x 4) = 9 W to a 4 ohm load, at 50 percent efficiency.

Formula: KCL: sum of currents at a node = 0; KVL: sum of voltages around a loop = 0; Vth = open-circuit voltage; Rth = Vth/I_sc; IN = Vth/Rth; maximum power when R_L = Rth, P_max = Vth^2/(4 Rth).

KCL says the currents entering a node sum to zero (charge conservation) and KVL says the voltages around a loop sum to zero (energy conservation); nodal and mesh analysis are systematic ways of writing these equations. Any linear network seen from two terminals is a Thevenin source Vth in series with Rth, or equivalently a Norton source IN = Vth/Rth in parallel with Rth. Superposition considers each independent source alone, and reciprocity says swapping a single source and the measurement point leaves the response unchanged. Maximum power is delivered when the load equals Rth (or the conjugate impedance for AC).

instruction: Give a worked example for Phasor analysis, resonance, locus diagrams and RLC filters [GATE IN - Electrical Circuits]
response:
Worked example: An RC low-pass with R = 1 k ohm and C = 0.16 uF has fc = 1/(2 pi x 1000 x 0.16e-6) = about 995 Hz. At 995 Hz a 10 V input gives about 7.07 V out; at 10 kHz it gives about 1 V.

Formula: Z_L = j omega L; Z_C = 1/(j omega C); S = V_rms I_rms* = P + jQ; f0 = 1/(2 pi sqrt(LC)); RC low-pass cutoff fc = 1/(2 pi RC); at fc the output is 1/sqrt(2) (about -3 dB) of the input.

In sinusoidal steady state, impedances are complex (j omega L, 1/(j omega C)) and voltages and currents are phasors. Apparent power S = P + jQ, with P the average power and Q the reactive power; series and parallel resonance both occur at f0 = 1/(2 pi sqrt(LC)), where the impedance is purely resistive. A locus diagram traces the tip of the current or voltage phasor as a parameter (such as frequency or resistance) varies. Simple RC and RL networks are first-order low-pass or high-pass filters with cutoff fc = 1/(2 pi RC) (or R/(2 pi L)), passing frequencies below (or above) the cutoff with -3 dB at fc.

instruction: Give a worked example for Single-phase transformer and three-phase induction motor [GATE IN - Electrical Circuits]
response:
Worked example: A 4-pole, 50 Hz motor has Ns = 1500 rpm; at Nr = 1440 rpm, slip is 0.04 and rotor frequency is 2 Hz. A transformer delivering 8 kW with 200 W iron and 300 W copper loss is 8000/8500 = 94.1 percent efficient.

Formula: V2/V1 = N2/N1; regulation = (V_nl - V_fl)/V_fl x 100 percent; eta = output/(output + Pi + Pcu), maximum when Pi = Pcu; Ns = 120 f/P; s = (Ns - Nr)/Ns; rotor frequency = s f.

A transformer transfers power by mutual induction: V2/V1 = N2/N1 = I1/I2 for an ideal transformer. The open-circuit test (rated voltage, secondary open) gives iron loss and the magnetising branch; the short-circuit test (rated current, low voltage) gives copper loss and series impedance. Voltage regulation is (V_no-load - V_full-load)/V_full-load, and efficiency is maximum when iron loss equals copper loss. A three-phase induction motor runs at slip s = (Ns - Nr)/Ns with Ns = 120 f/P; torque is proportional to s R2/(R2^2 + (s X2)^2), maximum at s = R2/X2, and the no-load and blocked-rotor tests give the equivalent circuit.

instruction: Give a worked example for Laplace, Fourier and Z-transforms [GATE IN - Signals & Systems]
response:
Worked example: y' + 2y = 0 with y(0) = 3 gives Y(s) = 3/(s + 2), so y(t) = 3 e^{-2t}. The discrete sequence (0.5)^n u[n] has Z-transform z/(z - 0.5) with pole at 0.5, inside the unit circle, so it is stable.

Formula: Laplace: X(s) = integral_0^inf x(t) e^{-s t} dt; L{dx/dt} = s X(s) - x(0); Fourier: X(omega) = integral x(t) e^{-j omega t} dt; Z: X(z) = sum x[n] z^{-n}; a^n u[n] <-> 1/(1 - a z^{-1}), ROC |z| > |a|.

The Laplace transform turns differential equations into algebra (differentiation becomes multiplication by s, minus initial values), the Fourier transform decomposes a signal into frequencies (convolution becomes multiplication), and the Z-transform does the same for discrete-time signals and difference equations. The transfer function H(s) = Y(s)/X(s) is the Laplace transform of the impulse response, and poles in the left half-plane mean stability for continuous systems, inside the unit circle for discrete ones. The region of convergence decides causality and stability of a Z-transform.

instruction: Give a worked example for Impulse response, convolution and correlation [GATE IN - Signals & Systems]
response:
Worked example: x = [1, 2] convolved with h = [1, 1] gives y = [1, 3, 2]. The autocorrelation of a signal at zero lag equals its energy; a delayed copy of a signal cross-correlates maximally at a lag equal to the delay.

Formula: y(t) = integral x(tau) h(t - tau) d tau; y[n] = sum_k x[k] h[n-k]; H(s) = Y(s)/X(s); autocorrelation R_xx(tau) = integral x(t) x(t + tau) dt, R_xx(0) = signal power.

The impulse response h(t) of an LTI system is its output for a unit impulse, and the output for any input is the convolution of the input with h. In the frequency domain convolution becomes multiplication by the transfer function H, whose magnitude and phase give the frequency response; first-order systems roll off at 20 dB/decade past their corner, second-order at 40 dB/decade. Correlation measures similarity between two signals as a function of lag: autocorrelation peaks at zero lag with the signal power, and cross-correlation peaks at the lag where the signals best align, which is how time delay is measured.

instruction: Give a worked example for DFT, FFT, IIR and FIR digital filters [GATE IN - Signals & Systems]
response:
Worked example: x = [1, 0, 1, 0], N = 4: X[0] = 2, X[1] = 0, X[2] = 2, X[3] = 0. A 3-tap moving-average FIR y[n] = (x[n] + x[n-1] + x[n-2])/3 is a simple low-pass filter.

Formula: DFT: X[k] = sum_{n=0}^{N-1} x[n] e^{-j 2 pi k n / N}; FIR: y[n] = sum_{k=0}^{M} b_k x[n-k]; IIR: y[n] = sum b_k x[n-k] - sum a_k y[n-k]; FIR always stable, linear phase possible; IIR stable iff poles inside the unit circle.

The DFT samples the DTFT at N equally spaced frequencies, X[k] = sum_{n=0}^{N-1} x[n] e^{-j 2 pi k n / N}, and the FFT computes it in O(N log N). FIR filters use only feedforward taps, so they are always stable and can have exactly linear phase, but need many taps for sharp cutoffs. IIR filters use feedback, so they achieve sharp cutoffs with few coefficients but can be unstable and have non-linear phase. Filter design starts from the required passband, stopband and transition width, then picks the order and the window (FIR) or prototype (IIR, e.g. Butterworth or Chebyshev).

instruction: Give a worked example for Signal flow graphs and Mason gain formula [GATE IN - Control Systems]
response:
Worked example: A system with one forward path of gain 10 and one feedback loop of gain -2 has Delta = 1 - (-2) = 3 and T = 10/3 = 3.33. Adding a second loop that does not touch the first contributes its product to Delta.

Formula: T = (sum_k M_k Delta_k) / Delta; Delta = 1 - sum L1 + sum L2 - sum L3 + ...; M_k = gain of k-th forward path; Delta_k = Delta with loops touching path k removed.

A signal flow graph represents a system as nodes (signals) joined by directed branches (gains). Mason gain formula gives the overall transfer function from the forward paths and loops: sum over forward paths of (path gain x its cofactor) divided by the determinant Delta. Delta is 1 minus the sum of individual loop gains, plus the sum of products of pairs of non-touching loops, minus the sum of products of triples of non-touching loops, and so on; a path cofactor is Delta with all loops touching that path removed.

instruction: Give a worked example for Stability criteria, compensators, state space and time-delay systems [GATE IN - Control Systems]
response:
Worked example: s^3 + 4 s^2 + 5 s + 2 has Routh rows 1, 5; 4, 2; 4.5; 2, all positive in the first column, so it is stable. A 0.1 s delay at 10 rad/s adds phase lag of 1 rad, about 57 deg, which can erase a phase margin.

Formula: Routh: stable iff first column has no sign changes; Nyquist: Z = N + P, stable iff Z = 0; phase margin = 180 deg + angle G(j omega_gc); state space: x-dot = A x + B u, y = C x + D u; delay: e^{-sT} adds phase -omega T.

Routh-Hurwitz tests stability from the characteristic polynomial (no sign changes in the first column means stable); Nyquist counts encirclements of -1 by the open-loop frequency response; root locus traces closed-loop poles as gain varies. Bode plots give gain and phase margins, the usual robustness measures. Lead compensation adds phase near crossover and speeds up the response, lag raises low-frequency gain and cuts steady-state error, and lag-lead does both. In state space, x-dot = A x + B u and y = C x + D u, and stability is decided by the eigenvalues of A. A pure time delay e^{-sT} adds phase lag proportional to frequency and hurts stability margins.

instruction: Give a worked example for Diode, Zener diode, BJT and MOSFET: characteristics and small-signal analysis [GATE IN - Instrumentation]
response:
Worked example: A BJT at Ic = 2 mA has gm = 2e-3/0.026 = about 77 mS, so with Rc = 1 k ohm the voltage gain is about -77. A 5.1 V Zener holds about 5.1 V across its load in reverse breakdown.

Formula: Diode: I = Is (e^{V/(eta Vt)} - 1); BJT: Ic = beta Ib, gm = Ic/Vt; MOSFET saturation: Id = (1/2) mu Cox (W/L)(Vgs - Vth)^2, gm = 2 Id/(Vgs - Vth); common-emitter gain about -gm Rc.

A diode conducts exponentially in forward bias, I = Is (e^{V/(eta Vt)} - 1) with Vt about 26 mV at 300 K, and blocks in reverse until breakdown; a Zener diode breaks down at a controlled reverse voltage and regulates it. A BJT in active mode has Ic = beta Ib and transconductance gm = Ic/Vt, so it is a current-controlled current source. A MOSFET in saturation has Id = (1/2) mu Cox (W/L) (Vgs - Vth)^2 and is voltage-controlled. Small-signal analysis replaces each device by its gm and output resistance to find gain and input/output resistance; feedback trades gain for bandwidth, linearity and stable resistance.

instruction: Give a worked example for Op-amp applications, instrumentation amplifier, PLL and noise [GATE IN - Instrumentation]
response:
Worked example: An instrumentation amplifier with R = 10 k ohm and Rg = 1 k ohm and a unity second stage has gain 1 + 20 = 21, so a 10 mV bridge output becomes 210 mV. A PLL with f_ref = 1 MHz and N = 50 outputs 50 MHz.

Formula: Inverting gain = -Rf/R1; non-inverting = 1 + Rf/R1; integrator Vo = -(1/RC) integral Vi dt; instrumentation amplifier gain = (1 + 2R/Rg) x (Rf/R1); PLL: f_out = N f_ref; thermal noise voltage density = sqrt(4 k T R) V/sqrt(Hz).

An ideal op-amp with negative feedback keeps its inputs at equal voltage and draws no input current, giving adder, subtractor, integrator (Vo = -1/(RC) integral Vi dt), differentiator, difference amplifier and precision rectifier (a diode inside the loop removes the 0.7 V diode drop). An instrumentation amplifier uses two non-inverting stages plus a difference stage to give high input impedance, high CMRR and gain set by one resistor Rg. A phase-locked loop locks a VCO to a reference: with a divide-by-N counter in the loop, f_out = N f_ref. Noise in circuits comes from thermal noise (4 k T R per hertz), shot noise and 1/f noise, and shielding and grounding keep interference out of low-level measurements.

instruction: Give a worked example for Active filters, oscillators and signal generators [GATE IN - Instrumentation]
response:
Worked example: A Sallen-Key low-pass with R1 = R2 = 15.9 k ohm and C1 = C2 = 10 nF has fc = 1/(2 pi x 15900 x 10e-9) = about 1000 Hz. A Wien-bridge oscillator with R = 16 k ohm and C = 10 nF oscillates near 995 Hz.

Formula: Sallen-Key low-pass: fc = 1/(2 pi sqrt(R1 R2 C1 C2)); Butterworth Q = 0.707; Barkhausen: loop gain >= 1 at 0 deg (360 deg) total phase; Wien bridge: f0 = 1/(2 pi RC); first-order roll-off 20 dB/decade, second-order 40 dB/decade.

Active filters use op-amps with RC networks instead of inductors: a first-order stage rolls off at 20 dB/decade, a second-order Sallen-Key stage at 40 dB/decade, with fc = 1/(2 pi sqrt(R1 R2 C1 C2)) and Q = 0.707 for a Butterworth (maximally flat) response. An oscillator needs loop gain of at least 1 with zero total phase shift (Barkhausen criterion); RC phase-shift and Wien-bridge oscillators set frequency with RC networks, and LC oscillators with a tank circuit. A voltage-controlled oscillator tunes its frequency with a control voltage, and a function generator combines oscillators, integrators and comparators to produce sine, square and triangle waves.

instruction: Give a worked example for Boolean minimisation and IC families: TTL and CMOS [GATE IN - Instrumentation]
response:
Worked example: F = sum m(1,3,5,7) over three variables is 1 exactly when C = 1, so the minimised form is F = C. A CMOS gate switching 10 pF at 5 V and 10 MHz dissipates about 10e-12 x 25 x 10e6 = 2.5 mW of dynamic power.

Formula: De Morgan: NOT(A B) = (NOT A) + (NOT B); K-map groups must be powers of 2; CMOS static power about 0, dynamic power = C V^2 f; TTL supply 5 V, typical noise margin about 0.4 V.

Boolean functions are minimised with algebra or Karnaugh maps, grouping 1s in powers of two (pairs, quads, octets) with wrap-around and don't-care cells, to get the smallest sum-of-products form. TTL logic uses bipolar transistors, runs on 5 V, and has fast switching but higher static power; CMOS uses complementary PMOS/NMOS pairs, draws almost no static power, has high noise margins and wide supply range, and dominates modern digital ICs. Key datasheet figures are propagation delay, fan-out (how many inputs one output can drive), noise margin and power dissipation.

instruction: Give a worked example for Sequential circuits, multivibrators, timers and counters [GATE IN - Instrumentation]
response:
Worked example: A 555 astable with R1 = 1 k ohm, R2 = 10 k ohm and C = 10 uF gives T = 0.693 x (1000 + 20000) x 10e-6 = 0.146 s, so f = about 6.9 Hz. A mod-10 counter needs 4 flip-flops.

Formula: Mod-n counter needs ceil(log2 n) flip-flops; 555 astable: f = 1.44 / ((R1 + 2 R2) C); T = 0.693 (R1 + 2 R2) C; f_max = 1 / (t_clk-to-Q + t_comb(max) + t_setup).

Flip-flops (D, JK, T) store one bit on a clock edge; latches are level-sensitive. Shift registers move bits along on each clock, counters divide the clock (a mod-n counter needs ceil(log2 n) flip-flops), and comparators and Schmitt triggers clean up and compare levels. An astable multivibrator free-runs as a clock; the 555 timer in astable mode gives frequency f = 1.44/((R1 + 2 R2) C) with duty cycle set by R1 and R2. Setup and hold times must be met, and the critical path sets the maximum clock frequency.

instruction: Give a worked example for ADCs, DACs, embedded systems, DCS and PLC [GATE IN - Instrumentation]
response:
Worked example: A 10-bit ADC with Vref = 5 V has LSB = 5/1024 = 4.88 mV, so a 1.00 V input reads about code 205. A 4-bit flash ADC needs 15 comparators.

Formula: ADC LSB = Vref / 2^n; quantisation error <= LSB/2; flash comparators = 2^n - 1; DAC R-2R output steps by Vref/2^n per LSB; sample-and-hold freezes the input during conversion.

An ADC quantises an analog voltage into an n-bit code with step LSB = Vref/2^n: successive-approximation ADCs are the common middle ground, flash ADCs are fastest (2^n - 1 comparators), integrating (dual-slope) ADCs are slow but reject mains noise, and sigma-delta ADCs oversample for high resolution. DACs use weighted resistors or an R-2R ladder. Key ADC/DAC figures are resolution, quantisation error (+/- LSB/2), conversion/settling time and effective number of bits. A microprocessor/microcontroller runs the data-acquisition system: sensor, signal conditioning, ADC, processor, memory and I/O; a DCS distributes control across many controllers in a plant, and a PLC runs rugged ladder-logic control of machines and processes.

instruction: Give a worked example for AC bridges: Maxwell, Anderson, Schering, Wien and Q-meter [GATE IN - Measurements]
response:
Worked example: A Maxwell bridge with R2 = 100 ohm, R3 = 200 ohm and C1 = 1 uF measures Lx = 100 x 200 x 1e-6 = 20 mH. A Wien bridge with R = 16 k ohm and C = 10 nF balances at f = 1/(2 pi x 16000 x 10e-9) = about 995 Hz.

Formula: Maxwell bridge: Lx = R2 R3 C1; Schering bridge: Cx = C1 (R3/R4), tan(delta) = omega C1 R1; Wien bridge: f = 1/(2 pi R C); Q-meter: Q = Vc / V at resonance; Q = omega L / R for a coil.

AC bridges measure inductance, capacitance and frequency by balancing arms at null, like the Wheatstone bridge does for resistance. The Maxwell bridge measures inductance against a known capacitance (Lx = R2 R3 C1); the Anderson bridge is a modified Maxwell that suits low-Q coils; the Schering bridge measures capacitance and dissipation factor (tan delta); the Wien bridge measures frequency, f = 1/(2 pi RC), and is also the basis of the Wien-bridge oscillator. A Q-meter measures the quality factor of a coil directly by resonance: Q = Vc/V, the ratio of the capacitor voltage to the applied voltage at resonance.

instruction: Give a worked example for Instrument transformers, true-RMS meters, timer/counter and oscilloscope [GATE IN - Measurements]
response:
Worked example: A 100/5 A CT with 4 A in its secondary carries 4 x (100/5) = 80 A in the primary. A timer counting 50000 cycles in a 1 s gate reads 50 kHz.

Formula: PT: V_secondary = V_primary x (N2/N1); CT: I_secondary = I_primary x (N1/N2); true RMS = sqrt(mean of v^2); frequency = counts / gate time; oscilloscope bandwidth should exceed the highest signal frequency of interest.

Instrument transformers scale high voltages and currents down for meters: a potential transformer (PT) scales voltage by its turns ratio, a current transformer (CT) scales current, and its secondary must never be open-circuited while the primary carries current. A true-RMS meter reads the RMS value of any waveform, while an average-responding meter is calibrated for sine waves only and reads wrong on distorted waveforms. A timer/counter measures frequency, period and time interval by counting cycles against a reference clock. An oscilloscope shows voltage against time (or X-Y), with time base, volts/division, triggering and bandwidth setting what can be seen; shielding and grounding keep interference out of the measurement.

instruction: Give a worked example for Sensors: resistive, capacitive, inductive, piezoelectric and Hall effect [GATE IN - Instrumentation]
response:
Worked example: A parallel-plate sensor with A = 1 cm^2, d = 1 mm in air has C = 8.85e-12 x 1e-4 / 1e-3 = 0.885 pF; halving the gap doubles the capacitance to 1.77 pF. A Hall sensor with a 10 mA current in a 0.1 T field gives a voltage proportional to B, used to measure current without breaking the circuit.

Formula: Capacitance C = epsilon A / d; Hall voltage V_H = I B / (n q t); piezoelectric charge Q = d x F (d = piezoelectric coefficient); LVDT output is linear in core displacement with a null at centre; strain gauge: delta R/R = G_f x strain.

Resistive sensors change resistance with the measured quantity (strain gauge, RTD, thermistor, LDR); capacitive sensors change C = epsilon A/d with gap or overlap or dielectric; inductive sensors change inductance with a moving core (LVDT gives a linear AC output versus core position); piezoelectric sensors generate charge under force or vibration (high impedance, needs a charge amplifier); Hall sensors give a voltage proportional to magnetic field times current. Signal conditioning matches the sensor to the ADC: bridge completion, amplification (often an instrumentation amplifier), filtering, isolation and linearisation.

instruction: Give a worked example for Temperature measurement: thermocouple, RTD, thermistor, pyrometer and bolometer [GATE IN - Instrumentation]
response:
Worked example: A Pt100 at 100 C reads R = 100 x (1 + 0.00385 x 100) = 138.5 ohm. A type-K thermocouple gives about 41 uV per deg C, so a 250 deg C difference gives about 10.3 mV.

Formula: Thermocouple: V about S x (T_hot - T_ref), S = Seebeck coefficient; RTD: R = R0 (1 + alpha T), Pt100 alpha = 0.00385 /deg C; thermistor (NTC): R falls exponentially with T; radiation: emitted power proportional to T^4 (Stefan-Boltzmann).

A thermocouple joins two dissimilar metals; the Seebeck effect gives a voltage roughly proportional to the temperature difference between the hot junction and the cold (reference) junction, so the reference temperature must be known or compensated. An RTD (usually Pt100, 100 ohm at 0 C) has resistance rising almost linearly with temperature, R = R0 (1 + alpha T) with alpha = 0.00385 per deg C for platinum, and 3- or 4-wire connection cancels lead resistance. A thermistor is a semiconductor whose resistance falls steeply (NTC) with temperature, very sensitive over a narrow range. A pyrometer measures temperature from thermal radiation without contact, and a bolometer detects radiation by the heating it causes.

instruction: Give a worked example for Flow, pressure, level, pH, conductivity and viscosity measurement [GATE IN - Instrumentation]
response:
Worked example: A venturi whose differential pressure quadruples has its flow doubled, since Q is proportional to sqrt(delta p). A tank of water 2 m deep gives a differential pressure of 1000 x 9.81 x 2 = 19.6 kPa at the bottom.

Formula: Orifice/venturi: Q proportional to sqrt(delta p); electromagnetic: E = B d v; turbine: flow proportional to rotor frequency; pH electrode: about 59.16 mV per pH unit at 25 C (Nernst); differential-pressure level: delta p = rho g h.

Variable-head meters (orifice, venturi) infer flow from the pressure drop, Q proportional to sqrt(delta p); variable-area (rotameter) meters read flow from a float position; electromagnetic meters use the voltage induced in a conductive fluid moving in a magnetic field, E = B d v; turbine meters count rotor speed; ultrasonic meters use transit time or Doppler shift; open-channel meters use a weir or flume. Pressure is measured by Bourdon tubes, diaphragms and strain-gauge transducers, and very low pressure by a McLeod gauge. Liquid level uses floats, capacitance, ultrasonic or differential pressure. pH is measured with a glass electrode (about 59 mV per pH at 25 C), conductivity with a conductance cell, and viscosity with rotational or capillary viscometers.

instruction: Give a worked example for Modulation, PCM, multiplexing and digital modulation [GATE IN - Instrumentation]
response:
Worked example: Telephone PCM samples at 8 kHz with 8 bits per sample, giving a bit rate of 64 kbps. An AM signal carrying 5 kHz audio occupies 10 kHz of bandwidth.

Formula: Sampling theorem: fs > 2 f_max; PCM bit rate = fs x n bits; AM bandwidth = 2 f_m; FM Carson bandwidth about 2 (delta_f + f_m); FDM stacks in frequency, TDM interleaves in time.

Amplitude modulation varies the carrier amplitude with the message, frequency modulation varies its frequency; both shift the message to a carrier frequency for transmission, and Shannon sampling theorem says a bandlimited signal is recovered from samples taken faster than twice its highest frequency. Pulse code modulation samples, quantises and encodes the signal into bits, with bit rate = sampling frequency x bits per sample. Frequency-division multiplexing stacks channels in frequency, time-division multiplexing interleaves them in time. Digital modulation (ASK, PSK, FSK, QAM) maps bits to carrier amplitude, phase, frequency or combinations, with QAM packing the most bits per symbol.

instruction: Give a worked example for Optical instrumentation: sources, detectors, interferometry, fibre sensing and spectrometry [GATE IN - Instrumentation]
response:
Worked example: A solution with molar absorptivity 1000 L/mol/cm in a 1 cm cuvette at 0.001 mol/L has absorbance A = 1000 x 0.001 x 1 = 1, so it transmits 10 percent of the light. An interferometer with 600 nm light moves one fringe per 300 nm of mirror displacement.

Formula: Beer-Lambert: A = epsilon c l; interferometer fringe shift: one fringe per half-wavelength of path change (delta = lambda/2 per fringe); mass spectrometer: ions separated by m/z; photodiode current proportional to incident optical power.

Optical sources are LEDs (incoherent, broad spectrum) and lasers (coherent, narrow spectrum); detectors are photodiodes (current proportional to light), light-dependent resistors (resistance falls with light) and square-law detectors (output proportional to optical power). An interferometer splits light into two paths and recombines it; the fringe shift measures displacement or refractive-index change to a fraction of a wavelength, which is the basis of precision metrology and fibre-optic sensing (where the measurand changes the fibre phase, intensity or wavelength). A UV-VIS spectrophotometer measures absorbance (Beer-Lambert law, A = epsilon c l), and a mass spectrometer separates ions by mass-to-charge ratio m/z, giving composition from the mass spectrum.

instruction: What is the formula for Wheatstone bridge balance condition? When is it used? [GATE IN - Measurements]
response:
Formula: Balance condition: R1 / R2 = R3 / R4, where R1, R2, R3 and R4 are the four arm resistances. Unknown resistance Rx = R2 * R3 / R1 (with the labelling R1 / R2 = R3 / Rx). At balance the galvanometer current is zero.

A Wheatstone bridge has four resistors in a diamond, with a supply across one diagonal and a galvanometer across the other. It is balanced when no current flows through the galvanometer, which happens when the two voltage dividers give equal midpoint voltages. At balance an unknown resistance can be found accurately from the three known resistances.

instruction: What is the formula for ADC resolution and LSB step size? When is it used? [GATE IN - Instrumentation]
response:
Formula: Number of levels = 2^N. LSB step = Vref / 2^N (for a unipolar range 0 to Vref), where N is the number of bits and Vref is the reference voltage. Maximum quantisation error is about plus or minus LSB / 2.

An N-bit ADC divides its full-scale input range into 2^N discrete levels. The resolution, or one LSB step, is the smallest change in input voltage that changes the output code by one count. More bits give a smaller step and smaller quantisation error, at the cost of slower or more expensive conversion.

instruction: What is the formula for Strain gauge and gauge factor? When is it used? [GATE IN - Instrumentation]
response:
Formula: Gauge factor GF = (Delta R / R) / (Delta L / L) = (Delta R / R) / epsilon, where epsilon = Delta L / L is strain (dimensionless). Change in resistance: Delta R = GF * R * epsilon. Typical GF is about 2 for metallic gauges.

A strain gauge is a resistive transducer whose resistance changes when it is stretched or compressed. The gauge factor relates the fractional change in resistance to the mechanical strain, and for common metallic foil gauges it is about 2. Because the resistance change is tiny, strain gauges are usually read with a Wheatstone bridge.

instruction: What is the formula for Measurement error: absolute, relative and percentage error? When is it used? [GATE IN - Measurements]
response:
Formula: Absolute error = measured value - true value. Relative error = absolute error / true value. Percentage error = (absolute error / true value) * 100 percent.

Absolute error is the difference between the measured value and the true value, while relative error expresses that difference as a fraction of the true value. Percentage error is the relative error multiplied by 100 and is the usual way to report accuracy. Systematic errors repeat in the same direction, while random errors vary unpredictably.

instruction: What is the formula for PID controller? When is it used? [GATE IN - Control Systems]
response:
Formula: u(t) = Kp * e(t) + Ki * integral of e(t) dt + Kd * de(t)/dt, where u(t) is the control output, e(t) is the error, and Kp, Ki and Kd are the proportional, integral and derivative gains. In the s-domain: U(s)/E(s) = Kp + Ki/s + Kd * s.

A PID controller combines proportional, integral and derivative action on the error between setpoint and measured output. The proportional term reacts to the present error, the integral term removes steady-state error by acting on past error, and the derivative term damps overshoot by acting on the rate of change of error. It is the most widely used controller in industry.

instruction: What is the formula for Nyquist sampling theorem for data acquisition? When is it used? [GATE IN - Signals & Systems]
response:
Formula: fs >= 2 * fm, where fs is sampling frequency and fm is the highest frequency in the signal. Nyquist rate = 2 * fm. Nyquist frequency = fs / 2.

To digitise an analogue signal without losing information, it must be sampled at least twice as fast as its highest frequency component. Sampling slower causes aliasing, in which higher frequencies appear as lower ones in the sampled data. Practical data-acquisition systems therefore use an anti-aliasing filter before the ADC and sample above the Nyquist rate.

instruction: What is the formula for Ohm's law for measurement circuits? When is it used? [GATE IN - Electrical Circuits]
response:
Formula: V = I * R, I = V / R, R = V / I. Voltage divider: Vout = Vin * R2 / (R1 + R2). Power: P = V * I = I^2 * R.

Ohm's law is the basic relation used to size shunts, series resistors and loads in measurement circuits. A current is often measured as the voltage drop across a known shunt resistor, and a voltage is scaled down with a resistive divider. The law holds for linear resistors at constant temperature.

instruction: What is the formula for Linear algebra: matrix algebra, rank, eigenvalues? When is it used? [GATE IN - Engineering Mathematics]
response:
Formula: Consistent iff rank(A) = rank([A | b]); unique iff rank = n; det(A - lambda I) = 0; det(A) = product of eigenvalues; trace(A) = sum of eigenvalues.

The rank of a matrix is the number of independent rows or columns. A system A x = b is consistent if and only if rank(A) = rank([A|b]), with a unique solution when the rank equals the number of unknowns. Eigenvalues come from det(A - lambda I) = 0; their product is the determinant and their sum is the trace. Eigenvectors give the directions a matrix only scales, which is how vibration modes and system poles are understood.

instruction: What is the formula for Fourier series and vector integral theorems? When is it used? [GATE IN - Engineering Mathematics]
response:
Formula: f(x) = a0/2 + sum [a_n cos(n pi x / L) + b_n sin(n pi x / L)]; Gauss: integral_V div F dV = integral_S F . dS; Stokes: integral_S curl F . dS = integral_C F . dr; Green: integral_C (P dx + Q dy) = integral_D (dQ/dx - dP/dy) dA.

A periodic function expands into sines and cosines; even functions need only cosines, odd functions only sines, and the coefficients come from integrating over one period. The vector theorems convert between integrals: Gauss turns a volume integral of divergence into surface flux, Stokes turns a surface integral of curl into a line integral around the boundary, and Green is the planar form of Stokes. These are the integral forms behind Gauss law and Faraday law.

instruction: What is the formula for Complex variables: analytic functions and residue theorem? When is it used? [GATE IN - Engineering Mathematics]
response:
Formula: Cauchy-Riemann: du/dx = dv/dy, du/dy = -dv/dx; integral_C f(z) dz = 2 pi i x sum of residues; Res at simple pole z0 = lim_{z->z0} (z - z0) f(z); Cauchy integral formula: f(a) = (1/2 pi i) integral_C f(z)/(z - a) dz.

A function is analytic where it satisfies the Cauchy-Riemann equations; such functions have Taylor expansions, and functions with isolated singularities have Laurent expansions including negative powers. The residue theorem says the integral around a closed contour equals 2 pi i times the sum of residues at singularities inside it, and the residue at a simple pole z0 is the limit of (z - z0) f(z). This evaluates real integrals of rational and trigonometric functions that are hard to do directly.

instruction: What is the formula for Numerical methods: matrix inversion, nonlinear equations, integration and regression? When is it used? [GATE IN - Engineering Mathematics]
response:
Formula: Newton-Raphson: x_{n+1} = x_n - f(x_n)/f'(x_n); trapezoidal: integral about (h/2)[f0 + 2 f1 + ... + 2 f_{n-1} + fn]; Simpson: integral about (h/3)[f0 + 4 f1 + 2 f2 + 4 f3 + ... + fn]; least squares slope b = sum (x - xbar)(y - ybar) / sum (x - xbar)^2.

Newton-Raphson solves f(x) = 0 by iterating x_{n+1} = x_n - f(x_n)/f'(x_n), converging fast near a simple root but needing a good start and a non-zero derivative. Matrix inversion (Gauss-Jordan) solves linear systems directly. Numerical integration uses the trapezoidal rule (error order h^2) or Simpson rule (error order h^4, needs an even number of intervals). Linear regression fits y = a + b x by least squares, minimising the sum of squared residuals, and correlation r in [-1, 1] measures linear association.

instruction: What is the formula for Electricity and magnetism: Gauss law, Biot-Savart law and magnetic circuits? When is it used? [GATE IN - Electrical Circuits]
response:
Formula: integral_S D . dS = Q_enclosed; E = Q/(4 pi epsilon r^2) point charge; B = mu_0 I/(2 pi r) long wire; MMF = N I; reluctance R = l/(mu A); Phi = MMF/R; L = N Phi/I; M = k sqrt(L1 L2).

Gauss law says the electric flux through a closed surface equals the enclosed charge over epsilon; by symmetry a point charge gives E = Q/(4 pi epsilon r^2), a line charge gives E falling as 1/r, and a plane sheet gives a constant field. A current element produces magnetic field by the Biot-Savart law, and Ampere law gives B = mu_0 I/(2 pi r) around a long straight wire. A magnetic circuit follows MMF = N I driving flux through reluctance R = l/(mu A), and self-inductance is L = N Phi/I with mutual inductance M = k sqrt(L1 L2) between coupled coils.

instruction: What is the formula for Kirchhoff laws, Thevenin, Norton, superposition and reciprocity? When is it used? [GATE IN - Electrical Circuits]
response:
Formula: KCL: sum of currents at a node = 0; KVL: sum of voltages around a loop = 0; Vth = open-circuit voltage; Rth = Vth/I_sc; IN = Vth/Rth; maximum power when R_L = Rth, P_max = Vth^2/(4 Rth).

KCL says the currents entering a node sum to zero (charge conservation) and KVL says the voltages around a loop sum to zero (energy conservation); nodal and mesh analysis are systematic ways of writing these equations. Any linear network seen from two terminals is a Thevenin source Vth in series with Rth, or equivalently a Norton source IN = Vth/Rth in parallel with Rth. Superposition considers each independent source alone, and reciprocity says swapping a single source and the measurement point leaves the response unchanged. Maximum power is delivered when the load equals Rth (or the conjugate impedance for AC).

instruction: What is the formula for Phasor analysis, resonance, locus diagrams and RLC filters? When is it used? [GATE IN - Electrical Circuits]
response:
Formula: Z_L = j omega L; Z_C = 1/(j omega C); S = V_rms I_rms* = P + jQ; f0 = 1/(2 pi sqrt(LC)); RC low-pass cutoff fc = 1/(2 pi RC); at fc the output is 1/sqrt(2) (about -3 dB) of the input.

In sinusoidal steady state, impedances are complex (j omega L, 1/(j omega C)) and voltages and currents are phasors. Apparent power S = P + jQ, with P the average power and Q the reactive power; series and parallel resonance both occur at f0 = 1/(2 pi sqrt(LC)), where the impedance is purely resistive. A locus diagram traces the tip of the current or voltage phasor as a parameter (such as frequency or resistance) varies. Simple RC and RL networks are first-order low-pass or high-pass filters with cutoff fc = 1/(2 pi RC) (or R/(2 pi L)), passing frequencies below (or above) the cutoff with -3 dB at fc.

instruction: What is the formula for Single-phase transformer and three-phase induction motor? When is it used? [GATE IN - Electrical Circuits]
response:
Formula: V2/V1 = N2/N1; regulation = (V_nl - V_fl)/V_fl x 100 percent; eta = output/(output + Pi + Pcu), maximum when Pi = Pcu; Ns = 120 f/P; s = (Ns - Nr)/Ns; rotor frequency = s f.

A transformer transfers power by mutual induction: V2/V1 = N2/N1 = I1/I2 for an ideal transformer. The open-circuit test (rated voltage, secondary open) gives iron loss and the magnetising branch; the short-circuit test (rated current, low voltage) gives copper loss and series impedance. Voltage regulation is (V_no-load - V_full-load)/V_full-load, and efficiency is maximum when iron loss equals copper loss. A three-phase induction motor runs at slip s = (Ns - Nr)/Ns with Ns = 120 f/P; torque is proportional to s R2/(R2^2 + (s X2)^2), maximum at s = R2/X2, and the no-load and blocked-rotor tests give the equivalent circuit.

instruction: What is the formula for Laplace, Fourier and Z-transforms? When is it used? [GATE IN - Signals & Systems]
response:
Formula: Laplace: X(s) = integral_0^inf x(t) e^{-s t} dt; L{dx/dt} = s X(s) - x(0); Fourier: X(omega) = integral x(t) e^{-j omega t} dt; Z: X(z) = sum x[n] z^{-n}; a^n u[n] <-> 1/(1 - a z^{-1}), ROC |z| > |a|.

The Laplace transform turns differential equations into algebra (differentiation becomes multiplication by s, minus initial values), the Fourier transform decomposes a signal into frequencies (convolution becomes multiplication), and the Z-transform does the same for discrete-time signals and difference equations. The transfer function H(s) = Y(s)/X(s) is the Laplace transform of the impulse response, and poles in the left half-plane mean stability for continuous systems, inside the unit circle for discrete ones. The region of convergence decides causality and stability of a Z-transform.

instruction: What is the formula for Impulse response, convolution and correlation? When is it used? [GATE IN - Signals & Systems]
response:
Formula: y(t) = integral x(tau) h(t - tau) d tau; y[n] = sum_k x[k] h[n-k]; H(s) = Y(s)/X(s); autocorrelation R_xx(tau) = integral x(t) x(t + tau) dt, R_xx(0) = signal power.

The impulse response h(t) of an LTI system is its output for a unit impulse, and the output for any input is the convolution of the input with h. In the frequency domain convolution becomes multiplication by the transfer function H, whose magnitude and phase give the frequency response; first-order systems roll off at 20 dB/decade past their corner, second-order at 40 dB/decade. Correlation measures similarity between two signals as a function of lag: autocorrelation peaks at zero lag with the signal power, and cross-correlation peaks at the lag where the signals best align, which is how time delay is measured.

instruction: What is the formula for DFT, FFT, IIR and FIR digital filters? When is it used? [GATE IN - Signals & Systems]
response:
Formula: DFT: X[k] = sum_{n=0}^{N-1} x[n] e^{-j 2 pi k n / N}; FIR: y[n] = sum_{k=0}^{M} b_k x[n-k]; IIR: y[n] = sum b_k x[n-k] - sum a_k y[n-k]; FIR always stable, linear phase possible; IIR stable iff poles inside the unit circle.

The DFT samples the DTFT at N equally spaced frequencies, X[k] = sum_{n=0}^{N-1} x[n] e^{-j 2 pi k n / N}, and the FFT computes it in O(N log N). FIR filters use only feedforward taps, so they are always stable and can have exactly linear phase, but need many taps for sharp cutoffs. IIR filters use feedback, so they achieve sharp cutoffs with few coefficients but can be unstable and have non-linear phase. Filter design starts from the required passband, stopband and transition width, then picks the order and the window (FIR) or prototype (IIR, e.g. Butterworth or Chebyshev).

instruction: What is the formula for Signal flow graphs and Mason gain formula? When is it used? [GATE IN - Control Systems]
response:
Formula: T = (sum_k M_k Delta_k) / Delta; Delta = 1 - sum L1 + sum L2 - sum L3 + ...; M_k = gain of k-th forward path; Delta_k = Delta with loops touching path k removed.

A signal flow graph represents a system as nodes (signals) joined by directed branches (gains). Mason gain formula gives the overall transfer function from the forward paths and loops: sum over forward paths of (path gain x its cofactor) divided by the determinant Delta. Delta is 1 minus the sum of individual loop gains, plus the sum of products of pairs of non-touching loops, minus the sum of products of triples of non-touching loops, and so on; a path cofactor is Delta with all loops touching that path removed.

instruction: What is the formula for Stability criteria, compensators, state space and time-delay systems? When is it used? [GATE IN - Control Systems]
response:
Formula: Routh: stable iff first column has no sign changes; Nyquist: Z = N + P, stable iff Z = 0; phase margin = 180 deg + angle G(j omega_gc); state space: x-dot = A x + B u, y = C x + D u; delay: e^{-sT} adds phase -omega T.

Routh-Hurwitz tests stability from the characteristic polynomial (no sign changes in the first column means stable); Nyquist counts encirclements of -1 by the open-loop frequency response; root locus traces closed-loop poles as gain varies. Bode plots give gain and phase margins, the usual robustness measures. Lead compensation adds phase near crossover and speeds up the response, lag raises low-frequency gain and cuts steady-state error, and lag-lead does both. In state space, x-dot = A x + B u and y = C x + D u, and stability is decided by the eigenvalues of A. A pure time delay e^{-sT} adds phase lag proportional to frequency and hurts stability margins.

instruction: What is the formula for Diode, Zener diode, BJT and MOSFET: characteristics and small-signal analysis? When is it used? [GATE IN - Instrumentation]
response:
Formula: Diode: I = Is (e^{V/(eta Vt)} - 1); BJT: Ic = beta Ib, gm = Ic/Vt; MOSFET saturation: Id = (1/2) mu Cox (W/L)(Vgs - Vth)^2, gm = 2 Id/(Vgs - Vth); common-emitter gain about -gm Rc.

A diode conducts exponentially in forward bias, I = Is (e^{V/(eta Vt)} - 1) with Vt about 26 mV at 300 K, and blocks in reverse until breakdown; a Zener diode breaks down at a controlled reverse voltage and regulates it. A BJT in active mode has Ic = beta Ib and transconductance gm = Ic/Vt, so it is a current-controlled current source. A MOSFET in saturation has Id = (1/2) mu Cox (W/L) (Vgs - Vth)^2 and is voltage-controlled. Small-signal analysis replaces each device by its gm and output resistance to find gain and input/output resistance; feedback trades gain for bandwidth, linearity and stable resistance.

instruction: What is the formula for Op-amp applications, instrumentation amplifier, PLL and noise? When is it used? [GATE IN - Instrumentation]
response:
