Formula: Inverting gain = -Rf/R1; non-inverting = 1 + Rf/R1; integrator Vo = -(1/RC) integral Vi dt; instrumentation amplifier gain = (1 + 2R/Rg) x (Rf/R1); PLL: f_out = N f_ref; thermal noise voltage density = sqrt(4 k T R) V/sqrt(Hz).

An ideal op-amp with negative feedback keeps its inputs at equal voltage and draws no input current, giving adder, subtractor, integrator (Vo = -1/(RC) integral Vi dt), differentiator, difference amplifier and precision rectifier (a diode inside the loop removes the 0.7 V diode drop). An instrumentation amplifier uses two non-inverting stages plus a difference stage to give high input impedance, high CMRR and gain set by one resistor Rg. A phase-locked loop locks a VCO to a reference: with a divide-by-N counter in the loop, f_out = N f_ref. Noise in circuits comes from thermal noise (4 k T R per hertz), shot noise and 1/f noise, and shielding and grounding keep interference out of low-level measurements.

instruction: What is the formula for Active filters, oscillators and signal generators? When is it used? [GATE IN - Instrumentation]
response:
Formula: Sallen-Key low-pass: fc = 1/(2 pi sqrt(R1 R2 C1 C2)); Butterworth Q = 0.707; Barkhausen: loop gain >= 1 at 0 deg (360 deg) total phase; Wien bridge: f0 = 1/(2 pi RC); first-order roll-off 20 dB/decade, second-order 40 dB/decade.

Active filters use op-amps with RC networks instead of inductors: a first-order stage rolls off at 20 dB/decade, a second-order Sallen-Key stage at 40 dB/decade, with fc = 1/(2 pi sqrt(R1 R2 C1 C2)) and Q = 0.707 for a Butterworth (maximally flat) response. An oscillator needs loop gain of at least 1 with zero total phase shift (Barkhausen criterion); RC phase-shift and Wien-bridge oscillators set frequency with RC networks, and LC oscillators with a tank circuit. A voltage-controlled oscillator tunes its frequency with a control voltage, and a function generator combines oscillators, integrators and comparators to produce sine, square and triangle waves.

instruction: What is the formula for Boolean minimisation and IC families: TTL and CMOS? When is it used? [GATE IN - Instrumentation]
response:
Formula: De Morgan: NOT(A B) = (NOT A) + (NOT B); K-map groups must be powers of 2; CMOS static power about 0, dynamic power = C V^2 f; TTL supply 5 V, typical noise margin about 0.4 V.

Boolean functions are minimised with algebra or Karnaugh maps, grouping 1s in powers of two (pairs, quads, octets) with wrap-around and don't-care cells, to get the smallest sum-of-products form. TTL logic uses bipolar transistors, runs on 5 V, and has fast switching but higher static power; CMOS uses complementary PMOS/NMOS pairs, draws almost no static power, has high noise margins and wide supply range, and dominates modern digital ICs. Key datasheet figures are propagation delay, fan-out (how many inputs one output can drive), noise margin and power dissipation.

instruction: What is the formula for Sequential circuits, multivibrators, timers and counters? When is it used? [GATE IN - Instrumentation]
response:
Formula: Mod-n counter needs ceil(log2 n) flip-flops; 555 astable: f = 1.44 / ((R1 + 2 R2) C); T = 0.693 (R1 + 2 R2) C; f_max = 1 / (t_clk-to-Q + t_comb(max) + t_setup).

Flip-flops (D, JK, T) store one bit on a clock edge; latches are level-sensitive. Shift registers move bits along on each clock, counters divide the clock (a mod-n counter needs ceil(log2 n) flip-flops), and comparators and Schmitt triggers clean up and compare levels. An astable multivibrator free-runs as a clock; the 555 timer in astable mode gives frequency f = 1.44/((R1 + 2 R2) C) with duty cycle set by R1 and R2. Setup and hold times must be met, and the critical path sets the maximum clock frequency.

instruction: What is the formula for ADCs, DACs, embedded systems, DCS and PLC? When is it used? [GATE IN - Instrumentation]
response:
Formula: ADC LSB = Vref / 2^n; quantisation error <= LSB/2; flash comparators = 2^n - 1; DAC R-2R output steps by Vref/2^n per LSB; sample-and-hold freezes the input during conversion.

An ADC quantises an analog voltage into an n-bit code with step LSB = Vref/2^n: successive-approximation ADCs are the common middle ground, flash ADCs are fastest (2^n - 1 comparators), integrating (dual-slope) ADCs are slow but reject mains noise, and sigma-delta ADCs oversample for high resolution. DACs use weighted resistors or an R-2R ladder. Key ADC/DAC figures are resolution, quantisation error (+/- LSB/2), conversion/settling time and effective number of bits. A microprocessor/microcontroller runs the data-acquisition system: sensor, signal conditioning, ADC, processor, memory and I/O; a DCS distributes control across many controllers in a plant, and a PLC runs rugged ladder-logic control of machines and processes.

instruction: What is the formula for AC bridges: Maxwell, Anderson, Schering, Wien and Q-meter? When is it used? [GATE IN - Measurements]
response:
Formula: Maxwell bridge: Lx = R2 R3 C1; Schering bridge: Cx = C1 (R3/R4), tan(delta) = omega C1 R1; Wien bridge: f = 1/(2 pi R C); Q-meter: Q = Vc / V at resonance; Q = omega L / R for a coil.

AC bridges measure inductance, capacitance and frequency by balancing arms at null, like the Wheatstone bridge does for resistance. The Maxwell bridge measures inductance against a known capacitance (Lx = R2 R3 C1); the Anderson bridge is a modified Maxwell that suits low-Q coils; the Schering bridge measures capacitance and dissipation factor (tan delta); the Wien bridge measures frequency, f = 1/(2 pi RC), and is also the basis of the Wien-bridge oscillator. A Q-meter measures the quality factor of a coil directly by resonance: Q = Vc/V, the ratio of the capacitor voltage to the applied voltage at resonance.

instruction: What is the formula for Instrument transformers, true-RMS meters, timer/counter and oscilloscope? When is it used? [GATE IN - Measurements]
response:
Formula: PT: V_secondary = V_primary x (N2/N1); CT: I_secondary = I_primary x (N1/N2); true RMS = sqrt(mean of v^2); frequency = counts / gate time; oscilloscope bandwidth should exceed the highest signal frequency of interest.

Instrument transformers scale high voltages and currents down for meters: a potential transformer (PT) scales voltage by its turns ratio, a current transformer (CT) scales current, and its secondary must never be open-circuited while the primary carries current. A true-RMS meter reads the RMS value of any waveform, while an average-responding meter is calibrated for sine waves only and reads wrong on distorted waveforms. A timer/counter measures frequency, period and time interval by counting cycles against a reference clock. An oscilloscope shows voltage against time (or X-Y), with time base, volts/division, triggering and bandwidth setting what can be seen; shielding and grounding keep interference out of the measurement.

instruction: What is the formula for Sensors: resistive, capacitive, inductive, piezoelectric and Hall effect? When is it used? [GATE IN - Instrumentation]
response:
Formula: Capacitance C = epsilon A / d; Hall voltage V_H = I B / (n q t); piezoelectric charge Q = d x F (d = piezoelectric coefficient); LVDT output is linear in core displacement with a null at centre; strain gauge: delta R/R = G_f x strain.

Resistive sensors change resistance with the measured quantity (strain gauge, RTD, thermistor, LDR); capacitive sensors change C = epsilon A/d with gap or overlap or dielectric; inductive sensors change inductance with a moving core (LVDT gives a linear AC output versus core position); piezoelectric sensors generate charge under force or vibration (high impedance, needs a charge amplifier); Hall sensors give a voltage proportional to magnetic field times current. Signal conditioning matches the sensor to the ADC: bridge completion, amplification (often an instrumentation amplifier), filtering, isolation and linearisation.

instruction: What is the formula for Temperature measurement: thermocouple, RTD, thermistor, pyrometer and bolometer? When is it used? [GATE IN - Instrumentation]
response:
Formula: Thermocouple: V about S x (T_hot - T_ref), S = Seebeck coefficient; RTD: R = R0 (1 + alpha T), Pt100 alpha = 0.00385 /deg C; thermistor (NTC): R falls exponentially with T; radiation: emitted power proportional to T^4 (Stefan-Boltzmann).

A thermocouple joins two dissimilar metals; the Seebeck effect gives a voltage roughly proportional to the temperature difference between the hot junction and the cold (reference) junction, so the reference temperature must be known or compensated. An RTD (usually Pt100, 100 ohm at 0 C) has resistance rising almost linearly with temperature, R = R0 (1 + alpha T) with alpha = 0.00385 per deg C for platinum, and 3- or 4-wire connection cancels lead resistance. A thermistor is a semiconductor whose resistance falls steeply (NTC) with temperature, very sensitive over a narrow range. A pyrometer measures temperature from thermal radiation without contact, and a bolometer detects radiation by the heating it causes.

instruction: What is the formula for Flow, pressure, level, pH, conductivity and viscosity measurement? When is it used? [GATE IN - Instrumentation]
response:
Formula: Orifice/venturi: Q proportional to sqrt(delta p); electromagnetic: E = B d v; turbine: flow proportional to rotor frequency; pH electrode: about 59.16 mV per pH unit at 25 C (Nernst); differential-pressure level: delta p = rho g h.

Variable-head meters (orifice, venturi) infer flow from the pressure drop, Q proportional to sqrt(delta p); variable-area (rotameter) meters read flow from a float position; electromagnetic meters use the voltage induced in a conductive fluid moving in a magnetic field, E = B d v; turbine meters count rotor speed; ultrasonic meters use transit time or Doppler shift; open-channel meters use a weir or flume. Pressure is measured by Bourdon tubes, diaphragms and strain-gauge transducers, and very low pressure by a McLeod gauge. Liquid level uses floats, capacitance, ultrasonic or differential pressure. pH is measured with a glass electrode (about 59 mV per pH at 25 C), conductivity with a conductance cell, and viscosity with rotational or capillary viscometers.

instruction: What is the formula for Modulation, PCM, multiplexing and digital modulation? When is it used? [GATE IN - Instrumentation]
response:
Formula: Sampling theorem: fs > 2 f_max; PCM bit rate = fs x n bits; AM bandwidth = 2 f_m; FM Carson bandwidth about 2 (delta_f + f_m); FDM stacks in frequency, TDM interleaves in time.

Amplitude modulation varies the carrier amplitude with the message, frequency modulation varies its frequency; both shift the message to a carrier frequency for transmission, and Shannon sampling theorem says a bandlimited signal is recovered from samples taken faster than twice its highest frequency. Pulse code modulation samples, quantises and encodes the signal into bits, with bit rate = sampling frequency x bits per sample. Frequency-division multiplexing stacks channels in frequency, time-division multiplexing interleaves them in time. Digital modulation (ASK, PSK, FSK, QAM) maps bits to carrier amplitude, phase, frequency or combinations, with QAM packing the most bits per symbol.

instruction: What is the formula for Optical instrumentation: sources, detectors, interferometry, fibre sensing and spectrometry? When is it used? [GATE IN - Instrumentation]
response:
Formula: Beer-Lambert: A = epsilon c l; interferometer fringe shift: one fringe per half-wavelength of path change (delta = lambda/2 per fringe); mass spectrometer: ions separated by m/z; photodiode current proportional to incident optical power.

Optical sources are LEDs (incoherent, broad spectrum) and lasers (coherent, narrow spectrum); detectors are photodiodes (current proportional to light), light-dependent resistors (resistance falls with light) and square-law detectors (output proportional to optical power). An interferometer splits light into two paths and recombines it; the fringe shift measures displacement or refractive-index change to a fraction of a wavelength, which is the basis of precision metrology and fibre-optic sensing (where the measurand changes the fibre phase, intensity or wavelength). A UV-VIS spectrophotometer measures absorbance (Beer-Lambert law, A = epsilon c l), and a mass spectrometer separates ions by mass-to-charge ratio m/z, giving composition from the mass spectrum.

instruction: Why does Wheatstone bridge balance condition matter in Measurements? Where is it used? [GATE IN]
response:
A Wheatstone bridge has four resistors in a diamond, with a supply across one diagonal and a galvanometer across the other. It is balanced when no current flows through the galvanometer, which happens when the two voltage dividers give equal midpoint voltages. At balance an unknown resistance can be found accurately from the three known resistances.

Formula: Balance condition: R1 / R2 = R3 / R4, where R1, R2, R3 and R4 are the four arm resistances. Unknown resistance Rx = R2 * R3 / R1 (with the labelling R1 / R2 = R3 / Rx). At balance the galvanometer current is zero.

instruction: What is Eigenvalues and eigenvectors? Explain it briefly. [GATE MA - Linear Algebra]
response:
For a square matrix A, a non-zero vector v is an eigenvector with eigenvalue lambda if A v = lambda v, so A only scales v. Eigenvalues are the roots of the characteristic equation det(A - lambda I) = 0. They determine stability, principal components and many other properties, and a matrix is singular if and only if 0 is one of its eigenvalues.

Formula: A v = lambda v, v != 0. Characteristic equation: det(A - lambda I) = 0. For a 2x2 matrix [[a, b], [c, d]], det(A - lambda I) = (a - lambda)(d - lambda) - bc = 0. Trace = sum of eigenvalues; determinant = product of eigenvalues.

Worked example: For A = [[4, 1], [2, 3]], det(A - lambda I) = (4 - lambda)(3 - lambda) - 2 = lambda^2 - 7 lambda + 10 = 0, so lambda = 5 or lambda = 2. The eigenvalues are 5 and 2; their sum 7 equals the trace and their product 10 equals the determinant.

instruction: What is Inverse of a 2x2 matrix? Explain it briefly. [GATE MA - Linear Algebra]
response:
A square matrix A has an inverse A^-1 with A A^-1 = A^-1 A = I exactly when its determinant is non-zero. For a 2x2 matrix the inverse is found by swapping the diagonal entries, negating the off-diagonal entries and dividing by the determinant. Solving A x = b is then x = A^-1 b.

Formula: For A = [[a, b], [c, d]], det(A) = ad - bc. If det(A) != 0, A^-1 = (1 / (ad - bc)) x [[d, -b], [-c, a]].

Worked example: For A = [[2, 1], [3, 4]], det(A) = 2x4 - 1x3 = 5, so A^-1 = (1/5) x [[4, -1], [-3, 2]] = [[0.8, -0.2], [-0.6, 0.4]]. Check: A x A^-1 gives [[1, 0], [0, 1]].

instruction: What is Taylor series? Explain it briefly. [GATE MA - Calculus]
response:
A Taylor series represents a smooth function as an infinite sum of powers of (x - a), using the function's derivatives at a. The Maclaurin series is the case a = 0. Truncating the series gives a polynomial approximation whose error is controlled by the next term when x is close to a.

Formula: f(x) = f(a) + f'(a)(x - a) + f''(a)(x - a)^2 / 2! + f'''(a)(x - a)^3 / 3! + ... . Maclaurin series: e^x = 1 + x + x^2/2! + x^3/3! + ... ; sin x = x - x^3/3! + x^5/5! - ... ; cos x = 1 - x^2/2! + x^4/4! - ...

Worked example: Approximate sin(0.1) using sin x approx x - x^3/6: 0.1 - 0.001/6 = 0.1 - 0.0001667 = 0.0998333. The true value sin(0.1) = 0.0998334, so the error is about 0.0000001.

instruction: What is Fundamental theorem of calculus? Explain it briefly. [GATE MA - Calculus]
response:
The fundamental theorem of calculus links differentiation and integration. If F is an antiderivative of f, the definite integral of f from a to b is F(b) - F(a). Equivalently, differentiating the integral of f from a fixed point to x recovers f(x). It turns area and accumulation problems into antiderivative problems.

Formula: If F'(x) = f(x), then integral from a to b of f(x) dx = F(b) - F(a). Also, d/dx [integral from a to x of f(t) dt] = f(x). Power rule: integral of x^n dx = x^(n+1)/(n+1) + C for n != -1.

Worked example: Integral from 0 to 1 of x^2 dx = [x^3/3] from 0 to 1 = 1/3 - 0 = 1/3, about 0.3333. This is the area under y = x^2 between x = 0 and x = 1.

instruction: What is Bayes theorem? Explain it briefly. [GATE MA - Probability & Statistics]
response:
Bayes theorem updates the probability of a hypothesis after seeing evidence, combining the prior probability with the likelihood of the evidence. It follows directly from the definition of conditional probability, P(A|B) = P(A and B) / P(B). It is the basis of Bayesian inference and of many classifiers and diagnostic calculations.

Formula: P(A|B) = P(B|A) x P(A) / P(B), where P(B) = P(B|A) x P(A) + P(B|not A) x P(not A). P(A) is the prior, P(B|A) the likelihood, P(A|B) the posterior.

Worked example: A disease affects 1% of people. A test is 99% sensitive and 95% specific. P(disease | positive) = 0.99 x 0.01 / (0.99 x 0.01 + 0.05 x 0.99) = 0.0099 / 0.0594 = 0.1667, about 16.7%, despite the test's high accuracy.

instruction: What is First-order linear ODE? Explain it briefly. [GATE MA - Differential Equations]
response:
A first-order linear ordinary differential equation has the form dy/dx + P(x) y = Q(x). It is solved with an integrating factor mu(x) = exp(integral of P(x) dx), which turns the left side into the derivative of mu(x) y. Integrating then gives the general solution, and an initial condition fixes the constant.

Formula: dy/dx + P(x) y = Q(x). Integrating factor: mu(x) = exp(integral P(x) dx). Solution: y = (1 / mu(x)) x [integral mu(x) Q(x) dx + C].

Worked example: Solve dy/dx + 2y = 4. Here P = 2, so mu = e^(2x). Then d/dx (e^(2x) y) = 4 e^(2x), so e^(2x) y = 2 e^(2x) + C, giving y = 2 + C e^(-2x). Check: y' + 2y = -2C e^(-2x) + 4 + 2C e^(-2x) = 4.

instruction: What is Newton-Raphson method? Explain it briefly. [GATE MA - Numerical Methods]
response:
The Newton-Raphson method finds a root of f(x) = 0 by repeatedly following the tangent line at the current guess to its x-intercept. Near a simple root it converges quadratically, roughly doubling the number of correct digits per iteration, provided the starting guess is close enough and f'(x) is not zero.

Formula: x(n+1) = x(n) - f(x(n)) / f'(x(n)), with f'(x(n)) != 0. Stop when |x(n+1) - x(n)| is below the tolerance. Convergence is quadratic near a simple root.

Worked example: Find sqrt(2), so f(x) = x^2 - 2 and f'(x) = 2x. From x0 = 1.5, x1 = 1.5 - (1.5^2 - 2) / (2 x 1.5) = 1.5 - 0.25/3 = 1.4167. The true sqrt(2) is 1.4142, so one step already gives about 3 correct digits.

instruction: What is Trapezoidal rule? Explain it briefly. [GATE MA - Numerical Methods]
response:
The trapezoidal rule approximates a definite integral by dividing the interval into n equal subintervals and replacing the curve on each subinterval by a straight line, forming a trapezium. Its error decreases as 1/n^2, so doubling n roughly quarters the error. It is exact for linear functions.

Formula: Integral from a to b of f(x) dx approx (h/2) x [f(x0) + 2 f(x1) + 2 f(x2) + ... + 2 f(x(n-1)) + f(xn)], where h = (b - a)/n and xi = a + i h. Error is O(h^2).

Worked example: Approximate the integral from 0 to 1 of x^2 dx with n = 2, h = 0.5: (0.5/2) x [f(0) + 2 f(0.5) + f(1)] = 0.25 x [0 + 2 x 0.25 + 1] = 0.25 x 1.5 = 0.375. The exact value is 1/3 = 0.3333, so the error is 0.0417.

instruction: What is Functions of several variables: partial derivatives, maxima, minima and Lagrange multipliers? Explain it briefly. [GATE MA - Calculus]
response:
For f(x,y), the partial derivatives f_x and f_y measure change along each axis, and the gradient points in the direction of steepest increase. The total derivative combines them: df = f_x dx + f_y dy. A critical point has zero gradient; the second derivative test uses the Hessian determinant D = f_xx f_yy - f_xy^2 to classify it as a max, min or saddle point. Lagrange multipliers handle constrained extrema by solving grad f = lambda grad g.

Formula: df = f_x dx + f_y dy; D = f_xx f_yy - (f_xy)^2: D > 0 and f_xx > 0 gives local min, D > 0 and f_xx < 0 gives local max, D < 0 gives saddle point; constrained: grad f = lambda grad g

Worked example: Maximizing f = xy subject to x + y = 10: grad f = (y, x) = lambda (1, 1) gives x = y = 5, so the maximum is 25. For f = x^2 + y^2, the origin has D = 4 > 0 and f_xx = 2 > 0, a local minimum.

instruction: What is Double and triple integrals and their applications? Explain it briefly. [GATE MA - Calculus]
response:
A double integral over a region gives volume under a surface or area when the integrand is 1; a triple integral gives volume or mass of a solid. Changing to polar coordinates (x = r cos theta, y = r sin theta) introduces the Jacobian r, and cylindrical or spherical coordinates simplify symmetric solids. Fubini's theorem lets iterated integrals be computed in either order when the function is continuous.

Formula: Area = double integral of dA; volume = double integral of f(x,y) dA; polar: dA = r dr dtheta; triple integral in spherical coordinates: dV = rho^2 sin(phi) d rho d phi d theta

Worked example: The area of a circle of radius a is the integral over r from 0 to a and theta from 0 to 2 pi of r dr dtheta = pi a^2. The volume of a sphere of radius a is (4/3) pi a^3 by a triple integral.

instruction: What is Vector calculus: gradient, divergence, curl and integral theorems? Explain it briefly. [GATE MA - Calculus]
response:
The gradient of a scalar field is a vector pointing in the direction of greatest increase; the divergence of a vector field measures net outflow per unit volume; the curl measures local rotation. Green's theorem relates a line integral around a closed curve to a double integral over the enclosed region. Stokes' theorem generalizes this to surfaces, and Gauss's divergence theorem relates flux through a closed surface to the volume integral of divergence.

Formula: Green: line integral of (P dx + Q dy) = double integral of (dQ/dx - dP/dy) dA; Stokes: line integral of F . dr = surface integral of (curl F) . n dS; Gauss: surface integral of F . n dS = triple integral of div F dV

Worked example: For F = (x, y, 0), div F = 2, so the flux through a sphere of radius a is 2 times its volume, (8/3) pi a^3. For F = (-y, x, 0), curl F = (0,0,2), giving circulation 2 pi a^2 around a circle of radius a.

instruction: What is Vector spaces, linear transformations, rank and nullity? Explain it briefly. [GATE MA - Linear Algebra]
response:
A vector space is a set closed under addition and scalar multiplication; a basis is a linearly independent spanning set, and its size is the dimension. A linear transformation T is determined by its action on a basis and is represented by a matrix once bases are fixed. The rank-nullity theorem says rank(T) + nullity(T) = dim(domain), and a system Ax = b is consistent exactly when b lies in the column space of A.

Formula: rank(T) + nullity(T) = dim(V); rank(A) = number of pivots in row echelon form; Ax = b is consistent iff rank(A) = rank([A|b])

Worked example: T: R^3 -> R^2 defined by T(x,y,z) = (x + y, y + z) has rank 2 and nullity 1 (kernel spanned by (1,-1,1)). The system x + y = 1, 2x + 2y = 3 is inconsistent since rank(A) = 1 but rank([A|b]) = 2.

instruction: What is Diagonalization, characteristic polynomial, minimal polynomial and Cayley-Hamilton theorem? Explain it briefly. [GATE MA - Linear Algebra]
response:
A matrix is diagonalizable if it has a basis of eigenvectors, equivalently if its minimal polynomial has distinct linear factors; symmetric matrices are always diagonalizable. The characteristic polynomial p(lambda) = det(A - lambda I) has the eigenvalues as roots, and the Cayley-Hamilton theorem says every matrix satisfies its own characteristic equation, p(A) = 0. The minimal polynomial is the smallest-degree monic polynomial annihilating A and divides the characteristic polynomial.

Formula: Cayley-Hamilton: p(A) = 0 where p(lambda) = det(A - lambda I); A is diagonalizable iff its minimal polynomial splits into distinct linear factors; A = PDP^-1 with D diagonal

Worked example: For A = [[2,1],[1,2]], p(lambda) = (lambda-3)(lambda-1), so A^2 - 4A + 3I = 0, and A^2 = 4A - 3I without multiplying matrices. The matrix [[1,1],[0,1]] has minimal polynomial (lambda-1)^2 and is not diagonalizable.

instruction: What is Inner product spaces, Gram-Schmidt and special matrices? Explain it briefly. [GATE MA - Linear Algebra]
response:
An inner product space has an inner product generalizing the dot product, giving lengths and orthogonality. The Gram-Schmidt process turns a basis into an orthonormal one by subtracting projections onto earlier vectors. Symmetric and Hermitian matrices have real eigenvalues and orthogonal eigenvectors; normal matrices are unitarily diagonalizable; orthogonal and unitary matrices preserve lengths and have orthonormal columns.

Formula: Gram-Schmidt: u1 = v1, u_k = v_k - sum_{i<k} proj_{u_i}(v_k); proj_u(v) = (<v,u>/<u,u>) u; unitary: U*U = I; Hermitian: A* = A

Worked example: Applying Gram-Schmidt to (1,1,0) and (1,0,1) gives orthonormal vectors (1/sqrt2, 1/sqrt2, 0) and (1/sqrt6, -1/sqrt6, 2/sqrt6). The rotation matrix [[cos t, -sin t],[sin t, cos t]] is orthogonal with determinant 1.

instruction: What is Jordan canonical form and bilinear and quadratic forms? Explain it briefly. [GATE MA - Linear Algebra]
response:
Every square matrix over the complex numbers is similar to a Jordan canonical form: a block diagonal matrix whose blocks have an eigenvalue on the diagonal and 1s just above it. The number and sizes of Jordan blocks for an eigenvalue are fixed by the dimensions of kernels of powers of (A - lambda I). A bilinear form is linear in each argument; a quadratic form Q(x) = x^T A x with symmetric A is classified by its eigenvalues as positive definite, negative definite, indefinite or semidefinite, and can be diagonalized by an orthogonal change of variables.

Formula: Jordan block J = lambda I + N with N nilpotent having 1s on the superdiagonal; quadratic form Q(x) = x^T A x; Sylvester's law of inertia: the numbers of positive, negative and zero eigenvalues are invariant under congruence

Worked example: The matrix [[2,1],[0,2]] is a single Jordan block for eigenvalue 2 and is not diagonalizable. The form 2x^2 + 2xy + 2y^2 has matrix [[2,1],[1,2]] with eigenvalues 3 and 1, so it is positive definite.

instruction: What is Metric spaces: connectedness, compactness and completeness? Explain it briefly. [GATE MA - Real Analysis]
response:
A metric space has a distance function satisfying non-negativity, symmetry and the triangle inequality. A set is compact if every open cover has a finite subcover; in R^n this is equivalent to being closed and bounded (Heine-Borel). A sequence is Cauchy if its terms get arbitrarily close to each other, and a space is complete if every Cauchy sequence converges inside it. A connected set cannot be split into two disjoint non-empty open pieces.

Formula: Heine-Borel: in R^n, compact iff closed and bounded; R is complete but (0,1) and Q are not; continuous image of a compact set is compact

Worked example: The closed interval [0,1] is compact, so a continuous function on it attains its maximum. The sequence 1, 1.4, 1.41, 1.414, ... is Cauchy in Q but converges to sqrt(2), which is not in Q, showing Q is incomplete.

instruction: What is Sequences and series of functions and uniform convergence? Explain it briefly. [GATE MA - Real Analysis]
response:
A sequence of functions can converge pointwise (at each x separately) or uniformly (the worst-case error over all x goes to zero). Uniform convergence preserves continuity, and lets limits pass through integrals and (with uniformly convergent derivatives) through differentiation. The Weierstrass M-test proves uniform convergence by dominating terms with a convergent numeric series. The contraction mapping principle says a contraction on a complete metric space has a unique fixed point, found by iteration.

Formula: M-test: if |f_n(x)| <= M_n for all x and sum M_n converges, then sum f_n converges uniformly; contraction: d(Tx, Ty) <= k d(x,y) with k < 1 implies a unique fixed point

Worked example: f_n(x) = x^n on [0,1] converges pointwise to 0 for x < 1 and 1 at x = 1, so the limit is discontinuous and convergence is not uniform. The Weierstrass approximation theorem says every continuous function on [a,b] is a uniform limit of polynomials.

instruction: What is Lebesgue measure and integral? Explain it briefly. [GATE MA - Real Analysis]
response:
Lebesgue measure extends length to a large class of sets, including all intervals and countable sets (which have measure zero). A function is measurable if preimages of intervals are measurable sets, and the Lebesgue integral is built by partitioning the range rather than the domain, so it handles many more functions than the Riemann integral. The monotone convergence theorem, Fatou's lemma and the dominated convergence theorem justify passing limits through integrals under mild conditions.

Formula: Monotone convergence: if 0 <= f_n increasing to f, then integral f_n -> integral f; dominated convergence: if f_n -> f pointwise and |f_n| <= g integrable, then integral f_n -> integral f; Fatou: integral liminf f_n <= liminf integral f_n

Worked example: The Dirichlet function (1 on rationals, 0 on irrationals) is not Riemann integrable but is Lebesgue integrable with integral 0, since the rationals have measure zero. Dominated convergence justifies differentiating under the integral sign for e^{-tx} type integrands.

instruction: What is Differentiation of several variables, inverse and implicit function theorems? Explain it briefly. [GATE MA - Real Analysis]
response:
A function of several variables is differentiable at a point if it is well approximated by a linear map, its derivative matrix being the Jacobian. The inverse function theorem says that if the Jacobian determinant is non-zero at a point, the function is locally invertible with a differentiable inverse. The implicit function theorem says an equation F(x,y) = 0 with F_y != 0 locally defines y as a differentiable function of x, with dy/dx = -F_x / F_y.

Formula: Implicit differentiation: dy/dx = -F_x / F_y when F(x,y) = 0 and F_y != 0; inverse function theorem needs det(J) != 0 at the point

Worked example: The circle x^2 + y^2 = 1 near (0,1) defines y = sqrt(1 - x^2), and dy/dx = -x/y = 0 at x = 0. The polar map (r, theta) -> (r cos theta, r sin theta) has Jacobian determinant r, so it is locally invertible where r != 0.

instruction: What is Analytic functions, Cauchy-Riemann equations and harmonic functions? Explain it briefly. [GATE MA - Complex Analysis]
response:
A complex function f(z) = u + iv is differentiable at z0 if the limit of the difference quotient exists independent of direction; it is analytic if differentiable in a neighbourhood. Differentiability is equivalent to the Cauchy-Riemann equations u_x = v_y and u_y = -v_x (with continuous partials). The real and imaginary parts of an analytic function are harmonic (their Laplacian is zero) and are conjugate to each other.

Formula: Cauchy-Riemann: du/dx = dv/dy and du/dy = -dv/dx; f'(z) = u_x + i v_x; Laplace: u_xx + u_yy = 0 for analytic f

Worked example: f(z) = z^2 = (x^2 - y^2) + i(2xy) satisfies u_x = 2x = v_y and u_y = -2y = -v_x, so it is analytic everywhere with f'(z) = 2z. The function f(z) = conjugate(z) fails Cauchy-Riemann everywhere and is nowhere differentiable.

instruction: What is Cauchy's integral theorem and formula, Liouville's theorem and maximum modulus principle? Explain it briefly. [GATE MA - Complex Analysis]
response:
Cauchy's integral theorem says the integral of an analytic function around a closed contour is zero. Cauchy's integral formula recovers values inside a contour from boundary values: f(a) = (1/2 pi i) times the integral of f(z)/(z-a) dz. From this follow Liouville's theorem (a bounded entire function is constant), the maximum modulus principle (a non-constant analytic function attains no maximum inside a domain), and Morera's theorem (vanishing integrals over all closed contours imply analyticity).

Formula: Cauchy integral formula: f(a) = (1/(2 pi i)) integral_C f(z)/(z - a) dz; f^(n)(a) = (n!/(2 pi i)) integral_C f(z)/(z - a)^(n+1) dz; Liouville: bounded entire f is constant

Worked example: The integral of 1/z around the unit circle is 2 pi i, showing 1/z is not analytic inside (it has a pole at 0). Liouville's theorem gives a one-line proof of the fundamental theorem of algebra.

instruction: What is Taylor and Laurent series, singularities and the residue theorem? Explain it briefly. [GATE MA - Complex Analysis]
response:
An analytic function expands as a Taylor series inside its disk of convergence; near an isolated singularity it expands as a Laurent series with negative powers. Singularities are removable, poles (of some finite order) or essential. The residue at a pole is the coefficient of (z-a)^-1, and the residue theorem says the integral around a closed contour equals 2 pi i times the sum of residues inside, which evaluates many real integrals.

Formula: Residue theorem: integral_C f(z) dz = 2 pi i * sum of residues inside C; for a simple pole, Res(f, a) = lim_{z->a} (z-a) f(z); radius of convergence reaches the nearest singularity

Worked example: The integral from -infinity to infinity of dx/(1 + x^2) equals pi: close the contour in the upper half-plane, where the only pole is at i with residue 1/(2i), giving 2 pi i * 1/(2i) = pi.

instruction: What is Conformal mappings, Mobius transformations, Rouche's theorem and Schwarz lemma? Explain it briefly. [GATE MA - Complex Analysis]
response:
A conformal map is an analytic function with non-zero derivative, preserving angles and local shape. Mobius transformations (az+b)/(cz+d) map circles and lines to circles and lines and are determined by the images of three points. Rouche's theorem counts zeros inside a contour by comparing a function with a dominant term on the boundary. The Schwarz lemma bounds analytic maps of the unit disk fixing the origin: |f(z)| <= |z|.

Formula: Mobius: w = (a z + b)/(c z + d), ad - bc != 0; Rouche: if |f| > |g| on C then f and f+g have the same number of zeros inside C; Schwarz: |f(z)| <= |z| and |f'(0)| <= 1

Worked example: The map w = (z - i)/(z + i) sends the upper half-plane onto the unit disk. Rouche's theorem shows z^5 + 3z + 1 has exactly one zero inside |z| < 1, since |3z| = 3 dominates |z^5 + 1| <= 2 on |z| = 1.

instruction: What is Higher order linear ODEs with constant coefficients? Explain it briefly. [GATE MA - Differential Equations]
What is Second order ODEs with variable coefficients, Cauchy-Euler equation and Laplace transforms? Explain it briefly. [GATE MA - Differential Equations]
response:
The Cauchy-Euler equation a x^2 y'' + b x y' + c y = 0 becomes constant-coefficient under x = e^t, with trial solutions y = x^m. Laplace transforms turn differential equations into algebraic ones: the transform of y' is sY(s) - y(0), so initial conditions enter directly, and the solution follows by partial fractions and inverse transforms. This is especially handy for equations with discontinuous forcing or impulses.

Formula: Cauchy-Euler: try y = x^m, giving a m(m-1) + b m + c = 0; Laplace: L{y'} = sY(s) - y(0), L{y''} = s^2 Y(s) - s y(0) - y'(0); L{1} = 1/s, L{e^{at}} = 1/(s-a)

Worked example: x^2 y'' - 2y = 0 gives m(m-1) - 2 = 0, so m = 2 or -1 and y = C1 x^2 + C2/x. Solving y' + y = 0 with y(0) = 1 by Laplace gives (s+1)Y = 1, so Y = 1/(s+1) and y = e^{-t}.

instruction: What is Series solutions, Legendre and Bessel functions? Explain it briefly. [GATE MA - Differential Equations]
response:
Near an ordinary point, an ODE has power-series solutions found by substituting y = sum a_n x^n and matching coefficients. At a regular singular point the Frobenius method uses y = x^r sum a_n x^n, with r from the indicial equation. Legendre's equation produces Legendre polynomials P_n(x), orthogonal on [-1,1]; Bessel's equation produces Bessel functions J_n(x), orthogonal with a weight on [0,1] and central to circular and cylindrical problems.

Formula: Legendre: (1-x^2) y'' - 2x y' + n(n+1) y = 0; integral_{-1}^{1} P_m P_n dx = 0 for m != n, = 2/(2n+1) for m = n; Bessel: x^2 y'' + x y' + (x^2 - n^2) y = 0

Worked example: P_0 = 1, P_1 = x, P_2 = (3x^2 - 1)/2. The Frobenius method on Bessel's equation of order 0 gives J_0(x) = 1 - x^2/4 + x^4/64 - ...

instruction: What is Systems of linear ODEs and Sturm-Liouville eigenvalue problems? Explain it briefly. [GATE MA - Differential Equations]
response:
A system x' = Ax of first-order linear ODEs is solved by the matrix exponential; eigenvalues of A give exponential modes, and the solution is a combination of them. Sturm's oscillation and separation theorems describe how zeros of solutions interlace. A Sturm-Liouville problem (p y')' + (lambda w - q) y = 0 with boundary conditions has real eigenvalues lambda_n increasing to infinity and eigenfunctions orthogonal with weight w, forming a basis for expansions.

Formula: System solution: x(t) = e^{At} x(0); Sturm-Liouville: (p(x) y')' + (lambda w(x) - q(x)) y = 0; orthogonality: integral w y_m y_n dx = 0 for m != n

Worked example: The system x' = y, y' = -x has eigenvalues +-i and solutions x = A cos t + B sin t. The problem y'' + lambda y = 0 with y(0) = y(pi) = 0 has eigenvalues lambda_n = n^2 and eigenfunctions sin(nx).

instruction: What is Planar autonomous systems and stability? Explain it briefly. [GATE MA - Differential Equations]
response:
A planar autonomous system x' = f(x,y), y' = g(x,y) has stationary points where f = g = 0. Linearized stability examines the Jacobian at the point: eigenvalues with negative real parts give asymptotic stability, positive real parts give instability, and a zero or purely imaginary pair is inconclusive by linearization. Lyapunov functions give a direct method: if a positive definite function decreases along trajectories, the equilibrium is stable.

Formula: Linearized system: u' = J u where J is the Jacobian at the equilibrium; trace-determinant test: stable node/spiral when trace < 0 and det > 0; Lyapunov: V > 0 and dV/dt < 0 implies asymptotic stability

Worked example: For the pendulum linearized at the bottom, the Jacobian has eigenvalues +-i sqrt(g/l), a centre; at the top the eigenvalues are real of opposite sign, a saddle and unstable. The damped oscillator x'' + 2x' + x = 0 has eigenvalues -1 (repeated), a stable node.

instruction: What is Partial differential equations: classification and separation of variables? Explain it briefly. [GATE MA - Differential Equations]
response:
Second-order PDEs in two variables are classified by the discriminant B^2 - AC: elliptic (Laplace, steady state), parabolic (heat, diffusion) or hyperbolic (wave, propagation). The method of characteristics solves first-order linear and quasilinear PDEs by reducing them to ODEs along characteristic curves. Separation of variables writes u(x,t) = X(x)T(t), turning a PDE into ODEs whose solutions superpose to satisfy boundary conditions, as in Laplace's equation in Cartesian and polar coordinates and the heat and wave equations in one space variable.

Formula: Classification: B^2 - AC < 0 elliptic, = 0 parabolic, > 0 hyperbolic; Laplace: u_xx + u_yy = 0; heat: u_t = k u_xx; wave: u_tt = c^2 u_xx

Worked example: The heat equation u_t = u_xx on 0 < x < pi with u = 0 at both ends separates to modes sin(nx) e^{-n^2 t}. Laplace's equation in a disk gives solutions r^n cos(n theta) and r^n sin(n theta).

instruction: What is Wave and heat equations: d'Alembert formula and Cauchy problems? Explain it briefly. [GATE MA - Differential Equations]
response:
The wave equation's Cauchy problem has d'Alembert's explicit solution: the initial displacement splits into left- and right-moving waves, and the initial velocity contributes an integral over the interval between the wave fronts. The domain of dependence of a point (x,t) is the interval [x-ct, x+ct] on the initial line, expressing finite propagation speed. The heat equation's Cauchy problem is solved by convolution with the Gaussian heat kernel, which instantly smooths and spreads data.

Formula: d'Alembert: u(x,t) = (1/2)[g(x-ct) + g(x+ct)] + (1/(2c)) integral_{x-ct}^{x+ct} h(s) ds for u_tt = c^2 u_xx, u(x,0) = g(x), u_t(x,0) = h(x)

Worked example: For a plucked string with u(x,0) = sin x and u_t(x,0) = 0, d'Alembert gives u(x,t) = (1/2)[sin(x-ct) + sin(x+ct)] = sin x cos ct, a standing wave.

instruction: What is Numerical solution of linear systems: direct and iterative methods? Explain it briefly. [GATE MA - Numerical Methods]
response:
Direct methods finish in a fixed number of steps: Gaussian elimination reduces a system to triangular form, LU decomposition reuses the factorization for many right-hand sides, and Cholesky factorization applies to symmetric positive definite matrices. Iterative methods (Jacobi and Gauss-Seidel) start from a guess and refine it; they converge for strictly diagonally dominant matrices, with Gauss-Seidel usually faster since it uses updated values immediately.

Formula: Jacobi: x_i^(k+1) = (b_i - sum_{j != i} a_ij x_j^(k)) / a_ii; Gauss-Seidel uses x_j^(k+1) for j < i; strict diagonal dominance: |a_ii| > sum_{j != i} |a_ij| guarantees convergence

Worked example: For 4x + y = 9 and x + 3y = 8, Jacobi from (0,0) gives (2.25, 2.67), then (1.58, 1.92), converging to (2, 2). Gaussian elimination on the same system gives x = 2, y = 2 directly.

instruction: What is Numerical solution of nonlinear equations: bisection, secant and fixed point iteration? Explain it briefly. [GATE MA - Numerical Methods]
response:
The bisection method halves a bracketing interval each step and always converges, but slowly (linearly). The secant method replaces the derivative in Newton's method by a finite difference and converges superlinearly, while fixed point iteration x = g(x) converges when |g'(x)| < 1 near the root. These methods trade reliability (bisection) against speed (secant, Newton).

Formula: Bisection: error after n steps <= (b - a)/2^n; secant: x_{n+1} = x_n - f(x_n)(x_n - x_{n-1})/(f(x_n) - f(x_{n-1})); fixed point converges if |g'(x)| < 1

Worked example: Solving x^2 - 2 = 0 on [1,2] by bisection: after 10 steps the interval width is 1/1024, so sqrt(2) is pinned to about 3 decimal places. Fixed point iteration x = (x + 2/x)/2 is Newton's method for this equation.

instruction: What is Interpolation: Lagrange and Newton forms and error? Explain it briefly. [GATE MA - Numerical Methods]
response:
Given n+1 points, there is a unique interpolating polynomial of degree at most n. Lagrange's form builds it as a sum of basis polynomials, each 1 at one node and 0 at the others. Newton's form uses divided differences, which makes adding a new point cheap. The interpolation error at x is f^(n+1)(xi)/(n+1)! times the product of (x - x_i), so error grows with the spacing and the size of the next derivative.

Formula: Lagrange: P(x) = sum y_i l_i(x), l_i(x) = product_{j != i} (x - x_j)/(x_i - x_j); error: f(x) - P(x) = f^(n+1)(xi)/(n+1)! * product (x - x_i)

Worked example: Interpolating (0,1), (1,2), (2,5) gives P(x) = x^2 + 1: at x = 1.5 it predicts 3.25. Adding the point (3,10) to Newton's form needs only one new divided difference.

instruction: What is Numerical differentiation and integration: Simpson's rule and Newton-Cotes formulas? Explain it briefly. [GATE MA - Numerical Methods]
response:
Numerical differentiation approximates derivatives by difference quotients; the central difference is second-order accurate. Numerical integration replaces the integrand by an interpolating polynomial: the trapezoidal rule uses linear pieces (error O(h^2)), Simpson's rule uses parabolas (error O(h^4)) and needs an even number of intervals, and composite rules split the range into many small panels. Newton-Cotes formulas are this family with equally spaced nodes.

Formula: Trapezoidal: integral = (h/2)[f0 + 2f1 + ... + 2f_{n-1} + fn]; Simpson: integral = (h/3)[f0 + 4f1 + 2f2 + 4f3 + ... + fn] with n even; central difference: f'(x) = (f(x+h) - f(x-h))/(2h) + O(h^2)

Worked example: Simpson's rule with h = 0.5 on the integral of x^2 from 0 to 1 gives (0.5/3)[0 + 4(0.25) + 1] = 1/3 exactly, since Simpson is exact for cubics. The trapezoidal rule on the same integral gives 0.375.

instruction: What is Numerical solution of ODE initial value problems: Euler and Runge-Kutta methods? Explain it briefly. [GATE MA - Numerical Methods]
response:
Euler's method advances the solution by the tangent slope: y_{n+1} = y_n + h f(x_n, y_n); its local error is O(h^2) and global error O(h), so it needs small steps. Second-order Runge-Kutta (RK2, e.g. Heun's method) averages the slopes at the start and a predicted end of the step, giving global error O(h^2). Smaller step size or higher order both improve accuracy, at the cost of more function evaluations.

Formula: Euler: y_{n+1} = y_n + h f(x_n, y_n); Heun (RK2): y_{n+1} = y_n + (h/2)[f(x_n, y_n) + f(x_{n+1}, y_n + h f(x_n, y_n))]; Euler global error O(h), RK2 global error O(h^2)

Worked example: For y' = y with y(0) = 1 and h = 0.1, Euler gives y(0.1) = 1.1 (true e^0.1 = 1.1052); Heun gives 1.105, much closer. Halving h roughly halves Euler's error but quarters RK2's.

instruction: Give a worked example for Eigenvalues and eigenvectors [GATE MA - Linear Algebra]
response:
Worked example: For A = [[4, 1], [2, 3]], det(A - lambda I) = (4 - lambda)(3 - lambda) - 2 = lambda^2 - 7 lambda + 10 = 0, so lambda = 5 or lambda = 2. The eigenvalues are 5 and 2; their sum 7 equals the trace and their product 10 equals the determinant.

Formula: A v = lambda v, v != 0. Characteristic equation: det(A - lambda I) = 0. For a 2x2 matrix [[a, b], [c, d]], det(A - lambda I) = (a - lambda)(d - lambda) - bc = 0. Trace = sum of eigenvalues; determinant = product of eigenvalues.

For a square matrix A, a non-zero vector v is an eigenvector with eigenvalue lambda if A v = lambda v, so A only scales v. Eigenvalues are the roots of the characteristic equation det(A - lambda I) = 0. They determine stability, principal components and many other properties, and a matrix is singular if and only if 0 is one of its eigenvalues.

instruction: Give a worked example for Inverse of a 2x2 matrix [GATE MA - Linear Algebra]
response:
Worked example: For A = [[2, 1], [3, 4]], det(A) = 2x4 - 1x3 = 5, so A^-1 = (1/5) x [[4, -1], [-3, 2]] = [[0.8, -0.2], [-0.6, 0.4]]. Check: A x A^-1 gives [[1, 0], [0, 1]].

Formula: For A = [[a, b], [c, d]], det(A) = ad - bc. If det(A) != 0, A^-1 = (1 / (ad - bc)) x [[d, -b], [-c, a]].

A square matrix A has an inverse A^-1 with A A^-1 = A^-1 A = I exactly when its determinant is non-zero. For a 2x2 matrix the inverse is found by swapping the diagonal entries, negating the off-diagonal entries and dividing by the determinant. Solving A x = b is then x = A^-1 b.

instruction: Give a worked example for Taylor series [GATE MA - Calculus]
response:
Worked example: Approximate sin(0.1) using sin x approx x - x^3/6: 0.1 - 0.001/6 = 0.1 - 0.0001667 = 0.0998333. The true value sin(0.1) = 0.0998334, so the error is about 0.0000001.

Formula: f(x) = f(a) + f'(a)(x - a) + f''(a)(x - a)^2 / 2! + f'''(a)(x - a)^3 / 3! + ... . Maclaurin series: e^x = 1 + x + x^2/2! + x^3/3! + ... ; sin x = x - x^3/3! + x^5/5! - ... ; cos x = 1 - x^2/2! + x^4/4! - ...

A Taylor series represents a smooth function as an infinite sum of powers of (x - a), using the function's derivatives at a. The Maclaurin series is the case a = 0. Truncating the series gives a polynomial approximation whose error is controlled by the next term when x is close to a.

instruction: Give a worked example for Fundamental theorem of calculus [GATE MA - Calculus]
response:
Worked example: Integral from 0 to 1 of x^2 dx = [x^3/3] from 0 to 1 = 1/3 - 0 = 1/3, about 0.3333. This is the area under y = x^2 between x = 0 and x = 1.

Formula: If F'(x) = f(x), then integral from a to b of f(x) dx = F(b) - F(a). Also, d/dx [integral from a to x of f(t) dt] = f(x). Power rule: integral of x^n dx = x^(n+1)/(n+1) + C for n != -1.

The fundamental theorem of calculus links differentiation and integration. If F is an antiderivative of f, the definite integral of f from a to b is F(b) - F(a). Equivalently, differentiating the integral of f from a fixed point to x recovers f(x). It turns area and accumulation problems into antiderivative problems.

instruction: Give a worked example for Bayes theorem [GATE MA - Probability & Statistics]
response:
Worked example: A disease affects 1% of people. A test is 99% sensitive and 95% specific. P(disease | positive) = 0.99 x 0.01 / (0.99 x 0.01 + 0.05 x 0.99) = 0.0099 / 0.0594 = 0.1667, about 16.7%, despite the test's high accuracy.

Formula: P(A|B) = P(B|A) x P(A) / P(B), where P(B) = P(B|A) x P(A) + P(B|not A) x P(not A). P(A) is the prior, P(B|A) the likelihood, P(A|B) the posterior.

Bayes theorem updates the probability of a hypothesis after seeing evidence, combining the prior probability with the likelihood of the evidence. It follows directly from the definition of conditional probability, P(A|B) = P(A and B) / P(B). It is the basis of Bayesian inference and of many classifiers and diagnostic calculations.

instruction: Give a worked example for First-order linear ODE [GATE MA - Differential Equations]
response:
Worked example: Solve dy/dx + 2y = 4. Here P = 2, so mu = e^(2x). Then d/dx (e^(2x) y) = 4 e^(2x), so e^(2x) y = 2 e^(2x) + C, giving y = 2 + C e^(-2x). Check: y' + 2y = -2C e^(-2x) + 4 + 2C e^(-2x) = 4.

Formula: dy/dx + P(x) y = Q(x). Integrating factor: mu(x) = exp(integral P(x) dx). Solution: y = (1 / mu(x)) x [integral mu(x) Q(x) dx + C].

A first-order linear ordinary differential equation has the form dy/dx + P(x) y = Q(x). It is solved with an integrating factor mu(x) = exp(integral of P(x) dx), which turns the left side into the derivative of mu(x) y. Integrating then gives the general solution, and an initial condition fixes the constant.

instruction: Give a worked example for Newton-Raphson method [GATE MA - Numerical Methods]
response:
Worked example: Find sqrt(2), so f(x) = x^2 - 2 and f'(x) = 2x. From x0 = 1.5, x1 = 1.5 - (1.5^2 - 2) / (2 x 1.5) = 1.5 - 0.25/3 = 1.4167. The true sqrt(2) is 1.4142, so one step already gives about 3 correct digits.

Formula: x(n+1) = x(n) - f(x(n)) / f'(x(n)), with f'(x(n)) != 0. Stop when |x(n+1) - x(n)| is below the tolerance. Convergence is quadratic near a simple root.

The Newton-Raphson method finds a root of f(x) = 0 by repeatedly following the tangent line at the current guess to its x-intercept. Near a simple root it converges quadratically, roughly doubling the number of correct digits per iteration, provided the starting guess is close enough and f'(x) is not zero.

instruction: Give a worked example for Trapezoidal rule [GATE MA - Numerical Methods]
response:
Worked example: Approximate the integral from 0 to 1 of x^2 dx with n = 2, h = 0.5: (0.5/2) x [f(0) + 2 f(0.5) + f(1)] = 0.25 x [0 + 2 x 0.25 + 1] = 0.25 x 1.5 = 0.375. The exact value is 1/3 = 0.3333, so the error is 0.0417.

Formula: Integral from a to b of f(x) dx approx (h/2) x [f(x0) + 2 f(x1) + 2 f(x2) + ... + 2 f(x(n-1)) + f(xn)], where h = (b - a)/n and xi = a + i h. Error is O(h^2).

The trapezoidal rule approximates a definite integral by dividing the interval into n equal subintervals and replacing the curve on each subinterval by a straight line, forming a trapezium. Its error decreases as 1/n^2, so doubling n roughly quarters the error. It is exact for linear functions.

instruction: Give a worked example for Functions of several variables: partial derivatives, maxima, minima and Lagrange multipliers [GATE MA - Calculus]
response:
Worked example: Maximizing f = xy subject to x + y = 10: grad f = (y, x) = lambda (1, 1) gives x = y = 5, so the maximum is 25. For f = x^2 + y^2, the origin has D = 4 > 0 and f_xx = 2 > 0, a local minimum.

Formula: df = f_x dx + f_y dy; D = f_xx f_yy - (f_xy)^2: D > 0 and f_xx > 0 gives local min, D > 0 and f_xx < 0 gives local max, D < 0 gives saddle point; constrained: grad f = lambda grad g

For f(x,y), the partial derivatives f_x and f_y measure change along each axis, and the gradient points in the direction of steepest increase. The total derivative combines them: df = f_x dx + f_y dy. A critical point has zero gradient; the second derivative test uses the Hessian determinant D = f_xx f_yy - f_xy^2 to classify it as a max, min or saddle point. Lagrange multipliers handle constrained extrema by solving grad f = lambda grad g.

instruction: Give a worked example for Double and triple integrals and their applications [GATE MA - Calculus]
response:
Worked example: The area of a circle of radius a is the integral over r from 0 to a and theta from 0 to 2 pi of r dr dtheta = pi a^2. The volume of a sphere of radius a is (4/3) pi a^3 by a triple integral.

Formula: Area = double integral of dA; volume = double integral of f(x,y) dA; polar: dA = r dr dtheta; triple integral in spherical coordinates: dV = rho^2 sin(phi) d rho d phi d theta

A double integral over a region gives volume under a surface or area when the integrand is 1; a triple integral gives volume or mass of a solid. Changing to polar coordinates (x = r cos theta, y = r sin theta) introduces the Jacobian r, and cylindrical or spherical coordinates simplify symmetric solids. Fubini's theorem lets iterated integrals be computed in either order when the function is continuous.

instruction: Give a worked example for Vector calculus: gradient, divergence, curl and integral theorems [GATE MA - Calculus]
response:
Worked example: For F = (x, y, 0), div F = 2, so the flux through a sphere of radius a is 2 times its volume, (8/3) pi a^3. For F = (-y, x, 0), curl F = (0,0,2), giving circulation 2 pi a^2 around a circle of radius a.

Formula: Green: line integral of (P dx + Q dy) = double integral of (dQ/dx - dP/dy) dA; Stokes: line integral of F . dr = surface integral of (curl F) . n dS; Gauss: surface integral of F . n dS = triple integral of div F dV

The gradient of a scalar field is a vector pointing in the direction of greatest increase; the divergence of a vector field measures net outflow per unit volume; the curl measures local rotation. Green's theorem relates a line integral around a closed curve to a double integral over the enclosed region. Stokes' theorem generalizes this to surfaces, and Gauss's divergence theorem relates flux through a closed surface to the volume integral of divergence.

instruction: Give a worked example for Vector spaces, linear transformations, rank and nullity [GATE MA - Linear Algebra]
response:
Worked example: T: R^3 -> R^2 defined by T(x,y,z) = (x + y, y + z) has rank 2 and nullity 1 (kernel spanned by (1,-1,1)). The system x + y = 1, 2x + 2y = 3 is inconsistent since rank(A) = 1 but rank([A|b]) = 2.

Formula: rank(T) + nullity(T) = dim(V); rank(A) = number of pivots in row echelon form; Ax = b is consistent iff rank(A) = rank([A|b])

A vector space is a set closed under addition and scalar multiplication; a basis is a linearly independent spanning set, and its size is the dimension. A linear transformation T is determined by its action on a basis and is represented by a matrix once bases are fixed. The rank-nullity theorem says rank(T) + nullity(T) = dim(domain), and a system Ax = b is consistent exactly when b lies in the column space of A.

instruction: Give a worked example for Diagonalization, characteristic polynomial, minimal polynomial and Cayley-Hamilton theorem [GATE MA - Linear Algebra]
response:
Worked example: For A = [[2,1],[1,2]], p(lambda) = (lambda-3)(lambda-1), so A^2 - 4A + 3I = 0, and A^2 = 4A - 3I without multiplying matrices. The matrix [[1,1],[0,1]] has minimal polynomial (lambda-1)^2 and is not diagonalizable.

Formula: Cayley-Hamilton: p(A) = 0 where p(lambda) = det(A - lambda I); A is diagonalizable iff its minimal polynomial splits into distinct linear factors; A = PDP^-1 with D diagonal

A matrix is diagonalizable if it has a basis of eigenvectors, equivalently if its minimal polynomial has distinct linear factors; symmetric matrices are always diagonalizable. The characteristic polynomial p(lambda) = det(A - lambda I) has the eigenvalues as roots, and the Cayley-Hamilton theorem says every matrix satisfies its own characteristic equation, p(A) = 0. The minimal polynomial is the smallest-degree monic polynomial annihilating A and divides the characteristic polynomial.

instruction: Give a worked example for Inner product spaces, Gram-Schmidt and special matrices [GATE MA - Linear Algebra]
response:
Worked example: Applying Gram-Schmidt to (1,1,0) and (1,0,1) gives orthonormal vectors (1/sqrt2, 1/sqrt2, 0) and (1/sqrt6, -1/sqrt6, 2/sqrt6). The rotation matrix [[cos t, -sin t],[sin t, cos t]] is orthogonal with determinant 1.

Formula: Gram-Schmidt: u1 = v1, u_k = v_k - sum_{i<k} proj_{u_i}(v_k); proj_u(v) = (<v,u>/<u,u>) u; unitary: U*U = I; Hermitian: A* = A

An inner product space has an inner product generalizing the dot product, giving lengths and orthogonality. The Gram-Schmidt process turns a basis into an orthonormal one by subtracting projections onto earlier vectors. Symmetric and Hermitian matrices have real eigenvalues and orthogonal eigenvectors; normal matrices are unitarily diagonalizable; orthogonal and unitary matrices preserve lengths and have orthonormal columns.

instruction: Give a worked example for Jordan canonical form and bilinear and quadratic forms [GATE MA - Linear Algebra]
response:
Worked example: The matrix [[2,1],[0,2]] is a single Jordan block for eigenvalue 2 and is not diagonalizable. The form 2x^2 + 2xy + 2y^2 has matrix [[2,1],[1,2]] with eigenvalues 3 and 1, so it is positive definite.

Formula: Jordan block J = lambda I + N with N nilpotent having 1s on the superdiagonal; quadratic form Q(x) = x^T A x; Sylvester's law of inertia: the numbers of positive, negative and zero eigenvalues are invariant under congruence

Every square matrix over the complex numbers is similar to a Jordan canonical form: a block diagonal matrix whose blocks have an eigenvalue on the diagonal and 1s just above it. The number and sizes of Jordan blocks for an eigenvalue are fixed by the dimensions of kernels of powers of (A - lambda I). A bilinear form is linear in each argument; a quadratic form Q(x) = x^T A x with symmetric A is classified by its eigenvalues as positive definite, negative definite, indefinite or semidefinite, and can be diagonalized by an orthogonal change of variables.

instruction: Give a worked example for Metric spaces: connectedness, compactness and completeness [GATE MA - Real Analysis]
response:
Worked example: The closed interval [0,1] is compact, so a continuous function on it attains its maximum. The sequence 1, 1.4, 1.41, 1.414, ... is Cauchy in Q but converges to sqrt(2), which is not in Q, showing Q is incomplete.

Formula: Heine-Borel: in R^n, compact iff closed and bounded; R is complete but (0,1) and Q are not; continuous image of a compact set is compact

A metric space has a distance function satisfying non-negativity, symmetry and the triangle inequality. A set is compact if every open cover has a finite subcover; in R^n this is equivalent to being closed and bounded (Heine-Borel). A sequence is Cauchy if its terms get arbitrarily close to each other, and a space is complete if every Cauchy sequence converges inside it. A connected set cannot be split into two disjoint non-empty open pieces.

instruction: Give a worked example for Sequences and series of functions and uniform convergence [GATE MA - Real Analysis]
response:
Worked example: f_n(x) = x^n on [0,1] converges pointwise to 0 for x < 1 and 1 at x = 1, so the limit is discontinuous and convergence is not uniform. The Weierstrass approximation theorem says every continuous function on [a,b] is a uniform limit of polynomials.

Formula: M-test: if |f_n(x)| <= M_n for all x and sum M_n converges, then sum f_n converges uniformly; contraction: d(Tx, Ty) <= k d(x,y) with k < 1 implies a unique fixed point

A sequence of functions can converge pointwise (at each x separately) or uniformly (the worst-case error over all x goes to zero). Uniform convergence preserves continuity, and lets limits pass through integrals and (with uniformly convergent derivatives) through differentiation. The Weierstrass M-test proves uniform convergence by dominating terms with a convergent numeric series. The contraction mapping principle says a contraction on a complete metric space has a unique fixed point, found by iteration.

instruction: Give a worked example for Lebesgue measure and integral [GATE MA - Real Analysis]
response:
Worked example: The Dirichlet function (1 on rationals, 0 on irrationals) is not Riemann integrable but is Lebesgue integrable with integral 0, since the rationals have measure zero. Dominated convergence justifies differentiating under the integral sign for e^{-tx} type integrands.

Formula: Monotone convergence: if 0 <= f_n increasing to f, then integral f_n -> integral f; dominated convergence: if f_n -> f pointwise and |f_n| <= g integrable, then integral f_n -> integral f; Fatou: integral liminf f_n <= liminf integral f_n

Lebesgue measure extends length to a large class of sets, including all intervals and countable sets (which have measure zero). A function is measurable if preimages of intervals are measurable sets, and the Lebesgue integral is built by partitioning the range rather than the domain, so it handles many more functions than the Riemann integral. The monotone convergence theorem, Fatou's lemma and the dominated convergence theorem justify passing limits through integrals under mild conditions.

instruction: Give a worked example for Differentiation of several variables, inverse and implicit function theorems [GATE MA - Real Analysis]
response:
Worked example: The circle x^2 + y^2 = 1 near (0,1) defines y = sqrt(1 - x^2), and dy/dx = -x/y = 0 at x = 0. The polar map (r, theta) -> (r cos theta, r sin theta) has Jacobian determinant r, so it is locally invertible where r != 0.

Formula: Implicit differentiation: dy/dx = -F_x / F_y when F(x,y) = 0 and F_y != 0; inverse function theorem needs det(J) != 0 at the point

A function of several variables is differentiable at a point if it is well approximated by a linear map, its derivative matrix being the Jacobian. The inverse function theorem says that if the Jacobian determinant is non-zero at a point, the function is locally invertible with a differentiable inverse. The implicit function theorem says an equation F(x,y) = 0 with F_y != 0 locally defines y as a differentiable function of x, with dy/dx = -F_x / F_y.

instruction: Give a worked example for Analytic functions, Cauchy-Riemann equations and harmonic functions [GATE MA - Complex Analysis]
response:
Worked example: f(z) = z^2 = (x^2 - y^2) + i(2xy) satisfies u_x = 2x = v_y and u_y = -2y = -v_x, so it is analytic everywhere with f'(z) = 2z. The function f(z) = conjugate(z) fails Cauchy-Riemann everywhere and is nowhere differentiable.

Formula: Cauchy-Riemann: du/dx = dv/dy and du/dy = -dv/dx; f'(z) = u_x + i v_x; Laplace: u_xx + u_yy = 0 for analytic f

A complex function f(z) = u + iv is differentiable at z0 if the limit of the difference quotient exists independent of direction; it is analytic if differentiable in a neighbourhood. Differentiability is equivalent to the Cauchy-Riemann equations u_x = v_y and u_y = -v_x (with continuous partials). The real and imaginary parts of an analytic function are harmonic (their Laplacian is zero) and are conjugate to each other.

instruction: Give a worked example for Cauchy's integral theorem and formula, Liouville's theorem and maximum modulus principle [GATE MA - Complex Analysis]
response:
Worked example: The integral of 1/z around the unit circle is 2 pi i, showing 1/z is not analytic inside (it has a pole at 0). Liouville's theorem gives a one-line proof of the fundamental theorem of algebra.

Formula: Cauchy integral formula: f(a) = (1/(2 pi i)) integral_C f(z)/(z - a) dz; f^(n)(a) = (n!/(2 pi i)) integral_C f(z)/(z - a)^(n+1) dz; Liouville: bounded entire f is constant

Cauchy's integral theorem says the integral of an analytic function around a closed contour is zero. Cauchy's integral formula recovers values inside a contour from boundary values: f(a) = (1/2 pi i) times the integral of f(z)/(z-a) dz. From this follow Liouville's theorem (a bounded entire function is constant), the maximum modulus principle (a non-constant analytic function attains no maximum inside a domain), and Morera's theorem (vanishing integrals over all closed contours imply analyticity).

instruction: Give a worked example for Taylor and Laurent series, singularities and the residue theorem [GATE MA - Complex Analysis]
response:
Worked example: The integral from -infinity to infinity of dx/(1 + x^2) equals pi: close the contour in the upper half-plane, where the only pole is at i with residue 1/(2i), giving 2 pi i * 1/(2i) = pi.

Formula: Residue theorem: integral_C f(z) dz = 2 pi i * sum of residues inside C; for a simple pole, Res(f, a) = lim_{z->a} (z-a) f(z); radius of convergence reaches the nearest singularity

An analytic function expands as a Taylor series inside its disk of convergence; near an isolated singularity it expands as a Laurent series with negative powers. Singularities are removable, poles (of some finite order) or essential. The residue at a pole is the coefficient of (z-a)^-1, and the residue theorem says the integral around a closed contour equals 2 pi i times the sum of residues inside, which evaluates many real integrals.

instruction: Give a worked example for Conformal mappings, Mobius transformations, Rouche's theorem and Schwarz lemma [GATE MA - Complex Analysis]
response:
Worked example: The map w = (z - i)/(z + i) sends the upper half-plane onto the unit disk. Rouche's theorem shows z^5 + 3z + 1 has exactly one zero inside |z| < 1, since |3z| = 3 dominates |z^5 + 1| <= 2 on |z| = 1.

Formula: Mobius: w = (a z + b)/(c z + d), ad - bc != 0; Rouche: if |f| > |g| on C then f and f+g have the same number of zeros inside C; Schwarz: |f(z)| <= |z| and |f'(0)| <= 1

A conformal map is an analytic function with non-zero derivative, preserving angles and local shape. Mobius transformations (az+b)/(cz+d) map circles and lines to circles and lines and are determined by the images of three points. Rouche's theorem counts zeros inside a contour by comparing a function with a dominant term on the boundary. The Schwarz lemma bounds analytic maps of the unit disk fixing the origin: |f(z)| <= |z|.

instruction: Give a worked example for Higher order linear ODEs with constant coefficients [GATE MA - Differential Equations]
Give a worked example for Second order ODEs with variable coefficients, Cauchy-Euler equation and Laplace transforms [GATE MA - Differential Equations]
response:
Worked example: x^2 y'' - 2y = 0 gives m(m-1) - 2 = 0, so m = 2 or -1 and y = C1 x^2 + C2/x. Solving y' + y = 0 with y(0) = 1 by Laplace gives (s+1)Y = 1, so Y = 1/(s+1) and y = e^{-t}.

Formula: Cauchy-Euler: try y = x^m, giving a m(m-1) + b m + c = 0; Laplace: L{y'} = sY(s) - y(0), L{y''} = s^2 Y(s) - s y(0) - y'(0); L{1} = 1/s, L{e^{at}} = 1/(s-a)

The Cauchy-Euler equation a x^2 y'' + b x y' + c y = 0 becomes constant-coefficient under x = e^t, with trial solutions y = x^m. Laplace transforms turn differential equations into algebraic ones: the transform of y' is sY(s) - y(0), so initial conditions enter directly, and the solution follows by partial fractions and inverse transforms. This is especially handy for equations with discontinuous forcing or impulses.

instruction: Give a worked example for Series solutions, Legendre and Bessel functions [GATE MA - Differential Equations]
response:
Worked example: P_0 = 1, P_1 = x, P_2 = (3x^2 - 1)/2. The Frobenius method on Bessel's equation of order 0 gives J_0(x) = 1 - x^2/4 + x^4/64 - ...

Formula: Legendre: (1-x^2) y'' - 2x y' + n(n+1) y = 0; integral_{-1}^{1} P_m P_n dx = 0 for m != n, = 2/(2n+1) for m = n; Bessel: x^2 y'' + x y' + (x^2 - n^2) y = 0

Near an ordinary point, an ODE has power-series solutions found by substituting y = sum a_n x^n and matching coefficients. At a regular singular point the Frobenius method uses y = x^r sum a_n x^n, with r from the indicial equation. Legendre's equation produces Legendre polynomials P_n(x), orthogonal on [-1,1]; Bessel's equation produces Bessel functions J_n(x), orthogonal with a weight on [0,1] and central to circular and cylindrical problems.

instruction: Give a worked example for Systems of linear ODEs and Sturm-Liouville eigenvalue problems [GATE MA - Differential Equations]
response:
Worked example: The system x' = y, y' = -x has eigenvalues +-i and solutions x = A cos t + B sin t. The problem y'' + lambda y = 0 with y(0) = y(pi) = 0 has eigenvalues lambda_n = n^2 and eigenfunctions sin(nx).

Formula: System solution: x(t) = e^{At} x(0); Sturm-Liouville: (p(x) y')' + (lambda w(x) - q(x)) y = 0; orthogonality: integral w y_m y_n dx = 0 for m != n

A system x' = Ax of first-order linear ODEs is solved by the matrix exponential; eigenvalues of A give exponential modes, and the solution is a combination of them. Sturm's oscillation and separation theorems describe how zeros of solutions interlace. A Sturm-Liouville problem (p y')' + (lambda w - q) y = 0 with boundary conditions has real eigenvalues lambda_n increasing to infinity and eigenfunctions orthogonal with weight w, forming a basis for expansions.

instruction: Give a worked example for Planar autonomous systems and stability [GATE MA - Differential Equations]
response:
Worked example: For the pendulum linearized at the bottom, the Jacobian has eigenvalues +-i sqrt(g/l), a centre; at the top the eigenvalues are real of opposite sign, a saddle and unstable. The damped oscillator x'' + 2x' + x = 0 has eigenvalues -1 (repeated), a stable node.

Formula: Linearized system: u' = J u where J is the Jacobian at the equilibrium; trace-determinant test: stable node/spiral when trace < 0 and det > 0; Lyapunov: V > 0 and dV/dt < 0 implies asymptotic stability

A planar autonomous system x' = f(x,y), y' = g(x,y) has stationary points where f = g = 0. Linearized stability examines the Jacobian at the point: eigenvalues with negative real parts give asymptotic stability, positive real parts give instability, and a zero or purely imaginary pair is inconclusive by linearization. Lyapunov functions give a direct method: if a positive definite function decreases along trajectories, the equilibrium is stable.

instruction: Give a worked example for Partial differential equations: classification and separation of variables [GATE MA - Differential Equations]
response:
Worked example: The heat equation u_t = u_xx on 0 < x < pi with u = 0 at both ends separates to modes sin(nx) e^{-n^2 t}. Laplace's equation in a disk gives solutions r^n cos(n theta) and r^n sin(n theta).

Formula: Classification: B^2 - AC < 0 elliptic, = 0 parabolic, > 0 hyperbolic; Laplace: u_xx + u_yy = 0; heat: u_t = k u_xx; wave: u_tt = c^2 u_xx

Second-order PDEs in two variables are classified by the discriminant B^2 - AC: elliptic (Laplace, steady state), parabolic (heat, diffusion) or hyperbolic (wave, propagation). The method of characteristics solves first-order linear and quasilinear PDEs by reducing them to ODEs along characteristic curves. Separation of variables writes u(x,t) = X(x)T(t), turning a PDE into ODEs whose solutions superpose to satisfy boundary conditions, as in Laplace's equation in Cartesian and polar coordinates and the heat and wave equations in one space variable.

instruction: Give a worked example for Wave and heat equations: d'Alembert formula and Cauchy problems [GATE MA - Differential Equations]
response:
Worked example: For a plucked string with u(x,0) = sin x and u_t(x,0) = 0, d'Alembert gives u(x,t) = (1/2)[sin(x-ct) + sin(x+ct)] = sin x cos ct, a standing wave.

Formula: d'Alembert: u(x,t) = (1/2)[g(x-ct) + g(x+ct)] + (1/(2c)) integral_{x-ct}^{x+ct} h(s) ds for u_tt = c^2 u_xx, u(x,0) = g(x), u_t(x,0) = h(x)

The wave equation's Cauchy problem has d'Alembert's explicit solution: the initial displacement splits into left- and right-moving waves, and the initial velocity contributes an integral over the interval between the wave fronts. The domain of dependence of a point (x,t) is the interval [x-ct, x+ct] on the initial line, expressing finite propagation speed. The heat equation's Cauchy problem is solved by convolution with the Gaussian heat kernel, which instantly smooths and spreads data.

instruction: Give a worked example for Numerical solution of linear systems: direct and iterative methods [GATE MA - Numerical Methods]
response:
Worked example: For 4x + y = 9 and x + 3y = 8, Jacobi from (0,0) gives (2.25, 2.67), then (1.58, 1.92), converging to (2, 2). Gaussian elimination on the same system gives x = 2, y = 2 directly.

Formula: Jacobi: x_i^(k+1) = (b_i - sum_{j != i} a_ij x_j^(k)) / a_ii; Gauss-Seidel uses x_j^(k+1) for j < i; strict diagonal dominance: |a_ii| > sum_{j != i} |a_ij| guarantees convergence

Direct methods finish in a fixed number of steps: Gaussian elimination reduces a system to triangular form, LU decomposition reuses the factorization for many right-hand sides, and Cholesky factorization applies to symmetric positive definite matrices. Iterative methods (Jacobi and Gauss-Seidel) start from a guess and refine it; they converge for strictly diagonally dominant matrices, with Gauss-Seidel usually faster since it uses updated values immediately.

instruction: Give a worked example for Numerical solution of nonlinear equations: bisection, secant and fixed point iteration [GATE MA - Numerical Methods]
response:
Worked example: Solving x^2 - 2 = 0 on [1,2] by bisection: after 10 steps the interval width is 1/1024, so sqrt(2) is pinned to about 3 decimal places. Fixed point iteration x = (x + 2/x)/2 is Newton's method for this equation.

Formula: Bisection: error after n steps <= (b - a)/2^n; secant: x_{n+1} = x_n - f(x_n)(x_n - x_{n-1})/(f(x_n) - f(x_{n-1})); fixed point converges if |g'(x)| < 1

The bisection method halves a bracketing interval each step and always converges, but slowly (linearly). The secant method replaces the derivative in Newton's method by a finite difference and converges superlinearly, while fixed point iteration x = g(x) converges when |g'(x)| < 1 near the root. These methods trade reliability (bisection) against speed (secant, Newton).

instruction: Give a worked example for Interpolation: Lagrange and Newton forms and error [GATE MA - Numerical Methods]
response:
Worked example: Interpolating (0,1), (1,2), (2,5) gives P(x) = x^2 + 1: at x = 1.5 it predicts 3.25. Adding the point (3,10) to Newton's form needs only one new divided difference.

Formula: Lagrange: P(x) = sum y_i l_i(x), l_i(x) = product_{j != i} (x - x_j)/(x_i - x_j); error: f(x) - P(x) = f^(n+1)(xi)/(n+1)! * product (x - x_i)

Given n+1 points, there is a unique interpolating polynomial of degree at most n. Lagrange's form builds it as a sum of basis polynomials, each 1 at one node and 0 at the others. Newton's form uses divided differences, which makes adding a new point cheap. The interpolation error at x is f^(n+1)(xi)/(n+1)! times the product of (x - x_i), so error grows with the spacing and the size of the next derivative.

instruction: Give a worked example for Numerical differentiation and integration: Simpson's rule and Newton-Cotes formulas [GATE MA - Numerical Methods]
response:
Worked example: Simpson's rule with h = 0.5 on the integral of x^2 from 0 to 1 gives (0.5/3)[0 + 4(0.25) + 1] = 1/3 exactly, since Simpson is exact for cubics. The trapezoidal rule on the same integral gives 0.375.

Formula: Trapezoidal: integral = (h/2)[f0 + 2f1 + ... + 2f_{n-1} + fn]; Simpson: integral = (h/3)[f0 + 4f1 + 2f2 + 4f3 + ... + fn] with n even; central difference: f'(x) = (f(x+h) - f(x-h))/(2h) + O(h^2)

Numerical differentiation approximates derivatives by difference quotients; the central difference is second-order accurate. Numerical integration replaces the integrand by an interpolating polynomial: the trapezoidal rule uses linear pieces (error O(h^2)), Simpson's rule uses parabolas (error O(h^4)) and needs an even number of intervals, and composite rules split the range into many small panels. Newton-Cotes formulas are this family with equally spaced nodes.

instruction: Give a worked example for Numerical solution of ODE initial value problems: Euler and Runge-Kutta methods [GATE MA - Numerical Methods]
response:
Worked example: For y' = y with y(0) = 1 and h = 0.1, Euler gives y(0.1) = 1.1 (true e^0.1 = 1.1052); Heun gives 1.105, much closer. Halving h roughly halves Euler's error but quarters RK2's.

Formula: Euler: y_{n+1} = y_n + h f(x_n, y_n); Heun (RK2): y_{n+1} = y_n + (h/2)[f(x_n, y_n) + f(x_{n+1}, y_n + h f(x_n, y_n))]; Euler global error O(h), RK2 global error O(h^2)

Euler's method advances the solution by the tangent slope: y_{n+1} = y_n + h f(x_n, y_n); its local error is O(h^2) and global error O(h), so it needs small steps. Second-order Runge-Kutta (RK2, e.g. Heun's method) averages the slopes at the start and a predicted end of the step, giving global error O(h^2). Smaller step size or higher order both improve accuracy, at the cost of more function evaluations.

instruction: What is the formula for Eigenvalues and eigenvectors? When is it used? [GATE MA - Linear Algebra]
response:
Formula: A v = lambda v, v != 0. Characteristic equation: det(A - lambda I) = 0. For a 2x2 matrix [[a, b], [c, d]], det(A - lambda I) = (a - lambda)(d - lambda) - bc = 0. Trace = sum of eigenvalues; determinant = product of eigenvalues.

For a square matrix A, a non-zero vector v is an eigenvector with eigenvalue lambda if A v = lambda v, so A only scales v. Eigenvalues are the roots of the characteristic equation det(A - lambda I) = 0. They determine stability, principal components and many other properties, and a matrix is singular if and only if 0 is one of its eigenvalues.

instruction: What is the formula for Inverse of a 2x2 matrix? When is it used? [GATE MA - Linear Algebra]
response:
Formula: For A = [[a, b], [c, d]], det(A) = ad - bc. If det(A) != 0, A^-1 = (1 / (ad - bc)) x [[d, -b], [-c, a]].

A square matrix A has an inverse A^-1 with A A^-1 = A^-1 A = I exactly when its determinant is non-zero. For a 2x2 matrix the inverse is found by swapping the diagonal entries, negating the off-diagonal entries and dividing by the determinant. Solving A x = b is then x = A^-1 b.

instruction: What is the formula for Taylor series? When is it used? [GATE MA - Calculus]
response:
Formula: f(x) = f(a) + f'(a)(x - a) + f''(a)(x - a)^2 / 2! + f'''(a)(x - a)^3 / 3! + ... . Maclaurin series: e^x = 1 + x + x^2/2! + x^3/3! + ... ; sin x = x - x^3/3! + x^5/5! - ... ; cos x = 1 - x^2/2! + x^4/4! - ...

A Taylor series represents a smooth function as an infinite sum of powers of (x - a), using the function's derivatives at a. The Maclaurin series is the case a = 0. Truncating the series gives a polynomial approximation whose error is controlled by the next term when x is close to a.

instruction: What is the formula for Fundamental theorem of calculus? When is it used? [GATE MA - Calculus]
response:
Formula: If F'(x) = f(x), then integral from a to b of f(x) dx = F(b) - F(a). Also, d/dx [integral from a to x of f(t) dt] = f(x). Power rule: integral of x^n dx = x^(n+1)/(n+1) + C for n != -1.
