Heat treatment exploits this: annealing softens, normalising refines grain, quenching forms hard martensite, and tempering restores toughness.

instruction: Give a worked example for Failure theories and Mohr's circle for stress [GATE PI - Manufacturing]
response:
Worked example: For plane stress sigma_x = 100 MPa, sigma_y = 0, tau_xy = 0: von Mises sigma_eq = 100 MPa and Tresca equivalent is also 100 MPa, so both predict yielding at sigma_y = 100 MPa.

Formula: von Mises: sigma_eq = sqrt(((sigma1-sigma2)^2 + (sigma2-sigma3)^2 + (sigma3-sigma1)^2)/2); Tresca: sigma1 - sigma3 = sigma_y at yield; Mohr: sigma_1,2 = sigma_avg +/- sqrt(((sigma_x-sigma_y)/2)^2 + tau_xy^2)

A part under combined loading fails when some equivalent stress reaches the material's limit. The maximum shear stress (Tresca) theory says yielding starts when the largest shear stress reaches half the yield strength; the distortion-energy (von Mises) theory uses the equivalent stress from all principal stresses and matches ductile metals better. For brittle materials the maximum principal stress theory applies. Mohr's circle gives the principal stresses and maximum shear from sigma_x, sigma_y and tau_xy.

instruction: Give a worked example for Sand casting: patterns, gating and risers [GATE PI - Manufacturing]
response:
Worked example: A cube of side 100 mm has modulus V/A = 16.7 mm and solidifies in time proportional to 16.7^2; its riser needs a larger modulus so it freezes later.

Formula: Chvorinov's rule: solidification time t = C (V/A)^2; Riser modulus must exceed casting modulus: (V/A)_riser > (V/A)_casting; Pattern shrinkage allowance is about 1-2% for cast iron and steel

Sand casting starts with a pattern, oversized by the shrinkage allowance and with draft so it withdraws cleanly from the mould. The gating system (pouring basin, sprue, runner, gates) fills the mould smoothly; the choke controls the filling rate. The casting solidifies from the walls inward and shrinks, so a riser — a reservoir of molten metal with a larger modulus (volume/surface area) than the casting — feeds the shrinkage and must solidify last, per Chvorinov's rule. Defects include porosity, cold shuts and misruns, checked by non-destructive testing.

instruction: Give a worked example for Bulk metal forming: forging, rolling, extrusion and drawing [GATE PI - Manufacturing]
response:
Worked example: Forging a disc of area 0.01 m^2 with flow stress 100 MPa needs an ideal load of about 100e6 x 0.01 = 1000 kN before friction is added.

Formula: Ideal work per volume w = integral sigma d(epsilon); Forging load P approx sigma_f x A x (1 + mu factor); Rolling: contact length L = sqrt(R delta h); Flow stress sigma_f = K epsilon^n (strain hardening)

Bulk forming shapes metal by plastic deformation above or below the recrystallisation temperature (hot, warm or cold working). Ideal work per volume is the area under the true stress-strain curve, and slab analysis adds friction to estimate the real load: forging load is roughly flow stress times projected area, with a friction factor. Rolling load depends on the contact length and mean flow stress; extrusion and wire drawing are analysed the same way, with redundant work raising the load. Common defects are laps, cracks, barrelling in forging and centre burst in drawing.

instruction: Give a worked example for Fusion and solid-state welding processes [GATE PI - Manufacturing]
response:
Worked example: An arc at 25 V, 200 A, 70% efficiency and travel speed 5 mm/s gives heat input (25 x 200 x 0.7)/5 = 700 J/mm.

Formula: Heat input per unit length H = (V I eta)/v, where eta is arc efficiency and v is travel speed; Higher heat input widens the heat-affected zone and slows cooling

Welding joins metals by melting (fusion) or by pressure without melting (solid state). Arc processes dominate: SMAW (stick), GMAW/MIG, GTAW/TIG, plasma arc and submerged arc, each with its own heat source, shielding and deposition rate. Solid-state processes — friction, friction-stir and ultrasonic welding — join without melting the base metal. Weld defects include porosity, slag inclusion, undercut, lack of fusion and cracking, and heat-affected-zone cracking is checked by inspection. Brazing and soldering join with a filler metal that melts below the base metal.

instruction: Give a worked example for Orthogonal machining and Merchant's analysis [GATE PI - Manufacturing]
response:
Worked example: With rake angle 10 deg and chip thickness ratio r = 0.4: tan phi = 0.4 cos10/(1 - 0.4 sin10) = 0.423, so phi = 22.9 degrees.

Formula: tan phi = r cos(alpha)/(1 - r sin(alpha)); Shear force Fs = Fc cos phi - Ft sin phi; Material removal rate MRR = v f d; Specific cutting energy u = Fc/(f d)

In orthogonal cutting the tool edge is perpendicular to the cutting velocity and the chip forms by shear along a shear plane at angle phi. Merchant's circle relates the cutting force Fc, thrust force Ft, shear force and friction force on the rake face. The shear angle follows from the chip thickness ratio r = t1/t2, and specific cutting energy is cutting force per unit material removed. Machining parameters set the material removal rate, and tool materials, wear and cutting fluids decide tool life and surface quality.

instruction: Give a worked example for Non-traditional machining: EDM, ECM, USM, AJM, LBM and EBM [GATE PI - Manufacturing]
response:
Worked example: ECM of iron (atomic weight 56, valency 2) at 1000 A removes mass at a rate proportional to 56 x 1000/(2 x 96485) = 0.29 g/s before efficiency losses.

Formula: ECM material removal: MRR = (A I)/(F rho z) in Faraday terms, i.e. mass removed proportional to current and time; EDM: MRR rises with discharge current and pulse on-time; USM: MRR rises with abrasive grain size and vibration amplitude

Non-traditional processes remove material without a conventional cutting edge, so they can machine very hard materials and complex shapes. EDM removes metal by electric sparks between tool and workpiece; wire EDM cuts profiles with a travelling wire. ECM dissolves metal anodically in an electrolyte, giving a stress-free surface. USM and AJM erode material with abrasive particles in a slurry or gas jet; LBM and EBM melt or vaporise material with a focused beam. Material removal rate, surface roughness and power consumption all depend on the process parameters, such as current in EDM or voltage in ECM.

instruction: Give a worked example for Computer integrated manufacturing: CAD/CAM, CNC and robots [GATE PI - Manufacturing]
response:
Worked example: A CNC program line G01 X50 Y25 F100 moves the tool in a straight line to (50, 25) at a feed of 100 mm/min.

Formula: CNC positioning: absolute (G90) vs incremental (G91) coordinates; Robot degrees of freedom decide the reachable workspace; Group technology uses part-family coding to form manufacturing cells

CAD builds the geometric model of a part; CAM turns it into tool paths and CNC code (G-code) that drives the machine tool. A CNC machine positions the tool by programmed coordinates, giving repeatability that manual machines cannot match. Industrial robots — articulated, SCARA, Cartesian and cylindrical configurations — automate handling, welding and assembly, with drives and controls setting speed and accuracy. Group technology groups similar parts into families for cellular manufacturing, and flexible manufacturing systems link cells with automated material handling.

instruction: Give a worked example for Metrology: limits, fits, tolerances and gauge design [GATE PI - Metrology]
response:
Worked example: A 50 H7/g6 fit: the H7 hole is 50.000 to 50.025 mm and the g6 shaft is 49.975 to 49.991 mm, so clearance is always between 0.009 and 0.050 mm — a clearance fit.

Formula: Maximum clearance = max hole - min shaft; Maximum interference = max shaft - min hole; Tolerance = upper deviation - lower deviation; Gauge tolerance is about 10% of the work tolerance

No part can be made exactly to size, so a tolerance band is specified around the nominal size. A fit describes how mating parts assemble: clearance fits always leave space, interference fits always overlap, and transition fits may do either. The hole-basis system is standard, with IT grades setting tolerance magnitude. Limit gauges check parts quickly: a GO gauge must enter and a NO-GO gauge must not, and Taylor's principle says the GO gauge checks the maximum-material condition over the full feature length while the NO-GO gauge checks a single cross-section.

instruction: Give a worked example for Surface roughness measurement [GATE PI - Metrology]
response:
Worked example: A turned surface specified as Ra 1.6 microns is smoother than a rough-milled surface at Ra 6.3 microns; grinding is typically needed to reach Ra below 0.8 microns.

Formula: Ra = (1/l) integral |y| dx over the sampling length; Rz = average of the five largest peak-to-valley heights; Rq = root mean square roughness

Surface finish is described by the roughness profile after form and waviness are filtered out. The common parameter Ra is the arithmetic average of absolute deviations from the mean line; Rz is the average of the five highest peaks and five deepest valleys. Roughness is measured by contact (stylus profilometer) or non-contact (optical interferometry) methods. Finish affects friction, wear, fatigue and sealing, and is specified with the lay and the sampling length.

instruction: Give a worked example for Acceptance sampling and OC curves [GATE PI - Quality Control]
response:
Worked example: A plan n = 50, c = 1 accepts a lot with 2% defectives with probability about (0.98)^50 + 50 x 0.02 x (0.98)^49 = 0.74.

Formula: OC curve: P(accept) = sum from d=0 to c of C(n,d) p^d (1-p)^(n-d) (binomial); Producer's risk alpha at AQL; Consumer's risk beta at LTPD

Acceptance sampling inspects a sample from a lot and accepts or rejects the whole lot by a rule such as accept if defectives are at most c in a sample of n. The operating characteristic (OC) curve plots the probability of acceptance against the lot's fraction defective, summarised by the producer's risk (rejecting a good lot, at AQL) and the consumer's risk (accepting a bad lot, at LTPD). Single, double and multiple sampling plans trade inspection effort against discrimination.

instruction: Give a worked example for Reliability, availability and maintainability [GATE PI - Quality Control]
response:
Worked example: A machine with MTBF 500 h and MTTR 20 h has availability 500/520 = 0.962; two such machines in parallel have system reliability 1 - (1-0.9)^2 = 0.99 if each has R = 0.9.

Formula: Exponential reliability: R(t) = e^(-lambda t); MTBF = 1/lambda; Availability A = MTBF/(MTBF + MTTR); Series: R_sys = product of R_i; Parallel: R_sys = 1 - product of (1 - R_i)

Reliability R(t) is the probability that a system survives to time t. For a constant failure rate lambda (exponential life), R(t) = e^(-lambda t) and the mean time between failures MTBF = 1/lambda. Maintainability is captured by mean time to repair MTTR, and steady-state availability is MTBF/(MTBF + MTTR). System reliability follows from the configuration: series systems multiply reliabilities, parallel systems multiply unreliabilities. Preventive maintenance, predictive maintenance and total productive maintenance aim to raise availability and cut unplanned downtime.

instruction: Give a worked example for Work study: method study and time study [GATE PI - Industrial Engineering]
response:
Worked example: An operation observed at 2.0 min with a rating of 110% has normal time 2.2 min; with 15% allowances the standard time is 2.2 x 1.15 = 2.53 min.

Formula: Normal time = observed time x rating factor; Standard time = normal time x (1 + allowance fraction); Work sampling: proportion estimate p with standard error sqrt(p(1-p)/n)

Work study improves productivity by examining how work is done. Method study (Taylor, Gilbreth) records and questions the present method and designs a better one, using process charts and the principles of motion economy. Time study measures the work: observed time is rated for pace to give normal time, and allowances for fatigue, delays and personal needs give the standard time. Work sampling estimates the proportion of time spent on activities from random observations, and predetermined motion-time systems (PMTS) build times from basic motions.

instruction: Give a worked example for Facility design: plant layout and assembly line balancing [GATE PI - Industrial Engineering]
response:
Worked example: A line must make 480 units in an 8-hour shift: cycle time = 480/480 = 1 min/unit. With total work content 4.2 min, at least 5 stations are needed (4.2/1 = 4.2, rounded up).

Formula: Cycle time C = available time per period / demand per period; Minimum stations = total work content / cycle time; Balance efficiency = total work content/(number of stations x cycle time); Balance delay = 1 - efficiency

Plant layout arranges machines and workstations to minimise material movement: process layout groups similar machines, product layout follows the line, and cellular layout groups part families. Assembly line balancing assigns tasks to workstations so that each station's time is as close as possible to the cycle time, which is set by demand: cycle time = available time / required output. Balance efficiency is the total work content divided by the number of stations times the cycle time; the balance delay is what remains.

instruction: Give a worked example for Production control: MRP, MRP-II and ERP [GATE PI - Industrial Engineering]
response:
Worked example: A product needing 2 units of part X per unit, with a schedule of 100 products and 50 X in stock, has gross requirement 200, net requirement 150, to be ordered one lead time ahead.

Formula: Net requirements = gross requirements - on-hand - scheduled receipts; Planned order release = net requirements offset backwards by lead time; MRP inputs: master production schedule, bill of materials, inventory records

Material requirements planning explodes the master production schedule through the bill of materials, netting gross requirements against on-hand stock and scheduled receipts to time orders for components. MRP-II adds capacity planning and shop-floor control; ERP integrates the whole business — production, inventory, purchasing, finance and sales — in one system. Push systems (MRP) schedule from a plan, while pull systems (JIT/kanban) produce only on actual demand, and lean manufacturing targets the elimination of waste.

instruction: Give a worked example for Transportation and assignment models [GATE PI - Operations Research]
response:
Worked example: A 3-source, 4-destination problem needs 3+4-1 = 6 occupied cells for a non-degenerate basic feasible solution.

Formula: Transportation: minimise sum c_ij x_ij subject to supply and demand constraints; Degeneracy when occupied cells < m + n - 1; Hungarian method: subtract row minima, then column minima, cover zeros with minimum lines, iterate to an assignment

The transportation problem ships from sources to destinations at minimum cost, subject to supply and demand. An initial basic feasible solution comes from the north-west corner, least-cost or Vogel's approximation method (VAM gives the best start); optimality is tested by the MODI (u-v) method, and degeneracy is handled when occupied cells are fewer than m+n-1. The assignment problem is the special case of one-to-one matching (one worker per job), solved in polynomial time by the Hungarian method.

instruction: Give a worked example for Markovian queuing models [GATE PI - Operations Research]
response:
Worked example: A single-server counter with arrivals 10/hour and service 15/hour has rho = 0.67, average number in system L = 2, and average time in system W = 1/(15-10) = 0.2 h = 12 min.

Formula: M/M/1: utilisation rho = lambda/mu; L = rho/(1-rho); W = 1/(mu - lambda); Little's law: L = lambda W; Stability requires rho < 1

Queues are described by Kendall notation A/B/c: arrival process, service process and number of servers, with M for Markovian (Poisson arrivals, exponential service). The M/M/1 queue has utilisation rho = lambda/mu, average number in system L = rho/(1-rho) and average time in system W = 1/(mu - lambda), linked by Little's law L = lambda W. Stability needs rho < 1; multi-server M/M/c models follow the same logic with Erlang formulas.

instruction: Give a worked example for Project management: PERT, CPM and Gantt charts [GATE PI - Operations Research]
response:
Worked example: An activity with to = 4, tm = 7, tp = 16 days has te = (4+28+16)/6 = 8 days and standard deviation (16-4)/6 = 2 days.

Formula: PERT expected time te = (to + 4 tm + tp)/6; Variance sigma^2 = ((tp - to)/6)^2; CPM: total float = latest start - earliest start; critical path has zero total float

CPM schedules a project with known activity durations: the critical path is the longest chain through the network, it sets the project duration, and activities on it have zero float (slack). PERT handles uncertain durations with three estimates per activity — optimistic, most likely and pessimistic — and an expected time that weights the most likely estimate fourfold. The project variance is the sum of variances of critical activities, giving the probability of meeting a deadline from the normal distribution. Gantt charts show the same schedule as bars against time.

instruction: What is the formula for Economic order quantity (EOQ)? When is it used? [GATE PI - Operations Research]
response:
Formula: EOQ = sqrt(2 * D * S / H); total annual cost TC(Q) = (D / Q) * S + (Q / 2) * H, where D is annual demand, S is ordering cost per order and H is holding cost per unit per year.

The economic order quantity is the order size that minimises total annual inventory cost by balancing ordering cost against holding cost. Ordering more often raises ordering cost but lowers average stock; ordering in larger lots does the reverse. At the EOQ the annual ordering cost exactly equals the annual holding cost. The classic model assumes constant demand, fixed ordering cost and instant replenishment.

instruction: What is the formula for Exponential smoothing forecast? When is it used? [GATE PI - Industrial Engineering]
response:
Formula: F_t = alpha * A_(t-1) + (1 - alpha) * F_(t-1), where F_t is the forecast for period t, A_(t-1) is the actual demand in the previous period, F_(t-1) is the previous forecast and alpha is the smoothing constant.

Exponential smoothing forecasts the next period as a weighted average of the latest actual demand and the latest forecast. The smoothing constant alpha (between 0 and 1) controls responsiveness: a larger alpha reacts faster to recent changes, a smaller alpha gives a steadier forecast. It needs only the previous forecast and the latest actual value, so it is widely used for short-term demand forecasting.

instruction: What is the formula for Control chart limits (X-bar chart)? When is it used? [GATE PI - Quality Control]
response:
Formula: For an X-bar chart: UCL = mu + 3 * sigma / sqrt(n); LCL = mu - 3 * sigma / sqrt(n), where mu is the process mean, sigma is the process standard deviation and n is the subgroup size.

A control chart separates common-cause variation from special-cause variation in a process. The centre line is the process mean, and control limits are set three standard errors from it: about 99.73% of sample means from a stable normal process fall inside. A point outside the limits, or a non-random pattern inside them, signals that the process has shifted and should be investigated.

instruction: What is the formula for Process capability indices Cp and Cpk? When is it used? [GATE PI - Quality Control]
response:
Formula: Cp = (USL - LSL) / (6 * sigma); Cpk = min[(USL - mu) / (3 * sigma), (mu - LSL) / (3 * sigma)], where USL and LSL are the specification limits, mu is the process mean and sigma is the process standard deviation.

Cp measures whether a process spread fits inside the specification width, assuming the process is perfectly centred: Cp compares the tolerance band to six standard deviations. Cpk also penalises a process whose mean has drifted toward one limit, taking the smaller of the two one-sided ratios. A Cp or Cpk of 1 means the spread just fits the specification; 1.33 is the usual minimum target for a capable process.

instruction: What is the formula for Little's law? When is it used? [GATE PI - Operations Research]
response:
Formula: L = lambda * W, where L is the average number of items in the system, lambda is the average arrival rate and W is the average time spent in the system.

Little's law is a fundamental queueing result: the long-run average number of items in a system equals the average arrival rate multiplied by the average time each item spends in the system. It holds for almost any stable queueing system regardless of arrival pattern or service distribution, which makes it a standard check in production, service and inventory problems.

instruction: What is the formula for Taylor's tool life equation? When is it used? [GATE PI - Manufacturing]
response:
Formula: V * T^n = C, where V is cutting speed, T is tool life, n is the Taylor exponent (about 0.1 for high-speed steel, 0.2-0.25 for carbide) and C is the machining constant.

Taylor's tool life equation is the empirical relation between cutting speed and tool life in machining: tool life falls steeply as cutting speed rises. The exponent n and constant C depend on the tool and workpiece materials and the cutting conditions, and are found experimentally. A small n means tool life is very sensitive to cutting speed.

instruction: What is the formula for Linear programming formulation? When is it used? [GATE PI - Operations Research]
response:
Formula: Maximise (or minimise) Z = c1*x1 + c2*x2 + ... subject to a11*x1 + a12*x2 + ... <= b1, ... and x1, x2, ... >= 0.

Linear programming optimises a linear objective function subject to linear constraints. The decision variables are non-negative, and the feasible region is a polygon (or polyhedron) whose optimum, when it exists, occurs at a corner point. This corner-point property is why the graphical method and the simplex method work, and LP is the standard model for product-mix, blending and transportation problems.

instruction: What is the formula for Eigenvalues and eigenvectors? When is it used? [GATE PI - Engineering Mathematics]
response:
Formula: det(A - lambda I) = 0; A x = lambda x; sum of eigenvalues = trace(A); product of eigenvalues = det(A)

For a square matrix A, a non-zero vector x is an eigenvector if A x = lambda x, where lambda is the eigenvalue. Eigenvalues are the roots of det(A - lambda I) = 0; their sum is the trace and their product is the determinant. In PI they appear in vibration analysis, principal stresses and the stability of linear systems.

instruction: What is the formula for Laplace transforms? When is it used? [GATE PI - Engineering Mathematics]
response:
Formula: L{1} = 1/s; L{e^(at)} = 1/(s-a); L{sin(at)} = a/(s^2+a^2); L{f'(t)} = sF(s) - f(0)

The Laplace transform converts a differential equation in time into an algebraic equation in s. It is defined as L{f(t)} = integral from 0 to infinity of e^(-st) f(t) dt. It is the standard GATE tool for initial-value problems and for the dynamic response of mechanical and process systems.

instruction: What is the formula for Probability distributions: binomial, Poisson, normal and exponential? When is it used? [GATE PI - Engineering Mathematics]
response:
Formula: Binomial mean np; Poisson: P(X=k) = e^(-lambda) lambda^k/k!; Normal: Z = (X - mu)/sigma; Exponential: f(t) = lambda e^(-lambda t), mean 1/lambda; Least-squares slope b = sum((x-xbar)(y-ybar))/sum((x-xbar)^2)

A random variable is described by its distribution. Binomial counts successes in n fixed trials; Poisson counts rare events in a fixed interval with mean lambda; normal is the bell curve of mean mu and standard deviation sigma; exponential describes the time between Poisson events and is memoryless. Mean, median, mode and standard deviation summarise a data set, and linear regression fits a straight line by least squares.

instruction: What is the formula for Numerical integration: trapezoidal and Simpson's rules? When is it used? [GATE PI - Engineering Mathematics]
response:
Formula: Trapezoidal: integral approx (h/2)[f0 + 2(f1+...+f(n-1)) + fn]; Simpson 1/3: (h/3)[f0 + 4(f1+f3+...) + 2(f2+f4+...) + fn]

When an integral has no closed form, it is approximated from sampled values. The trapezoidal rule joins points with straight lines; Simpson's 1/3 rule fits parabolas through triples of points and is exact for polynomials up to degree 3. Simpson's rule needs an even number of intervals, and both rules are used for numerical solution of differential equations by single- and multi-step methods.

instruction: What is the formula for Iron-carbon diagram and heat treatment of steels? When is it used? [GATE PI - Manufacturing]
response:
Formula: Eutectoid: 0.77% C at 727 deg C, austenite -> pearlite; Eutectic: 4.3% C at 1147 deg C; Lever rule: fraction of a phase = opposite arm length / total tie-line length

The iron-carbon diagram maps the phases of steel against temperature and carbon content. The eutectoid point at 0.77% C and 727 deg C is where austenite transforms to pearlite, a lamellar mix of ferrite and cementite. Below 0.77% C steels are hypoeutectoid (ferrite + pearlite); above are hypereutectoid (pearlite + cementite). Heat treatment exploits this: annealing softens, normalising refines grain, quenching forms hard martensite, and tempering restores toughness.

A fit describes how mating parts assemble: clearance fits always leave space, interference fits always overlap, and transition fits may do either. The hole-basis system is standard, with IT grades setting tolerance magnitude. Limit gauges check parts quickly: a GO gauge must enter and a NO-GO gauge must not, and Taylor's principle says the GO gauge checks the maximum-material condition over the full feature length while the NO-GO gauge checks a single cross-section.

instruction: What is the formula for Surface roughness measurement? When is it used? [GATE PI - Metrology]
response:
Formula: Ra = (1/l) integral |y| dx over the sampling length; Rz = average of the five largest peak-to-valley heights; Rq = root mean square roughness

Surface finish is described by the roughness profile after form and waviness are filtered out. The common parameter Ra is the arithmetic average of absolute deviations from the mean line; Rz is the average of the five highest peaks and five deepest valleys. Roughness is measured by contact (stylus profilometer) or non-contact (optical interferometry) methods. Finish affects friction, wear, fatigue and sealing, and is specified with the lay and the sampling length.

instruction: What is the formula for Acceptance sampling and OC curves? When is it used? [GATE PI - Quality Control]
response:
Formula: OC curve: P(accept) = sum from d=0 to c of C(n,d) p^d (1-p)^(n-d) (binomial); Producer's risk alpha at AQL; Consumer's risk beta at LTPD

Acceptance sampling inspects a sample from a lot and accepts or rejects the whole lot by a rule such as accept if defectives are at most c in a sample of n. The operating characteristic (OC) curve plots the probability of acceptance against the lot's fraction defective, summarised by the producer's risk (rejecting a good lot, at AQL) and the consumer's risk (accepting a bad lot, at LTPD). Single, double and multiple sampling plans trade inspection effort against discrimination.

instruction: What is the formula for Reliability, availability and maintainability? When is it used? [GATE PI - Quality Control]
response:
Formula: Exponential reliability: R(t) = e^(-lambda t); MTBF = 1/lambda; Availability A = MTBF/(MTBF + MTTR); Series: R_sys = product of R_i; Parallel: R_sys = 1 - product of (1 - R_i)

Reliability R(t) is the probability that a system survives to time t. For a constant failure rate lambda (exponential life), R(t) = e^(-lambda t) and the mean time between failures MTBF = 1/lambda. Maintainability is captured by mean time to repair MTTR, and steady-state availability is MTBF/(MTBF + MTTR). System reliability follows from the configuration: series systems multiply reliabilities, parallel systems multiply unreliabilities. Preventive maintenance, predictive maintenance and total productive maintenance aim to raise availability and cut unplanned downtime.

instruction: What is the formula for Work study: method study and time study? When is it used? [GATE PI - Industrial Engineering]
response:
Formula: Normal time = observed time x rating factor; Standard time = normal time x (1 + allowance fraction); Work sampling: proportion estimate p with standard error sqrt(p(1-p)/n)

Work study improves productivity by examining how work is done. Method study (Taylor, Gilbreth) records and questions the present method and designs a better one, using process charts and the principles of motion economy. Time study measures the work: observed time is rated for pace to give normal time, and allowances for fatigue, delays and personal needs give the standard time. Work sampling estimates the proportion of time spent on activities from random observations, and predetermined motion-time systems (PMTS) build times from basic motions.

instruction: What is the formula for Facility design: plant layout and assembly line balancing? When is it used? [GATE PI - Industrial Engineering]
response:
Formula: Cycle time C = available time per period / demand per period; Minimum stations = total work content / cycle time; Balance efficiency = total work content/(number of stations x cycle time); Balance delay = 1 - efficiency

Plant layout arranges machines and workstations to minimise material movement: process layout groups similar machines, product layout follows the line, and cellular layout groups part families. Assembly line balancing assigns tasks to workstations so that each station's time is as close as possible to the cycle time, which is set by demand: cycle time = available time / required output. Balance efficiency is the total work content divided by the number of stations times the cycle time; the balance delay is what remains.

instruction: What is the formula for Production control: MRP, MRP-II and ERP? When is it used? [GATE PI - Industrial Engineering]
response:
Formula: Net requirements = gross requirements - on-hand - scheduled receipts; Planned order release = net requirements offset backwards by lead time; MRP inputs: master production schedule, bill of materials, inventory records

Material requirements planning explodes the master production schedule through the bill of materials, netting gross requirements against on-hand stock and scheduled receipts to time orders for components. MRP-II adds capacity planning and shop-floor control; ERP integrates the whole business — production, inventory, purchasing, finance and sales — in one system. Push systems (MRP) schedule from a plan, while pull systems (JIT/kanban) produce only on actual demand, and lean manufacturing targets the elimination of waste.

instruction: What is the formula for Transportation and assignment models? When is it used? [GATE PI - Operations Research]
response:
Formula: Transportation: minimise sum c_ij x_ij subject to supply and demand constraints; Degeneracy when occupied cells < m + n - 1; Hungarian method: subtract row minima, then column minima, cover zeros with minimum lines, iterate to an assignment

The transportation problem ships from sources to destinations at minimum cost, subject to supply and demand. An initial basic feasible solution comes from the north-west corner, least-cost or Vogel's approximation method (VAM gives the best start); optimality is tested by the MODI (u-v) method, and degeneracy is handled when occupied cells are fewer than m+n-1. The assignment problem is the special case of one-to-one matching (one worker per job), solved in polynomial time by the Hungarian method.

instruction: What is the formula for Markovian queuing models? When is it used? [GATE PI - Operations Research]
response:
Formula: M/M/1: utilisation rho = lambda/mu; L = rho/(1-rho); W = 1/(mu - lambda); Little's law: L = lambda W; Stability requires rho < 1

Queues are described by Kendall notation A/B/c: arrival process, service process and number of servers, with M for Markovian (Poisson arrivals, exponential service). The M/M/1 queue has utilisation rho = lambda/mu, average number in system L = rho/(1-rho) and average time in system W = 1/(mu - lambda), linked by Little's law L = lambda W. Stability needs rho < 1; multi-server M/M/c models follow the same logic with Erlang formulas.

instruction: What is the formula for Project management: PERT, CPM and Gantt charts? When is it used? [GATE PI - Operations Research]
response:
Formula: PERT expected time te = (to + 4 tm + tp)/6; Variance sigma^2 = ((tp - to)/6)^2; CPM: total float = latest start - earliest start; critical path has zero total float

CPM schedules a project with known activity durations: the critical path is the longest chain through the network, it sets the project duration, and activities on it have zero float (slack). PERT handles uncertain durations with three estimates per activity — optimistic, most likely and pessimistic — and an expected time that weights the most likely estimate fourfold. The project variance is the sum of variances of critical activities, giving the probability of meeting a deadline from the normal distribution. Gantt charts show the same schedule as bars against time.

instruction: Why does Economic order quantity (EOQ) matter in Operations Research? Where is it used? [GATE PI]
response:
The economic order quantity is the order size that minimises total annual inventory cost by balancing ordering cost against holding cost. Ordering more often raises ordering cost but lowers average stock; ordering in larger lots does the reverse. At the EOQ the annual ordering cost exactly equals the annual holding cost. The classic model assumes constant demand, fixed ordering cost and instant replenishment.

Formula: EOQ = sqrt(2 * D * S / H); total annual cost TC(Q) = (D / Q) * S + (Q / 2) * H, where D is annual demand, S is ordering cost per order and H is holding cost per unit per year.

instruction: Why does Exponential smoothing forecast matter in Industrial Engineering? Where is it used? [GATE PI]
response:
Exponential smoothing forecasts the next period as a weighted average of the latest actual demand and the latest forecast. The smoothing constant alpha (between 0 and 1) controls responsiveness: a larger alpha reacts faster to recent changes, a smaller alpha gives a steadier forecast. It needs only the previous forecast and the latest actual value, so it is widely used for short-term demand forecasting.

Formula: F_t = alpha * A_(t-1) + (1 - alpha) * F_(t-1), where F_t is the forecast for period t, A_(t-1) is the actual demand in the previous period, F_(t-1) is the previous forecast and alpha is the smoothing constant.

instruction: Why does Control chart limits (X-bar chart) matter in Quality Control? Where is it used? [GATE PI]
response:
A control chart separates common-cause variation from special-cause variation in a process. The centre line is the process mean, and control limits are set three standard errors from it: about 99.73% of sample means from a stable normal process fall inside. A point outside the limits, or a non-random pattern inside them, signals that the process has shifted and should be investigated.

Formula: For an X-bar chart: UCL = mu + 3 * sigma / sqrt(n); LCL = mu - 3 * sigma / sqrt(n), where mu is the process mean, sigma is the process standard deviation and n is the subgroup size.

instruction: Why does Process capability indices Cp and Cpk matter in Quality Control? Where is it used? [GATE PI]
response:
Cp measures whether a process spread fits inside the specification width, assuming the process is perfectly centred: Cp compares the tolerance band to six standard deviations. Cpk also penalises a process whose mean has drifted toward one limit, taking the smaller of the two one-sided ratios. A Cp or Cpk of 1 means the spread just fits the specification; 1.33 is the usual minimum target for a capable process.

Formula: Cp = (USL - LSL) / (6 * sigma); Cpk = min[(USL - mu) / (3 * sigma), (mu - LSL) / (3 * sigma)], where USL and LSL are the specification limits, mu is the process mean and sigma is the process standard deviation.

instruction: Why does Little's law matter in Operations Research? Where is it used? [GATE PI]
response:
Little's law is a fundamental queueing result: the long-run average number of items in a system equals the average arrival rate multiplied by the average time each item spends in the system. It holds for almost any stable queueing system regardless of arrival pattern or service distribution, which makes it a standard check in production, service and inventory problems.

Formula: L = lambda * W, where L is the average number of items in the system, lambda is the average arrival rate and W is the average time spent in the system.

instruction: Why does Taylor's tool life equation matter in Manufacturing? Where is it used? [GATE PI]
response:
Taylor's tool life equation is the empirical relation between cutting speed and tool life in machining: tool life falls steeply as cutting speed rises. The exponent n and constant C depend on the tool and workpiece materials and the cutting conditions, and are found experimentally. A small n means tool life is very sensitive to cutting speed.

Formula: V * T^n = C, where V is cutting speed, T is tool life, n is the Taylor exponent (about 0.1 for high-speed steel, 0.2-0.25 for carbide) and C is the machining constant.

instruction: Why does Linear programming formulation matter in Operations Research? Where is it used? [GATE PI]
response:
Linear programming optimises a linear objective function subject to linear constraints. The decision variables are non-negative, and the feasible region is a polygon (or polyhedron) whose optimum, when it exists, occurs at a corner point. This corner-point property is why the graphical method and the simplex method work, and LP is the standard model for product-mix, blending and transportation problems.

Formula: Maximise (or minimise) Z = c1*x1 + c2*x2 + ... subject to a11*x1 + a12*x2 + ... <= b1, ... and x1, x2, ... >= 0.

instruction: Why does Eigenvalues and eigenvectors matter in Engineering Mathematics? Where is it used? [GATE PI]
response:
For a square matrix A, a non-zero vector x is an eigenvector if A x = lambda x, where lambda is the eigenvalue. Eigenvalues are the roots of det(A - lambda I) = 0; their sum is the trace and their product is the determinant. In PI they appear in vibration analysis, principal stresses and the stability of linear systems.

Formula: det(A - lambda I) = 0; A x = lambda x; sum of eigenvalues = trace(A); product of eigenvalues = det(A)

instruction: Why does Laplace transforms matter in Engineering Mathematics? Where is it used? [GATE PI]
response:
The Laplace transform converts a differential equation in time into an algebraic equation in s. It is defined as L{f(t)} = integral from 0 to infinity of e^(-st) f(t) dt. It is the standard GATE tool for initial-value problems and for the dynamic response of mechanical and process systems.

Formula: L{1} = 1/s; L{e^(at)} = 1/(s-a); L{sin(at)} = a/(s^2+a^2); L{f'(t)} = sF(s) - f(0)

instruction: Why does Probability distributions: binomial, Poisson, normal and exponential matter in Engineering Mathematics? Where is it used? [GATE PI]
response:
A random variable is described by its distribution. Binomial counts successes in n fixed trials; Poisson counts rare events in a fixed interval with mean lambda; normal is the bell curve of mean mu and standard deviation sigma; exponential describes the time between Poisson events and is memoryless. Mean, median, mode and standard deviation summarise a data set, and linear regression fits a straight line by least squares.

Formula: Binomial mean np; Poisson: P(X=k) = e^(-lambda) lambda^k/k!; Normal: Z = (X - mu)/sigma; Exponential: f(t) = lambda e^(-lambda t), mean 1/lambda; Least-squares slope b = sum((x-xbar)(y-ybar))/sum((x-xbar)^2)

instruction: Why does Numerical integration: trapezoidal and Simpson's rules matter in Engineering Mathematics? Where is it used? [GATE PI]
response:
When an integral has no closed form, it is approximated from sampled values. The trapezoidal rule joins points with straight lines; Simpson's 1/3 rule fits parabolas through triples of points and is exact for polynomials up to degree 3. Simpson's rule needs an even number of intervals, and both rules are used for numerical solution of differential equations by single- and multi-step methods.

Formula: Trapezoidal: integral approx (h/2)[f0 + 2(f1+...+f(n-1)) + fn]; Simpson 1/3: (h/3)[f0 + 4(f1+f3+...) + 2(f2+f4+...) + fn]

instruction: Why does Iron-carbon diagram and heat treatment of steels matter in Manufacturing? Where is it used? [GATE PI]
response:
The iron-carbon diagram maps the phases of steel against temperature and carbon content. The eutectoid point at 0.77% C and 727 deg C is where austenite transforms to pearlite, a lamellar mix of ferrite and cementite. Below 0.77% C steels are hypoeutectoid (ferrite + pearlite); above are hypereutectoid (pearlite + cementite). Heat treatment exploits this: annealing softens, normalising refines grain, quenching forms hard martensite, and tempering restores toughness.

Formula: Eutectoid: 0.77% C at 727 deg C, austenite -> pearlite; Eutectic: 4.3% C at 1147 deg C; Lever rule: fraction of a phase = opposite arm length / total tie-line length

instruction: Why does Failure theories and Mohr's circle for stress matter in Manufacturing? Where is it used? [GATE PI]
response:
A part under combined loading fails when some equivalent stress reaches the material's limit. The maximum shear stress (Tresca) theory says yielding starts when the largest shear stress reaches half the yield strength; the distortion-energy (von Mises) theory uses the equivalent stress from all principal stresses and matches ductile metals better. For brittle materials the maximum principal stress theory applies. Mohr's circle gives the principal stresses and maximum shear from sigma_x, sigma_y and tau_xy.

Formula: von Mises: sigma_eq = sqrt(((sigma1-sigma2)^2 + (sigma2-sigma3)^2 + (sigma3-sigma1)^2)/2); Tresca: sigma1 - sigma3 = sigma_y at yield; Mohr: sigma_1,2 = sigma_avg +/- sqrt(((sigma_x-sigma_y)/2)^2 + tau_xy^2)

instruction: What is Denavit-Hartenberg parameters? Explain it briefly. [GATE RA - Kinematics]
response:
The Denavit-Hartenberg (DH) convention describes each joint of a serial robot with just four parameters: link length a, link twist alpha, link offset d, and joint angle theta. For a revolute joint theta is the variable and a, alpha and d are constants; for a prismatic joint d is the variable. Substituting the four parameters into the standard homogeneous matrix gives the pose of frame i relative to frame i-1, and multiplying the matrices of all joints gives the end-effector pose relative to the base.

Formula: A_i = [[cos(theta_i), -sin(theta_i)cos(alpha_i), sin(theta_i)sin(alpha_i), a_i cos(theta_i)], [sin(theta_i), cos(theta_i)cos(alpha_i), -cos(theta_i)sin(alpha_i), a_i sin(theta_i)], [0, sin(alpha_i), cos(alpha_i), d_i], [0, 0, 0, 1]]; T_0n = A_1 A_2 ... A_n

Worked example: For one planar link with a = 0.5 m, alpha = 0, d = 0 and theta = 90 degrees, A = [[0, -1, 0, 0], [1, 0, 0, 0.5], [0, 0, 1, 0], [0, 0, 0, 1]], so the end of the link is at position (0, 0.5, 0) m relative to the base frame.

instruction: What is Forward and inverse kinematics of a 2R planar arm? Explain it briefly. [GATE RA - Kinematics]
response:
Forward kinematics computes the end-effector position from the joint angles, and is unique. Inverse kinematics computes the joint angles from a desired end-effector position, and is generally harder: a 2R planar arm has no solution outside its reachable workspace (|L1 - L2| <= r <= L1 + L2), one solution on the workspace boundary, and two solutions (elbow-up and elbow-down) inside it.

Formula: Forward: x = L1 cos(theta1) + L2 cos(theta1 + theta2); y = L1 sin(theta1) + L2 sin(theta1 + theta2). Inverse: cos(theta2) = (x^2 + y^2 - L1^2 - L2^2) / (2 L1 L2); theta1 = atan2(y, x) - atan2(L2 sin(theta2), L1 + L2 cos(theta2))

Worked example: With L1 = 2 m, L2 = 1.5 m and target (x, y) = (2, 1) m: cos(theta2) = (5 - 4 - 2.25) / 6 = -0.2083, so theta2 = +/-102.02 degrees. For the elbow-up solution (theta2 = +102.02 degrees), theta1 = atan2(1, 2) - atan2(1.467, 1.688) = 26.57 - 41.00 = -14.44 degrees. Forward kinematics with these angles returns (2.0, 1.0) m.

instruction: What is Degrees of freedom - Gruebler (Kutzbach) criterion? Explain it briefly. [GATE RA - Kinematics]
response:
The degree of freedom (mobility) of a mechanism is the number of independent inputs needed to define the configuration of all its links. Gruebler's criterion counts it from the number of links and joints: each free link in a plane has 3 degrees of freedom, each 1-DOF joint (revolute or prismatic) removes 2, and each 2-DOF joint (cam or gear pair) removes 1. A result F = 1 means one input drives the mechanism; F = 0 is a structure and F < 0 is over-constrained.

Formula: Planar: F = 3(n - 1) - 2 j1 - j2, where n = number of links including the ground link, j1 = number of 1-DOF joints, j2 = number of 2-DOF joints. Spatial: F = 6(n - 1) - 5 j1 - 4 j2 - 3 j3 - 2 j4 - j5

Worked example: A four-bar linkage has n = 4 links (including ground) and j1 = 4 revolute joints, j2 = 0. Then F = 3(4 - 1) - 2(4) - 0 = 9 - 8 = 1, so it has one degree of freedom and needs one input (one driven crank) to define its motion.

instruction: What is Manipulator Jacobian? Explain it briefly. [GATE RA - Kinematics]
response:
The Jacobian matrix J(q) relates joint velocities to end-effector velocity: it is the matrix of partial derivatives of the end-effector position and orientation with respect to the joint variables. For a spatial manipulator it is 6 x n (3 rows for linear velocity, 3 for angular velocity), where n is the number of joints. When J loses rank the manipulator is at a singularity, where it cannot move in some Cartesian direction and the inverse-velocity solution fails or blows up.

Formula: x_dot = J(q) q_dot, where J(q) = partial x / partial q; for a square non-singular Jacobian, q_dot = J(q)^-1 x_dot, and in general q_dot = J(q)^+ x_dot using the pseudoinverse. For a 2R planar arm: J = [[-L1 sin(theta1) - L2 sin(theta1+theta2), -L2 sin(theta1+theta2)], [L1 cos(theta1) + L2 cos(theta1+theta2), L2 cos(theta1+theta2)]]

Worked example: For a 2R arm with L1 = L2 = 1 m, theta1 = 0 degrees and theta2 = 90 degrees, J = [[-1, -1], [1, 0]]. With joint velocities q_dot = [1, 0] rad/s, the end-effector velocity is [vx, vy] = J q_dot = [-1, 1] m/s.

instruction: What is PID control? Explain it briefly. [GATE RA - Dynamics & Control]
response:
A PID controller drives the error e(t) = setpoint - measured value to zero using three terms: proportional (present error), integral (accumulated past error) and derivative (rate of change of error, anticipating the future). The proportional term gives speed, the integral term removes steady-state error, and the derivative term damps overshoot. Choosing Kp, Ki and Kd is called tuning; too much integral gain causes windup and oscillation, and the derivative term amplifies measurement noise.

Formula: u(t) = Kp e(t) + Ki integral_0^t e(tau) d tau + Kd de(t)/dt, where e(t) = r(t) - y(t); transfer function Gc(s) = Kp + Ki/s + Kd s

Worked example: At one instant, e = 4, the accumulated integral of e is 10, de/dt = -1, with Kp = 2, Ki = 0.5 and Kd = 0.1. Then u = 2(4) + 0.5(10) + 0.1(-1) = 8 + 5 - 0.1 = 12.9 (in the controller's output units).

instruction: What is PLC ladder logic basics? Explain it briefly. [GATE RA - Automation & PLC]
response:
A PLC (programmable logic controller) runs a scan cycle: read inputs, execute the program, update outputs. Ladder logic, one of the IEC 61131-3 languages, draws the program like a relay ladder with two vertical power rails and horizontal rungs. Contacts on the left are conditions and a coil on the right is the output: a normally open (NO) contact passes power when its input is ON, a normally closed (NC) contact passes power when its input is OFF (NOT), contacts in series give AND, and contacts in parallel give OR.

Formula: Series contacts = AND; parallel contacts = OR; NC contact = NOT. Motor start/stop seal-in (latching) rung: Y = (Start OR Y) AND (NOT Stop), where Y is the motor output coil; a NO contact of Y in parallel with Start keeps the motor running after Start is released until Stop breaks the rung.

Worked example: Start is a momentary NO pushbutton and Stop is an NC pushbutton. Pressing Start makes (Start OR Y) true and Stop not pressed makes (NOT Stop) true, so Y energises and its own contact seals the rung in, so the motor keeps running after Start is released. Pressing Stop makes (NOT Stop) false, the rung opens and Y = 0, so the motor stops.

instruction: What is Manipulator singularities? Explain it briefly. [GATE RA - Kinematics]
response:
A manipulator is at a singularity when its Jacobian loses rank, i.e. det(J) = 0 for a square Jacobian, so the end-effector loses the ability to move (or exert force) in some Cartesian direction. At a singularity, inverse kinematics has no unique solution and joint velocities needed for a given tip velocity blow up. Common types are wrist singularities (axes of joints 4 and 6 align), elbow singularities (arm fully stretched or folded) and shoulder singularities (wrist centre lies on the first joint axis).

Formula: Singularity when det(J(q)) = 0 (square J) or rank(J(q)) < min(6, n). For a 2R planar arm: det(J) = l1*l2*sin(theta2). Near a singularity, joint velocity qdot = J^(-1) * xdot grows without bound.

Worked example: For a 2R planar arm with link lengths l1 = l2 = 1 m, det(J) = l1*l2*sin(theta2) = sin(theta2). At theta2 = 0 (arm fully stretched) or theta2 = 180 degrees (fully folded), det(J) = 0: the arm is singular and cannot move its tip in the radial direction, however large the joint torques.

instruction: What is Lagrangian dynamics and the manipulator equation? Explain it briefly. [GATE RA - Dynamics & Control]
response:
Lagrangian dynamics derives a robot's equations of motion from energy, not from free-body diagrams. With generalised coordinates q, kinetic energy T and potential energy U, the Lagrangian is L = T - U, and each joint obeys the Euler-Lagrange equation. Collecting terms for all joints gives the manipulator equation, in which M(q) is the symmetric positive-definite inertia matrix, C(q, qdot) carries Coriolis and centrifugal effects, and g(q) is gravity. At rest only the gravity term remains, so tau = g(q) is the holding torque.

Formula: L = T - U; d/dt(dL/dqdot_i) - dL/dq_i = tau_i. Manipulator equation: M(q)*qddot + C(q, qdot)*qdot + g(q) = tau. Kinetic energy: T = (1/2)*qdot^T*M(q)*qdot.

Worked example: A single pendulum link (point mass m = 2 kg at length l = 0.5 m): L = (1/2)*m*l^2*thetadot^2 + m*g*l*cos(theta). The equation of motion is m*l^2*thetaddot + m*g*l*sin(theta) = tau. At theta = 30 degrees the gravity torque to hold it still is m*g*l*sin(30) = 2*9.81*0.5*0.5 = 4.91 Nm.

instruction: What is Newton-Euler recursive dynamics? Explain it briefly. [GATE RA - Dynamics & Control]
response:
The Newton-Euler method derives the same equations of motion as Lagrange, but by applying Newton's law (F = m*a) and Euler's rotational law (N = I*alpha + omega x (I*omega)) to each link in turn. A forward recursion propagates velocities and accelerations from the base to the tip; a backward recursion propagates forces and moments from the tip to the base, giving the joint torques. It is computationally efficient (O(n) in the number of joints) and is the basis of the recursive Newton-Euler algorithm used for inverse dynamics in real controllers.

Formula: Newton: F = m*a_cm. Euler: N = I*alpha + omega x (I*omega). Inverse dynamics (RNEA): given q, qdot, qddot, the recursion returns tau; forward dynamics: qddot = M(q)^(-1)*(tau - C(q, qdot)*qdot - g(q)).

Worked example: Holding a 5 kg link horizontally with its centre of mass 0.3 m from the joint: the static joint torque is m*g*r = 5*9.81*0.3 = 14.7 Nm. Newton-Euler computes this (and the dynamic torques) link by link instead of from one big energy expression, which is why it is the standard O(n) algorithm in robot controllers.

instruction: What is Computed-torque trajectory tracking control? Explain it briefly. [GATE RA - Dynamics & Control]
response:
Computed-torque (inverse-dynamics) control cancels the robot's nonlinear dynamics by feeding back the model: the controller computes the torque that would make the arm behave like a set of independent double integrators, then adds PD terms on the tracking error. If the model is exact, each joint's error obeys a linear second-order equation, so Kp and Kd can be set from a desired natural frequency and damping ratio. Its weakness is model error: wrong masses or friction leave residual dynamics, so in practice it is combined with robust or adaptive terms.

Formula: tau = M(q)*(qddot_d + Kp*e + Kd*edot) + C(q, qdot)*qdot + g(q), where e = q_d - q. Ideal error dynamics: eddot + Kd*edot + Kp*e = 0. Damping ratio: zeta = Kd/(2*sqrt(Kp)); wn = sqrt(Kp).

Worked example: Choose Kp = 100, Kd = 20 for one joint. The error dynamics are eddot + 20*edot + 100*e = 0, i.e. natural frequency wn = sqrt(100) = 10 rad/s and damping ratio zeta = Kd/(2*sqrt(Kp)) = 20/20 = 1, so the tracking error decays critically damped, with no overshoot.

instruction: What is Lyapunov stability and Routh-Hurwitz criterion? Explain it briefly. [GATE RA - Dynamics & Control]
response:
Lyapunov stability proves a control system is stable without solving its differential equations: find a positive-definite energy-like function V (V = 0 only at the equilibrium, V > 0 elsewhere) and show its time derivative Vdot <= 0 along trajectories. If Vdot is strictly negative (except at the equilibrium), the equilibrium is asymptotically stable. The classical Routh-Hurwitz criterion is the complementary algebraic test: a linear system's characteristic polynomial has all roots in the left half-plane (stable) iff all entries in the first column of the Routh array are positive.

Formula: Lyapunov: V(x) > 0 for x != 0, V(0) = 0, and Vdot(x) <= 0 => stable; Vdot(x) < 0 for x != 0 => asymptotically stable. Routh-Hurwitz: stability iff the first column of the Routh array has no sign changes.

Worked example: For a PD-controlled joint with error e and error rate edot, take V = (1/2)*edot^2 + (1/2)*Kp*e^2 (kinetic-like plus potential-like energy). Then Vdot = -Kd*edot^2 <= 0, so the energy never grows and the equilibrium e = 0 is stable; with Kd > 0 the error decays.

instruction: What is DC servo and stepper motors? Explain it briefly. [GATE RA - Sensors & Actuators]
response:
Robot joints are usually driven by DC servo motors (brushed or brushless) through a gearbox, because they give smooth, controllable torque proportional to current and are easily closed-loop controlled with an encoder. The back-EMF grows with speed, so at high speed less voltage is left to drive current and torque falls. Stepper motors move in fixed angular steps and hold position open-loop, which suits low-cost positioning, but they lose steps under overload and are noisier and less efficient than servos at high speed. Gear reduction multiplies torque by the gear ratio (and divides speed), at the cost of added friction and backlash.

Formula: DC motor: tau = Kt*I; back-EMF Eb = Ke*omega; V = I*R + Eb (steady state). Stepper step angle = 360 degrees / steps per revolution. Gearbox: tau_out = N*tau_motor, omega_out = omega_motor/N (ideal, N = gear ratio).

Worked example: A DC servo motor with torque constant Kt = 0.1 Nm/A driven at 3 A produces tau = 0.1*3 = 0.3 Nm. A 200-step-per-revolution stepper motor moves 360/200 = 1.8 degrees per step, so 50 steps rotate it 90 degrees, with no position sensor needed if no steps are missed.

instruction: What is Encoders and resolvers for position sensing? Explain it briefly. [GATE RA - Sensors & Actuators]
response:
An encoder measures joint angle: an optical or magnetic disc with slots interrupts a light beam (or changes a magnetic field) as it turns, producing pulses. Incremental encoders count pulses from a reference mark, so they lose absolute position at power-off and need homing; quadrature decoding (two channels A and B, 90 degrees apart) gives direction and four counts per pulse period. Absolute encoders output a unique code for each angle, so position is known immediately. A resolver is a rugged analogue alternative that outputs sine/cosine signals proportional to angle and survives harsh factory environments better than optical encoders.

Formula: Resolution (degrees) = 360 / counts per revolution. Quadrature counts per rev = 4 * pulses per rev (PPR). Angle = counts * (360 / counts per rev).

Worked example: A 1024-pulse-per-revolution incremental encoder with quadrature decoding gives 4*1024 = 4096 counts per revolution, so the angular resolution is 360/4096 = 0.088 degrees per count. An absolute encoder instead reports the exact angle at power-on, with no homing move needed.

instruction: What is Force/torque, tactile and proximity sensors? Explain it briefly. [GATE RA - Sensors & Actuators]
response:
Force/torque sensors, usually strain-gauge based, measure the six components of force and moment at the wrist or in a joint, enabling force control, assembly (peg-in-hole), and safe human-robot contact. Tactile sensors measure distributed pressure over a gripper surface, proximity sensors (ultrasonic, infrared, capacitive) detect nearby objects without contact, and vision (cameras) gives the richest sensing but needs processing. Sensor choice trades accuracy, bandwidth, cost and robustness.

Formula: Torque from a force at a distance: tau = r x F (magnitude r*F*sin(theta)). Strain-gauge bridge output is proportional to applied strain, hence to force.

Worked example: A wrist force sensor reads 10 N of contact force applied 0.2 m from the joint axis: the joint feels a torque of tau = r x F = 0.2*10 = 2 Nm. A controller can use that reading to cap contact force, e.g. to stop before damaging a part or hurting a person.

instruction: What is Pneumatic and hydraulic actuators? Explain it briefly. [GATE RA - Sensors & Actuators]
response:
Pneumatic actuators use compressed air (typically 5-7 bar): they are fast, clean, cheap and safe in explosive atmospheres, but air is compressible, so force and position control are soft and imprecise. Hydraulic actuators use pressurised oil (typically 100-200 bar): they deliver very large forces in a compact size and are stiff and precise, but need pumps, seals and maintenance and can leak. The choice is force and precision (hydraulic) versus speed, cleanliness and cost (pneumatic); electric servos beat both on controllability.

Formula: Actuator force: F = P*A, where P is pressure and A is piston area. Cylinder speed: v = Q/A, where Q is volume flow rate.

Worked example: A pneumatic cylinder at 6 bar (600,000 Pa) with a 50 mm bore (area pi*0.025^2 = 0.00196 m2) pushes with F = P*A = 600,000*0.00196 = 1,178 N, about 1.18 kN. The same force from a hydraulic cylinder needs far less area because hydraulic pressure is typically 100-200 bar.

instruction: What is Configuration space and free space? Explain it briefly. [GATE RA - Motion Planning]
response:
The configuration space (C-space) is the space of all joint configurations q of a robot; for an n-joint arm it is n-dimensional. Obstacles in the workspace map to forbidden regions C_obs in C-space, and the free space C_free is everything else. Motion planning is then a geometric problem in C-space: find a continuous path from the start configuration to the goal that stays inside C_free. The workspace is where the task is described; the C-space is where the planning is done, because joint limits and self-collision are simple bounds there.

Formula: C-space: q in R^n (or a torus for revolute joints). C = C_free union C_obs. A valid path is a continuous curve q(t) with q(t) in C_free for all t, q(0) = q_start, q(1) = q_goal.

Worked example: A 2R planar arm has two joint angles, so its configuration space is a torus: each angle wraps around at 360 degrees, and the point (350 degrees, 10 degrees) is adjacent to (0 degrees, 10 degrees). An obstacle in the workspace becomes a forbidden region in this torus, and a valid motion is a continuous curve that stays in the free part.

instruction: What is RRT and PRM sampling-based planning? Explain it briefly. [GATE RA - Motion Planning]
response:
Sampling-based planners avoid building the C-space explicitly. RRT (Rapidly-exploring Random Tree) grows a tree from the start by sampling random configurations, steering a small step from the nearest tree node toward each sample, and keeping the step if it is collision-free; it is fast and explores large spaces well, but the path is jagged and only probabilistically complete. PRM (Probabilistic Roadmap) instead samples many collision-free configurations, connects nearby ones into a roadmap graph, and then searches the graph with A*; the roadmap can be reused for many queries in the same environment. RRT* rewires the tree to converge toward the optimal path.

Formula: RRT step: q_new = q_near + eta*(q_rand - q_near)/||q_rand - q_near||, kept only if the segment q_near to q_new is collision-free. PRM: roadmap graph G = (V, E) of sampled free configurations; query = graph search (e.g. A*) from q_start to q_goal.

Worked example: An RRT planning for a mobile robot samples a random point, finds the nearest tree node, and extends one step of size 0.1 m toward it. After a few thousand iterations the tree has spread through the free space and reached the goal region, even in a cluttered room where a grid search would be far too large.

instruction: What is Artificial potential field planning? Explain it briefly. [GATE RA - Motion Planning]
response:
Artificial potential fields plan by treating the goal as an attractor and obstacles as repellers: the robot follows the negative gradient of the total potential, i.e. it rolls downhill. The method is simple, fast and reactive, so it is popular for mobile-robot obstacle avoidance. Its main flaw is local minima, where attractive and repulsive forces cancel away from the goal and the robot gets stuck; narrow passages and oscillations near obstacles are other known problems. It is a local method, unlike RRT/PRM which plan globally.

Formula: U_att(q) = (1/2)*k_att*||q - q_goal||^2. U_rep(q) = (1/2)*k_rep*(1/d - 1/d0)^2 if d < d0, else 0, where d is distance to the nearest obstacle and d0 the influence range. U_total = U_att + U_rep; motion follows F = -grad(U_total).

Worked example: With attractive gain k_att = 1 and the robot 2 m from the goal, U_att = (1/2)*1*2^2 = 2 and the attractive force magnitude is k_att*2 = 2 (in force units), pulling it toward the goal. The classic failure is a U-shaped obstacle: the repulsive push balances the attraction and the robot stalls in a local minimum short of the goal.

instruction: What is Joint-space trajectory planning: cubic, quintic and trapezoidal profiles? Explain it briefly. [GATE RA - Trajectory Planning]
response:
A path is the geometry of the motion; a trajectory adds the timing law. In joint space, a cubic polynomial fits position and velocity at both ends (four conditions, four coefficients) and gives smooth position and velocity, but acceleration jumps at the ends. A quintic polynomial also fixes the end accelerations (six conditions). The trapezoidal velocity profile is the industrial workhorse: constant acceleration, constant velocity, constant deceleration, which makes it easy to respect vmax and amax, but acceleration is discontinuous at the phase switches. Via points are handled by joining polynomial segments with continuous velocity.

Formula: Cubic: q(t) = a0 + a1*t + a2*t^2 + a3*t^3, with q(0) = q0, q(tf) = qf, qdot(0) = v0, qdot(tf) = vf. Rest-to-rest: a0 = q0, a1 = 0, a2 = 3*(qf - q0)/tf^2, a3 = -2*(qf - q0)/tf^3; peak velocity = 1.5*(qf - q0)/tf. Trapezoidal: distance = (1/2)*vmax*(tf + t_cruise), where t_cruise is the constant-velocity time.

Worked example: Move one joint from 0 to 90 degrees (pi/2 = 1.571 rad) in tf = 2 s, at rest at both ends, with a cubic polynomial: a0 = 0, a1 = 0, a2 = 3*(1.571)/2^2 = 1.178, a3 = -2*(1.571)/2^3 = -0.393, so q(t) = 1.178*t^2 - 0.393*t^3. Peak velocity is 1.5*(1.571)/2 = 1.18 rad/s at t = 1 s. A trapezoidal profile would instead accelerate at constant amax, cruise at vmax, then decelerate, which respects velocity and acceleration limits directly.

instruction: What is SCADA and the industrial automation hierarchy? Explain it briefly. [GATE RA - Automation & PLC]
response:
Industrial automation is organised in layers: field devices (sensors, actuators) at the bottom, PLCs and controllers doing real-time control, SCADA (Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition) monitoring, logging and alarming from a control room, then MES for production scheduling and ERP for business planning. SCADA supervises but does not replace the PLC's real-time loop: if SCADA goes down, the PLCs keep running the process. Modern plants link these layers over industrial Ethernet and fieldbus networks.

Formula: Automation hierarchy (bottom to top): field devices -> PLC / DCS (real-time control) -> SCADA (supervision, logging, alarms) -> MES (production management) -> ERP (business planning). Rule: SCADA monitors and commands; the PLC controls.

Worked example: In a bottling plant, field sensors and actuators wire into PLCs that run the filling sequence in real time; the SCADA system in the control room shows tank levels and line speed on one screen, logs every batch, and raises an alarm if a tank runs low, while the plant MES above it schedules the day's orders.

instruction: What is Homogeneous transformations and rotation matrices? Explain it briefly. [GATE RA - Kinematics]
response:
A rotation matrix R maps coordinates between frames: it is orthonormal (R-transpose times R = identity, determinant +1). A homogeneous transform T combines rotation R and translation p in one 4x4 matrix, and chaining transforms maps a point through several frames: T02 = T01 x T12. Forward kinematics of a robot is a chain of such transforms, one per joint.

Formula: 2D rotation: R(theta) = [[cos theta, -sin theta],[sin theta, cos theta]]; T = [[R, p],[0 0 0, 1]]; composition T02 = T01 x T12

Worked example: Rotating the point (1, 0) by 90 degrees: R(90) x (1, 0) = (0, 1).

instruction: What is KCL, KVL, Thevenin and Norton theorems? Explain it briefly. [GATE RA - Mechatronics Basics]
response:
Kirchhoff's current law: the currents entering a node sum to zero. Kirchhoff's voltage law: the voltages around any closed loop sum to zero. Thevenin's theorem: any linear network seen from two terminals behaves like a voltage source Vth (the open-circuit voltage) in series with a resistance Rth. Norton's equivalent is a current source Isc in parallel with the same Rth. Maximum power is delivered when the load equals Rth.

Formula: Vth = open-circuit voltage; Rth = Vth / Isc; maximum power when R_load = Rth, Pmax = Vth^2 / (4 x Rth)

Worked example: A source with Vth = 12 V and Rth = 3 ohm delivers maximum power 12^2 / (4 x 3) = 12 W to a 3 ohm load.

instruction: What is Ideal op-amp: inverting and non-inverting amplifiers? Explain it briefly. [GATE RA - Analog Circuits & Embedded Systems]
response:
An ideal op-amp has infinite gain, infinite input impedance and zero output impedance. In negative feedback the two inputs sit at the same voltage (virtual short) and draw no current (virtual ground at the inverting input). That gives clean gain formulas set by two resistors, and the same building block makes integrators, filters, Schmitt triggers and comparators.

Formula: Inverting gain A = -Rf / R1; non-inverting gain A = 1 + Rf / R1

Worked example: With Rf = 100 k ohm and R1 = 10 k ohm, an inverting amplifier has gain -10: 0.5 V in gives -5 V out.

instruction: What is Fourier, Laplace and Z-transforms? Explain it briefly. [GATE RA - Signals & Systems]
response:
The Fourier transform moves a signal between time and frequency. The Laplace transform moves differential equations into algebra in the s-domain, handling initial conditions, which is why control design lives in s. The Z-transform is the discrete-time counterpart for sampled signals and digital control: sampling with period T maps s to z = e^(sT).

Formula: Laplace: L{df/dt} = sF(s) - f(0); Z-transform: X(z) = sum over n of x[n] z^(-n); sampling: z = e^(sT)

Worked example: A unit step u(t) has Laplace transform 1/s; the same step sampled has Z-transform z/(z - 1).

instruction: What is Transfer functions, Bode plots and root locus? Explain it briefly. [GATE RA - Dynamics & Control]
response:
For a linear time-invariant system the transfer function G(s) = Y(s)/U(s) captures all input-output behaviour. Its poles decide stability: all poles in the left half-plane means stable. A Bode plot shows gain and phase against frequency; the root locus shows how the poles move as a gain K grows. Gain margin and phase margin measure how far the system is from instability.

Formula: Gain margin = 1/|G| at the phase -180 degree frequency; phase margin = 180 degrees + phase of G at the gain crossover frequency; stable when both margins are positive

Worked example: G(s) = 1/(s + 1): Bode magnitude falls at 20 dB per decade after omega = 1 rad/s and phase tends to -90 degrees.

instruction: What is PID control and tuning? Explain it briefly. [GATE RA - Dynamics & Control]
response:
A PID controller acts on the error e: the proportional term corrects the present error, the integral term accumulates past error and removes steady-state offset, and the derivative term anticipates future error and adds damping. Too much integral action causes overshoot and oscillation; derivative action amplifies measurement noise. Ziegler-Nichols tuning finds the ultimate gain Ku and period Tu at the edge of oscillation and sets gains from them.

Formula: u(t) = Kp x e + Ki x integral of e dt + Kd x de/dt; Ziegler-Nichols: Kp = 0.6 Ku, Ti = Tu/2, Td = Tu/8

Worked example: A motor position loop with proportional-only control holds a steady offset under load; adding integral action removes it.

instruction: What is Mohr's circle for plane stress? Explain it briefly. [GATE RA - Mechanics of Materials]
response:
Mohr's circle plots normal stress against shear stress for every orientation of a material element. Its centre is the average normal stress and its radius comes from the stress differences; the circle's ends give the principal stresses (where shear is zero) and its top and bottom give the maximum shear stress, which acts on planes at 45 degrees to the principal planes.

Formula: Principal stresses: sigma1,2 = (sigma_x + sigma_y)/2 +- sqrt(((sigma_x - sigma_y)/2)^2 + tau_xy^2); tau_max = (sigma1 - sigma2)/2

Worked example: With sigma_x = 80 MPa, sigma_y = 20 MPa, tau_xy = 30 MPa: sigma1 = 50 + sqrt(900 + 900) = 92.4 MPa and sigma2 = 7.6 MPa.

instruction: What is Torsion of shafts and bending stress? Explain it briefly. [GATE RA - Mechanics of Materials]
response:
Twisting a circular shaft produces shear stress proportional to radius: maximum at the outer surface, zero at the centre. Bending a beam produces normal stress proportional to distance from the neutral axis. Both formulas share the same idea: stress = (load x distance) / (section property). Combined torsion and bending in a shaft is checked with von Mises stress.

Formula: Torsion: tau = T x r / J, twist angle phi = T x L / (G x J); bending: sigma = M x y / I

Worked example: Solid shaft diameter 40 mm under torque 500 N m: J = pi x d^4 / 32 = 2.51 x 10^-7 m^4, tau_max = T x (d/2) / J = 39.8 MPa.

instruction: What is Euler column buckling? Explain it briefly. [GATE RA - Mechanics of Materials]
response:
A long slender column buckles sideways before the material yields. The critical load depends on stiffness EI and on the effective length KL, which the end conditions set: pinned-pinned K = 1, fixed-fixed K = 0.5, fixed-free K = 2. The slenderness ratio KL/r decides whether Euler buckling or yielding governs.

Formula: Critical load Pcr = pi^2 x E x I / (K x L)^2; critical stress sigma_cr = pi^2 x E / (K x L / r)^2

Worked example: Steel column E = 200 GPa, I = 8 x 10^-6 m^4, L = 3 m, pinned ends: Pcr = pi^2 x 200e9 x 8e-6 / 9 = 1.75 MN.

instruction: What is Gear trains and gear ratio? Explain it briefly. [GATE RA - Kinematics]
response:
A gear pair's velocity ratio is the inverse of its teeth ratio: a small gear driving a large one reduces speed and raises torque. Compound trains multiply the ratios of their stages; epicyclic (planetary) trains give large reductions in a compact package. The same ratio logic applies to belt-pulley drives.

Formula: Velocity ratio = N_driver / N_driven = T_driven / T_driver; compound ratio = product of the stage ratios

Worked example: A 20-tooth gear driving a 60-tooth gear, then a 15-tooth gear driving a 45-tooth gear: total ratio = (60/20) x (45/15) = 9:1 reduction.

instruction: What is SDOF vibration: natural frequency and damping? Explain it briefly. [GATE RA - Dynamics & Control]
response:
A single-degree-of-freedom mass-spring-damper has one natural frequency set by stiffness and mass. The damping ratio zeta decides the behaviour: underdamped (zeta < 1) oscillates, critically damped (zeta = 1) returns fastest without oscillating, overdamped creeps back. Forcing near the natural frequency causes resonance, with large amplitudes limited only by damping.

Formula: Natural frequency omega_n = sqrt(k/m); damping ratio zeta = c / (2 x sqrt(k x m)); damped frequency omega_d = omega_n x sqrt(1 - zeta^2)

Worked example: Mass 2 kg, spring 800 N/m: omega_n = sqrt(400) = 20 rad/s, about 3.18 Hz.

instruction: What is Fatigue, S-N diagram and failure theories? Explain it briefly. [GATE RA - Machine Design]
response:
Under cyclic loading a part can fail by fatigue far below its yield strength: cracks start at stress raisers and grow a little each cycle. The S-N curve plots stress against cycles to failure; steels show an endurance limit below which life is effectively infinite (about half the ultimate strength, before correction factors). Ductile yielding under combined stress is checked with von Mises (distortion energy); Tresca (maximum shear) is more conservative.

Formula: von Mises stress: sigma' = sqrt(sigma_x^2 - sigma_x x sigma_y + sigma_y^2 + 3 x tau_xy^2); design rule sigma' <= Sy / N

Worked example: A steel with ultimate strength 600 MPa has an endurance limit near 300 MPa before surface, size and reliability corrections pull it lower.

instruction: What is Python data structures: stack, queue, linked list, BST? Explain it briefly. [GATE RA - Mechatronics Basics]
response:
A stack is last-in-first-out (push and pop); a queue is first-in-first-out (enqueue and dequeue). A linked list is nodes joined by pointers, so inserting at the head is O(1). A binary search tree keeps keys ordered, so search and insert average O(log n) when balanced. A graph is nodes plus edges, traversed by breadth-first or depth-first search.

Formula: Stack push/pop and queue enqueue/dequeue are O(1); binary search tree search is O(h), O(log n) when balanced

Worked example: Function calls use a stack, so recursion depth is limited by stack size; breadth-first search uses a queue.

instruction: Give a worked example for Denavit-Hartenberg parameters [GATE RA - Kinematics]
response:
Worked example: For one planar link with a = 0.5 m, alpha = 0, d = 0 and theta = 90 degrees, A = [[0, -1, 0, 0], [1, 0, 0, 0.5], [0, 0, 1, 0], [0, 0, 0, 1]], so the end of the link is at position (0, 0.5, 0) m relative to the base frame.

Formula: A_i = [[cos(theta_i), -sin(theta_i)cos(alpha_i), sin(theta_i)sin(alpha_i), a_i cos(theta_i)], [sin(theta_i), cos(theta_i)cos(alpha_i), -cos(theta_i)sin(alpha_i), a_i sin(theta_i)], [0, sin(alpha_i), cos(alpha_i), d_i], [0, 0, 0, 1]]; T_0n = A_1 A_2 ... A_n

The Denavit-Hartenberg (DH) convention describes each joint of a serial robot with just four parameters: link length a, link twist alpha, link offset d, and joint angle theta. For a revolute joint theta is the variable and a, alpha and d are constants; for a prismatic joint d is the variable. Substituting the four parameters into the standard homogeneous matrix gives the pose of frame i relative to frame i-1, and multiplying the matrices of all joints gives the end-effector pose relative to the base.

instruction: Give a worked example for Forward and inverse kinematics of a 2R planar arm [GATE RA - Kinematics]
response:
Worked example: With L1 = 2 m, L2 = 1.5 m and target (x, y) = (2, 1) m: cos(theta2) = (5 - 4 - 2.25) / 6 = -0.2083, so theta2 = +/-102.02 degrees. For the elbow-up solution (theta2 = +102.02 degrees), theta1 = atan2(1, 2) - atan2(1.467, 1.688) = 26.57 - 41.00 = -14.44 degrees. Forward kinematics with these angles returns (2.0, 1.0) m.

Formula: Forward: x = L1 cos(theta1) + L2 cos(theta1 + theta2); y = L1 sin(theta1) + L2 sin(theta1 + theta2). Inverse: cos(theta2) = (x^2 + y^2 - L1^2 - L2^2) / (2 L1 L2); theta1 = atan2(y, x) - atan2(L2 sin(theta2), L1 + L2 cos(theta2))

Forward kinematics computes the end-effector position from the joint angles, and is unique. Inverse kinematics computes the joint angles from a desired end-effector position, and is generally harder: a 2R planar arm has no solution outside its reachable workspace (|L1 - L2| <= r <= L1 + L2), one solution on the workspace boundary, and two solutions (elbow-up and elbow-down) inside it.

instruction: Give a worked example for Degrees of freedom - Gruebler (Kutzbach) criterion [GATE RA - Kinematics]
response:
Worked example: A four-bar linkage has n = 4 links (including ground) and j1 = 4 revolute joints, j2 = 0. Then F = 3(4 - 1) - 2(4) - 0 = 9 - 8 = 1, so it has one degree of freedom and needs one input (one driven crank) to define its motion.

Formula: Planar: F = 3(n - 1) - 2 j1 - j2, where n = number of links including the ground link, j1 = number of 1-DOF joints, j2 = number of 2-DOF joints. Spatial: F = 6(n - 1) - 5 j1 - 4 j2 - 3 j3 - 2 j4 - j5

The degree of freedom (mobility) of a mechanism is the number of independent inputs needed to define the configuration of all its links. Gruebler's criterion counts it from the number of links and joints: each free link in a plane has 3 degrees of freedom, each 1-DOF joint (revolute or prismatic) removes 2, and each 2-DOF joint (cam or gear pair) removes 1. A result F = 1 means one input drives the mechanism; F = 0 is a structure and F < 0 is over-constrained.

instruction: Give a worked example for Manipulator Jacobian [GATE RA - Kinematics]
response:
Worked example: For a 2R arm with L1 = L2 = 1 m, theta1 = 0 degrees and theta2 = 90 degrees, J = [[-1, -1], [1, 0]]. With joint velocities q_dot = [1, 0] rad/s, the end-effector velocity is [vx, vy] = J q_dot = [-1, 1] m/s.

Formula: x_dot = J(q) q_dot, where J(q) = partial x / partial q; for a square non-singular Jacobian, q_dot = J(q)^-1 x_dot, and in general q_dot = J(q)^+ x_dot using the pseudoinverse.
