For a 2R planar arm: J = [[-L1 sin(theta1) - L2 sin(theta1+theta2), -L2 sin(theta1+theta2)], [L1 cos(theta1) + L2 cos(theta1+theta2), L2 cos(theta1+theta2)]]

The Jacobian matrix J(q) relates joint velocities to end-effector velocity: it is the matrix of partial derivatives of the end-effector position and orientation with respect to the joint variables. For a spatial manipulator it is 6 x n (3 rows for linear velocity, 3 for angular velocity), where n is the number of joints. When J loses rank the manipulator is at a singularity, where it cannot move in some Cartesian direction and the inverse-velocity solution fails or blows up.

instruction: Give a worked example for PID control [GATE RA - Dynamics & Control]
response:
Worked example: At one instant, e = 4, the accumulated integral of e is 10, de/dt = -1, with Kp = 2, Ki = 0.5 and Kd = 0.1. Then u = 2(4) + 0.5(10) + 0.1(-1) = 8 + 5 - 0.1 = 12.9 (in the controller's output units).

Formula: u(t) = Kp e(t) + Ki integral_0^t e(tau) d tau + Kd de(t)/dt, where e(t) = r(t) - y(t); transfer function Gc(s) = Kp + Ki/s + Kd s

A PID controller drives the error e(t) = setpoint - measured value to zero using three terms: proportional (present error), integral (accumulated past error) and derivative (rate of change of error, anticipating the future). The proportional term gives speed, the integral term removes steady-state error, and the derivative term damps overshoot. Choosing Kp, Ki and Kd is called tuning; too much integral gain causes windup and oscillation, and the derivative term amplifies measurement noise.

instruction: Give a worked example for PLC ladder logic basics [GATE RA - Automation & PLC]
response:
Worked example: Start is a momentary NO pushbutton and Stop is an NC pushbutton. Pressing Start makes (Start OR Y) true and Stop not pressed makes (NOT Stop) true, so Y energises and its own contact seals the rung in, so the motor keeps running after Start is released. Pressing Stop makes (NOT Stop) false, the rung opens and Y = 0, so the motor stops.

Formula: Series contacts = AND; parallel contacts = OR; NC contact = NOT. Motor start/stop seal-in (latching) rung: Y = (Start OR Y) AND (NOT Stop), where Y is the motor output coil; a NO contact of Y in parallel with Start keeps the motor running after Start is released until Stop breaks the rung.

A PLC (programmable logic controller) runs a scan cycle: read inputs, execute the program, update outputs. Ladder logic, one of the IEC 61131-3 languages, draws the program like a relay ladder with two vertical power rails and horizontal rungs. Contacts on the left are conditions and a coil on the right is the output: a normally open (NO) contact passes power when its input is ON, a normally closed (NC) contact passes power when its input is OFF (NOT), contacts in series give AND, and contacts in parallel give OR.

instruction: Give a worked example for Manipulator singularities [GATE RA - Kinematics]
response:
Worked example: For a 2R planar arm with link lengths l1 = l2 = 1 m, det(J) = l1*l2*sin(theta2) = sin(theta2). At theta2 = 0 (arm fully stretched) or theta2 = 180 degrees (fully folded), det(J) = 0: the arm is singular and cannot move its tip in the radial direction, however large the joint torques.

Formula: Singularity when det(J(q)) = 0 (square J) or rank(J(q)) < min(6, n). For a 2R planar arm: det(J) = l1*l2*sin(theta2). Near a singularity, joint velocity qdot = J^(-1) * xdot grows without bound.

A manipulator is at a singularity when its Jacobian loses rank, i.e. det(J) = 0 for a square Jacobian, so the end-effector loses the ability to move (or exert force) in some Cartesian direction. At a singularity, inverse kinematics has no unique solution and joint velocities needed for a given tip velocity blow up. Common types are wrist singularities (axes of joints 4 and 6 align), elbow singularities (arm fully stretched or folded) and shoulder singularities (wrist centre lies on the first joint axis).

instruction: Give a worked example for Lagrangian dynamics and the manipulator equation [GATE RA - Dynamics & Control]
response:
Worked example: A single pendulum link (point mass m = 2 kg at length l = 0.5 m): L = (1/2)*m*l^2*thetadot^2 + m*g*l*cos(theta). The equation of motion is m*l^2*thetaddot + m*g*l*sin(theta) = tau. At theta = 30 degrees the gravity torque to hold it still is m*g*l*sin(30) = 2*9.81*0.5*0.5 = 4.91 Nm.

Formula: L = T - U; d/dt(dL/dqdot_i) - dL/dq_i = tau_i. Manipulator equation: M(q)*qddot + C(q, qdot)*qdot + g(q) = tau. Kinetic energy: T = (1/2)*qdot^T*M(q)*qdot.

Lagrangian dynamics derives a robot's equations of motion from energy, not from free-body diagrams. With generalised coordinates q, kinetic energy T and potential energy U, the Lagrangian is L = T - U, and each joint obeys the Euler-Lagrange equation. Collecting terms for all joints gives the manipulator equation, in which M(q) is the symmetric positive-definite inertia matrix, C(q, qdot) carries Coriolis and centrifugal effects, and g(q) is gravity. At rest only the gravity term remains, so tau = g(q) is the holding torque.

instruction: Give a worked example for Newton-Euler recursive dynamics [GATE RA - Dynamics & Control]
response:
Worked example: Holding a 5 kg link horizontally with its centre of mass 0.3 m from the joint: the static joint torque is m*g*r = 5*9.81*0.3 = 14.7 Nm. Newton-Euler computes this (and the dynamic torques) link by link instead of from one big energy expression, which is why it is the standard O(n) algorithm in robot controllers.

Formula: Newton: F = m*a_cm. Euler: N = I*alpha + omega x (I*omega). Inverse dynamics (RNEA): given q, qdot, qddot, the recursion returns tau; forward dynamics: qddot = M(q)^(-1)*(tau - C(q, qdot)*qdot - g(q)).

The Newton-Euler method derives the same equations of motion as Lagrange, but by applying Newton's law (F = m*a) and Euler's rotational law (N = I*alpha + omega x (I*omega)) to each link in turn. A forward recursion propagates velocities and accelerations from the base to the tip; a backward recursion propagates forces and moments from the tip to the base, giving the joint torques. It is computationally efficient (O(n) in the number of joints) and is the basis of the recursive Newton-Euler algorithm used for inverse dynamics in real controllers.

instruction: Give a worked example for Computed-torque trajectory tracking control [GATE RA - Dynamics & Control]
response:
Worked example: Choose Kp = 100, Kd = 20 for one joint. The error dynamics are eddot + 20*edot + 100*e = 0, i.e. natural frequency wn = sqrt(100) = 10 rad/s and damping ratio zeta = Kd/(2*sqrt(Kp)) = 20/20 = 1, so the tracking error decays critically damped, with no overshoot.

Formula: tau = M(q)*(qddot_d + Kp*e + Kd*edot) + C(q, qdot)*qdot + g(q), where e = q_d - q. Ideal error dynamics: eddot + Kd*edot + Kp*e = 0. Damping ratio: zeta = Kd/(2*sqrt(Kp)); wn = sqrt(Kp).

Computed-torque (inverse-dynamics) control cancels the robot's nonlinear dynamics by feeding back the model: the controller computes the torque that would make the arm behave like a set of independent double integrators, then adds PD terms on the tracking error. If the model is exact, each joint's error obeys a linear second-order equation, so Kp and Kd can be set from a desired natural frequency and damping ratio. Its weakness is model error: wrong masses or friction leave residual dynamics, so in practice it is combined with robust or adaptive terms.

instruction: Give a worked example for Lyapunov stability and Routh-Hurwitz criterion [GATE RA - Dynamics & Control]
response:
Worked example: For a PD-controlled joint with error e and error rate edot, take V = (1/2)*edot^2 + (1/2)*Kp*e^2 (kinetic-like plus potential-like energy). Then Vdot = -Kd*edot^2 <= 0, so the energy never grows and the equilibrium e = 0 is stable; with Kd > 0 the error decays.

Formula: Lyapunov: V(x) > 0 for x != 0, V(0) = 0, and Vdot(x) <= 0 => stable; Vdot(x) < 0 for x != 0 => asymptotically stable. Routh-Hurwitz: stability iff the first column of the Routh array has no sign changes.

Lyapunov stability proves a control system is stable without solving its differential equations: find a positive-definite energy-like function V (V = 0 only at the equilibrium, V > 0 elsewhere) and show its time derivative Vdot <= 0 along trajectories. If Vdot is strictly negative (except at the equilibrium), the equilibrium is asymptotically stable. The classical Routh-Hurwitz criterion is the complementary algebraic test: a linear system's characteristic polynomial has all roots in the left half-plane (stable) iff all entries in the first column of the Routh array are positive.

instruction: Give a worked example for DC servo and stepper motors [GATE RA - Sensors & Actuators]
response:
Worked example: A DC servo motor with torque constant Kt = 0.1 Nm/A driven at 3 A produces tau = 0.1*3 = 0.3 Nm. A 200-step-per-revolution stepper motor moves 360/200 = 1.8 degrees per step, so 50 steps rotate it 90 degrees, with no position sensor needed if no steps are missed.

Formula: DC motor: tau = Kt*I; back-EMF Eb = Ke*omega; V = I*R + Eb (steady state). Stepper step angle = 360 degrees / steps per revolution. Gearbox: tau_out = N*tau_motor, omega_out = omega_motor/N (ideal, N = gear ratio).

Robot joints are usually driven by DC servo motors (brushed or brushless) through a gearbox, because they give smooth, controllable torque proportional to current and are easily closed-loop controlled with an encoder. The back-EMF grows with speed, so at high speed less voltage is left to drive current and torque falls. Stepper motors move in fixed angular steps and hold position open-loop, which suits low-cost positioning, but they lose steps under overload and are noisier and less efficient than servos at high speed. Gear reduction multiplies torque by the gear ratio (and divides speed), at the cost of added friction and backlash.

instruction: Give a worked example for Encoders and resolvers for position sensing [GATE RA - Sensors & Actuators]
response:
Worked example: A 1024-pulse-per-revolution incremental encoder with quadrature decoding gives 4*1024 = 4096 counts per revolution, so the angular resolution is 360/4096 = 0.088 degrees per count. An absolute encoder instead reports the exact angle at power-on, with no homing move needed.

Formula: Resolution (degrees) = 360 / counts per revolution. Quadrature counts per rev = 4 * pulses per rev (PPR). Angle = counts * (360 / counts per rev).

An encoder measures joint angle: an optical or magnetic disc with slots interrupts a light beam (or changes a magnetic field) as it turns, producing pulses. Incremental encoders count pulses from a reference mark, so they lose absolute position at power-off and need homing; quadrature decoding (two channels A and B, 90 degrees apart) gives direction and four counts per pulse period. Absolute encoders output a unique code for each angle, so position is known immediately. A resolver is a rugged analogue alternative that outputs sine/cosine signals proportional to angle and survives harsh factory environments better than optical encoders.

instruction: Give a worked example for Force/torque, tactile and proximity sensors [GATE RA - Sensors & Actuators]
response:
Worked example: A wrist force sensor reads 10 N of contact force applied 0.2 m from the joint axis: the joint feels a torque of tau = r x F = 0.2*10 = 2 Nm. A controller can use that reading to cap contact force, e.g. to stop before damaging a part or hurting a person.

Formula: Torque from a force at a distance: tau = r x F (magnitude r*F*sin(theta)). Strain-gauge bridge output is proportional to applied strain, hence to force.

Force/torque sensors, usually strain-gauge based, measure the six components of force and moment at the wrist or in a joint, enabling force control, assembly (peg-in-hole), and safe human-robot contact. Tactile sensors measure distributed pressure over a gripper surface, proximity sensors (ultrasonic, infrared, capacitive) detect nearby objects without contact, and vision (cameras) gives the richest sensing but needs processing. Sensor choice trades accuracy, bandwidth, cost and robustness.

instruction: Give a worked example for Pneumatic and hydraulic actuators [GATE RA - Sensors & Actuators]
response:
Worked example: A pneumatic cylinder at 6 bar (600,000 Pa) with a 50 mm bore (area pi*0.025^2 = 0.00196 m2) pushes with F = P*A = 600,000*0.00196 = 1,178 N, about 1.18 kN. The same force from a hydraulic cylinder needs far less area because hydraulic pressure is typically 100-200 bar.

Formula: Actuator force: F = P*A, where P is pressure and A is piston area. Cylinder speed: v = Q/A, where Q is volume flow rate.

Pneumatic actuators use compressed air (typically 5-7 bar): they are fast, clean, cheap and safe in explosive atmospheres, but air is compressible, so force and position control are soft and imprecise. Hydraulic actuators use pressurised oil (typically 100-200 bar): they deliver very large forces in a compact size and are stiff and precise, but need pumps, seals and maintenance and can leak. The choice is force and precision (hydraulic) versus speed, cleanliness and cost (pneumatic); electric servos beat both on controllability.

instruction: Give a worked example for Configuration space and free space [GATE RA - Motion Planning]
response:
Worked example: A 2R planar arm has two joint angles, so its configuration space is a torus: each angle wraps around at 360 degrees, and the point (350 degrees, 10 degrees) is adjacent to (0 degrees, 10 degrees). An obstacle in the workspace becomes a forbidden region in this torus, and a valid motion is a continuous curve that stays in the free part.

Formula: C-space: q in R^n (or a torus for revolute joints). C = C_free union C_obs. A valid path is a continuous curve q(t) with q(t) in C_free for all t, q(0) = q_start, q(1) = q_goal.

The configuration space (C-space) is the space of all joint configurations q of a robot; for an n-joint arm it is n-dimensional. Obstacles in the workspace map to forbidden regions C_obs in C-space, and the free space C_free is everything else. Motion planning is then a geometric problem in C-space: find a continuous path from the start configuration to the goal that stays inside C_free. The workspace is where the task is described; the C-space is where the planning is done, because joint limits and self-collision are simple bounds there.

instruction: Give a worked example for RRT and PRM sampling-based planning [GATE RA - Motion Planning]
response:
Worked example: An RRT planning for a mobile robot samples a random point, finds the nearest tree node, and extends one step of size 0.1 m toward it. After a few thousand iterations the tree has spread through the free space and reached the goal region, even in a cluttered room where a grid search would be far too large.

Formula: RRT step: q_new = q_near + eta*(q_rand - q_near)/||q_rand - q_near||, kept only if the segment q_near to q_new is collision-free. PRM: roadmap graph G = (V, E) of sampled free configurations; query = graph search (e.g. A*) from q_start to q_goal.

Sampling-based planners avoid building the C-space explicitly. RRT (Rapidly-exploring Random Tree) grows a tree from the start by sampling random configurations, steering a small step from the nearest tree node toward each sample, and keeping the step if it is collision-free; it is fast and explores large spaces well, but the path is jagged and only probabilistically complete. PRM (Probabilistic Roadmap) instead samples many collision-free configurations, connects nearby ones into a roadmap graph, and then searches the graph with A*; the roadmap can be reused for many queries in the same environment. RRT* rewires the tree to converge toward the optimal path.

instruction: Give a worked example for Artificial potential field planning [GATE RA - Motion Planning]
response:
Worked example: With attractive gain k_att = 1 and the robot 2 m from the goal, U_att = (1/2)*1*2^2 = 2 and the attractive force magnitude is k_att*2 = 2 (in force units), pulling it toward the goal. The classic failure is a U-shaped obstacle: the repulsive push balances the attraction and the robot stalls in a local minimum short of the goal.

Formula: U_att(q) = (1/2)*k_att*||q - q_goal||^2. U_rep(q) = (1/2)*k_rep*(1/d - 1/d0)^2 if d < d0, else 0, where d is distance to the nearest obstacle and d0 the influence range. U_total = U_att + U_rep; motion follows F = -grad(U_total).

Artificial potential fields plan by treating the goal as an attractor and obstacles as repellers: the robot follows the negative gradient of the total potential, i.e. it rolls downhill. The method is simple, fast and reactive, so it is popular for mobile-robot obstacle avoidance. Its main flaw is local minima, where attractive and repulsive forces cancel away from the goal and the robot gets stuck; narrow passages and oscillations near obstacles are other known problems. It is a local method, unlike RRT/PRM which plan globally.

instruction: Give a worked example for Joint-space trajectory planning: cubic, quintic and trapezoidal profiles [GATE RA - Trajectory Planning]
response:
Worked example: Move one joint from 0 to 90 degrees (pi/2 = 1.571 rad) in tf = 2 s, at rest at both ends, with a cubic polynomial: a0 = 0, a1 = 0, a2 = 3*(1.571)/2^2 = 1.178, a3 = -2*(1.571)/2^3 = -0.393, so q(t) = 1.178*t^2 - 0.393*t^3. Peak velocity is 1.5*(1.571)/2 = 1.18 rad/s at t = 1 s. A trapezoidal profile would instead accelerate at constant amax, cruise at vmax, then decelerate, which respects velocity and acceleration limits directly.

Formula: Cubic: q(t) = a0 + a1*t + a2*t^2 + a3*t^3, with q(0) = q0, q(tf) = qf, qdot(0) = v0, qdot(tf) = vf. Rest-to-rest: a0 = q0, a1 = 0, a2 = 3*(qf - q0)/tf^2, a3 = -2*(qf - q0)/tf^3; peak velocity = 1.5*(qf - q0)/tf. Trapezoidal: distance = (1/2)*vmax*(tf + t_cruise), where t_cruise is the constant-velocity time.

A path is the geometry of the motion; a trajectory adds the timing law. In joint space, a cubic polynomial fits position and velocity at both ends (four conditions, four coefficients) and gives smooth position and velocity, but acceleration jumps at the ends. A quintic polynomial also fixes the end accelerations (six conditions). The trapezoidal velocity profile is the industrial workhorse: constant acceleration, constant velocity, constant deceleration, which makes it easy to respect vmax and amax, but acceleration is discontinuous at the phase switches. Via points are handled by joining polynomial segments with continuous velocity.

instruction: Give a worked example for SCADA and the industrial automation hierarchy [GATE RA - Automation & PLC]
response:
Worked example: In a bottling plant, field sensors and actuators wire into PLCs that run the filling sequence in real time; the SCADA system in the control room shows tank levels and line speed on one screen, logs every batch, and raises an alarm if a tank runs low, while the plant MES above it schedules the day's orders.

Formula: Automation hierarchy (bottom to top): field devices -> PLC / DCS (real-time control) -> SCADA (supervision, logging, alarms) -> MES (production management) -> ERP (business planning). Rule: SCADA monitors and commands; the PLC controls.

Industrial automation is organised in layers: field devices (sensors, actuators) at the bottom, PLCs and controllers doing real-time control, SCADA (Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition) monitoring, logging and alarming from a control room, then MES for production scheduling and ERP for business planning. SCADA supervises but does not replace the PLC's real-time loop: if SCADA goes down, the PLCs keep running the process. Modern plants link these layers over industrial Ethernet and fieldbus networks.

instruction: Give a worked example for Homogeneous transformations and rotation matrices [GATE RA - Kinematics]
response:
Worked example: Rotating the point (1, 0) by 90 degrees: R(90) x (1, 0) = (0, 1).

Formula: 2D rotation: R(theta) = [[cos theta, -sin theta],[sin theta, cos theta]]; T = [[R, p],[0 0 0, 1]]; composition T02 = T01 x T12

A rotation matrix R maps coordinates between frames: it is orthonormal (R-transpose times R = identity, determinant +1). A homogeneous transform T combines rotation R and translation p in one 4x4 matrix, and chaining transforms maps a point through several frames: T02 = T01 x T12. Forward kinematics of a robot is a chain of such transforms, one per joint.

instruction: Give a worked example for KCL, KVL, Thevenin and Norton theorems [GATE RA - Mechatronics Basics]
response:
Worked example: A source with Vth = 12 V and Rth = 3 ohm delivers maximum power 12^2 / (4 x 3) = 12 W to a 3 ohm load.

Formula: Vth = open-circuit voltage; Rth = Vth / Isc; maximum power when R_load = Rth, Pmax = Vth^2 / (4 x Rth)

Kirchhoff's current law: the currents entering a node sum to zero. Kirchhoff's voltage law: the voltages around any closed loop sum to zero. Thevenin's theorem: any linear network seen from two terminals behaves like a voltage source Vth (the open-circuit voltage) in series with a resistance Rth. Norton's equivalent is a current source Isc in parallel with the same Rth. Maximum power is delivered when the load equals Rth.

instruction: Give a worked example for Ideal op-amp: inverting and non-inverting amplifiers [GATE RA - Analog Circuits & Embedded Systems]
response:
Worked example: With Rf = 100 k ohm and R1 = 10 k ohm, an inverting amplifier has gain -10: 0.5 V in gives -5 V out.

Formula: Inverting gain A = -Rf / R1; non-inverting gain A = 1 + Rf / R1

An ideal op-amp has infinite gain, infinite input impedance and zero output impedance. In negative feedback the two inputs sit at the same voltage (virtual short) and draw no current (virtual ground at the inverting input). That gives clean gain formulas set by two resistors, and the same building block makes integrators, filters, Schmitt triggers and comparators.

instruction: Give a worked example for Fourier, Laplace and Z-transforms [GATE RA - Signals & Systems]
response:
Worked example: A unit step u(t) has Laplace transform 1/s; the same step sampled has Z-transform z/(z - 1).

Formula: Laplace: L{df/dt} = sF(s) - f(0); Z-transform: X(z) = sum over n of x[n] z^(-n); sampling: z = e^(sT)

The Fourier transform moves a signal between time and frequency. The Laplace transform moves differential equations into algebra in the s-domain, handling initial conditions, which is why control design lives in s. The Z-transform is the discrete-time counterpart for sampled signals and digital control: sampling with period T maps s to z = e^(sT).

instruction: Give a worked example for Transfer functions, Bode plots and root locus [GATE RA - Dynamics & Control]
response:
Worked example: G(s) = 1/(s + 1): Bode magnitude falls at 20 dB per decade after omega = 1 rad/s and phase tends to -90 degrees.

Formula: Gain margin = 1/|G| at the phase -180 degree frequency; phase margin = 180 degrees + phase of G at the gain crossover frequency; stable when both margins are positive

For a linear time-invariant system the transfer function G(s) = Y(s)/U(s) captures all input-output behaviour. Its poles decide stability: all poles in the left half-plane means stable. A Bode plot shows gain and phase against frequency; the root locus shows how the poles move as a gain K grows. Gain margin and phase margin measure how far the system is from instability.

instruction: Give a worked example for PID control and tuning [GATE RA - Dynamics & Control]
response:
Worked example: A motor position loop with proportional-only control holds a steady offset under load; adding integral action removes it.

Formula: u(t) = Kp x e + Ki x integral of e dt + Kd x de/dt; Ziegler-Nichols: Kp = 0.6 Ku, Ti = Tu/2, Td = Tu/8

A PID controller acts on the error e: the proportional term corrects the present error, the integral term accumulates past error and removes steady-state offset, and the derivative term anticipates future error and adds damping. Too much integral action causes overshoot and oscillation; derivative action amplifies measurement noise. Ziegler-Nichols tuning finds the ultimate gain Ku and period Tu at the edge of oscillation and sets gains from them.

instruction: Give a worked example for Mohr's circle for plane stress [GATE RA - Mechanics of Materials]
response:
Worked example: With sigma_x = 80 MPa, sigma_y = 20 MPa, tau_xy = 30 MPa: sigma1 = 50 + sqrt(900 + 900) = 92.4 MPa and sigma2 = 7.6 MPa.

Formula: Principal stresses: sigma1,2 = (sigma_x + sigma_y)/2 +- sqrt(((sigma_x - sigma_y)/2)^2 + tau_xy^2); tau_max = (sigma1 - sigma2)/2

Mohr's circle plots normal stress against shear stress for every orientation of a material element. Its centre is the average normal stress and its radius comes from the stress differences; the circle's ends give the principal stresses (where shear is zero) and its top and bottom give the maximum shear stress, which acts on planes at 45 degrees to the principal planes.

instruction: Give a worked example for Torsion of shafts and bending stress [GATE RA - Mechanics of Materials]
response:
Worked example: Solid shaft diameter 40 mm under torque 500 N m: J = pi x d^4 / 32 = 2.51 x 10^-7 m^4, tau_max = T x (d/2) / J = 39.8 MPa.

Formula: Torsion: tau = T x r / J, twist angle phi = T x L / (G x J); bending: sigma = M x y / I

Twisting a circular shaft produces shear stress proportional to radius: maximum at the outer surface, zero at the centre. Bending a beam produces normal stress proportional to distance from the neutral axis. Both formulas share the same idea: stress = (load x distance) / (section property). Combined torsion and bending in a shaft is checked with von Mises stress.

instruction: Give a worked example for Euler column buckling [GATE RA - Mechanics of Materials]
response:
Worked example: Steel column E = 200 GPa, I = 8 x 10^-6 m^4, L = 3 m, pinned ends: Pcr = pi^2 x 200e9 x 8e-6 / 9 = 1.75 MN.

Formula: Critical load Pcr = pi^2 x E x I / (K x L)^2; critical stress sigma_cr = pi^2 x E / (K x L / r)^2

A long slender column buckles sideways before the material yields. The critical load depends on stiffness EI and on the effective length KL, which the end conditions set: pinned-pinned K = 1, fixed-fixed K = 0.5, fixed-free K = 2. The slenderness ratio KL/r decides whether Euler buckling or yielding governs.

instruction: Give a worked example for Gear trains and gear ratio [GATE RA - Kinematics]
response:
Worked example: A 20-tooth gear driving a 60-tooth gear, then a 15-tooth gear driving a 45-tooth gear: total ratio = (60/20) x (45/15) = 9:1 reduction.

Formula: Velocity ratio = N_driver / N_driven = T_driven / T_driver; compound ratio = product of the stage ratios

A gear pair's velocity ratio is the inverse of its teeth ratio: a small gear driving a large one reduces speed and raises torque. Compound trains multiply the ratios of their stages; epicyclic (planetary) trains give large reductions in a compact package. The same ratio logic applies to belt-pulley drives.

instruction: Give a worked example for SDOF vibration: natural frequency and damping [GATE RA - Dynamics & Control]
response:
Worked example: Mass 2 kg, spring 800 N/m: omega_n = sqrt(400) = 20 rad/s, about 3.18 Hz.

Formula: Natural frequency omega_n = sqrt(k/m); damping ratio zeta = c / (2 x sqrt(k x m)); damped frequency omega_d = omega_n x sqrt(1 - zeta^2)

A single-degree-of-freedom mass-spring-damper has one natural frequency set by stiffness and mass. The damping ratio zeta decides the behaviour: underdamped (zeta < 1) oscillates, critically damped (zeta = 1) returns fastest without oscillating, overdamped creeps back. Forcing near the natural frequency causes resonance, with large amplitudes limited only by damping.

instruction: Give a worked example for Fatigue, S-N diagram and failure theories [GATE RA - Machine Design]
response:
Worked example: A steel with ultimate strength 600 MPa has an endurance limit near 300 MPa before surface, size and reliability corrections pull it lower.

Formula: von Mises stress: sigma' = sqrt(sigma_x^2 - sigma_x x sigma_y + sigma_y^2 + 3 x tau_xy^2); design rule sigma' <= Sy / N

Under cyclic loading a part can fail by fatigue far below its yield strength: cracks start at stress raisers and grow a little each cycle. The S-N curve plots stress against cycles to failure; steels show an endurance limit below which life is effectively infinite (about half the ultimate strength, before correction factors). Ductile yielding under combined stress is checked with von Mises (distortion energy); Tresca (maximum shear) is more conservative.

instruction: Give a worked example for Python data structures: stack, queue, linked list, BST [GATE RA - Mechatronics Basics]
response:
Worked example: Function calls use a stack, so recursion depth is limited by stack size; breadth-first search uses a queue.

Formula: Stack push/pop and queue enqueue/dequeue are O(1); binary search tree search is O(h), O(log n) when balanced

A stack is last-in-first-out (push and pop); a queue is first-in-first-out (enqueue and dequeue). A linked list is nodes joined by pointers, so inserting at the head is O(1). A binary search tree keeps keys ordered, so search and insert average O(log n) when balanced. A graph is nodes plus edges, traversed by breadth-first or depth-first search.

instruction: What is the formula for Denavit-Hartenberg parameters? When is it used? [GATE RA - Kinematics]
response:
Formula: A_i = [[cos(theta_i), -sin(theta_i)cos(alpha_i), sin(theta_i)sin(alpha_i), a_i cos(theta_i)], [sin(theta_i), cos(theta_i)cos(alpha_i), -cos(theta_i)sin(alpha_i), a_i sin(theta_i)], [0, sin(alpha_i), cos(alpha_i), d_i], [0, 0, 0, 1]]; T_0n = A_1 A_2 ... A_n

The Denavit-Hartenberg (DH) convention describes each joint of a serial robot with just four parameters: link length a, link twist alpha, link offset d, and joint angle theta. For a revolute joint theta is the variable and a, alpha and d are constants; for a prismatic joint d is the variable. Substituting the four parameters into the standard homogeneous matrix gives the pose of frame i relative to frame i-1, and multiplying the matrices of all joints gives the end-effector pose relative to the base.

instruction: What is the formula for Forward and inverse kinematics of a 2R planar arm? When is it used? [GATE RA - Kinematics]
response:
Formula: Forward: x = L1 cos(theta1) + L2 cos(theta1 + theta2); y = L1 sin(theta1) + L2 sin(theta1 + theta2). Inverse: cos(theta2) = (x^2 + y^2 - L1^2 - L2^2) / (2 L1 L2); theta1 = atan2(y, x) - atan2(L2 sin(theta2), L1 + L2 cos(theta2))

Forward kinematics computes the end-effector position from the joint angles, and is unique. Inverse kinematics computes the joint angles from a desired end-effector position, and is generally harder: a 2R planar arm has no solution outside its reachable workspace (|L1 - L2| <= r <= L1 + L2), one solution on the workspace boundary, and two solutions (elbow-up and elbow-down) inside it.

instruction: What is the formula for Degrees of freedom - Gruebler (Kutzbach) criterion? When is it used? [GATE RA - Kinematics]
response:
Formula: Planar: F = 3(n - 1) - 2 j1 - j2, where n = number of links including the ground link, j1 = number of 1-DOF joints, j2 = number of 2-DOF joints. Spatial: F = 6(n - 1) - 5 j1 - 4 j2 - 3 j3 - 2 j4 - j5

The degree of freedom (mobility) of a mechanism is the number of independent inputs needed to define the configuration of all its links. Gruebler's criterion counts it from the number of links and joints: each free link in a plane has 3 degrees of freedom, each 1-DOF joint (revolute or prismatic) removes 2, and each 2-DOF joint (cam or gear pair) removes 1. A result F = 1 means one input drives the mechanism; F = 0 is a structure and F < 0 is over-constrained.

instruction: What is the formula for Manipulator Jacobian? When is it used? [GATE RA - Kinematics]
response:
Formula: x_dot = J(q) q_dot, where J(q) = partial x / partial q; for a square non-singular Jacobian, q_dot = J(q)^-1 x_dot, and in general q_dot = J(q)^+ x_dot using the pseudoinverse. For a 2R planar arm: J = [[-L1 sin(theta1) - L2 sin(theta1+theta2), -L2 sin(theta1+theta2)], [L1 cos(theta1) + L2 cos(theta1+theta2), L2 cos(theta1+theta2)]]

The Jacobian matrix J(q) relates joint velocities to end-effector velocity: it is the matrix of partial derivatives of the end-effector position and orientation with respect to the joint variables. For a spatial manipulator it is 6 x n (3 rows for linear velocity, 3 for angular velocity), where n is the number of joints. When J loses rank the manipulator is at a singularity, where it cannot move in some Cartesian direction and the inverse-velocity solution fails or blows up.

instruction: What is the formula for PID control? When is it used? [GATE RA - Dynamics & Control]
response:
Formula: u(t) = Kp e(t) + Ki integral_0^t e(tau) d tau + Kd de(t)/dt, where e(t) = r(t) - y(t); transfer function Gc(s) = Kp + Ki/s + Kd s

A PID controller drives the error e(t) = setpoint - measured value to zero using three terms: proportional (present error), integral (accumulated past error) and derivative (rate of change of error, anticipating the future). The proportional term gives speed, the integral term removes steady-state error, and the derivative term damps overshoot. Choosing Kp, Ki and Kd is called tuning; too much integral gain causes windup and oscillation, and the derivative term amplifies measurement noise.

instruction: What is the formula for PLC ladder logic basics? When is it used? [GATE RA - Automation & PLC]
response:
Formula: Series contacts = AND; parallel contacts = OR; NC contact = NOT. Motor start/stop seal-in (latching) rung: Y = (Start OR Y) AND (NOT Stop), where Y is the motor output coil; a NO contact of Y in parallel with Start keeps the motor running after Start is released until Stop breaks the rung.

A PLC (programmable logic controller) runs a scan cycle: read inputs, execute the program, update outputs. Ladder logic, one of the IEC 61131-3 languages, draws the program like a relay ladder with two vertical power rails and horizontal rungs. Contacts on the left are conditions and a coil on the right is the output: a normally open (NO) contact passes power when its input is ON, a normally closed (NC) contact passes power when its input is OFF (NOT), contacts in series give AND, and contacts in parallel give OR.

instruction: What is the formula for Manipulator singularities? When is it used? [GATE RA - Kinematics]
response:
Formula: Singularity when det(J(q)) = 0 (square J) or rank(J(q)) < min(6, n). For a 2R planar arm: det(J) = l1*l2*sin(theta2). Near a singularity, joint velocity qdot = J^(-1) * xdot grows without bound.

A manipulator is at a singularity when its Jacobian loses rank, i.e. det(J) = 0 for a square Jacobian, so the end-effector loses the ability to move (or exert force) in some Cartesian direction. At a singularity, inverse kinematics has no unique solution and joint velocities needed for a given tip velocity blow up. Common types are wrist singularities (axes of joints 4 and 6 align), elbow singularities (arm fully stretched or folded) and shoulder singularities (wrist centre lies on the first joint axis).

instruction: What is the formula for Lagrangian dynamics and the manipulator equation? When is it used? [GATE RA - Dynamics & Control]
response:
Formula: L = T - U; d/dt(dL/dqdot_i) - dL/dq_i = tau_i. Manipulator equation: M(q)*qddot + C(q, qdot)*qdot + g(q) = tau. Kinetic energy: T = (1/2)*qdot^T*M(q)*qdot.

Lagrangian dynamics derives a robot's equations of motion from energy, not from free-body diagrams. With generalised coordinates q, kinetic energy T and potential energy U, the Lagrangian is L = T - U, and each joint obeys the Euler-Lagrange equation. Collecting terms for all joints gives the manipulator equation, in which M(q) is the symmetric positive-definite inertia matrix, C(q, qdot) carries Coriolis and centrifugal effects, and g(q) is gravity. At rest only the gravity term remains, so tau = g(q) is the holding torque.

instruction: What is the formula for Newton-Euler recursive dynamics? When is it used? [GATE RA - Dynamics & Control]
response:
Formula: Newton: F = m*a_cm. Euler: N = I*alpha + omega x (I*omega). Inverse dynamics (RNEA): given q, qdot, qddot, the recursion returns tau; forward dynamics: qddot = M(q)^(-1)*(tau - C(q, qdot)*qdot - g(q)).

The Newton-Euler method derives the same equations of motion as Lagrange, but by applying Newton's law (F = m*a) and Euler's rotational law (N = I*alpha + omega x (I*omega)) to each link in turn. A forward recursion propagates velocities and accelerations from the base to the tip; a backward recursion propagates forces and moments from the tip to the base, giving the joint torques. It is computationally efficient (O(n) in the number of joints) and is the basis of the recursive Newton-Euler algorithm used for inverse dynamics in real controllers.

instruction: What is the formula for Computed-torque trajectory tracking control? When is it used? [GATE RA - Dynamics & Control]
response:
Formula: tau = M(q)*(qddot_d + Kp*e + Kd*edot) + C(q, qdot)*qdot + g(q), where e = q_d - q. Ideal error dynamics: eddot + Kd*edot + Kp*e = 0. Damping ratio: zeta = Kd/(2*sqrt(Kp)); wn = sqrt(Kp).

Computed-torque (inverse-dynamics) control cancels the robot's nonlinear dynamics by feeding back the model: the controller computes the torque that would make the arm behave like a set of independent double integrators, then adds PD terms on the tracking error. If the model is exact, each joint's error obeys a linear second-order equation, so Kp and Kd can be set from a desired natural frequency and damping ratio. Its weakness is model error: wrong masses or friction leave residual dynamics, so in practice it is combined with robust or adaptive terms.

instruction: What is the formula for Lyapunov stability and Routh-Hurwitz criterion? When is it used? [GATE RA - Dynamics & Control]
response:
Formula: Lyapunov: V(x) > 0 for x != 0, V(0) = 0, and Vdot(x) <= 0 => stable; Vdot(x) < 0 for x != 0 => asymptotically stable. Routh-Hurwitz: stability iff the first column of the Routh array has no sign changes.

Lyapunov stability proves a control system is stable without solving its differential equations: find a positive-definite energy-like function V (V = 0 only at the equilibrium, V > 0 elsewhere) and show its time derivative Vdot <= 0 along trajectories. If Vdot is strictly negative (except at the equilibrium), the equilibrium is asymptotically stable. The classical Routh-Hurwitz criterion is the complementary algebraic test: a linear system's characteristic polynomial has all roots in the left half-plane (stable) iff all entries in the first column of the Routh array are positive.

instruction: What is the formula for DC servo and stepper motors? When is it used? [GATE RA - Sensors & Actuators]
response:
Formula: DC motor: tau = Kt*I; back-EMF Eb = Ke*omega; V = I*R + Eb (steady state). Stepper step angle = 360 degrees / steps per revolution. Gearbox: tau_out = N*tau_motor, omega_out = omega_motor/N (ideal, N = gear ratio).

Robot joints are usually driven by DC servo motors (brushed or brushless) through a gearbox, because they give smooth, controllable torque proportional to current and are easily closed-loop controlled with an encoder. The back-EMF grows with speed, so at high speed less voltage is left to drive current and torque falls. Stepper motors move in fixed angular steps and hold position open-loop, which suits low-cost positioning, but they lose steps under overload and are noisier and less efficient than servos at high speed. Gear reduction multiplies torque by the gear ratio (and divides speed), at the cost of added friction and backlash.

instruction: What is the formula for Encoders and resolvers for position sensing? When is it used? [GATE RA - Sensors & Actuators]
response:
Formula: Resolution (degrees) = 360 / counts per revolution. Quadrature counts per rev = 4 * pulses per rev (PPR). Angle = counts * (360 / counts per rev).

An encoder measures joint angle: an optical or magnetic disc with slots interrupts a light beam (or changes a magnetic field) as it turns, producing pulses. Incremental encoders count pulses from a reference mark, so they lose absolute position at power-off and need homing; quadrature decoding (two channels A and B, 90 degrees apart) gives direction and four counts per pulse period. Absolute encoders output a unique code for each angle, so position is known immediately. A resolver is a rugged analogue alternative that outputs sine/cosine signals proportional to angle and survives harsh factory environments better than optical encoders.

instruction: What is the formula for Force/torque, tactile and proximity sensors? When is it used? [GATE RA - Sensors & Actuators]
response:
Formula: Torque from a force at a distance: tau = r x F (magnitude r*F*sin(theta)). Strain-gauge bridge output is proportional to applied strain, hence to force.

Force/torque sensors, usually strain-gauge based, measure the six components of force and moment at the wrist or in a joint, enabling force control, assembly (peg-in-hole), and safe human-robot contact. Tactile sensors measure distributed pressure over a gripper surface, proximity sensors (ultrasonic, infrared, capacitive) detect nearby objects without contact, and vision (cameras) gives the richest sensing but needs processing. Sensor choice trades accuracy, bandwidth, cost and robustness.

instruction: What is the formula for Pneumatic and hydraulic actuators? When is it used? [GATE RA - Sensors & Actuators]
response:
Formula: Actuator force: F = P*A, where P is pressure and A is piston area. Cylinder speed: v = Q/A, where Q is volume flow rate.

Pneumatic actuators use compressed air (typically 5-7 bar): they are fast, clean, cheap and safe in explosive atmospheres, but air is compressible, so force and position control are soft and imprecise. Hydraulic actuators use pressurised oil (typically 100-200 bar): they deliver very large forces in a compact size and are stiff and precise, but need pumps, seals and maintenance and can leak. The choice is force and precision (hydraulic) versus speed, cleanliness and cost (pneumatic); electric servos beat both on controllability.

instruction: What is the formula for Configuration space and free space? When is it used? [GATE RA - Motion Planning]
response:
Formula: C-space: q in R^n (or a torus for revolute joints). C = C_free union C_obs. A valid path is a continuous curve q(t) with q(t) in C_free for all t, q(0) = q_start, q(1) = q_goal.

The configuration space (C-space) is the space of all joint configurations q of a robot; for an n-joint arm it is n-dimensional. Obstacles in the workspace map to forbidden regions C_obs in C-space, and the free space C_free is everything else. Motion planning is then a geometric problem in C-space: find a continuous path from the start configuration to the goal that stays inside C_free. The workspace is where the task is described; the C-space is where the planning is done, because joint limits and self-collision are simple bounds there.

instruction: What is the formula for RRT and PRM sampling-based planning? When is it used? [GATE RA - Motion Planning]
response:
Formula: RRT step: q_new = q_near + eta*(q_rand - q_near)/||q_rand - q_near||, kept only if the segment q_near to q_new is collision-free. PRM: roadmap graph G = (V, E) of sampled free configurations; query = graph search (e.g. A*) from q_start to q_goal.

Sampling-based planners avoid building the C-space explicitly. RRT (Rapidly-exploring Random Tree) grows a tree from the start by sampling random configurations, steering a small step from the nearest tree node toward each sample, and keeping the step if it is collision-free; it is fast and explores large spaces well, but the path is jagged and only probabilistically complete. PRM (Probabilistic Roadmap) instead samples many collision-free configurations, connects nearby ones into a roadmap graph, and then searches the graph with A*; the roadmap can be reused for many queries in the same environment. RRT* rewires the tree to converge toward the optimal path.

instruction: What is the formula for Artificial potential field planning? When is it used? [GATE RA - Motion Planning]
response:
Formula: U_att(q) = (1/2)*k_att*||q - q_goal||^2. U_rep(q) = (1/2)*k_rep*(1/d - 1/d0)^2 if d < d0, else 0, where d is distance to the nearest obstacle and d0 the influence range. U_total = U_att + U_rep; motion follows F = -grad(U_total).

Artificial potential fields plan by treating the goal as an attractor and obstacles as repellers: the robot follows the negative gradient of the total potential, i.e. it rolls downhill. The method is simple, fast and reactive, so it is popular for mobile-robot obstacle avoidance. Its main flaw is local minima, where attractive and repulsive forces cancel away from the goal and the robot gets stuck; narrow passages and oscillations near obstacles are other known problems. It is a local method, unlike RRT/PRM which plan globally.

instruction: What is the formula for Joint-space trajectory planning: cubic, quintic and trapezoidal profiles? When is it used? [GATE RA - Trajectory Planning]
response:
Formula: Cubic: q(t) = a0 + a1*t + a2*t^2 + a3*t^3, with q(0) = q0, q(tf) = qf, qdot(0) = v0, qdot(tf) = vf. Rest-to-rest: a0 = q0, a1 = 0, a2 = 3*(qf - q0)/tf^2, a3 = -2*(qf - q0)/tf^3; peak velocity = 1.5*(qf - q0)/tf. Trapezoidal: distance = (1/2)*vmax*(tf + t_cruise), where t_cruise is the constant-velocity time.

A path is the geometry of the motion; a trajectory adds the timing law. In joint space, a cubic polynomial fits position and velocity at both ends (four conditions, four coefficients) and gives smooth position and velocity, but acceleration jumps at the ends. A quintic polynomial also fixes the end accelerations (six conditions). The trapezoidal velocity profile is the industrial workhorse: constant acceleration, constant velocity, constant deceleration, which makes it easy to respect vmax and amax, but acceleration is discontinuous at the phase switches. Via points are handled by joining polynomial segments with continuous velocity.

instruction: What is the formula for SCADA and the industrial automation hierarchy? When is it used? [GATE RA - Automation & PLC]
response:
Formula: Automation hierarchy (bottom to top): field devices -> PLC / DCS (real-time control) -> SCADA (supervision, logging, alarms) -> MES (production management) -> ERP (business planning). Rule: SCADA monitors and commands; the PLC controls.

Industrial automation is organised in layers: field devices (sensors, actuators) at the bottom, PLCs and controllers doing real-time control, SCADA (Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition) monitoring, logging and alarming from a control room, then MES for production scheduling and ERP for business planning. SCADA supervises but does not replace the PLC's real-time loop: if SCADA goes down, the PLCs keep running the process. Modern plants link these layers over industrial Ethernet and fieldbus networks.

instruction: What is the formula for Homogeneous transformations and rotation matrices? When is it used? [GATE RA - Kinematics]
response:
Formula: 2D rotation: R(theta) = [[cos theta, -sin theta],[sin theta, cos theta]]; T = [[R, p],[0 0 0, 1]]; composition T02 = T01 x T12

A rotation matrix R maps coordinates between frames: it is orthonormal (R-transpose times R = identity, determinant +1). A homogeneous transform T combines rotation R and translation p in one 4x4 matrix, and chaining transforms maps a point through several frames: T02 = T01 x T12. Forward kinematics of a robot is a chain of such transforms, one per joint.

instruction: What is the formula for KCL, KVL, Thevenin and Norton theorems? When is it used? [GATE RA - Mechatronics Basics]
response:
Formula: Vth = open-circuit voltage; Rth = Vth / Isc; maximum power when R_load = Rth, Pmax = Vth^2 / (4 x Rth)

Kirchhoff's current law: the currents entering a node sum to zero. Kirchhoff's voltage law: the voltages around any closed loop sum to zero. Thevenin's theorem: any linear network seen from two terminals behaves like a voltage source Vth (the open-circuit voltage) in series with a resistance Rth. Norton's equivalent is a current source Isc in parallel with the same Rth. Maximum power is delivered when the load equals Rth.

instruction: What is the formula for Ideal op-amp: inverting and non-inverting amplifiers? When is it used? [GATE RA - Analog Circuits & Embedded Systems]
response:
Formula: Inverting gain A = -Rf / R1; non-inverting gain A = 1 + Rf / R1

An ideal op-amp has infinite gain, infinite input impedance and zero output impedance. In negative feedback the two inputs sit at the same voltage (virtual short) and draw no current (virtual ground at the inverting input). That gives clean gain formulas set by two resistors, and the same building block makes integrators, filters, Schmitt triggers and comparators.

instruction: What is the formula for Fourier, Laplace and Z-transforms? When is it used? [GATE RA - Signals & Systems]
response:
Formula: Laplace: L{df/dt} = sF(s) - f(0); Z-transform: X(z) = sum over n of x[n] z^(-n); sampling: z = e^(sT)

The Fourier transform moves a signal between time and frequency. The Laplace transform moves differential equations into algebra in the s-domain, handling initial conditions, which is why control design lives in s. The Z-transform is the discrete-time counterpart for sampled signals and digital control: sampling with period T maps s to z = e^(sT).

instruction: What is the formula for Transfer functions, Bode plots and root locus? When is it used? [GATE RA - Dynamics & Control]
response:
Formula: Gain margin = 1/|G| at the phase -180 degree frequency; phase margin = 180 degrees + phase of G at the gain crossover frequency; stable when both margins are positive

For a linear time-invariant system the transfer function G(s) = Y(s)/U(s) captures all input-output behaviour. Its poles decide stability: all poles in the left half-plane means stable. A Bode plot shows gain and phase against frequency; the root locus shows how the poles move as a gain K grows. Gain margin and phase margin measure how far the system is from instability.

instruction: What is the formula for PID control and tuning? When is it used? [GATE RA - Dynamics & Control]
response:
Formula: u(t) = Kp x e + Ki x integral of e dt + Kd x de/dt; Ziegler-Nichols: Kp = 0.6 Ku, Ti = Tu/2, Td = Tu/8

A PID controller acts on the error e: the proportional term corrects the present error, the integral term accumulates past error and removes steady-state offset, and the derivative term anticipates future error and adds damping. Too much integral action causes overshoot and oscillation; derivative action amplifies measurement noise. Ziegler-Nichols tuning finds the ultimate gain Ku and period Tu at the edge of oscillation and sets gains from them.

instruction: What is the formula for Mohr's circle for plane stress? When is it used? [GATE RA - Mechanics of Materials]
response:
Formula: Principal stresses: sigma1,2 = (sigma_x + sigma_y)/2 +- sqrt(((sigma_x - sigma_y)/2)^2 + tau_xy^2); tau_max = (sigma1 - sigma2)/2

Mohr's circle plots normal stress against shear stress for every orientation of a material element. Its centre is the average normal stress and its radius comes from the stress differences; the circle's ends give the principal stresses (where shear is zero) and its top and bottom give the maximum shear stress, which acts on planes at 45 degrees to the principal planes.

instruction: What is the formula for Torsion of shafts and bending stress? When is it used? [GATE RA - Mechanics of Materials]
response:
Formula: Torsion: tau = T x r / J, twist angle phi = T x L / (G x J); bending: sigma = M x y / I

Twisting a circular shaft produces shear stress proportional to radius: maximum at the outer surface, zero at the centre. Bending a beam produces normal stress proportional to distance from the neutral axis. Both formulas share the same idea: stress = (load x distance) / (section property). Combined torsion and bending in a shaft is checked with von Mises stress.

instruction: What is the formula for Euler column buckling? When is it used? [GATE RA - Mechanics of Materials]
response:
Formula: Critical load Pcr = pi^2 x E x I / (K x L)^2; critical stress sigma_cr = pi^2 x E / (K x L / r)^2

A long slender column buckles sideways before the material yields. The critical load depends on stiffness EI and on the effective length KL, which the end conditions set: pinned-pinned K = 1, fixed-fixed K = 0.5, fixed-free K = 2. The slenderness ratio KL/r decides whether Euler buckling or yielding governs.

instruction: What is the formula for Gear trains and gear ratio? When is it used? [GATE RA - Kinematics]
response:
Formula: Velocity ratio = N_driver / N_driven = T_driven / T_driver; compound ratio = product of the stage ratios

A gear pair's velocity ratio is the inverse of its teeth ratio: a small gear driving a large one reduces speed and raises torque. Compound trains multiply the ratios of their stages; epicyclic (planetary) trains give large reductions in a compact package. The same ratio logic applies to belt-pulley drives.

instruction: What is the formula for SDOF vibration: natural frequency and damping? When is it used? [GATE RA - Dynamics & Control]
response:
Formula: Natural frequency omega_n = sqrt(k/m); damping ratio zeta = c / (2 x sqrt(k x m)); damped frequency omega_d = omega_n x sqrt(1 - zeta^2)

A single-degree-of-freedom mass-spring-damper has one natural frequency set by stiffness and mass. The damping ratio zeta decides the behaviour: underdamped (zeta < 1) oscillates, critically damped (zeta = 1) returns fastest without oscillating, overdamped creeps back. Forcing near the natural frequency causes resonance, with large amplitudes limited only by damping.

instruction: What is the formula for Fatigue, S-N diagram and failure theories? When is it used? [GATE RA - Machine Design]
response:
Formula: von Mises stress: sigma' = sqrt(sigma_x^2 - sigma_x x sigma_y + sigma_y^2 + 3 x tau_xy^2); design rule sigma' <= Sy / N

Under cyclic loading a part can fail by fatigue far below its yield strength: cracks start at stress raisers and grow a little each cycle. The S-N curve plots stress against cycles to failure; steels show an endurance limit below which life is effectively infinite (about half the ultimate strength, before correction factors). Ductile yielding under combined stress is checked with von Mises (distortion energy); Tresca (maximum shear) is more conservative.

instruction: What is the formula for Python data structures: stack, queue, linked list, BST? When is it used? [GATE RA - Mechatronics Basics]
response:
Formula: Stack push/pop and queue enqueue/dequeue are O(1); binary search tree search is O(h), O(log n) when balanced

A stack is last-in-first-out (push and pop); a queue is first-in-first-out (enqueue and dequeue). A linked list is nodes joined by pointers, so inserting at the head is O(1). A binary search tree keeps keys ordered, so search and insert average O(log n) when balanced. A graph is nodes plus edges, traversed by breadth-first or depth-first search.

instruction: Why does Denavit-Hartenberg parameters matter in Kinematics? Where is it used? [GATE RA]
response:
The Denavit-Hartenberg (DH) convention describes each joint of a serial robot with just four parameters: link length a, link twist alpha, link offset d, and joint angle theta. For a revolute joint theta is the variable and a, alpha and d are constants; for a prismatic joint d is the variable. Substituting the four parameters into the standard homogeneous matrix gives the pose of frame i relative to frame i-1, and multiplying the matrices of all joints gives the end-effector pose relative to the base.

Formula: A_i = [[cos(theta_i), -sin(theta_i)cos(alpha_i), sin(theta_i)sin(alpha_i), a_i cos(theta_i)], [sin(theta_i), cos(theta_i)cos(alpha_i), -cos(theta_i)sin(alpha_i), a_i sin(theta_i)], [0, sin(alpha_i), cos(alpha_i), d_i], [0, 0, 0, 1]]; T_0n = A_1 A_2 ... A_n

instruction: What is Normal distribution? Explain it briefly. [GATE ST - Probability]
response:
The normal distribution is the bell-shaped distribution defined by its mean mu and standard deviation sigma. About 68.27% of values lie within one standard deviation of the mean, 95.45% within two, and 99.73% within three. Standardising a value gives its z-score, which measures how many standard deviations it is from the mean.

Formula: Probability density: f(x) = (1 / (sigma x sqrt(2 pi))) x exp(-(x - mu)^2 / (2 sigma^2)). z-score: z = (x - mu) / sigma. Empirical rule: P(mu - sigma < X < mu + sigma) = 0.6827; P(mu - 2 sigma < X < mu + 2 sigma) = 0.9545.

Worked example: For X ~ N(mu = 100, sigma = 15), the value x = 115 has z = (115 - 100)/15 = 1, so it is one standard deviation above the mean. About 68.27% of values lie between 85 and 115.

instruction: What is Central limit theorem? Explain it briefly. [GATE ST - Sampling]
response:
The central limit theorem says that the mean of a large random sample is approximately normally distributed, whatever the shape of the population, provided the population variance is finite. The sampling distribution of the sample mean has mean mu and standard deviation sigma / sqrt(n), called the standard error, which shrinks as n grows.

Formula: For a sample of size n from a population with mean mu and standard deviation sigma, the sample mean X-bar is approximately N(mu, sigma^2 / n). Standard error of the mean: SE = sigma / sqrt(n). A common rule of thumb is n >= 30 for the approximation to be reasonable.

Worked example: A population has sigma = 20. For a sample of n = 100, the standard error of the sample mean is SE = 20 / sqrt(100) = 20/10 = 2. So sample means typically fall within about 2 of mu, and about 95% fall within about 1.96 x 2 = 3.92 of mu.

instruction: What is Maximum likelihood estimation? Explain it briefly. [GATE ST - Statistical Inference]
response:
Maximum likelihood estimation picks the parameter values that make the observed data most probable. The likelihood is the joint density of the data viewed as a function of the parameters, and it is usually maximised by maximising the log-likelihood and setting its derivative to zero. MLEs are consistent and asymptotically efficient under regular conditions.

Formula: Likelihood: L(theta) = product over i of f(xi; theta). Log-likelihood: l(theta) = log L(theta). MLE: theta-hat = argmax L(theta), found by solving d l(theta) / d theta = 0. For a normal sample, the MLE of mu is the sample mean x-bar.

Worked example: For data 2, 4, 6 from a normal distribution with unknown mean mu, the log-likelihood is maximised at mu-hat = (2 + 4 + 6)/3 = 4. So the MLE of the mean is 4, the sample mean.

instruction: What is Confidence interval for a mean? Explain it briefly. [GATE ST - Statistical Inference]
response:
A confidence interval gives a range of plausible values for a population parameter, computed from a sample. A 95% confidence interval means that if the sampling were repeated many times, about 95% of the intervals so constructed would contain the true parameter. Wider intervals come from smaller samples, larger variability or higher confidence levels.

Formula: For a large sample with known sigma: x-bar +/- z(alpha/2) x sigma / sqrt(n). For 95% confidence, z = 1.96; for 90%, z = 1.645; for 99%, z = 2.576. With sigma unknown and a small sample, use t(alpha/2, n-1) x s / sqrt(n).

Worked example: A sample of n = 100 has mean 50 and sigma = 10. The standard error is 10/sqrt(100) = 1, so a 95% confidence interval is 50 +/- 1.96 x 1 = (48.04, 51.96).

instruction: What is p-value and hypothesis testing? Explain it briefly. [GATE ST - Hypothesis Testing]
response:
In hypothesis testing, the null hypothesis H0 is a default claim and the alternative H1 is what the test looks for evidence against. The p-value is the probability of getting a test statistic at least as extreme as the observed one, assuming H0 is true. If p is smaller than the chosen significance level alpha, usually 0.05, H0 is rejected. A p-value is not the probability that H0 is true.

Formula: p-value = P(test statistic at least as extreme as observed | H0 true). Decision: reject H0 if p < alpha; otherwise fail to reject H0. Type I error rate = alpha = P(reject H0 | H0 true).

Worked example: A test gives p = 0.03 with alpha = 0.05. Since 0.03 < 0.05, reject H0 at the 5% level. If instead p had been 0.20, we would fail to reject H0, which is not proof that H0 is true.

instruction: What is Simple linear regression? Explain it briefly. [GATE ST - Regression]
response:
Simple linear regression fits a straight line to the relationship between a predictor x and a response y by least squares, minimising the sum of squared residuals. The slope measures the average change in y per unit change in x, and the intercept is the predicted y when x is zero. The fitted values and residuals are used to judge the fit.

Formula: Model: y = beta0 + beta1 x + epsilon. Least-squares slope: beta1-hat = Cov(x, y) / Var(x) = sum((xi - x-bar)(yi - y-bar)) / sum((xi - x-bar)^2). Intercept: beta0-hat = y-bar - beta1-hat x-bar. Fitted value: y-hat = beta0-hat + beta1-hat x.

Worked example: For points (1, 2), (2, 4), (3, 5): x-bar = 2, y-bar = 11/3 = 3.667. The slope is [( -1 x -1.667) + (0 x 0.333) + (1 x 1.333)] / [1 + 0 + 1] = 3/2 = 1.5, and the intercept is 3.667 - 1.5 x 2 = 0.667. The fitted line is y-hat = 0.67 + 1.5 x.

instruction: What is One-way ANOVA? Explain it briefly. [GATE ST - Hypothesis Testing]
response:
One-way analysis of variance tests whether the means of three or more independent groups are all equal. It splits the total variation into variation between group means and variation within groups. If the between-group variation is large relative to the within-group variation, the F statistic is large and the null hypothesis of equal means is rejected.

Formula: F = MS_between / MS_within, where MS_between = SS_between / (k - 1) and MS_within = SS_within / (N - k), with k groups and N total observations. SS_between = sum n_i (x-bar_i - x-bar)^2; SS_within = sum sum (x_ij - x-bar_i)^2. Under H0, F follows an F distribution with (k - 1, N - k) degrees of freedom.

Worked example: With k = 3 groups, MS_between = 120 and MS_within = 30, F = 120/30 = 4.0, with degrees of freedom (2, 27) if N = 30. A large F like this suggests the group means differ more than chance alone would explain.

instruction: What is Axiomatic probability, conditional probability and Bayes theorem? Explain it briefly. [GATE ST - Probability]
response:
Kolmogorov's axioms define probability: P(A) >= 0 for every event, P(sample space) = 1, and probabilities add over disjoint events. From these follow the addition rule, the complement rule and monotonicity. Events A and B are independent if P(A and B) = P(A) P(B). Conditional probability P(A|B) = P(A and B)/P(B) updates beliefs with evidence, and Bayes' theorem reverses the conditioning.

Formula: P(A union B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A and B); P(A|B) = P(A and B)/P(B); Bayes: P(A|B) = P(B|A) P(A) / P(B); independence: P(A and B) = P(A) P(B)

Worked example: Drawing two cards without replacement: P(two aces) = (4/52)(3/51) = 1/221. If a test has 1% false positives and a disease affects 0.1% of people, a positive result still leaves the disease unlikely by Bayes' theorem.

instruction: What is Random variables, distributions, expectation and moment generating functions? Explain it briefly. [GATE ST - Probability]
response:
A random variable has a distribution function F(x) = P(X <= x); discrete variables use a probability mass function and continuous ones a density, with the density integrating to 1. Expectation E(X) is the long-run average, variance measures spread, and moments E(X^k) summarize shape. The moment generating function M(t) = E(e^{tX}) generates moments by differentiation and identifies distributions; the quantile function inverts F. A function of a random variable gets its distribution by transformation or the Jacobian method.

Formula: E(X) = sum x p(x) or integral x f(x) dx; Var(X) = E(X^2) - (E X)^2; MGF: M(t) = E(e^{tX}), E(X^k) = M^(k)(0); E(aX + b) = a E(X) + b

Worked example: For a fair die, E(X) = 3.5 and Var(X) = 35/12. For X uniform on (0,1), E(X) = 1/2 and the MGF is (e^t - 1)/t. If Y = 2X + 1, then E(Y) = 2 E(X) + 1 and Var(Y) = 4 Var(X).

instruction: What is Chebyshev, Markov and Jensen inequalities? Explain it briefly. [GATE ST - Probability]
response:
Markov's inequality bounds the tail of a non-negative random variable using only its mean: P(X >= a) <= E(X)/a. Chebyshev's inequality uses the variance: P(|X - mu| >= k sigma) <= 1/k^2, so most mass lies within a few standard deviations of the mean. Jensen's inequality says a convex function of an average is at most the average of the function: E(phi(X)) >= phi(E(X)), with the reverse for concave functions.

Formula: Markov: P(X >= a) <= E(X)/a for X >= 0, a > 0; Chebyshev: P(|X - mu| >= k sigma) <= 1/k^2; Jensen: E(phi(X)) >= phi(E X) for convex phi

Worked example: A variable with mean 10 and standard deviation 2 lies in [4, 16] with probability at least 1 - 1/9 = 89% by Chebyshev (k = 3). Jensen gives E(1/X) >= 1/E(X) for positive X, so the harmonic mean is below the arithmetic mean.

instruction: What is Standard discrete distributions? Explain it briefly. [GATE ST - Probability]
response:
The Bernoulli(p) distribution is a single 0/1 trial; the binomial(n,p) counts successes in n independent trials; the geometric(p) counts trials until the first success and is memoryless; the negative binomial counts trials until the r-th success; the hypergeometric counts successes in draws without replacement from a finite population; the discrete uniform gives equal probability to each of n values; the Poisson(lambda) models rare events in a fixed interval.

Formula: Binomial: P(X=k) = C(n,k) p^k (1-p)^(n-k), mean np, variance np(1-p); Geometric: P(X=k) = (1-p)^(k-1) p, mean 1/p; Poisson: P(X=k) = e^-lambda lambda^k/k!, mean = variance = lambda; Hypergeometric: P(X=k) = C(K,k) C(N-K,n-k)/C(N,n)

Worked example: The number of heads in 10 fair coin tosses is Binomial(10, 0.5) with mean 5. Calls arriving at 3 per minute follow Poisson(3): the chance of no calls in a minute is e^-3 = 5%. Drawing 5 cards, the number of aces is hypergeometric, not binomial.

instruction: What is Standard continuous distributions? Explain it briefly. [GATE ST - Probability]
What is Jointly distributed random variables? Explain it briefly. [GATE ST - Probability]
response:
Two random variables have a joint distribution (joint pmf or pdf) from which marginal distributions follow by summing or integrating out the other variable, and conditional distributions by dividing by the marginal. The conditional expectation E(Y|X) is itself a random variable, and the law of total expectation says E(Y) = E(E(Y|X)). Covariance and correlation measure linear association; the joint moment generating function extends the one-variable version; independent variables factor their joint distribution into the product of marginals.

Formula: f_{X,Y}(x,y) = f_X(x) f_Y(y) if independent; E(Y) = E(E(Y|X)); Cov(X,Y) = E(XY) - E(X)E(Y); correlation rho = Cov(X,Y)/(sigma_X sigma_Y); Var(X+Y) = Var X + Var Y + 2 Cov(X,Y)

Worked example: Rolling two dice, the sum S and the first die X have E(S|X = 4) = 4 + 3.5 = 7.5. For a bivariate normal with correlation rho, the conditional mean of Y given X = x is mu_Y + rho (sigma_Y/sigma_X)(x - mu_X).

instruction: What is Order statistics? Explain it briefly. [GATE ST - Probability]
response:
Order statistics X_(1) <= X_(2) <= ... <= X_(n) are the sorted values of a sample; the minimum and maximum are the extremes. Their distributions follow from the original CDF: the CDF of the maximum is F(x)^n and of the minimum is 1 - (1-F(x))^n. Joint densities of order statistics involve multinomial-type counting of how many observations fall in each interval, and they are the basis of rank-based tests and quantile estimation.

Formula: F_{X_(n)}(x) = F(x)^n; F_{X_(1)}(x) = 1 - (1 - F(x))^n; pdf of X_(k): n! / ((k-1)! (n-k)!) * F(x)^(k-1) (1-F(x))^(n-k) f(x)

Worked example: For 5 independent Uniform(0,1) draws, the maximum has CDF x^5 and mean 5/6, while the median (3rd order statistic) has mean 1/2. The sample range X_(n) - X_(1) measures spread without assuming a distribution.

instruction: What is Multinomial and bivariate normal distributions? Explain it briefly. [GATE ST - Probability]
response:
The multinomial distribution generalizes the binomial to k categories with probabilities p_1,...,p_k over n trials; its counts have means n p_i and covariances -n p_i p_j between different categories. The bivariate normal is determined by two means, two variances and a correlation rho; its marginals are normal, its conditionals are normal with a linear regression mean, and zero correlation is equivalent to independence for it (unlike in general).

Formula: Multinomial: P(X1=x1,...,Xk=xk) = n!/(x1! ... xk!) p1^x1 ... pk^xk; Cov(Xi, Xj) = -n pi pj; bivariate normal conditional mean: E(Y|X=x) = mu_Y + rho (sigma_Y/sigma_X)(x - mu_X)

Worked example: Rolling a die 60 times, the counts of the six faces are Multinomial(60, 1/6 each). For a bivariate normal with rho = 0.6, sigma_X = sigma_Y = 1, observing X = 1 shifts the mean of Y to 0.6.

instruction: What is Sampling distributions: chi-square, t and F? Explain it briefly. [GATE ST - Sampling]
response:
The chi-square distribution with nu degrees of freedom is the sum of squares of nu independent standard normals, and it describes the sampling distribution of the sample variance of normal data. The t distribution is a standard normal divided by the square root of an independent chi-square over its degrees of freedom, used for inference about a mean with unknown variance. The F distribution is the ratio of two independent chi-squares each divided by its degrees of freedom, used to compare variances and in ANOVA.

Formula: If Z_i are iid N(0,1), sum Z_i^2 is chi-square(nu); (n-1) S^2 / sigma^2 is chi-square(n-1); T = Z / sqrt(V/nu) is t(nu); F = (U/nu1)/(V/nu2) with U, V independent chi-squares

Worked example: With a sample of 10 from a normal population, the 95% confidence interval for the mean uses t_9 (critical value 2.262) rather than the normal 1.96, because sigma is estimated. The ratio of two sample variances follows an F distribution under equal population variances.

instruction: What is Modes of convergence, laws of large numbers and the delta method? Explain it briefly. [GATE ST - Probability]
response:
Convergence in probability means P(|X_n - X| > e) -> 0; almost sure convergence means X_n -> X with probability 1; convergence in distribution means CDFs converge at continuity points; convergence in r-th mean means E|X_n - X|^r -> 0. Almost sure implies in probability implies in distribution; r-th mean implies in probability. Slutsky's lemma lets limits be combined, Borel-Cantelli links summable tail probabilities to finitely-many occurrences, and the weak and strong laws of large numbers make sample averages converge to the mean. The delta method propagates asymptotic normality through a smooth function.

Formula: WLLN: Xbar -> mu in probability; SLLN: Xbar -> mu almost surely; delta method: if sqrt(n)(T_n - theta) -> N(0, sigma^2), then sqrt(n)(g(T_n) - g(theta)) -> N(0, (g'(theta))^2 sigma^2)

Worked example: For iid data with mean mu, the sample mean converges to mu by the laws of large numbers. If the sample proportion p-hat has asymptotic variance p(1-p)/n, the delta method gives log(p-hat) an asymptotic variance of (1-p)/(n p).

instruction: What is Markov chains? Explain it briefly. [GATE ST - Stochastic Processes]
response:
A Markov chain is a sequence where the future depends on the present only, described by transition probabilities P_ij. States are classified as transient or recurrent, and recurrent states split into positive recurrent and null recurrent; a state is periodic if returns are possible only at multiples of some period d > 1. An irreducible aperiodic positive recurrent chain has a unique stationary distribution pi with pi = pi P, and n-step transition probabilities converge to it. Finite irreducible chains are always positive recurrent.

Formula: Chapman-Kolmogorov: P^(m+n) = P^(m) P^(n); stationary distribution: pi = pi P with sum pi_i = 1; mean recurrence time of state i is 1/pi_i

Worked example: A two-state weather chain with P(sunny->rainy) = 0.3 and P(rainy->sunny) = 0.4 has stationary distribution pi_sunny = 0.4/0.7 = 4/7, pi_rainy = 3/7. A simple symmetric random walk on the integers is null recurrent.

instruction: What is Poisson process and birth-and-death processes? Explain it briefly. [GATE ST - Stochastic Processes]
response:
A Poisson process counts events occurring at constant rate lambda with independent increments: the count in any interval is Poisson(lambda * length) and inter-arrival times are independent exponentials. Birth-and-death processes generalize this with state-dependent birth rates lambda_n and death rates mu_n, covering queues (M/M/1) and population models. A pure-birth process has only births (e.g. the Yule process) and a pure-death process only deaths; the stationary distribution of a birth-death process follows from detailed balance when it exists.

Formula: Poisson process: P(N(t) = k) = e^{-lambda t} (lambda t)^k / k!; inter-arrival times iid Exponential(lambda); birth-death stationary: pi_n = pi_0 * product_{i=0}^{n-1} (lambda_i / mu_{i+1})

Worked example: Calls arriving at 5 per hour form a Poisson process: the chance of exactly 3 calls in the next hour is e^-5 5^3/6 = 14%. An M/M/1 queue with arrival rate 2 and service rate 3 per hour has stationary probabilities pi_n = (1/3)(2/3)^n.

instruction: What is Brownian motion? Explain it briefly. [GATE ST - Stochastic Processes]
response:
Brownian motion (the Wiener process) is a continuous-time process starting at 0 with independent, stationary, normally distributed increments: B(t) - B(s) is Normal(0, t - s). Its paths are continuous everywhere but differentiable nowhere, and it is the scaling limit of random walks (Donsker's theorem). It is the basic building block of stochastic calculus and diffusion models in finance and physics.

Formula: B(t) - B(s) ~ N(0, t - s) for t > s; Cov(B(s), B(t)) = min(s, t); Var(B(t)) = t

Worked example: A particle's position after t seconds of Brownian motion with diffusion coefficient D has variance 2Dt, so typical displacement grows like sqrt(t), not t. Simulating it means adding N(0, dt) steps.

instruction: What is Sufficiency, minimal sufficiency, completeness and Basu's theorem? Explain it briefly. [GATE ST - Statistical Inference]
response:
A statistic is sufficient if it captures all information about the parameter, so the conditional distribution of the data given the statistic does not depend on the parameter. The factorization theorem identifies sufficient statistics from the likelihood: f(x; theta) = g(T(x); theta) h(x). A minimal sufficient statistic is a coarsest sufficient one. A statistic is complete if no non-zero function of it has zero expectation for all theta; exponential families are complete under mild conditions. Basu's theorem says a complete sufficient statistic is independent of every ancillary statistic (one whose distribution is free of theta).

Formula: Factorization: f(x; theta) = g(T(x); theta) h(x) iff T is sufficient; Basu: complete sufficient T is independent of any ancillary statistic

Worked example: For a sample from N(mu, 1), the sample mean is sufficient and complete for mu, while the sample variance is ancillary for mu. For Uniform(0, theta), the maximum is sufficient and complete.

instruction: What is Unbiased estimation, UMVUE, Rao-Blackwell and Cramer-Rao inequality? Explain it briefly. [GATE ST - Statistical Inference]
response:
An estimator is unbiased if its expectation equals the parameter. The Rao-Blackwell theorem improves any unbiased estimator by conditioning on a sufficient statistic, never increasing variance. The Lehmann-Scheffe theorem says conditioning an unbiased estimator on a complete sufficient statistic gives the unique uniformly minimum variance unbiased estimator (UMVUE). The Cramer-Rao inequality lower-bounds the variance of any unbiased estimator by the reciprocal of the Fisher information, so an estimator attaining it is efficient.

Formula: Cramer-Rao: Var(T) >= 1 / I(theta) for unbiased T, where I(theta) = E[(d/d theta log f(X; theta))^2]; Rao-Blackwell: Var(E(T|S)) <= Var(T) for sufficient S

Worked example: For a sample from N(mu, sigma^2) with sigma known, the sample mean attains the Cramer-Rao bound  sigma^2/n and is the UMVUE. For Poisson(lambda), the sample mean is the UMVUE of lambda.

instruction: What is Method of moments estimators and consistency? Explain it briefly. [GATE ST - Statistical Inference]
response:
The method of moments estimates parameters by equating sample moments to population moments and solving; it is simple and often gives a starting value for maximum likelihood. An estimator is consistent if it converges in probability to the true parameter as the sample size grows; the sample mean and sample variance are consistent for their targets under mild conditions. Consistency is a minimal requirement: an inconsistent estimator stays wrong even with infinite data.

Formula: Method of moments: set (1/n) sum X_i^k = E_theta(X^k) for k = 1, 2, ... and solve for theta; consistent: T_n -> theta in probability as n -> infinity

Worked example: For Gamma(alpha, beta) data, equating the sample mean to alpha/beta and the sample variance to alpha/beta^2 gives moment estimators of both parameters. The sample proportion is consistent for a population proportion by the weak law of large numbers.

instruction: What is Interval estimation with pivotal quantities and coverage probability? Explain it briefly. [GATE ST - Statistical Inference]
response:
A confidence interval is built by inverting a pivotal quantity: a function of data and parameter whose distribution does not depend on the parameter. The classic pivot (Xbar - mu)/(S/sqrt(n)) follows a t distribution, giving the usual interval for a normal mean. Coverage probability is the long-run fraction of intervals that contain the true parameter; a 95% interval covers the truth in 95% of repeated samples, not with 95% probability for one realized interval.

Formula: 95% CI for a normal mean: Xbar +- t_{n-1, 0.975} * S/sqrt(n); pivot: (Xbar - mu)/(sigma/sqrt(n)) ~ N(0,1) when sigma is known

Worked example: With n = 16, Xbar = 10 and S = 4, the 95% CI for mu is 10 +- 2.131 * 4/4 = (7.87, 12.13). A pivotal quantity for an exponential scale parameter uses the ratio Xbar/theta.

instruction: What is Neyman-Pearson lemma, most powerful and uniformly most powerful tests? Explain it briefly. [GATE ST - Hypothesis Testing]
response:
For testing a simple null against a simple alternative, the Neyman-Pearson lemma says the most powerful test of a given size rejects for large values of the likelihood ratio. When the family has monotone likelihood ratio (MLR), the same one-sided test is uniformly most powerful (UMP) for all alternatives on one side.
