instruction: Floor Area Ratio (FAR / FSI) gurinchi oka worked example ivvu. [GATE AR - Planning]
response:
Worked example: A plot of 1000 sq m with FAR = 2.0 may have up to 2.0 x 1000 = 2000 sq m of total floor area, for example four floors of 500 sq m each.

Formula: FAR (FSI) = total built-up floor area / plot area. Permissible built-up area = FAR x plot area.

Floor Area Ratio (called Floor Space Index, FSI, in India) is the ratio of a building's total floor area to the area of its plot. It is the main planning control on how much can be built on a site: a higher FAR allows a taller or bulkier building. It is set by development control regulations and varies by zone, road width, and land use.

instruction: Water-cement ratio and Abrams' law gurinchi oka worked example ivvu. [GATE AR - Building Materials]
response:
Worked example: A mix uses 180 kg of water and 400 kg of cement. w/c = 180/400 = 0.45, which is the IS 456 maximum for reinforced concrete in severe exposure.

Formula: w/c = W / C;  Abrams' law: strength S = A / B^(w/c), where W is mass of water, C is mass of cement, and A and B are empirical constants for the materials and curing.

The water-cement ratio is the mass of free water divided by the mass of cement in a concrete mix. Abrams' law states that, for given materials and curing, the compressive strength of fully compacted concrete depends mainly on this ratio: a lower ratio gives denser paste and higher strength, while excess water leaves pores that weaken the concrete. Codes such as IS 456 set maximum ratios by exposure condition.

instruction: U-value and heat transfer through building fabric gurinchi oka worked example ivvu. [GATE AR - Architecture]
response:
Worked example: A wall with R_total = 2.5 m2 K/W has U = 1/2.5 = 0.4 W/(m2 K). For A = 10 m2 and delta T = 10 K, heat flow Q = 0.4 x 10 x 10 = 40 W.

Formula: U = 1 / R_total;  Q = U x A x delta T, where U is in W/(m2 K), R_total is total thermal resistance, Q is heat flow, A is area and delta T is temperature difference.

The U-value (thermal transmittance) measures how much heat passes through one square metre of a wall, roof, or window per degree of temperature difference. It is the reciprocal of the total thermal resistance of the layers. A lower U-value means better insulation and lower heating or cooling load, which is central to climate-responsive design.

instruction: Daylight factor gurinchi oka worked example ivvu. [GATE AR - Architecture]
response:
Worked example: If indoor illuminance is 300 lux and outdoor illuminance is 10,000 lux, DF = (300/10,000) x 100 = 3%.

Formula: Daylight factor DF = (Ei / Eo) x 100%, where Ei is indoor illuminance and Eo is outdoor illuminance under an overcast sky.

The daylight factor is the ratio of indoor illuminance at a point to the simultaneous outdoor illuminance under an overcast sky, expressed as a percentage. It is the standard measure of how well a room is daylit, independent of the time of day. Larger windows, lighter surfaces, and shallower rooms raise it; a living room typically needs an average daylight factor of about 2% or more.

instruction: Golden ratio in proportion gurinchi oka worked example ivvu. [GATE AR - History of Architecture]
response:
Worked example: A golden rectangle 1.618 m long is 1.0 m wide. Removing a 1 m x 1 m square leaves a smaller rectangle, 0.618 m by 1 m, which is again in the golden ratio.

Formula: phi = (1 + sqrt(5)) / 2 = 1.618... A golden rectangle has sides in the ratio 1 : 1.618.

The golden ratio, phi, is the proportion in which a line is divided so that the ratio of the whole to the longer part equals the ratio of the longer part to the shorter part. It has been used since antiquity as a proportioning system in architecture, from the Parthenon to Le Corbusier's Modulor, because rectangles in this ratio are widely judged harmonious. It is closely linked to the Fibonacci sequence.

instruction: Neighbourhood unit (Clarence Perry) gurinchi oka worked example ivvu. [GATE AR - Planning]
response:
Worked example: A neighbourhood of 6,000 people with one elementary school at the centre and homes within 400 m of it follows Perry's unit: children walk to school without crossing an arterial road.

Formula: Population about 5,000-10,000 per unit; radius about 400 m (1/4 mile) to the central school; area about 160 acres in Perry's original scheme.

Clarence Perry's neighbourhood unit (1929) is a foundational planning concept: a residential area of about 5,000-10,000 people organised around an elementary school at its centre, bounded by arterial roads, with shops at the edges and parks and open space inside. Every home is within about a quarter-mile (400 m), a five-minute walk, of the school. It shaped garden-city and new-town planning and remains the basis of walkable neighbourhood design.

instruction: PERT and CPM in Project Management gurinchi oka worked example ivvu. [GATE AR - Architecture]
response:
Worked example: An activity with a = 2, m = 4 and b = 12 days has expected time te = (2 + 16 + 12)/6 = 5 days; if it lies on the critical path, slipping by 2 days delays the project by 2 days.

Formula: PERT expected time te = (a + 4m + b)/6; total float = LS − ES = LF − EF; critical path float = 0

The Critical Path Method (CPM) schedules a project as a network of activities: for each activity the earliest start/finish and latest start/finish are computed, and the path with zero total float is the critical path that fixes the project duration. Any delay on it delays the whole project. PERT handles uncertain durations by taking optimistic (a), most likely (m) and pessimistic (b) estimates and computing an expected time. CPM is used for construction projects with well-defined activities.

instruction: Modular Coordination in Building Construction gurinchi oka worked example ivvu. [GATE AR - Building Materials]
response:
Worked example: A room planned on a 3M grid is 3.0 m, 3.3 m or 3.6 m wide, so standard 900 mm (9M) doors and 1,200 mm (12M) windows fit without on-site cutting.

Formula: Rule: basic module M = 100 mm; dimensions are multiples of M (e.g. 3M = 300 mm planning grid)

Modular coordination sizes building components on a standard module, conventionally M = 100 mm, so that parts from different manufacturers fit together on a common grid. Planning, structural and service dimensions are multiples of the module, which reduces cutting and waste, speeds prefabrication and allows standardised windows, doors and panels. It is a core principle of industrialised and prefabricated construction.

instruction: Natural and Mechanical Ventilation: Air Changes per Hour gurinchi oka worked example ivvu. [GATE AR - Architecture]
response:
Worked example: A 60 m3 bedroom supplied with 120 m3/h of fresh air has 2 air changes per hour, meaning its air is fully replaced every 30 minutes.

Formula: ACH = airflow (m3/h) / room volume (m3)

Ventilation replaces stale indoor air with fresh air, removing heat, moisture, odours and pollutants. Its rate is often expressed as air changes per hour (ACH): the volume of fresh air supplied per hour divided by the room volume. Natural ventilation relies on wind and stack effect through openings, while mechanical ventilation uses fans and ducts. Bedrooms and living rooms typically need 0.5-1 ACH, while kitchens and toilets need much higher rates.

instruction: Room Acoustics: Reverberation Time (Sabine's Formula) gurinchi oka worked example ivvu. [GATE AR - Architecture]
response:
Worked example: A hall of volume 500 m3 with total absorption 100 sabins has RT60 = 0.161 × 500/100 ≈ 0.81 s, suitable for speech; doubling the absorption would halve it to about 0.4 s.

Formula: RT60 = 0.161 × V/A; A = Σ(S × α), where S = surface area and α = absorption coefficient

Reverberation time RT60 is the time for sound to decay by 60 dB after the source stops, and it decides whether a room sounds echoey or dead. Sabine's formula relates it to the room volume V and the total absorption A, which is the sum of each surface's area times its absorption coefficient. Large, hard rooms reverberate longest; adding soft, absorptive material shortens it. Speech needs a short RT60 (about 0.5-1 s), while concert halls need longer (about 1.5-2 s).

instruction: Kevin Lynch's Five Elements of Urban Design gurinchi oka worked example ivvu. [GATE AR - Urban Design]
response:
Worked example: In a historic city the main street is a path, the river is an edge, the old quarter is a district, the central square is a node, and the cathedral tower is a landmark that orients visitors.

Formula: Rule: legibility = clear paths + edges + districts + nodes + landmarks

Kevin Lynch's The Image of the City (1960) identified five elements by which people read and remember a city: paths (streets and routes of movement), edges (boundaries such as rivers or walls), districts (areas with a recognisable character), nodes (focal points such as squares or junctions) and landmarks (reference points such as a tower or monument). A legible city with clear elements is easier to navigate and gives a stronger sense of place.

instruction: Garden City Movement (Ebenezer Howard) gurinchi oka worked example ivvu. [GATE AR - Planning]
response:
Worked example: Letchworth Garden City, founded in 1903, follows Howard's plan with a central square, radial avenues and a green belt that still limits its expansion today.

Formula: Rule: town of ~32,000 people + permanent green belt + town-country balance; growth by new towns, not sprawl

Ebenezer Howard's Garden City (1898) proposed self-contained towns combining the advantages of town and country — jobs and services with fresh air and gardens — surrounded by a permanent agricultural green belt. Each town was planned for about 32,000 people, with radial streets, a central park and civic buildings, and limited growth by building new towns instead of sprawling. Letchworth and Welwyn in England were the first examples, and the idea influenced new-town planning worldwide.

instruction: Residential Density: Net and Gross gurinchi oka worked example ivvu. [GATE AR - Planning]
response:
Worked example: 100 dwelling units on 2 hectares of residential plots is a net density of 50 DU/ha; if the same 100 units sit in a 4-hectare neighbourhood including roads and a park, the gross density is 25 DU/ha.

Formula: Density = dwelling units (or persons) / area in hectares; gross density counts the whole area, net density only residential plots

Residential density measures how intensively land is used for housing, expressed as dwelling units per hectare or persons per hectare. Net density counts only the residential plots, while gross density includes roads, open spaces and community facilities in the area, so gross is always lower. Density shapes infrastructure demand, transport viability and liveability: very low density makes public transport uneconomic, while very high density strains services and open space.

instruction: Gothic Architecture gurinchi oka worked example ivvu. [GATE AR - History of Architecture]
response:
Worked example: Notre-Dame de Paris uses flying buttresses to carry the vault thrust outside the walls, allowing its great rose windows and a nave height of about 33 m.

Formula: Rule: pointed arch + ribbed vault + flying buttress = tall, light-filled interior with large stained-glass windows

Gothic architecture, dominant in Europe from the 12th to the 16th century, is defined by the pointed arch, ribbed vault and flying buttress, which together channelled the weight of the roof outward and downward so walls could be thin and filled with stained glass. The result is soaring verticality and light-filled interiors expressing spiritual aspiration. Early masterpieces include Chartres and Notre-Dame de Paris, and the style revived in the 19th-century Gothic Revival.

instruction: Vernacular Architecture of India gurinchi oka worked example ivvu. [GATE AR - History of Architecture]
response:
Worked example: A Kerala Nalukettu uses a sloping clay-tile roof to shed monsoon rain, a central courtyard for light and ventilation, and laterite and timber from nearby sources.

Formula: Rule: local climate + local materials + local craft = climate-responsive, low-energy building

Vernacular architecture is building shaped by local climate, materials, crafts and ways of life, without a professional architect. In India it ranges from Kerala's Nalukettu houses with sloping tiled roofs and courtyards for the monsoon, to Rajasthan's havelis with thick walls, courtyards and jharokhas for hot-dry summers, to bamboo and mud houses of the north-east for earthquakes. Its lessons in climate response and low-energy design are widely reused in contemporary sustainable architecture.

instruction: Concrete Mix Design and Target Mean Strength gurinchi oka worked example ivvu. [GATE AR - Building Materials]
response:
Worked example: For M20 concrete with σ = 4 MPa, the target mean strength is 20 + 1.65 × 4 = 26.6 MPa, so the mix is proportioned to reach 26.6 MPa on average.

Formula: Target mean strength f'ck = fck + 1.65σ; Abrams' law: strength falls as water-cement ratio rises

Concrete is specified by its characteristic compressive strength fck (for example M20 means 20 MPa at 28 days). Because strength varies, the mix is designed for a target mean strength higher than fck by a margin depending on the standard deviation σ of site production: f'ck = fck + 1.65σ, so that no more than 5% of samples fall below fck. The water-cement ratio governs strength (Abrams' law) and durability: lower ratios give stronger, more durable concrete but need admixtures for workability.

instruction: Fire Safety and Means of Escape in Buildings gurinchi oka worked example ivvu. [GATE AR - Architecture]
response:
Worked example: A residential floor is typically limited to about 30 m of travel distance to a protected staircase, so that occupants can reach safety within a few minutes of an alarm.

Formula: Rule: protected escape stairs + limited travel distance to exits + fire compartmentation + detection/alarm; refuge areas required in high-rise buildings

Fire safety design provides safe escape before conditions become untenable: protected staircases, fire-rated doors, clear travel distances to exits, and refuge areas in high-rise buildings. Indian codes (National Building Code) set maximum travel distances, minimum stair widths and the number of exits based on occupancy and floor area. Detection and alarm, sprinklers, and compartmentation that slows fire spread complement escape design.

instruction: Transit Oriented Development (TOD) gurinchi oka worked example ivvu. [GATE AR - Planning]
response:
Worked example: Redeveloping land around a metro station with apartments, offices and shops above the station, with wide footpaths and no large parking lots, is a TOD project.

Formula: Rule: dense mixed-use development within ~500 m of transit; the five Ds = density, diversity, design, destination accessibility, distance to transit

Transit Oriented Development concentrates dense, mixed-use development within walking distance (about 500 m) of a transit station, so people can live, work and shop without a car. Its five Ds are density, diversity of uses, design (walkable streets), destination accessibility and distance to transit. TOD reduces car dependence, supports ridership and makes efficient use of expensive transit investment, and is a key policy in Indian urban planning guidelines.

instruction: Floor Area Ratio (FAR / FSI) par ek worked example dijiye. [GATE AR - Planning]
response:
Worked example: A plot of 1000 sq m with FAR = 2.0 may have up to 2.0 x 1000 = 2000 sq m of total floor area, for example four floors of 500 sq m each.

Formula: FAR (FSI) = total built-up floor area / plot area. Permissible built-up area = FAR x plot area.

Floor Area Ratio (called Floor Space Index, FSI, in India) is the ratio of a building's total floor area to the area of its plot. It is the main planning control on how much can be built on a site: a higher FAR allows a taller or bulkier building. It is set by development control regulations and varies by zone, road width, and land use.

instruction: Water-cement ratio and Abrams' law par ek worked example dijiye. [GATE AR - Building Materials]
response:
Worked example: A mix uses 180 kg of water and 400 kg of cement. w/c = 180/400 = 0.45, which is the IS 456 maximum for reinforced concrete in severe exposure.

Formula: w/c = W / C;  Abrams' law: strength S = A / B^(w/c), where W is mass of water, C is mass of cement, and A and B are empirical constants for the materials and curing.

The water-cement ratio is the mass of free water divided by the mass of cement in a concrete mix. Abrams' law states that, for given materials and curing, the compressive strength of fully compacted concrete depends mainly on this ratio: a lower ratio gives denser paste and higher strength, while excess water leaves pores that weaken the concrete. Codes such as IS 456 set maximum ratios by exposure condition.

instruction: U-value and heat transfer through building fabric par ek worked example dijiye. [GATE AR - Architecture]
response:
Worked example: A wall with R_total = 2.5 m2 K/W has U = 1/2.5 = 0.4 W/(m2 K). For A = 10 m2 and delta T = 10 K, heat flow Q = 0.4 x 10 x 10 = 40 W.

Formula: U = 1 / R_total;  Q = U x A x delta T, where U is in W/(m2 K), R_total is total thermal resistance, Q is heat flow, A is area and delta T is temperature difference.

The U-value (thermal transmittance) measures how much heat passes through one square metre of a wall, roof, or window per degree of temperature difference. It is the reciprocal of the total thermal resistance of the layers. A lower U-value means better insulation and lower heating or cooling load, which is central to climate-responsive design.

instruction: Daylight factor par ek worked example dijiye. [GATE AR - Architecture]
response:
Worked example: If indoor illuminance is 300 lux and outdoor illuminance is 10,000 lux, DF = (300/10,000) x 100 = 3%.

Formula: Daylight factor DF = (Ei / Eo) x 100%, where Ei is indoor illuminance and Eo is outdoor illuminance under an overcast sky.

The daylight factor is the ratio of indoor illuminance at a point to the simultaneous outdoor illuminance under an overcast sky, expressed as a percentage. It is the standard measure of how well a room is daylit, independent of the time of day. Larger windows, lighter surfaces, and shallower rooms raise it; a living room typically needs an average daylight factor of about 2% or more.

instruction: Golden ratio in proportion par ek worked example dijiye. [GATE AR - History of Architecture]
response:
Worked example: A golden rectangle 1.618 m long is 1.0 m wide. Removing a 1 m x 1 m square leaves a smaller rectangle, 0.618 m by 1 m, which is again in the golden ratio.

Formula: phi = (1 + sqrt(5)) / 2 = 1.618... A golden rectangle has sides in the ratio 1 : 1.618.

The golden ratio, phi, is the proportion in which a line is divided so that the ratio of the whole to the longer part equals the ratio of the longer part to the shorter part. It has been used since antiquity as a proportioning system in architecture, from the Parthenon to Le Corbusier's Modulor, because rectangles in this ratio are widely judged harmonious. It is closely linked to the Fibonacci sequence.

instruction: Neighbourhood unit (Clarence Perry) par ek worked example dijiye. [GATE AR - Planning]
response:
Worked example: A neighbourhood of 6,000 people with one elementary school at the centre and homes within 400 m of it follows Perry's unit: children walk to school without crossing an arterial road.

Formula: Population about 5,000-10,000 per unit; radius about 400 m (1/4 mile) to the central school; area about 160 acres in Perry's original scheme.

Clarence Perry's neighbourhood unit (1929) is a foundational planning concept: a residential area of about 5,000-10,000 people organised around an elementary school at its centre, bounded by arterial roads, with shops at the edges and parks and open space inside. Every home is within about a quarter-mile (400 m), a five-minute walk, of the school. It shaped garden-city and new-town planning and remains the basis of walkable neighbourhood design.

instruction: Michaelis-Menten enzyme kinetics gurinchi oka worked example ivvu. [GATE BT - Biochemistry]
response:
Worked example: If Vmax = 100 micromol/min, Km = 2 mM and [S] = 2 mM, v = (100 x 2)/(2 + 2) = 50 micromol/min, exactly half of Vmax.

Formula: v = (Vmax x [S]) / (Km + [S]), where v is reaction rate, Vmax is maximum rate, [S] is substrate concentration and Km is the Michaelis constant.

Michaelis-Menten kinetics describes the rate of an enzyme-catalysed reaction as a function of substrate concentration. At low substrate the rate rises almost linearly, and at high substrate it approaches a maximum rate Vmax when the enzyme is saturated. Km is the substrate concentration at half Vmax and measures affinity: a low Km means high affinity.

instruction: Monod growth kinetics gurinchi oka worked example ivvu. [GATE BT - Bioprocess Engineering]
response:
Worked example: If mu_max = 0.8 per hour, Ks = 0.5 g/L and S = 1.5 g/L, mu = (0.8 x 1.5)/(0.5 + 1.5) = 0.6 per hour. Doubling time = ln 2 / 0.6 = 1.16 hours.

Formula: mu = (mu_max x S) / (Ks + S), where mu is specific growth rate, mu_max is maximum specific growth rate, S is limiting substrate concentration and Ks is the half-saturation constant.

Monod kinetics is the microbial-growth analogue of Michaelis-Menten kinetics: the specific growth rate of a culture depends on the concentration of the limiting substrate. Growth is slow when substrate is scarce and approaches a maximum rate mu_max when substrate is plentiful. Ks is the substrate concentration at half the maximum growth rate.

instruction: PCR exponential amplification gurinchi oka worked example ivvu. [GATE BT - Molecular Biology]
response:
Worked example: Starting with 10 copies and running 30 cycles, N = 10 x 2^30 = about 1.07 x 10^10 copies.

Formula: N = N0 x 2^n, where N is the final copy number, N0 is the initial copy number and n is the number of cycles.

Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) amplifies a specific DNA segment through repeated cycles of denaturation, annealing of primers, and extension by a heat-stable DNA polymerase such as Taq. In ideal conditions the number of copies doubles each cycle, so amplification is exponential. After n cycles, one starting molecule yields about 2^n copies.

instruction: Central dogma of molecular biology gurinchi oka worked example ivvu. [GATE BT - Molecular Biology]
response:
Worked example: A coding sequence of 900 nucleotides contains 900/3 = 300 codons, so it encodes a protein of about 300 amino acids (before the stop codon).

Formula: DNA --transcription--> RNA --translation--> Protein. One codon (3 bases) codes for one amino acid.

The central dogma states that genetic information flows from DNA to RNA to protein: DNA is transcribed into messenger RNA, which is translated into protein on ribosomes. DNA replication copies the genome before cell division. In retroviruses, reverse transcriptase can copy RNA back into DNA, an exception to the usual flow.

instruction: Exponential growth and doubling time gurinchi oka worked example ivvu. [GATE BT - Bioprocess Engineering]
response:
Worked example: With X0 = 1 g/L, mu = 0.5 per hour and t = 4 hours, X = 1 x e^2 = 7.39 g/L. The doubling time is ln 2 / 0.5 = 1.39 hours.

Formula: X = X0 x e^(mu x t);  doubling time td = ln 2 / mu, where X is biomass, X0 is initial biomass, mu is specific growth rate and t is time.

In the exponential (log) phase, a microbial population grows at a constant specific growth rate, with cell number or biomass increasing exponentially with time. The doubling time is the time for the population to double and is inversely related to the specific growth rate. This phase ends when a nutrient is exhausted or waste accumulates.

instruction: Yield coefficients in fermentation gurinchi oka worked example ivvu. [GATE BT - Bioprocess Engineering]
response:
Worked example: If 20 g of glucose is consumed and 10 g of dry cells are produced, Yx/s = 10/20 = 0.5 g cells per g glucose.

Formula: Yx/s = (change in biomass) / (change in substrate consumed);  Yp/s = (change in product) / (change in substrate consumed).

A yield coefficient relates the amount of biomass or product formed to the amount of substrate consumed in a fermentation. The biomass yield Yx/s is the mass of cells produced per mass of substrate used. It is used in mass balances to size media, estimate substrate demand, and compare strains and processes.

instruction: Enzyme Inhibition: Competitive, Non-competitive and Uncompetitive gurinchi oka worked example ivvu. [GATE BT - Biochemistry]
response:
Worked example: If [I] = Ki for a competitive inhibitor, the apparent Km doubles, so twice as much substrate is needed to reach half of Vmax, while Vmax itself is unchanged.

Formula: Competitive: v = Vmax[S]/(Km(1 + [I]/Ki) + [S]); non-competitive: Vmax_app = Vmax/(1 + [I]/Ki)

A competitive inhibitor binds the active site and raises the apparent Km without changing Vmax, so its effect can be overcome by adding more substrate. A non-competitive inhibitor binds elsewhere and lowers Vmax without changing Km. An uncompetitive inhibitor binds only the enzyme-substrate complex, lowering both Vmax and Km. The inhibitor constant Ki measures binding strength; smaller Ki means stronger inhibition.

instruction: Linkage, Recombination and Chromosome Mapping gurinchi oka worked example ivvu. [GATE BT - Genetics]
response:
Worked example: In a test cross of 200 progeny, 30 are recombinant for genes A and B, so the distance is 30/200 × 100 = 15 cM.

Formula: Recombination frequency (%) = (recombinant progeny / total progeny) × 100; 1% RF = 1 cM

Genes on the same chromosome are linked and tend to be inherited together, but crossing over during meiosis produces recombinant gametes. The recombination frequency between two genes estimates their distance: 1% recombination equals 1 centiMorgan (cM). Genes 50 cM or more apart behave as if unlinked because multiple crossovers randomise their assortment.

instruction: The lac Operon: Regulation of Gene Expression gurinchi oka worked example ivvu. [GATE BT - Molecular Biology]
response:
Worked example: E. coli grown in glucose plus lactose keeps the lac operon off (catabolite repression); when glucose runs out, cAMP rises, CAP binds, and beta-galactosidase is produced to use lactose.

Formula: Rule: lac operon ON only when lactose present AND glucose absent (AND logic of repressor release + CAP activation)

The lac operon of E. coli contains the genes lacZ, lacY and lacA for lactose metabolism, controlled by the lacI repressor and the CAP-cAMP activator. Lactose (as allolactose) inactivates the repressor, while glucose lowers cAMP so CAP cannot activate transcription. The operon is therefore switched on only when lactose is present and glucose is absent, a classic example of combined negative and positive control.

instruction: Chemostat: Dilution Rate and Washout gurinchi oka worked example ivvu. [GATE BT - Bioprocess Engineering]
response:
Worked example: A 10 L chemostat fed at 2 L/h has D = 0.2 h−1, so the cells grow at μ = 0.2 h−1 at steady state; raising the feed above μmax × V would wash the culture out.

Formula: D = F/V; at steady state μ = D; washout when D > μmax; biomass X = Y(S0 − S)

A chemostat is a continuous culture in which fresh medium flows in at rate F and culture flows out at the same rate, keeping the volume V constant. At steady state the specific growth rate μ equals the dilution rate D = F/V. If D exceeds the maximum growth rate μmax, cells are washed out faster than they divide and the culture collapses.

instruction: Oxygen Transfer in Bioreactors: kLa gurinchi oka worked example ivvu. [GATE BT - Bioprocess Engineering]
response:
Worked example: With kLa = 100 h−1, C* = 8 mg/L and CL = 2 mg/L, OTR = 100 × (8 − 2) = 600 mg/L/h; a culture consuming oxygen faster than this becomes oxygen-limited.

Formula: OTR = kLa(C* − CL); OUR = qO2 × X; at steady state OTR = OUR

Aerobic cultures are usually limited by oxygen transfer from gas bubbles into the liquid. The volumetric mass-transfer coefficient kLa combines the liquid-side coefficient kL and the interfacial area a. The oxygen transfer rate OTR = kLa(C* − CL), where C* is the saturation concentration and CL the actual dissolved oxygen. At steady state OTR equals the oxygen uptake rate of the cells, so kLa must be high enough to meet demand.

instruction: Thiele Modulus and Effectiveness Factor gurinchi oka worked example ivvu. [GATE BT - Bioprocess Engineering]
response:
Worked example: For φ = 0.3, η = tanh(0.3)/0.3 ≈ 0.97, so the immobilised enzyme works at 97% of its intrinsic rate and diffusion is barely limiting.

Formula: φ = R√(k/Deff) (first order); η = tanh(φ)/φ for a slab; η → 1 when φ is small

When an enzyme is immobilised in a porous particle, substrate must diffuse in before it can react, so the observed rate is lower than the intrinsic rate. The Thiele modulus φ compares the reaction rate to the diffusion rate: small φ means reaction-limited (the whole particle is used), large φ means diffusion-limited (only the outer shell reacts). The effectiveness factor η is the ratio of the observed rate to the rate without diffusion resistance.

instruction: Ideal Reactors: Batch, CSTR and PFR Design Equations gurinchi oka worked example ivvu. [GATE BT - Bioprocess Engineering]
response:
Worked example: For a first-order reaction needing 90% conversion, the PFR volume is about half the CSTR volume, because the CSTR operates entirely at the low exit concentration where the rate is slowest.

Formula: Batch: t = ∫dX/(−rA); CSTR: V = FA0·X/(−rA); PFR: V = FA0·∫dX/(−rA)

A batch reactor holds the same material while reaction proceeds, so its time is found by integrating the rate over conversion. A CSTR is perfectly mixed, so the whole volume sits at the exit concentration and its volume is proportional to the rate at that concentration. A PFR has concentration changing along its length, so its volume is the integral of dX/(−rA). For a given conversion, a PFR is smaller than a CSTR when the rate falls with conversion.

instruction: Restriction Enzymes and Cloning Vectors gurinchi oka worked example ivvu. [GATE BT - Molecular Biology]
response:
Worked example: EcoRI cuts G^AATTC, leaving a 5' AATT overhang; a DNA fragment cut with EcoRI can be ligated into a plasmid cut with the same enzyme.

Formula: Rule: a vector needs an origin of replication + a selectable marker + a cloning site; sticky ends from the same enzyme ligate efficiently

Restriction endonucleases cut DNA at specific, usually palindromic, recognition sequences, producing sticky ends (with single-stranded overhangs) or blunt ends. Sticky ends from the same enzyme ligate efficiently, which is the basis of recombinant DNA cloning. A cloning vector must carry an origin of replication, a selectable marker such as an antibiotic-resistance gene, and a cloning site; common vectors are plasmids, lambda phage, cosmids and bacterial artificial chromosomes.

instruction: CRISPR-Cas9 Genome Editing gurinchi oka worked example ivvu. [GATE BT - Molecular Biology]
response:
Worked example: To knock out a gene, a sgRNA is designed against its early coding region; NHEJ repair introduces an indel that shifts the reading frame and destroys the protein.

Formula: Rule: Cas9 cuts ~3 bp upstream of the NGG PAM; NHEJ gives knockouts, HDR gives precise edits

CRISPR-Cas9 edits DNA using a single guide RNA (sgRNA) that directs the Cas9 nuclease to a target sequence next to a PAM site (NGG in the common Streptococcus pyogenes system). Cas9 makes a double-strand break about 3 bp upstream of the PAM. The cell repairs it by error-prone non-homologous end joining, which usually knocks the gene out, or by homology-directed repair with a supplied template, which makes a precise edit.

instruction: Antibody Structure and ELISA gurinchi oka worked example ivvu. [GATE BT - Biochemistry]
response:
Worked example: A sandwich ELISA for HIV p24 antigen uses a capture antibody on the plate and an enzyme-linked detection antibody, giving a colour signal that quantifies viral protein in the sample.

Formula: Rule: in ELISA, absorbance is proportional to antigen concentration; IgG = 2 heavy + 2 light chains (Fab binds antigen, Fc mediates effector functions)

An antibody is made of two heavy and two light chains forming a Y shape: the Fab arms bind antigen and the Fc stem carries out effector functions. There are five classes: IgG, IgA, IgM, IgE and IgD. In a sandwich ELISA the target antigen is captured by one antibody and detected by a second enzyme-linked antibody; the enzyme produces a coloured product whose absorbance is proportional to the antigen concentration.

instruction: Laplace Transforms for Growth and Reaction ODEs gurinchi oka worked example ivvu. [GATE BT - Engineering Mathematics]
response:
Worked example: For exponential cell growth dX/dt = μX with X(0) = X0, the transform gives sX̄ − X0 = μX̄, so X̄ = X0/(s − μ) and inverting gives X(t) = X0·e^(μt).

Formula: L{f'(t)} = sF(s) − f(0); L{e^(at)} = 1/(s − a)

The Laplace transform turns a linear ODE with constant coefficients into an algebraic equation in s, which is useful for first-order growth, decay and reactor balance equations. The transform of a derivative is L{f'} = sF(s) − f(0), and L{e^(at)} = 1/(s − a). Inverting the result returns the time-domain solution.

instruction: Chromatography: Resolution and Plate Number gurinchi oka worked example ivvu. [GATE BT - Bioprocess Engineering]
response:
Worked example: Two peaks at 5.0 and 5.5 min with widths of 0.2 min each give Rs = 2(0.5)/(0.4) = 2.5, so they are fully baseline-separated.

Formula: Rs = 2(tR2 − tR1)/(w1 + w2); N = 16(tR/w)^2

Chromatographic resolution Rs measures how well two adjacent peaks are separated; Rs ≥ 1.5 means baseline separation. It depends on the difference in retention times relative to peak widths. The plate number N measures column efficiency, and a taller column or smaller particles raise N. Ion-exchange, gel-filtration, hydrophobic-interaction and affinity chromatography separate proteins by charge, size, hydrophobicity and specific binding respectively.

instruction: Arrhenius equation and activation energy gurinchi oka worked example ivvu. [GATE CY - Physical Chemistry]
response:
Worked example: For Ea = 50 kJ/mol, warming from 300 K to 310 K gives ln(k2/k1) = -(50000/8.314) x (1/310 - 1/300) = 0.65, so k2/k1 = e^0.65 = about 1.9. The rate nearly doubles.

Formula: k = A x e^(-Ea / (R x T));  ln(k2/k1) = -(Ea/R) x (1/T2 - 1/T1), where k is the rate constant, A is the pre-exponential factor, Ea is activation energy, R is the gas constant and T is absolute temperature.

The Arrhenius equation relates the rate constant of a reaction to temperature and activation energy. A higher temperature increases the fraction of molecules with enough energy to overcome the activation barrier, so the rate rises exponentially. The activation energy Ea is the minimum energy reacting molecules must have.

instruction: Beer-Lambert law gurinchi oka worked example ivvu. [GATE CY - Spectroscopy]
response:
Worked example: If epsilon = 10,000 L/(mol cm), c = 2 x 10^-5 mol/L and l = 1 cm, A = 10,000 x 2 x 10^-5 x 1 = 0.20.

Formula: A = epsilon x c x l, where A is absorbance, epsilon is molar absorptivity, c is concentration and l is path length. Transmittance T = 10^(-A).

The Beer-Lambert law relates the absorbance of a solution to the concentration of the absorbing species and the path length of light through it. Absorbance is proportional to concentration, which is why UV-visible spectroscopy is used for quantitative analysis. The law holds for dilute solutions with monochromatic light.

instruction: Nernst equation gurinchi oka worked example ivvu. [GATE CY - Physical Chemistry]
response:
Worked example: For a cell with E0 = 1.10 V, n = 2 and Q = 0.01, E = 1.10 - (0.0592/2) x log10(0.01) = 1.10 - 0.0296 x (-2) = 1.16 V.

Formula: E = E0 - (RT/(nF)) x ln Q;  at 25 C, E = E0 - (0.0592/n) x log10 Q, where E0 is standard potential, n is electrons transferred, F is Faraday's constant and Q is the reaction quotient.

The Nernst equation gives the electrode or cell potential under non-standard conditions, correcting the standard potential for the concentrations of reactants and products. As the reaction proceeds and the reaction quotient changes, the cell potential falls, reaching zero at equilibrium. At 25 C the factor 2.303 RT/F is 0.0592 V.

instruction: Gibbs free energy and spontaneity gurinchi oka worked example ivvu. [GATE CY - Physical Chemistry]
response:
Worked example: If Delta H = -100 kJ/mol, Delta S = -0.20 kJ/(mol K) and T = 298 K, Delta G = -100 - 298 x (-0.20) = -100 + 59.6 = -40.4 kJ/mol, so the process is spontaneous.

Formula: Delta G = Delta H - T x Delta S;  Delta G0 = -R x T x ln K, where Delta G is Gibbs energy change, Delta H is enthalpy change, Delta S is entropy change, T is absolute temperature and K is the equilibrium constant.

Gibbs free energy determines whether a process is spontaneous at constant temperature and pressure: a negative change in Gibbs energy means the process is spontaneous, zero means equilibrium, and positive means non-spontaneous. Enthalpy favours exothermic processes, while entropy favours disorder; temperature decides which dominates.

instruction: Henderson-Hasselbalch equation and buffers gurinchi oka worked example ivvu. [GATE CY - Physical Chemistry]
response:
Worked example: For acetic acid, pKa = 4.76. If [acetate]/[acetic acid] = 10, pH = 4.76 + log10(10) = 4.76 + 1 = 5.76.

Formula: pH = pKa + log10([A-] / [HA]), where pKa is the acid dissociation constant, [A-] is conjugate base concentration and [HA] is weak acid concentration.

The Henderson-Hasselbalch equation gives the pH of a buffer made of a weak acid and its conjugate base. When the acid and base concentrations are equal, pH equals pKa. A buffer resists pH change because added acid or base is consumed by the conjugate pair, and it works best within about one pH unit of pKa.

instruction: Ideal gas law gurinchi oka worked example ivvu. [GATE CY - Physical Chemistry]
response:
Worked example: For 1 mol at 273 K and 1 atm, V = nRT/P = (1 x 0.0821 x 273)/1 = 22.4 L.

Formula: P x V = n x R x T, where P is pressure, V is volume, n is moles, R is the gas constant (0.0821 L atm/(mol K) or 8.314 J/(mol K)) and T is absolute temperature.

The ideal gas law combines Boyle's, Charles's and Avogadro's laws into one relation between pressure, volume, temperature and amount of gas. It assumes gas molecules have negligible volume and no intermolecular forces, which is a good approximation for most gases at ordinary temperature and pressure. One mole of an ideal gas occupies about 22.4 L at 0 C and 1 atm.

instruction: Bragg's law of X-ray diffraction gurinchi oka worked example ivvu. [GATE CY - Spectroscopy]
response:
Worked example: With lambda = 0.154 nm, d = 0.20 nm and n = 1, sin(theta) = 0.154/(2 x 0.20) = 0.385, so theta = about 22.6 degrees.

Formula: n x lambda = 2 x d x sin(theta), where n is the order of diffraction, lambda is X-ray wavelength, d is interplanar spacing and theta is the Bragg angle (angle between the ray and the crystal plane).

Bragg's law explains diffraction of X-rays by crystal planes: rays reflected from successive planes interfere constructively only when their path difference is a whole number of wavelengths. This gives sharp diffraction peaks at specific angles, from which interplanar spacings and crystal structure are determined.

instruction: Particle in a One-Dimensional Box gurinchi oka worked example ivvu. [GATE CY - Physical Chemistry]
response:
Worked example: An electron in a 1 nm box has E1 = (6.626×10^−34)^2/(8 × 9.11×10^−31 × (10^−9)^2) ≈ 6.0×10^−20 J ≈ 0.38 eV; the gap to n = 2 is 3E1.

Formula: En = n^2·h^2/(8mL^2), n = 1, 2, 3, ...; ψn = √(2/L)·sin(nπx/L)

A particle confined to a one-dimensional box of length L with infinitely high walls has quantised energy levels, because its wavefunction must vanish at the walls. Only standing waves fitting an integer number of half-wavelengths are allowed. The ground state (n = 1) still has non-zero energy, the zero-point energy, so a confined particle can never be at rest.

instruction: Clausius-Clapeyron Equation gurinchi oka worked example ivvu. [GATE CY - Physical Chemistry]
response:
Worked example: For water, ΔHvap ≈ 40.7 kJ/mol; the vapour pressure at 90 °C is about 0.70 atm, which is why water boils below 100 °C on a mountain where atmospheric pressure is lower.

Formula: dP/dT = ΔH/(T·ΔV); ln(P2/P1) = −ΔHvap/R × (1/T2 − 1/T1)

The Clausius-Clapeyron equation relates the slope of a phase boundary on a P-T diagram to the enthalpy change and volume change of the transition. For vaporisation, where the vapour volume dominates, it gives the vapour pressure as a function of temperature. It explains why vapour pressure rises steeply with temperature and why water boils at lower temperatures at altitude.

instruction: Debye-Hückel Limiting Law gurinchi oka worked example ivvu. [GATE CY - Physical Chemistry]
response:
Worked example: For 0.01 M NaCl, I = 0.01, so log γ± = −0.509 × 1 × 0.1 = −0.0509, giving γ± ≈ 0.89, meaning the ions behave as if only 89% as concentrated.

Formula: log10 γ± = −A|z+·z−|√I; I = (1/2)Σci·zi^2; A = 0.509 for water at 25 °C

In dilute electrolyte solutions, ions are surrounded by an oppositely charged ionic atmosphere that lowers their activity below their concentration. The Debye-Hückel limiting law gives the mean ionic activity coefficient from the ionic strength of the solution. It is valid only at low ionic strength (below about 0.01 M), where ion-ion interactions dominate and ion size can be ignored.

instruction: Langmuir Adsorption Isotherm gurinchi oka worked example ivvu. [GATE CY - Physical Chemistry]
response:
Worked example: When KP = 1, θ = 0.5, so the surface is half covered; doubling the pressure to KP = 9 raises coverage only to 0.9, showing the saturation behaviour.

Formula: θ = KP/(1 + KP); linear form: P/V = 1/(Vm·K) + P/Vm

The Langmuir isotherm models adsorption as a monolayer on identical surface sites with no interaction between adsorbed molecules. The fractional surface coverage θ rises with gas pressure and saturates at θ = 1 when all sites are filled. At low pressure coverage is proportional to pressure (Henry's-law region). The linearised form is used to find the monolayer capacity and the adsorption equilibrium constant from experimental data.

instruction: Crystal Field Theory and CFSE gurinchi oka worked example ivvu. [GATE CY - Inorganic Chemistry]
response:
Worked example: Fe2+ (d6) in a weak field is high-spin t2g^4 eg^2 with CFSE = (−1.6 + 1.2)Δo = −0.4Δo, while in a strong field it is low-spin t2g^6 with CFSE = −2.4Δo + 2P.

Formula: CFSE = (−0.4·n_t2g + 0.6·n_eg)Δo; high-spin if Δo < P, low-spin if Δo > P

In an octahedral complex, the five d orbitals split into a lower t2g set and an upper eg set separated by Δo, because the eg orbitals point directly at the ligands and are destabilised more. The crystal field stabilisation energy is CFSE = (−0.4·n_t2g + 0.6·n_eg)Δo. If Δo is smaller than the pairing energy P the complex is high-spin; if larger, it is low-spin. This splitting also explains the colours of transition-metal complexes through d-d transitions.

instruction: The 18-Electron Rule in Organometallic Chemistry gurinchi oka worked example ivvu. [GATE CY - Inorganic Chemistry]
response:
Worked example: Fe(CO)5: Fe is group 8 and each CO donates 2 electrons, so 8 + 5 × 2 = 18 electrons, a stable complex.

Formula: Total electron count = metal group number + 2 × (number of L-type ligands) + 1 × (number of X-type ligands); stable at 18

Stable organometallic complexes usually have 18 valence electrons around the metal, filling the nine valence orbitals (one s, three p, five d) like a noble-gas configuration. Count the metal's group number plus 2 electrons for each 2-electron donor ligand (CO, phosphine, alkene) and 1 electron per X-type ligand (halide, alkyl). Complexes with 16 electrons, such as square-planar d8 species, are common exceptions.

instruction: SN1 vs SN2 Nucleophilic Substitution gurinchi oka worked example ivvu. [GATE CY - Organic Chemistry]
response:
Worked example: tert-Butyl bromide with OH− reacts by SN1 to give racemic tert-butanol if the carbon were chiral, while methyl bromide reacts by SN2 with complete inversion.

Formula: SN2: rate = k[RX][Nu], inversion, 1° > 2° > 3°; SN1: rate = k[RX], racemisation, 3° > 2° > 1°

SN2 is a concerted one-step reaction: the nucleophile attacks from the back side as the leaving group departs, giving inversion of configuration (Walden inversion), with rate = k[RX][Nu]. It is favoured by primary substrates and strong nucleophiles. SN1 is two-step: ionisation to a planar carbocation is rate-determining, so rate = k[RX] and attack from either face gives racemisation. It is favoured by tertiary substrates and polar protic solvents that stabilise the carbocation.

instruction: Woodward-Hoffmann Rules for Pericyclic Reactions gurinchi oka worked example ivvu. [GATE CY - Organic Chemistry]
response:
Worked example: Butadiene + ethylene gives cyclohexene thermally by a [4+2] Diels-Alder reaction, but two ethylenes do not dimerise thermally because [2+2] cycloaddition is symmetry-forbidden in the ground state.

Formula: Thermal: (4n + 2)π suprafacial allowed, (4n)π photochemical; electrocyclic: 4n + 2 thermal disrotatory, 4n thermal conrotatory

Pericyclic reactions are concerted reactions through a cyclic transition state, and their feasibility depends on orbital symmetry. A thermal reaction is allowed when the total number of (4q + 2)s and (4r)a components is odd. In practice: a thermal [4+2] cycloaddition (Diels-Alder) is allowed suprafacial-suprafacial, while a thermal [2+2] is forbidden and needs light. Electrocyclic ring closure is disrotatory for 4n + 2 pi electrons thermally and conrotatory for 4n pi electrons thermally, reversing under light.

instruction: NMR Spectroscopy: Chemical Shift and Spin-Spin Splitting gurinchi oka worked example ivvu. [GATE CY - Spectroscopy]
response:
Worked example: Bromoethane CH3CH2Br shows a triplet near 1.7 ppm (3H, split by 2 neighbours) and a quartet near 3.4 ppm (2H, split by 3 neighbours), the CH2 being downfield because bromine deshields it.

Formula: δ (ppm) = (ν_sample − ν_TMS)/ν_spectrometer × 10^6; splitting: n + 1 rule

In proton NMR, the chemical shift δ measures how shielded a nucleus is relative to TMS (0 ppm): electron-withdrawing groups deshield and shift signals downfield. Equivalent neighbouring protons split a signal into n + 1 peaks, where n is the number of protons on adjacent carbons, with coupling constant J in Hz. Integration gives the relative number of protons, so NMR reveals both the environment and the connectivity of hydrogens.

instruction: Hückel's Rule and Aromaticity gurinchi oka worked example ivvu. [GATE CY - Organic Chemistry]
response:
Worked example: Benzene has 6 π electrons (n = 1) and is aromatic; cyclobutadiene has 4 π electrons and is antiaromatic; cyclopentadienyl anion has 6 π electrons and is aromatic.

Formula: Aromatic: cyclic, planar, conjugated, (4n + 2) π electrons; antiaromatic: 4n π electrons

A compound is aromatic if it is cyclic, planar, fully conjugated, and has (4n + 2) pi electrons, which gives extra stability from a closed shell of delocalised electrons. A planar cyclic conjugated system with 4n pi electrons is antiaromatic and especially unstable. Non-planar or non-conjugated rings are simply non-aromatic. The rule also applies to charged species such as the cyclopentadienyl anion (6 pi electrons, aromatic).

instruction: First-Order Reaction Kinetics and Half-Life gurinchi oka worked example ivvu. [GATE CY - Physical Chemistry]
response:
Worked example: A reaction with k = 0.0693 min−1 has t1/2 = 0.693/0.0693 = 10 min, so after 20 min only one-quarter of the reactant remains.

Formula: ln[A] = ln[A]0 − kt; t1/2 = ln 2/k = 0.693/k

In a first-order reaction the rate is proportional to the concentration of one reactant, so a plot of ln[A] against time is a straight line with slope −k. The half-life is independent of the initial concentration, which is the signature of first-order kinetics. Many processes, including radioactive decay and some drug eliminations, follow first-order kinetics.

instruction: Rotational Spectroscopy of Diatomic Molecules gurinchi oka worked example ivvu. [GATE CY - Spectroscopy]
response:
Worked example: For CO, B ≈ 1.93 cm−1, so its pure rotational lines are spaced by about 3.86 cm−1 in the microwave region, from which the C-O bond length (~1.13 Å) is calculated.

Formula: E_J = B·J(J + 1); B = h/(8π^2·I); line spacing = 2B; selection rule ΔJ = ±1

A diatomic molecule treated as a rigid rotor has quantised rotational energies E_J = BJ(J + 1), where B = h/(8π²I) is the rotational constant and I = μr² is the moment of inertia. Microwave absorption follows the selection rule ΔJ = ±1, so spectral lines appear spaced by 2B. Measuring the spacing gives B, hence the bond length.

instruction: Arrhenius equation and activation energy par ek worked example dijiye. [GATE CY - Physical Chemistry]
response:
Worked example: For Ea = 50 kJ/mol, warming from 300 K to 310 K gives ln(k2/k1) = -(50000/8.314) x (1/310 - 1/300) = 0.65, so k2/k1 = e^0.65 = about 1.9. The rate nearly doubles.

Formula: k = A x e^(-Ea / (R x T));  ln(k2/k1) = -(Ea/R) x (1/T2 - 1/T1), where k is the rate constant, A is the pre-exponential factor, Ea is activation energy, R is the gas constant and T is absolute temperature.

The Arrhenius equation relates the rate constant of a reaction to temperature and activation energy. A higher temperature increases the fraction of molecules with enough energy to overcome the activation barrier, so the rate rises exponentially. The activation energy Ea is the minimum energy reacting molecules must have.
